The reduced camera shake is what I think is meant in the description by “no wobbling”. The button itself exaggerates the play in the shutter button on the camera which is fairly loose (not firmly restrained from slight jiggling).

There are two of these little buttons in the pack. Properly installed, I suspect the second will never be needed. Both come in individual pouches and include a rubber gasket. Because if the size of the gasket, I’d recommend using a pair of tweezers to put it on the post - if you drop it there’s a fair chance you’ll lose it.

From the product listing’s photos this button looks convex. It is not - it is concave.

So far I am not unhappy with this soft release button. It fits my camera properly and it looks nice. It speeds shooting and reduces camera shake when pressing the button which for me is a win.

title: Got it Working Under Linux
text:
I am a little different when it comes to computer users. I use Windows for email and photo editing, but just about everything else I do on Linux. I selected this drive for use on my Linux laptop and so far I am happy with it. It's very fast and it works very well.

Linux recognizes the drive straight away. Note that Windows sees it too but it's not readily usable. I took the time to repartition and rebuild the drive with a different file system in order to optimize it for use under Linux, but that was the plan from the beginning. Once rebuilt I plugged it into the USB-C port and away we went.

This drive is FAST. I have been able to copy large ISO images (9GB) in short order and it doesn't miss a beat. So far it has been reliable too, so this has become my new backup drive.

This drive might be designed around Mac users but it does work under Linux (and I presume Windows as well) with some coaxing. It's fast and seems to be reliable.

title: Good Improvements Over Older Smart Watch Models
text:
I have used smart watches for a while now and I have seen a steady progression in the technology. This is my first Gen 6 watch. It is a big improvement from what I have used before (beyond just battery life) and so far I am pleased with it.

This is an Android-based smart watch, and it is similar in interface to previous smart watches I have seen and used. If you have used any generation of smart watch before this one the experience is very similar. I won't get too deep into the nuts and bolts of that or the WearOS app.

There are two big areas of improvement I have seen with this new watch. First, the battery life is much better than previous smart watches I have used which is very encouraging. I have a Gen 2 watch that I love but it lasts only about 3 days on a charge, and my Gen 5 is not much better. This one lasts several days before the battery runs out.

The more important improvement to me, though, is the way it doesn't interfere with the Bluetooth in my car. Previous watches messed up my ability to stream to the car's sound system to the point that the sound would sputter and simply die. I did trace it to the watch by powering off the watch completely after which the problem went away and would come back when the watch was powered on. This watch does not interfere at all and my car's Bluetooth works whether the watch is on or not.

This is a stylish watch, a bit more upscale than some of the others I have seen and used. The band is a non-stretch link band that is a little snug but not unworkable.

So far this watch works well for me. I am pleased with the improved battery life and even more happy that it doesn't mess with my car's Bluetooth connectivity.

title: Works with Linux; Bright and Clear
text:
I selected this monitor to work on a beefy laptop I use for building Linux virtual machines and testing software, so my use case is a little different than the target audience. I have been needing a larger monitor to go with said laptop and this one seemed to be a good one. So far I am pleased with it, though I have not pushed it to its full potential.

This is a 27" display capable of 2560x1440 resolution, fast refresh rates and bright colors. In the box comes the panel itself, a stand, and a DisplayPort cable. I was a little surprised that there was no HDMI cable in the box but this is all right, I have a couple of them so I was not left wanting.

My initial testing was disastrous, though the issue proved to be a fault with the laptop, not the monitor. My laptop has an HDMI output, and it does provide enough power to let the monitor know that something is there, but it intermittently sends a signal so I was not getting a consistent display. After a couple of hours, the monitor would display nothing at all. Thinking I had a dud, I connected a different system to verify and the monitor came right up. It did the same with a second system as well. After some research I determined that the issue was the graphics card in my main laptop which has known problems with HDMI. I bought an adapter to connect to the Thunderbolt port on the laptop and everything works fine now.

The system connected to this monitor is a gaming laptop that is running Linux with VMs installed. The system properly reports the model number of the display which is a very good sign. The OS does not push the monitor like a Windows gaming system might when used for actual gaming. For me, the screen real estate is what I needed. The adapter I bought caps the resolution at 1920x1200, so I am not getting the full resolution from this monitor but it is more than enough for my purposes.

The monitor responds to signal on both HDMI ports. So far I have not had occasion to try using the DisplayPorts on the back.

The display is very bright and clear, with no dead pixels. It seems to keep up very well with the system with no apparent lag, though again I am not pushing it as hard as I could. Because of the way I have it connected I can't bump up the refresh rate though it is happy at 60Hz. It doesn't appear to flicker to my eyes (though my camera disagrees), and it does not induce headaches.

If I could make any changes at all, I would change the design of the stand/base. The base is not height-adjustible so I cannot raise or lower the monitor without getting an arm harness. That's a minor complaint and is not enough to get myself upset about but it is worth mentioning.

Admittedly I am not the typical use case for a monitor like this, but I am happy with it nonetheless and it works well for me. The issues I have had with this monitor were related to other hardware, not the monitor itself. It seems to work very well, it is bright and clear and it gives me the screen real estate that I need. The fact that the Linux system recognizes its model number is a plus - it's supported.

title: Decent Slider, but Room for Improvement
text:
I am primarily a stills shooter. That said, I do have an excellent camera that is very capable of shooting video and I do need it for such on occasion. I was interested in this camera slider as a way to get smooth shots and to reduce reliance on lens-based stabilization which is not included in my camera body. This has been a learning experience and while I like this slider there is definitely room for improvement.

I will start with the basics. This is a large and fairly heavy animal, which is to be expected. It is roughly 3' long and in it’s most basic configuration rests on a flat surface with no issues. It does have some adjustments that can be made to the individual feet on the frame so it can be adjusted slightly for uneven but mostly level surfaces without using any other equipment. To get much more versatility out of it, though, it can be mounted on tripods on either end to raise it higher or to set up angular shots.

The motor on the frame is controlled by a remote which comes with a battery pack. The remote is not wireless and has to be connected to the motor via the provided cabling. This is all right, but wireless functionality would make it much more versatile. It should be noted that the remote controls the slider, not the camera. I had some concern about this in the very beginning, thinking that the remote would be incompatible with my camera and that this unit would not work for me.

I encountered some issues that bother me. First, when powered on and running the motor runs the slider down the track until it is either stopped or a stop point is set. If one is not set, it bumps into the end and keeps trying to go beyond, making an awful noise that will surely mess up any video that requires sound. In my mind, the motor should detect when it hits the end and stop, even if start and stop points are not set.

When the motor is running and it is not near a stop point, it runs at constant speed and it is very smooth. When manually paused, it stops quickly but it doesn’t jerk to an abrupt stop like it hit something. But, if one of the end points are set and is reached, the motor slows down, then jerks to a stop, enough to notice in video footage. This is most obvious when the remote is set up to film in a loop as the issue can be observed repeatedly.

The motor is not silent, though it is quiet. It is not loud enough to ruin a shot unless absolute quiet is needed, and the motor produces a low-volume, low-frequency hum that slightly resembles the sound of an electric trolling motor on a bass boat, but quieter. The point is that it is by no means silent, but it should be good enough in the majority of cases. This is out the window if the motor is allowed to reach the end of the track before it is stopped, in which case the noise is likely to be a serious issue.

This is a decent slider and if used with some thought will serve nicely. There are definitely some places where it could be improved, particularly in the way it fails to handle reaching the end of tracks.

title: Words Fine in My Dash Cam
text:
I selected this memory card because I needed one for a dash cam. When it comes to storage, name bands are usually the way to go when you need something really reliable, so I was a little hesitant at first to use a "store brand" card. So far, it has been fine and I have no complaints, though it will take time and more use to determine if it will hold up long-term.

The card I received is a 128GB MicroSD with an adapter. The adapter makes it work in a camera like my mirrorless, but I would not recommend this kind of set-up unless pressed. The adapter is really most useful when pulling data from the card in a machine that does not have a slot for a MicroSD, so the adapter does have its place.

The card fit in my dash cam with no issues and the cam seems to be happy with it. It detects the presence of the card and the full capacity of it which is good. Being a class 10 card it is fast enough to keep up with the recording and in a 45 minute trip it did not skip or stutter once. Quality seems to be fine. Using the adapter, my PC has no trouble reading the card and reformatting when I want to quickly erase it.

So far, this card has worked out just fine and I am pleased with it. It's priced well and it seems to work well in the way I need it to work. Time will tell if it will hold up, but so far all indicators are positive.

title: Made Well and Works Well
text:
USB-C cables are the one cable type I usually have trouble putting my hands on in my house, and I need them for charging my tablet as well as my video lights. I selected this one because I like cables with braided insulation and so far this one has worked out well for me.

This is a 6' cable which is just about right for my needs. It is long enough to reach my devices when I have it plugged into my USB brick on my desk without requiring rearrangement of everything on my desk just to make it fit. Longer would be handy but unnecessary, but shorter would make it a lot less useful for me.

I have not used it for data transfer, just charging up devices, and so far it has worked out well in that capacity. The connection is snug and I have not noticed any particular difference in charging speeds between this cable and the OEM cables that came with my devices.

I am especially pleased with the build quality. The cable is stiff (as to be expected) and it should hold up for a long time against kinks and twists. The junctions where the cable goes into the plastic casings for the connectors are tight and allow no play which is a big plus for me as these are the spots where I have had cables fail most often. Overall, I am not unhappy with the build quality.

This is a decent third-party USB-C cable that works very well for me. It is made well and it does a fine job charging my devices. It isn’t too expensive either, making it easy to recommend.

title: Very Versatile LED Video Light; Priced Very Well
text:
I do a lot of creative photography work and I look for tools and ideas that will help me along in that regard. I took a chance on this LED light, thinking it would be a good tool for adding color and light when I need it, and so far I am pleased with it.

This is not a very big light, about the size of an iPhone. It's small enough that finding a place for it in my camera bag takes little effort and it is always at the ready when I need it without requiring a bunch of storage. It comes in a carrying case and even the case is small. If you need a small light, keep reading.

This is advertised as a video light, so one of the most important things to consider is whether or not is strobes. A lot of cheap LEDs strobe which makes them inappropriate for video work (or high speed photography for that matter). This is not a super-cheap light, more expensive than many of the LED banks I have seen, so I assumed it would not strobe and this assumption was correct. When considering that it is a non-strobing LED that is priced around $70 (as I write this), this thing is a bargain - good video lights are often more than double the cost.

This light is a very interesting tool. I have other LED video lights, and these typically have a brightness setting, a few effects, and gel plates that can be used to tweak the color. This particular LED bank is different in that it allows for adjusting not only the brightness but also the colors, with RGB broken out into components that can be adjusted individually. So, if you need a really bright yellow light, a pale green light or a cool blue, this light can do it. Whatever color/brightness you need, there's a way to get it out of this light.

This light also has a number of effects that will suit a videographer. I spent some time playing with these and cycling through the different effect modes. There's lightning flash, police lights, faulty bulbs and more, and these can be adjusted like the solid modes can be. These modes are not really of any use to me at the moment, personally, as I do not do video work much at all, but I can see some things I can do with them for fun and I do like having them available should I decide to do any video work later.

When I received this light it was mostly discharged and I needed to plug it in to charge. The documentation says it takes about 2 hours to fully charge and that's fairly accurate. The display shows the charging level and it doesn't take too long from almost dead to fully changed.

Though I am unlikely to need it, I like that I can charge a USB device with this light, like it's a power bank. I have not tried charging/powering my camera with it yet, but I like the idea that I can do that.

This light comes with a hot shoe mount and USB-C charging cables. While it can be mounted on a tripod, a selfie stick is more versatile and makes getting this light in the right position easy.

This is a neat little light and it is worth more than the asking price in my opinion. It seems to work very well, it has a lot of neat creative modes and, most importantly, it does not strobe. If you need a well-priced LED light that works well for video and high-speed photography, this is a good one to consider.

title: Better than Average ANC Phones
text:
I have worked with a lot of active noise canceling (ANC) headphones by a lot of manufacturers, including an older pair of Philips headphones. I’ve seen a wide variance in ANC implementation and sound profiles, and to be honest few manufacturers get theirs right. With this set of headphones, Philips comes close.

These are over-ear phones which I prefer over on-ear phones. They fit snugly but not tight, and they actually do a good job of sound isolation. Even if you don’t like the ANC function (which would defeat the purpose of having these phones), these do a surprisingly good job of sound isolation. The pads are soft enough and comfortable enough that I can wear these for quite a while without discomfort. After a bit of time they do start to get a little warm but not to the point that I need to take them off.

These connect via Bluetooth and they connect very quickly. The connectivity of these phones is absolutely amazing: this is the very first pair of Bluetooth headphones I have used that maintains a steady connection up two flights of stairs with closed doors in between the phones and the source. The connectivity alone makes these very much worth checking out.

The ANC function is very good though it is not quite as aggressive as that of Bose or Sony. It is strong enough to mostly drown out a droning high-volume fan (my baseline for testing), such that music at a low volume while the ANC is turned on completely drowns out the fan. While Bose and Sony go to the extreme for noise cancellation, and other manufacturers often have ANC that’s barely there, Philips has implemented a system that is good enough for most. I am pleased with the ANC and will use these phones when I travel next.

The ANC function on these phones can be turned off if desired. There is also a special “awareness mode” that is an in-between mode that doesn’t completely turn off ANC but allows more environmental noise in, and this mode is really designed for permitting conversation without having to turn everything off completely. It works fairly well though the noise this mode produces via the external microphone is slightly harsh and shrill.

The default sound profile is not exactly perfect but it is better than many I have used and heard. These do boost the bass by default though not to an uncomfortable level. Bass boost is very common in headphones and it’s often too aggressive, but these actually give a modest boost. The midrange is a little soft though present. The highs sound bright and clear but not piercing. As a result, the sound profile is not quite perfectly balanced but it still good.

The sound profile can be tweaked via an app. I found the Philips Headphones app, installed it and started messing with it. The app works better than the reviews have suggested and it does a decent job of adjusting the headphones on the fly. The mode can be changed as well as the sound profile to adjust for different could quality based on music type, and there is a custom setting so that the equalizer can be adjusted to taste. The only complaint I have with the app is that there is about a 1s pause when changing modes between ANC. Awareness mode and Off, though this gap does not occur when changing the mode via the button on the headphones.

I like these ANC phones. They’re not perfect but they’re better than average with a good ANC function and decent sound. The have absolutely incredible connectivity, and they can be adjusted to taste via an app. This is a pair to keep on the short list if you need Bluethooth headphones that maintain a connection a long way from the source and provide ANC in the deal.

title: Love the Watch, the Software not so Much
text:
I have a smartwatch that I have worn now for over a year and I have been pleased with it. I was unfamiliar with the idea of a "hybrid smartwatch" and was interested in this one from Skagen. It's an interesting concept and the watch itself seems to work well, but I have some frustrations with the software.

This is basically a traditional analog watch with some smartwatch functions built into it. The smartwatches I have used usually have a full digital face with all manner of things on the display, and depending on the face chosen it may or may not be easy to read. This watch keeps things relatively simple and has the hour and minute displayed with moving hands, and around the center are displays for steps, heart rate and weather-at-a-glance. The whole is clean and easy on the eyes. Now, that said, if you cannot read an analog watch this one might not be the best choice.

Charging requires the special cable that comes with it and it takes a relatively short time to charge. The run time is much longer than most smartwatches I have used, getting well over a week on a single charge where a smartwatch is often 2-3 days or less.

Skagen has a special app for interacting with the watch and it was easy to find in the repository. It installs quickly and guides through the setup without too much issue. It is good for activity tracking and limited health monitoring as well as limited customization of the face. However, I have had some difficulty with connectivity and staying connected through the app, such that it has been an annoyance. This is the biggest complaint I have so far.

So far this watch has managed to keep good time, connected or not.

Overall I am happy with this watch though I am less than thrilled with the app. Hopefully an update will correct the connectivity issue I see with it. Otherwise, this is a good-looking and functional watch.

title: Seems to Work Well; Bad Documentation
text:
I have been interested in a device that can find hidden cameras for a while as we do tend to travel periodically. This device seemed like a good one and I wanted to try it out before I travel again. It seems like a pretty neat device that works fairly well, but it is hamstrung by very poor documentation.

This does more than just find hidden cameras. It is able to pick up Wi-fi signals, wireless phone signals and more. The sensitivity is very much like working with a metal detector - turn it up too high and it becomes nothing more than a sight and sound show; turned too low and it hardly sees anything.

With the unit turned on and set to a reasonable initial detection level I set about looking for devices in my home office. I have several Wi-fi connected devices and I usually have my smartphone there too, and I messed with this detector until I found the level where it was able to find everything. I did not try going near the router which is in another room but I imagine that one would require another sensitivity adjustment.

Most of the functions are self-explanatory, but some took a little trial and error to figure out. This is where good documentation would come in handy, and unfortunately the documentation with this device is poor. It's sufficient to identify the different functions of the device and where to find different components, but the actual descriptions and explanations of the functions are written in very poorly translated English.

Aside from the documentation, it would have been nice to have a carrying case for this device for storage and travel. That's a minor gripe, though.

I am happy with this device, though better documentation would make it much easier to use right away. It has some useful functions that will appeal to wary travelers, and it seems to work well once you figure out the right adjustments.

title: Works Very Well for Us; Easy to Understand and Operate. UPDATE - Failed after under two weeks
text:
UPDATE 05/15/2021 - It lasted less than two weeks and it died. During playback the player freezes on discs known to be good, and in order to get6 the player to respond I have to disconnect the power from it. It was great while it lasted, I guess.

Original review follows.

===

I have wanted a Blu-Ray player for a while and I have had reason to suspect that my DVD player is dying. I have a flat-screen Sony television so I figured this player would connect and work with it without too much effort. I was right and it has worked very well for my family and me.

This is a straightforward device. I connected it to the TV via the provided HDMI cable, selected that input and immediately was able to get signal from it. I popped in a disc and it loaded up to the menu. That’s exactly what I expected to happen. In operation using the remote it has worked very much like my old DVD player – remote is laid out a bit differently but the operation is the same and it provides buttons to stop, fast forward and reverse, pause, eject, select the root menu and more. The remote had given us no issues so far, though it does need to have near line-of-site with the player in order for the player to see it and respond.

The footprint is much smaller than my older DVD player and required a bit of rearrangement in my entertainment center. The whole unit is smaller than a ream of paper and weighs next to nothing.

It has built-in WiFi and makes it easy to access online streaming services. However, I will confess that I haven’t yet tried this as I try to keep my WiFi device list small. I will experiment with this when there is time.

So far we have seen no issues with playback – no skips or stutters or freezes. I have a couple of discs that I know to cause issues for my DVD player that I will try in this player and see if it fares better, though I believe the discs are actually bad.

So far I have had a positive experience with this player and based on that I am happy to recommend it. It seems to work well and it is easy to understand and operate. It isn’t particularly expensive either which is a big plus.

title: Decent Entry-Level Bluetooth-Only Headphones
text:
I have worked with a lot of different headphones, mostly active noise canceling (ANC) phones but also more traditional phones. Over the years I have had several Sennheiser phones and they typically have balanced sound and good build quality. This set is a step down from many of the others with which I have worked, though they’re still decent.

My preference on headphones is over-the-ear phones which for me are more comfortable. These particular phones are on-ear, and these pinch a little after extended wear. They’re better than some of the other on-ear phones with which I have worked, but I still prefer over-the-ear phones. One preference I have is a headphone that clamps down fairly tightly when worn so they’re less likely to slip off when I tilt my head down; these are a lighter fit.

These are Bluetooth-only phones and as such cannot be used with non-BT devices. This is unfortunate but isn’t a deal-breaker. These connect easily and quickly.

These are not ANC phones, but they have excellent passive noise canceling which is quite surprising for on-ear phones. They reduce ambient noise in my office considerably, which us especially noticeable when running a large fan that I use to generate white noise. I am pleased with that aspect of these phones. These are still not as effective as a set of ANC phones.

The sound profile is fairly typical of Sennheiser phones, though the bass is mildly beefed up.. The trend with phones these days is overdriven bass, and these do increase the bass response a little bit but not to a headache-inducing level. The midrange is full and warm, and that’s a good thing as many times the increased bass comes at the expense of the midrange. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. Overall, the sound is reasonably balanced, but certainly not audiophile quality.

Build-wise, these actually feel a bit on the cheaper side which is surprising. These aren’t exactly fragile, but they are definitely not of the same build quality as other Sennheisers I have used in the past.

These are probably best described as entry-level headphones. They’re not the highest quality, and they are not the most sturdy, but the sound quality is fine and the cost is right. The main thing I would change is the addition of an audio port so they could be used as wired phones.

title: Better ANC than Most; Outstanding in the Price Range
text:
I have worked with numerous pairs of active noise canceling (ANC phones) and I’ve seen a wide variation in sound profiles, features, and the quality of the ANC function. Some are better than others. I was a bit skeptical of these because of the price; most of the ANC phones I have used that were worth anything have a higher price tag. These are better than the price suggests.

Right out of the box, these headphones do not draw much attention to themselves. They’re not flashy and do not have any noticeable markings on them unless you’re looking for them. They are over-the-ear headphones which tend to be more comfortable than on-ear phones, and these have a snug fit without clamping down tightly. They adjust easily to fit almost any size head too. The padding on the cans is soft enough to not pinch, though after extended wear they do start to get a little warm.

Pairing and connection with my computer was a painless affair and these were ready very quickly after they were powered on.

The ANC function is far and away better than any other headphones I have worked with in this price range. They’re almost as aggressive as that of the Bose QC-15’s that I own, without that weird faux pressure sensation when the ANC is turned on. Even with the volume down low, these cancel out enough background noise to make them a serious contender. I have no complaints with the ANC.

The sound quality is very good, though not quite to my tastes. The bass is very strong – much stronger than I like personally, but not out of line with what has been trending in the last decade. Where Skullcandy got it right, though, is in how well they’ve implemented the bass enhancement. Even though the bass is very strong (enough to give me a headache at higher volumes), it does not distort or turn into just low-frequency noise. More importantly, the bass enhancement does not stomp on the midrange which is the usual casualty. The midrange is warm and fairly balanced. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. The end result is a sound profile that sounds full and rich. So many headphones with enhanced bass I have used have killed the midrange which makes music sound hollow, or distort the bass so much as to make music sound like a low-fidelity render. These are refreshing in that regard.

Some headphones detect when you take them off and pause music or playback when you take them off. These do not.

These come in a carry pouch that offers little in the way of drop and crush protection but it does keep them clean and free of scuffs and scratches. Also included is an audio cable for wired use as well as a USB Type C cable for charging.

Overall, these are far and away better than the price would suggest. They are very comfortable to wear, they have a good sound profile (particularly if you like heavy bass) and the ANC function is better than average and competitive with much more expensive headphones. These are budget-friendly ANC headphones with higher-end performance.

title: Works Well and Inexpensive
text:
I use rechargeable AA batteries frequently, specifically in my handheld GPS receivers, so keeping them charged up is sometimes a challenge when I have had more than one device in use. My previous charger only allowed for charging two batteries at a time, so I was excited to have the ability to charge eight at once. This charger works well for this, though it is on the slow side.

This is a very small and lightweight charger, without a lot of bells and whistles. It does not have a refresh option, it is simply a charger. The cost is lower than I would have expected, running about $13 as I write this.

I was startled when I opened the box and found that this is a USB-powered charger, not a AC-powered charger. It’s not even a USB-C device but a Micro USB device. My immediate thought was that it will be slow, and this thought was correct. To be fair, I missed the detail that it works via USB so that’s on me. The fact that it uses a Micro USB interface is listed as well, though it is buried in the details.

I popped in 8 batteries and let it go. I wasn’t sure how long it would take to charge them all, and it finished them at varying times over about a 4-hour period. Most had some charge already and finished earlier, while others had little power already and needed more time. It did charge them all, and it gave me a clear visual indicator when it had finished each battery. I’m not dissatisfied there.

While it is slower than my 2-battery charger that runs on AC power, it ultimately is faster as it can charge 4 times as many at once and the net time consumed is less.

The one improvement I would make for this charger would be to have it use USB-C instead of Micro USB, though that would likely drive up the asking price. Otherwise, I have no real complaints. This charger works well and it handles 8 batteries simultaneously. Price-wise, this is a good deal, too.

title: Cheaply Made and Overpriced
text:
I selected this little organizer for keeping my collection of thumb drives organized and in one place. I have a habit of misplacing one or more of them on occasion and I was hopeful this organization system would help keep them all together. It does work well for that purpose but in my opinion this is overpriced and cheaply made.

At a glance, this is a small and lightweight case, made of plastic with aluminum framing. The inside is a foam rubber sheet with grooves cut into it that hold on to small objects, in this case thumb drives and two slots for SSD or laptop hard drives. It’s not as big as a typical briefcase, and in fact will likely fit inside most briefcases.

My complaint is that it is cheaply made, especially when considering the price ($40 as I write this). The plastic handle and the clasp are both chrome-plated plastic that is easily scratched and flaked. The clasp itself isn’t even straight on my unit and there’s enough play in the hinge that I expect it to break off completely over time. The no-slip feet on the bottom aren’t even straight, and they’re installed loosely enough that they can be turned and wiggled freely. The foam insert has the feel and consistency of packing peanuts, cheap material.

There are better solutions for SSD and thumb drive storage. This one is so cheaply made and so overpriced that I have real difficulty recommending it.

title: These Work as Designed and are Made Well
text:
I selected these zip ties for a specific purpose, an outside task for which Velcro or twist ties are not suitable. These have worked out well for me and I am pleased with them.

There’s a limited amount that can be said about something as simple as a nylon zip tie. These are 4” long, seem to be made well and the latch definitely holds properly. I have only used a few of them so far and there has been no hint of any of them slipping or stretching. Overall, they’re working as designed and have held up even in the direct sunshine which has a tendency to fatigue plastics.

I’m happy with these. They work in the role for which I got them and they seem to be made well.

title: Works Great for Me
text:
I selected this audio extension cable for the office, where I need to use headphones to listen to content but am unable to move the source. A 6' audio cable is often too short, and having an extension cable instead of a full audio cable enables me to use different headphone sets. So far, this cable has worked out for me.

This is a nylon-wrapped cable which I prefer to plastic-insulated cables for durability. Unlike many other nylon cables, though, this one has some flex to it and it is not stiff and prone to knotting or kinking like others I have used. The end connectors are attached with a plastic sleeve that is stiff enough to keep the cable from getting bent at the connector without some effort, and this should greatly help in making this cable last longer since the point of connection is usually the failure point for me with audio cables.

The main concern I had when adding this cable to my configuration is if it would work seamlessly or would it introduce static or a hum to output. While this might not be a huge concern in this case it was still something I made a point to check. The sound was identical with this cable in place as it is without it. Even when turning the connector on either end, there was no static. That's all I can really ask of it.

This cable meets a need I had and it works very well. It's made nicely and it doesn't impact sound quality, good or bad (unless replacing a bad extension cable). Based on my working with it I am happy to recommend it.

title: Works Well, Seems to be Made Well
text:
I use headphones frequently in the office, and I have found that audio cables are often the weak link when it comes to headphones. I have gone through several cables just from daily wear and tear. I looked to this cable as a replacement for my last failed cable. So far I am pleased with it.

I prefer nylon braided cables as they seem to be more durable and tend to last longer. They do have a tendency to be more stiff and inflexible, though. This particular cable has more flex than most other nylon braided cables I have used while it also feels more substantial. I have been pleasantly surprised with how much more flexible this cable is compared to most.

The weak point in most cables is where the cable itself joins the connector. I have seen so many that have a rubbery, flimsy sleeve at the connector, and these have a tendency to rip before the cable connection fails. This particular cable has a nice, hard plastic sleeve instead, once that does have a small amount of flex but is hard and sturdy enough that it’s not going to rip or fail without deliberate effort to damage it.

As a nice plus, I like that this cable is bright red where most others are plain black or white. There will be no confusing this cable for someone else’s in a shared environment. I have paired this cable with a set of Munitio PRO40 headphones and it works well and looks great.

It’s another big plus that it comes in different sizes too, so you can choose the size you need.

Sound quality with my cable appears to be unchanged from other cables I have tried - no buzz or hum with different electronics I have tried, no crackle or hiss. That’s really all I can ask.

So far I have no complaints with this audio cable. It works well, appears to be made well and it is brightly colored which makes it stand out and distinguishable from most other audio cables I have seen and used. It is priced reasonably as well. Based on my experience with it so far this is an easy recommend.

title: Suitable for Vlogging or Photo Studio Use
text:
Note: There is more than one product attached to this listing. I am specifically reviewing the 18” light.

One of the things I have been researching for a while is ring lights. I have wanted one for a little while, but not the kind that sits on a desk and is only useful for making personal videos for upload. I wanted one that would be suitable for taking portrait photos and would be suitable for professional use. This is a nice ring light to that end and so far I am pleased with it, though I have not been using it long.

This is a large light, 18” in diameter which makes it quite a bit larger than most ring lights available right now. It is large enough that you can shoot photos or video through it using a full-sized camera with little effort, which is what I was looking for. It comes with a full-sized tripod (which it needs) as well as a nylon carry bag. It also comes with a mounting makeup mirror in the bag which is something I will not use with the ring light (I have other uses for it). In includes all of the hardware you need for mounting your camera, video camera or phone if you are a vlogger or content maker.

The very first thing I did with this light was point my camera right at it while using the electronic shutter, in order to determine if the LEDs in this light are strobing or not. I half expected these to strobe based on the price, but they do not which is a very good thing. It means steady, consistent light that does not flicker.

There are two adjustment knobs that are on the light assembly, one to control the brightness and the other to control the light temperature. The temperature range (speaking in generalized, observable terms rather than technical terms with numbers) allows for setting the light from an orangy golden-hour glow to a piercing frosty blue, and everywhere in between. So, though it may require some messing it allows for getting the light temperature just right based on skin tone and background. The brightness can be varied from a soft glow to bright enough to hurt your eyes when looking right at the ring. Thought not designed for such, this would work as a studio light in a pinch...

I do not have a light meter to check the actual light temperature or the lumens/lux output.

There’s a plastic cover over the LED array that helps to diffuse the lights and make them easier to face when using the light to illuminate a face for portraits.

The power source is AC 110/120. Some ring lights I have seen and used have USB-based power input instead. These tend to be smaller and less powerful.

Construction is good though I would stop short of saying it is solid and rugged. It is mostly plastic so it does have some flex to it but seems sturdy enough to handle getting moved around and jostled some. Because the housing is plastic instead of metal this is a lightweight unit and is easy to transport. This is a trade-off I have seen with tripods as well – lightweight for travel, heavier for less mobile work. This light seems geared for the traveler based on that.

Overall, I am pleased with this light. It is a bit better than I expected and it has everything you need in the package to be suitable for vlogging or studio use. It’s a big light so it does cost a bit more than a lot of the smaller, USB-powered lights out there but the cost is reasonable. If you’re looking for a ring light that can be used for either video content or of portrait work, give this one some consideration.

title: Versatile Camera Stabilization Tool
text:
I am no videographer though I have a camera that is well-suited for video recording (even though it is primarily a stills camera). I selected the Scorpion EX as a possible aid in taking shots close to the ground. In my case this device is absolutely overkill and likely will see less use than it would in the hands of someone shooting video, but I do have my uses for it and I do very much like it.

The concept is pretty simple. This is really just a fancy holster of sorts, not unrelated to a tripod, and it has all of the hardware you need to attach your camera, video camera, or even your phone to it (I will generically say just “camera” moving forward). It is roughly the shape of a horseshoe (hence the name) and it has numerous mounting holes for attaching your camera. It has an easy grip handle and is lightweight enough to be easy to handle, even for people with smaller hands.

There are no electronics involved here – no remote shutter, no stabilization like with a gimbal, or any other fancy electronic smarts that would drive up the cost. What stabilization is there is gravity-based and this works surprisingly well, though not as well as a gimbal. My camera does not have on-board stabilization, and in experimentation the Scorpion did reduce but not eliminate some of the shakes. So, do not expect miracles, but it will definitely make a stabilization improvement when you use it.

This has a surprising amount of flexibility built-in (not in the sense of being pliable, but versatile). The harnesses can be attached almost anywhere on the handle so that everything can be optimally positioned. I have found this to be especially useful for attaching a COB light near the forwardmost point, so that the light is cast wonderfully when I am trying to get a head-on shot.

As for being low to the ground when I need a ground level shot, this is better than a tripod because I can get the camera lower than with even the smallest tripod and I can use adjustable feet to make everything level. This is really useful for when I am taking long exposures.

While this is very definitely overkill for my uses I am pleased I have this in my toolbox. It is a simple tool but it is very useful, and in the hands of someone who needs to better stabilize a video recorder it will be more useful still. As I mentioned above, it won’t work absolute miracles, but it reduces the camera shakes enough to make a noticeable difference.

title: Excellent at the Price Point
text:
My son participates in an online meeting weekly, and he needed a new webcam to replace the one he was using. The old one worked but was not of good quality. Based on the asking price for this webcam I was not especially hopeful. That said, it has proven to be better than either of us expected.

It's easy to set up - plug it in and let the OS configure it. It's easy enough to use, too, by selecting the camera desired if there's more than one.

We have seen no issues with clarity or audio/video quality, which have both been solid and reliable. In his meeting, others have commented that his feed seems to be the clearest and most glitch-free.

At least one other reviewer noticed issues with lag and skipping. This has not been an issue for us and so far this little camera has performed well without incident.

The model we received did not have the mini tripod. However, it has a standard mount for a tripod and those little tripods are easy enough to find. If you already have a tripod of any size, this webcam will mount without issue.

Could it be better? Sure. But, improvement would drive up the cost, and the quality is good as it is. For the asking price, this is a great little webcam.

title: Works with Linux; Small and Fast
text:
Crucial is one of the first names that comes to mind when I have needed reliable RAM for my systems in the past. I have a Crucial 500MB SSD in one of my systems and it has served me well over the years so I was interested in this SSD as a back-up option for pictures and data. It has proven to be a fine solution for my needs.

Right up front – yes, it works with Linux right out of the box. I plugged it into my Peppermint Linux system and the kernel immediately recognized the drive and made it available. It was on me to mount the drive, but this was a simple matter and I was able to access the file system and see drive statistics. Obviously it works with Windows so I won’t go into that.

This is a physically small device, slightly less than half the size of a cell phone (iPhone 6s is what I used for comparison). It will easily fit inside the change pocket in my jeans and can tuck just about anywhere. This is a double-edged sword. On one hand it is convenient to have something this small and easy to store, but it is also easy to misplace or even lose. If this stays in your laptop bag or briefcase it should be secure, but if you are in a habit of keeping things in your pockets instead be cautious.

Transfer speeds are good. I have not done benchmarks on this drive but I copied thousands of pictures (average size about 8mb per file, some more and some less) and it was significantly faster than the USB drive I have been using for a while and faster than many of the thumb drives I have been using for backups. I have no complaints.

This is a small and fast drive that just works. It works with Linux which for me is important, and it is small enough to tuck in my camera bag for making backups in the field.

title: Works Perfectly Under Linux
text:
I selected this keyboard after doing a bit of research. I already have a solar keyboard (a Logitech) on my Windows system, and I needed a keyboard for my Linux system. I was a little hesitant to buy because I did not see any definitive information that it would work with Linux. I've had it several days, and I can say with some authority, it definitely works correctly under Linux.

The system in question is a Dell laptop running Peppermint Linux hosting a CentOS 8 VM. Most keyboards (with one notable exception) work on this system so I was hopeful it would work well, and it does. It behaves virtually identically to the Logitech keyboard and so far has given me no trouble.

Build-wise, this is a solid keyboard that should hold up to some abuse. It is sturdy and does not flex when I am typing. I like the fact that the dongle is held to the back of the keyboard magnetically so it can be transported with less concern of being misplaced when not in use.

One of the major issues I have with keyboards is that I have the hands of a gorilla and I frequently run into issues with hitting multiple keys at the same time, particularly with flat keyboards like this one. The keys are slightly bigger than average with this one, though, and hitting muliple keys simultaneously is less of a problem. This was an unexpected and welcome surprise.

Aesthetically, I love the feel of this keyboard. Most of the keys are concave and feel pleasant to the touch. Oddly, a good number of the keys on the bottom row are actually convex. While this is no issue at all, I do find it puzzling.

It is priced competitively against the Logitech too.

If I could change anything I would include some kind of indicator of how much charge this keyboard has at any given time. So far I have not run out of power, but eventually I expect to have a situation where there has not been enough light to keep it at a full charge and it would be good to know how much power it has retained.

I'm pleased with this keyboard. It works well under Linux and I don't need to replace batteries or plug it in. I really can't ask for much more than that.

title: Versatile Mount for Lighting Source or Camera/Phone
text:
I selected the OctoPad as much out of curiosity as out of need. I have a weighted platform that looks similar that I use for my GPS navigator in the car, and that has proven to be one of the best ways to support that device. I expected a similar experience from the OctoPad, and it has proven it’s worth. I would, however, stop short of calling it perfect.

The concept is simple. It is a weighted (sand-filled) pad with a non-skid bottom. It has a ball joint with a threaded mount attached, and the mount can accommodate a camera, selfie stick, smartphone harness, or even a harness for another device if it supports the thread. It serves the same base purpose as a miniature tripod but is more versatile as the flat, rubber base is designed to prevent slipping on smoother surfaces.

It is the non-skid base that stands between this being a good product and a great one. The rubbery material is thin and feels quite fragile, and I believe it is a matter of time before it either breaks down or just rips. Because of the material of the upper portion that covers the sand I believe a new base can be sewn in place when this happens but that is inconvenient at the very least.

Other than my reservations about the no-slip base, this has proven to be a valuable tool for me. I have a selfie stick permanently mounted on it and I use that to mount a small COB light, which all together provides me with a very useful mobile light source when I need to angle a light in a tight spot. It is not ideal but it brings me much closer than when I hand-hold the light. It also is more stable when the surface on which I put it isn’t quite level.

This is a useful tool in my photography arsenal. It works as designed and it provides me with some options when I need a mount that I can put almost anywhere. I would change the base material and make it more durable, even if it increased the cost a bit, but otherwise I have no complaints and am pleased with the OctoPad.

title: Excellent at the Price Point
text:
Note: There are multiple products attached to this listing. I am specifically reviewing the vertical mouse.

I have used a variety of trackballs, mice, writing tablets and more in my search for the most comfortable pointing device. My weapon of choice has been a higher-end trackball for the last couple of years, and I have a relatively cheap vertical mouse I use on occasion when I need to use that trackball on another system. I've used Kensington trackballs in the past and have had good experiences with them, so I was optimistic about this vertical mouse. So far, it has not disappointed me.

I have the hands of a gorilla so finding a mouse, trackball or any other pointing device usually requires some searching. What fits my hand is often too big for others and what I find too small is usually just right for everyone else. This vertical mouse seems to hit the sweet spot - it's comfortable in my hand and quite usable but it is also good for people with smaller hands. I will say that it is still slightly on the small side for me, and when I use it my pinky finger rests on the desk at the base of this mouse, but it is not uncomfortable and is a step up from others I have used.

In terms of the contour and fit, it is arguably one of the most comfortable vertical mice I have used. My thumb, index and middle fingers rest properly on it and I have no trouble controlling the mouse at all. I do not need to stretch to reach the buttons, but also I do not need to scrunch my hand either. It's a good balance.

Operation is smooth and easy. It is very responsive, it is not loud when the buttons are clicked, and it has a reasonable amount of range.

Considering the cost, it is as close to perfect as I have used. That said, there are a couple of things I would change if I had the opportunity to do so, though the cost would increase. First, I would add the ability to connect via Bluetooth and provide for switching between two connected systems. I have that ability with other peripherals and I like it, though it's a convenience feature. Second, I would add the ability to recharge it instead of replacing batteries. This is a double-edged sword, though - the difference between being up and running with replaceable batteries and rechargeable can be the difference between a minute and a couple of hours.

Because of the nature of vertical mice, it is not switchable between right and left hands. This is very much a right-handed mouse. If you are left-handed, you can use this mouse but it will be very awkward.

One odd thing occurred when I set it up under Windows 10. When I plugged in the receiver it reported it as a wireless keyboard. However, operation has been fine so this is a weird cosmetic issue and I assume that it is because it uses a common receiver.

I like this mouse and am pleased with it. It isn't absolutely perfect and there are some ways in which it could be improved, but to do so would increase the cost appreciably. At the price point, this is one of the best vertical mice I have used.

title: Better than Average Headphones; Very Balanced Sound
text:
Most of the headphones with which I have worked have been active noise canceling (ANC) phones which have their strengths and weaknesses. I have a few pairs of nice non-ANC phones, some of which are excellent for studio work, but this is my first pair of true studio phones. After working with them, I am very pleased with them. They are comfortable to wear for long periods of time and they sound great with a very balanced sound profile.

These are over-the-ear phones, not on-ear, and I prefer that. They do not pinch or press my ears and I can wear them for several hours without them getting uncomfortable. The pads are soft and do not irritate as some phone pads sometimes can. The pads do not breathe, though, so after some time they do eventually get a bit warm.

If using these as Bluetooth phones, operation is simple – turn them on. They’re immediately ready to pair and my system discovered them and paired without incident. The Bluetooth range is good and I was able to get between 30’ and 50’ with walls in between before the sound began to stutter a little.

If you prefer to use them corded, that works too and these come with several audio cords with which to connect. Speaking of the cords: these do not use a standard audio cable with a standard connector on the phone side, so you can’t simply use any audio cable with them (though they will work with extension cables). Bear this in mind.

Volume can be controlled by touching the connector on the left side – flick up to increase volume, flick down to decrease.

The most important aspect of any headphones is the sound quality and these definitely deliver. The highs are sharp and crisp without being piercing. The midlevels are full and warm, and the base is strong without being overdriven. Most headphones anymore are tuned to overdrive the bass at the expense of the midrange making music sound hollow while pounding the listener to a headache. It is refreshing to listen to music that is properly balanced without needing an equalizer to get the sound right. I would not call these audiophile phones, but they’re better than many headphones I have used that cost much more.

If I could change one thing… I prefer a headphone set that clamps down on my head and fits snugly. These are not as snug as I’d like, but they are better than some I have used. When I turn my head and look down, they remain in place without slipping which is an issue with loose-fitting phones. Since these don’t slip, I’m satisfied.

I’m happy with these phones and based on my experience with them I am pleased to recommend them. They sound great and they are comfortable enough for extended use.

title: Excellent Weather Radio
text:
Anymore, an emergency radio has been largely replaced by smart phones for getting emergency updates and it is not a common item that people frequently buy or have around. That said, having a radio like this is useful when traveling and either cell service is bad or using a phone is impractical. In such cases a radio like this is a really good resource. For us, while not a necessity this radio sees daily use as a weather radio.

One of the things that has been around our house for many, many years is a weather radio. We are in range of two weather stations and we have a dedicated emergency weather radio that provides us emergency notifications as well as current conditions and forecasts around the region. The difficulty we have had with it is that reception is not the greatest and we often have static over the broadcast. We have a secondary weather radio that has even worse reception that our main one.

I did not have high expectations of this radio at all. We tuned it to the closest station with the expectation of hearing a lot of static and interference. Much to our surprise, the broadcast is clear and uncluttered. We tuned to the other station and got the same – a clear broadcast. What was a real surprise for us is that we could suddenly pick up a third station. We had no idea we were close enough to any other station to hear their broadcasts. It’s not as clear as the others, but it is clear enough to be understood.

As a weather radio, this unit is excellent. We have no complaints.

Most of the other features we have tried though do not use regularly. It has a flashlight built in that is bright enough to navigate through the house during a power outage and it has a couple of different modes such as SOS flash that make it useful in different emergency situations. It has different charging modes so it is ready to go when needed, the most frequent of which we use is the solar charging but it can be plugged in and it also can be hand-cranked to generate enough power for emergency use. A particularly helpful emergency feature is the ability to charge your phone, and the battery is sufficient to give one full charge to a smaller smartphone with power to spare.

If I could change one thing I would make it more ruggedized. It is good in that regard and should be able to handle getting dropped or jostled and bumped, but there is definitely opportunity to go farther. This is by no means a show-stopper or even a complaint, but a data point – if you need something that can handle a lot of abuse, this isn’t it, though in the price range it would be difficult to find better.

This is a nice emergency radio and my family really likes it. Though designed and marketed as an emergency radio, it actually sees daily use solely on the basis of how well it performs as a weather radio.

title: Excellent Continuous LED Light with Good Feature Set
text:
I selected this light after doing some research on continuous LED lights. I had a situation where I had only a strobing light available to me and it made getting even a still exposure without banding very difficult. My requirements for a continuous LED were that it had to be compact, bright and have variable color output. This light met those requirements, and in addition I found some favorable write-ups of this light online. Though on the pricey side, I took the plunge and so far I have no regrets.

I will state right up front that this is not marketed as a general purpose light and it is not a proper substitute for such. There are less expensive and more practical lights available if you need general lighting. Yes, it will work as a general purpose light source, even as a flashlight in a pinch, but that’s akin to using a blowtorch to light candles when a simple match will do.

This is a very small light, about the side of a king-sized candy bar. Even after reading the description and reviews, I was surprised at just how small this light is. That’s good for me because it fits perfectly in my camera bag and can go with me without taking up extra room or requiring space in the car or luggage. When stored in the case it takes up about as much room as a small jar of peanut butter.

The light has ten brightness settings as well as a boost mode which makes it almost blinding. The lowest setting is quite dim but usable, and the brightest outside of boost mode is bright enough to illuminate a 10’x10’ space reasonably well. The light color is constant unless using the color “gels” (more on that in a moment). When using boost mode, it remains in that mode for a period of roughly a minute before switching back to one of the normal settings. It takes some time before boost mode can be used again, likely a safety measure due to increased heat output.

Included are several color “gels” that are more like hard plastic plates that fit in front of the light array. These allow for some adjustment in color. The colors tweak the color range to be warmer or colder. I used the darkest orange to give a scene a warmer, golden glow that worked remarkably well. These plates are held in place against the array with a clip-on harness that fits over the front of the unit.

Also included is a silicone diffuser that reduces the harshness of the array. When the clip-on harness is in place it is difficult at best to attach the diffuser.

There are several effects modes to emulate different lighting situations, including a flickering light, lightning strike, glow from a television and more. While these are interesting and some will find these modes useful, particularly for video, they do not serve my purposes.

What I did not realize is that this light has a mounting hole on the bottom that allows for attaching it to any standard tripod or even a monopod/selfie stick. I attached it to a higher-quality telescoping monopod with a swivel base and was able to get the exact lighting angle I needed. With a tripod it becomes hands-free.

Though it is waterproof I have no intention of using this in water.

It includes a couple of patches that allow it to be semi-permanently attached to a surface. I am contemplating building a large light box and attaching this light inside.

This is a really excellent and versatile continuous LED light. It is as bright or dim as you need it, it includes some color plates for adjusting the color output, it includes some special effect modes and it is small enough to fit in my bag without any trouble at all. This is a very easy light to recommend if you need a continuous LED light.

title: Better than I Expected; Doesn't Lose Power Like Canned Dusters Do
text:
I use canned dusters for a variety of purposes, from cleaning keyboards to cleaning up my electric shaver. These sometimes leave residue behind, so I was interested in trying this electric duster to see if it would cut down on residue and save money in the long run. I will confess that I was not very optimistic and thought it would be underpowered. However, it has proven to be as effective as a canned duster in cleaning keyboards and other equipment, without leaving any residue and without losing power like canned dusters tend to do as they get cold.

This device is smaller than a tea kettle and relatively light. It requires an AC outlet so it does need to be plugged in when you want to use it. I was hopeful I had missed something on the description and that there was a rechargeable battery but unfortunately this is not the case. This was me being hopeful, not a confusing write-up.

It comes with a few attachments to help direct the air flow over the surface of what you’re trying to clean. The most helpful attachment, to me, is the round nozzle, but all of them have their uses.

I took it to my office where we have an abundance of dirty keyboards that need to be cleaned, and I set to work. I was expecting it to do a mediocre cleaning job, but it gave me a very pleasant surprise and blew air with plenty of force to clean out the clumps of dust that collect under the keys. More importantly, though, the power didn’t diminish like what tends to happen with canned dusters as they get cold, and there was no problem with frost buildup either.

So far, this is proving to be a useful and helpful tool. It produces enough force to get the job done without losing power, and it leaves no residue behind.

title: Good Set of Filters
text:
I bought this set of filters to fit a 77mm Fujinon lens. I needed a UV filter, and I wanted a CPL filter. I bought a separate variable ND filter so I really didn’t need the ND4 filter but it’s a good addition to this set. So far I have been pleased with the set and am happy to recommend it.

The UV filter is useful as a basic protective cover for a lens, but it also does filter out UV light. This is a lot less of a problem when it comes to digital camera, as UV light was harmful to 35mm film. UV light can make images hazy and this filter can reduce that. In very specific situations, there can be reflections between the lens glass and the filter, so there are occasions when using the UV filter is not advisable.

I had the opportunity to use the CPL filter on a sunny day at a lake and I used the filter to cut through the reflections on the water. It worked well and I was able to get a picture of things on the bottom. That’s all I could really ask.

I have not used the ND4 filter.

This set comes in a nice carrying case that protects the filters when they’re not in use. The case is small enough that it fits inside my camera bag without any issue.

This is a decent filter set and I am pleased with it. The filters I have used have worked well for me.

title: Inexpensive Macro Filter Set
text:
I selected these macro filters to go with a 77mm Fujinon lens. I have used these types of filters with an older camera and wanted a set for my new camera, and after researching available options I chose these. These are decent macro filters though there is some room for improvement.

These are about as basic as it gets. They’re not fancy, they’re just screw-on filters designed to fit lenses with a 77mm thread. They fit my lens just fine and I have had no trouble removing them when I am done. These are straight glass and with the exception of the +10 filter there is little distortion. The +10 filter has a lot of edge distortion but clarity in the middle, which is very much like other sets like these I have used.

There is a problem with the +1 filter in my set. The glass is loose in the ring and it actually rattles when I handle it. It doesn’t seem to be loose enough to come out of the ring. It does concern me that it could come out, though. I would be more concerned about this if I used this particular filter more, but that’s not the point.

This is not a bad set, but the quality is not as good as it should be. The filters work well enough, but I am concerned that the glass might separate from the ring, based on one of them in my set. So far it hasn’t happened.

title: Superb Fit; Soft Midrange
text:
I have worked with a lot of different sets of headphones and ear buds and have gotten a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Specifically with ear buds I pay attention to the fit as well as the sound, which are two areas where many manufacturers get it wrong. Anker did a good job with these though there is a soft spot in the sound profile.

I used these with an iPhone 7, and initial pairing was very quick and painless. The buds found each other (another issue I have seen with other sets on occasion), and these paired without much fanfare or issue at all. That’s really all you could ask.

These fit like a dream. The package contains several silicone plugs of different sizes so you can get just the right fit for yourself, but I found that the ones already on the buds were actually a perfect fit. I popped these in, gave them a turn to lock them in place and they sealed perfectly. I am especially happy with how well these fit in my ears and actually stay there.

The sound isolation is on par with what you’d expect. When not powered on and streaming music they are the equivalent to a cheap set of ear plugs – enough to block out some sound but not completely silence the world.

The sound quality is very good but the sound profile could use a tweak. The bass is strong but not overdriven to the point of causing headaches. There is a tendency to overdrive the bass, so having good bass that’s not overpowering is nice. The highs are bright and clear too. The midrange is another matter and feels weak (though not non-existent). Music played through these buds lacks the warmth and fullness that the midrange brings to the table (and if it was overdriven everything would sound like it is coming through a tunnel). I would rather have under-driven midrange than overdriven, but it’s still soft enough to be noticeable.

They case in which these buds are stored also serves as the charger. What is interesting about these is how the case itself is charged. Instead of MicroUSB, this case uses a Type C connector which is not unwelcome but up to this point is unusual for this kind of device. There is a cable in the box so there’s no issue.

These are good ear buds and they have some nice features. They fit superbly and they pair to a source without problems. The sound profile is imperfect, though not terribly so, which is the only complaint I have with them.

title: Keyboard Slipped Past the QC Department
text:
For the most part I have had good fortune with Logitech peripherals. As I write this I am using an MX Ergo trackball which is the best mouse/trackball I have ever used. I looked to the MK470 mouse/keyboard combination with the idea of using it with a laptop running Linux. I had high expectations for the keyboard but lower expectations for the mouse due to the size and shape. Both failed me, but in completely different ways.

I will start with this: this combo does not use a unifying receiver so if you want to use another peripheral with this combo you’ll need either another USB port or connect via Bluetooth. That’s all right as long as you recognize that up front. It’s a mild disappointment, but it was clear up front so this was not a surprise.

The mouse and the keyboard both have the batteries installed already. The keyboard takes 2 AAA batteries and the mouse takes one AA battery. I question the logic behind using different battery sizes.

I plugged the receiver into my laptop running Linux with the latest kernel, and both peripherals were immediately usable. That’s a plus.

The first problem I have is with the mouse. The mouse works just fine but is such a low-profile device that it is uncomfortable for me to use. I have a travel mouse that actually fits my hand a little better and that says a lot. For someone with very small hands this one will serve acceptably as a basic two-button travel mouse. To be fair, I knew this ahead of time so I cannot complain too much. It does work correctly and in a pinch I can work with it.

The keyboard is a completely different matter entirely. It works just fine – except for the “P” key. For that specific key, I have to bear down very hard to get it to register at all. I tried leaning the keyboard on its side and tapping it gently in case something was caught in the switch and I have tried my best to clean it without disassembly. No matter what I have tried, the “P” key continues to be insensitive to the point of rendering the keyboard unusable.

I really wanted to like this keyboard, and I knew the mouse would be small. Unfortunately, because the keyboard I received doesn’t work properly I can’t use it and can’t rate it favorably. It’s a shame – I imagine I got a bad unit (it happens), but I cannot recommend a product based on an assumption.

UPDATE 10/31/2019:

I popped off the "P" key and looked at the mechanism underneath, since the keyboard was not otherwise useful. It does not appear to be broken, damaged or obstructed in any way. For this particular key, the plastic key cover needs a small bead in the center underneath to push down the silicone membrane to make contact. Using a very small piece of tape and a tiny ball (about the size of a pin head) I was able to add such to the key cover to get it working without damaging any parts, without changing the feel while typing, and without spending any money. However, this should not have been necessary as this should have been tested properly before pack-and-ship; my review and rating stand.

title: Versatile Digital Picture Frame
text:
This is the first digital picture frame with which I have worked so I do not have any basis of comparison with others to know if it compares well against other ones or not. That said, it does what it is supposed to do, it does it well and I am happy with it.

Setup is simple and easy. If you have your media ready to go, copy it to the included SD card and pop it in.

On a side note, the card that came with it is 32GB which is huge. That can hold literally thousands of full-resolution images from a digital camera. Assuming that the average high-resolution JPG image is 8mb (which is what comes off my mirrorless camera) it can hold about 4,000 pictures. That all said, this frame can also play back video and sound, so there is more to it than just showing pictures. In that light, the size of the card makes a lot of sense.

The frame is approximately 10” of viewing area. The images are bright and clear which should please most users.

The unit handles a number of audio, video and image formats. The list is not exhaustive, but it does handle the main types in each category.

Included is a little remote. The remote isn’t fancy but it is sufficient for changing settings, moving to the next media element, power on/off, etc.

There’s really only one negative, and that’s the documentation which is written in very poorly-translated English. I would lower my rating of the overall package on this basis except that the product is so self-explanatory and easy to use/understand that the documentation isn’t necessary.

Overall, we are happy with this frame. It works well and it is very easy and straightforward to understand. It handles a lot of formats and can play back audio and video in addition to showing still images.

title: Affordable Small-System Solution
text:
I selected this camera to mount on my front porch, with the intention of keeping a watchful eye on the front of the house. I was very skeptical of this camera because of the price and assumed that it would be a budget-grade solution as a result. It has proven to be better than I anticipated.

This is a single-camera solution with no dedicated monitoring station. It connects via the WiFi network and it can be monitored via phone which is handy when you’re away. It includes a power supply and all of the mounting equipment (minus the tools) to set it all up for outdoor use.

All of that sounds great, but as I write this the camera sells for under $40.

It has not performed like a $40 camera. It has been rock-solid so far – it’s stable, it has remained connected except for when I have had router issues, the image in the daytime is excellent and the night-vision mode is far and away better than I expected – I can read license plates on cars in the driveway at night.

This is not a complete security solution but rather is a single camera for zone security. There are more complete systems that offer more features and capabilities, but these cost a lot more and cover broader areas with multiple cameras. If you just need a single camera to monitor a fairly small area, and you have a wireless network to connect it to, this is a very affordable solution.

title: Works Well for Me
text:
Of the three main GPS receiver manufacturers - Garmin, TomTom and Magellan - I have had the most success with TomTom devices. My first GPS was a TomTom and it served me well for years until the map outgrew the memory. I was excited to have the opportunity to try this one; so far, it has been a good unit, though I do not care for the menu system.

This is a larger unit than the original one I had, upgrading from a 4.3" to a 6". I like the screen real estate. For all that screen space, TomTom has made good use of it, maximizing the visible map and keeping the interface clean and uncluttered. One area where I am slightly disappointed, though, is in the speed display which is a little small - it's good to keep it out of the way but it's a little smaller than I like and it a bit harder to read. If you use your GPS for watching your speed, this could be a problem.

Navigation is easy. I like the way this unit routes me to my destination yet does not nag me when I go off the chosen route. Others I have used (including my old TomTom) would badger me to make a U-turn for a while before deciding that there was another way to get where I was going. This unit does make that point sometimes, but it also is smart enough to reroute when I have multiple similar routes.

The biggest plus for this unit (and it seems to be a TomTom thing) is that the voice very clearly enunciates without distortion or the unit buzzing. I have had this issue with every other unit of every other brand, but my old TomTom was clear and understandible even at higher volumes. Since this one is the same, I believe TomTom has a better understanding of how to build a unit that sounds right.

Navigating from work to home is usually a straight shot down the interstate for 40+ miles and a little bit of backroads. To test, I instead took a long, out-of-the-way route that I use when there is heavy traffic volume. Knowing it would try to put me on the interstate, I set the farthest point as a first leg, then set it to take me home from there. The route it chose was actually only slightly different than the one I had chosen already, and the difference was that I accounted for rush hour traffic.

Speaking of traffic... This unit gathers traffic data without relying on mobile data. I greatly prefer this to having to run an app on my phone and letting it gather traffic info from online. So far I have not had it report a reroute due to traffic; I will come back here and update when it does.
