I knew that the newer display panel would have some advantages other than more resolution, and that the smart-TV functions would be an upgrade, but I had no idea how much of an upgrade it would be!

First of all, I obviously no longer need a Firestick. This TV has everything built in, and even has stick-style remote included so if you're used to that, this will be very familiar. All the streaming services I wanted are there, however I was nervous about some apps like Plex not being available since I have a Plex server of my own library and I didn't think it was such a popular mainstream thing to do. Sure enough, Plex IS an option and it performs flawlessly! The TV even has a browser built in, really making it feel like there's no reason to keep the Firestick around.

Not only that but it actually has a lot of built in live content straight from Samsung. Personally, I'm a cord-cutter and no longer subscribe to cable TV or even bother with local broadcast. I've been streaming only for years now, so I was surprised to find that Samsung offers me what appear to be live channels I can tune in complete with a guide like a cablebox. Some of the channels even have things I might be interested in, however I might look into disabling this feature since the idea of cutting the cord was partly to prevent my kids from mindlessly watching things "because it is on".

Since the menus are run on the TV itself, everything displays and moves at glorious high frame rate 4k resolution, which is awesome. Part of the problem with a high hz and resolution TV is that there usually is not a lot of content that takes advantage of all of that. Most of the time you're watching content only available in 1080/30p at best, unless you are lucky enough to find something available in full 4k and high frame rate. The menus and UI clearly do and you can see and feel the difference- navigating on this is a pleasure. It syncs up with Alexa (you can also use Bixby and Google Home), and allows me to make announcements that will be heard on the TV, such as "turn it off and come upstairs". As a parent, I like that- but then again, the Firestick could do that too. What supposedly makes this even better is that it implied I have the ability to also turn on or off the TV using Alexa (so I can ask her to, for example, shut it down at bedtime). I could not get that feature to work but I might not have set it up correctly yet.

One thing I DON'T like, which comes with every new TV, is their motion-smoothing picture thing that causes the dreaded "soap opera effect" on narratives films and shows. This can be turned off, but it took me a while to figure out where it was. It has moved since my last Samsung TV, and it was counterintuitive since I turned it off in the settings, but then found it set to auto within the program I was watching. I'm not sure if its a per-profile setting or something, but after turning it off there as well it finally is actually STAYING off. Motion looks like a movie theater again instead of like a video game cut scene.

I really like the way the remote has a solar panel on the back- I don't know yet if this is just a gimmick but it's a very cool idea. The fact that it is rechargeable and doesn't need batteries is huge as well.

All in all, this is a great upgrade to my old TV. The price is a little steep, but you get a lot for your money. The picture quality is astounding, especially on content that can take advantage of all it has to offer. I recommend it!

title: Great for headphones, not for microphones (not TRRS?)
text:
After finally needing to retire my last phone with a headphone jack, it was time to try out some of these USBC to 3.5mm adapters. The good news is, it works really well and actually is small enough to leave attached to the end of my favorite set of wired headphones. You're not going to get audiophile quad-dac quality out of it like my old LG phones, but it will drive a normal pair of headphones just fine for music or videos.
HOWEVER, there are a couple of things to note:
1) It seems to support the audio out channels but not the microphone, if your headphones have one. You know how phone earbuds usually have an extra pin for the microphone on the tip (3 rings instead of 2)? I think this doesn't support that. I believe this jack is TRS instead of TRRS. Or even if it IS a TRRS, it's only telling my phone that the left and right audio channels are there. Which leads me to item #2:
2) It tells the phone a headset is connected even if it is not. And I think this also is related to #1, because it doesn't seem to care what's plugged into the other side of it, as soon you plug this adapter into your phone, even empty, the headphones icon shows up and all audio is routed out to the empty 3.5mm jack. Plug something in, you hear the sound. Unplug it, the sound goes nowhere. This is why I'm happy to leave it semi-permanently attached to my earphones, and just considering it an extension of them. You don't want to leave this attached to your phone with nothing plugged in.

In a nutshell, this is great if you want to listen to music. Not if you want to use a wired headset for phone calls.

title: Premium IEM from Panasonic/Technics
text:
I work in live AV production, and usually keep a pair of Sony over-the-ear headphones in my gear bag for monitoring sound on location. Quality of the sound is important for concert and other live music gigs. But those big Sonys take up a lot of space, so I've been considering a good set of IEMs for a while now. In the past I haven't had good results from anything that wasn't a large over-the-ear set, and I have small ears that reject a lot of ear-bud style devices so I was excited to get a chance to try these out.

Ok, to be fair, I don't have any other IEMs to compare this to, but I'm BLOWN AWAY at how incredible they sound at such a miniscule size. I put on the smallest tips for my ears and they actually stay in relatively well, and create the passive noise cancellation I was expecting but without being uncomfortable to wear for an extended period of time. But the range of sound reproduced was something I have only experienced in larger studio headphones!
A perk of IEMs versus larger headphones on jobs like mine are that I can pull out one so I can hear the sound around me while monitoring with my other ear (great if working with an audio engineer who needs to communicate with me on the job), and it comes with a pretty nifty case to wrap it up and slide into my bag. The case makes it bigger than it needs to be, but honestly this is so much less space than my old headphones took up, and keeps the cord from getting tangled. I love it!
For personal use, they sound great even on consumer equipment, but they really shine on devices that can drive the additional range such as my old LG V20 with it's Quad DAC built in (one of the reasons I keep that old device around!).
The price tag is a little steep for me personally, but my Sony headphones retail somewhere around this (I had bought them used), and I KNOW there are pricier options out there, so it seems to fit right into the audiophile equipment range.

title: It plays correctly, but the remote issues = bad experience
text:
This is a great player for those of us with older DVDs that we want to play on a modern (or older, it does have RCA plugs!) TV. It works, and the TV displayed the upscaled image just fine, however the remote almost killed the experience.
For starters, the batteries it came with were physically warped, but no big deal- I don't usually expect batteries to be included, so I tossed them away and put fresh ones in. But then the remote did not seem to work. Fine, I'll just use the controls on the player, right? WRONG. The only option on the player is the play/pause button. So if your DVD has a menu that starts with the cursor over play, that's fine. But if you need to navigate the menus at all, you're out of luck without the remote working. There is no D-pad or any other obvious way to get the cursor to move.
But then I thankfully read another review here that described not getting the remote to work unless it was in direct line-of-sight with the TOP of the player (as if mounted to a wall in the picture- basically it isn't just that it CAN be wall mounted, it is designed to ONLY work properly in that angle!). Well folks, it does work if only in that exact scenario, which is kind of boggling. If this gets used in a classroom or senior center, the experience will not be intuitive without being told you have to hold the remote in a very specific orientation for it to work. I've never seen an IR remote that was so picky... usually if you point a remote at something nearby the sensor, it will still pick it up. But I guess the placement of the sensor here makes it very narrow, and to me that seems like an odd design flaw.

3 stars because it DOES work once you figure out how, but it is really not intuitive out of the box to expect others to use.

title: Not top of the line, but excellent value!
text:
This is a great CHEAP sata solid state drive. I want to emphasize that this is CHEAP- it is not going to be a speed demon, and it's not large enough to be a main storage drive to house mission-critical data. But it seems to deliver consistently over 400mbps in benchmark tests, which is more than enough to get the benefits of it over a mechanical drive in a SATA setup.
I can't vouch for the longevity of a brand I've never heard of, but again... the value here is the insanely low price of entry. That makes it great for refurbishing an old laptop or perhaps turning older hardware into a chrome book or a closet file server at home. I like to use it in HDMI recording devices such as an Atmos Ninja, as I can edit footage directly off the drive (it's fast enough!) when plugged into my computer, and it's nice to have a backup from my camera's SD card slot when recording events. If the drive dies one day, nothing major will have been lost. For what it is, so far I am impressed, just have realistic expectations for what you can use it for. I probably would not use this for my main computer C drive if only because it is a laughably small amount of storage. But as a fast SSD that uses legacy SATA connections, it definitely has uses!

title: Another winner from Sabrent
text:
I've had the opportunity to evaluate and own a quite a few Sabrent branded accessories for my editing setup, and my experience has been overwhelmingly positive. This memory DIMM is no different, after trying the 32GB version I wanted to also get this 16 in a laptop that could use a boost.
This laptop motherboard only supported 2400Mhz clocked ram, so the DIMM did not perform at its full 3200mhz advertised speed, however the benchmarks clocked appropriately for that speed and the overall performance of the computer was improved, as intended.

title: Great way to put a USB where you want it
text: I wanted to mount a USB port near where I put my phone's wireless charger, and just run a short cable to it so I don't have a giant honking wire all across my dashboard (I keep my phone on the left of the steering wheel). With this adapter, I was able to fish a wire behind my dash and come up right where I want my phone to be mounted. Drilling a hole in the plastic and putting this in was simple, use the nut to fasten it into place and keep it there. Connected it to a DC USB adapter hidden in my storage console, and used a short 3" cable to the phone charger from the port this gives. It works great to charge my phone without wires visible everywhere!

title: Decent quality from Sabrent
text: I've owned some SSDs, networking and other PC products from Sabrent, but this was my first RAM stick from them. Overall I've been impressed with the brand, and these are no different. The performance was pretty solid, however the laptop I used it in did not like using XMP profiles (something to do with shared vram or something like that) so I kept it clocked at a more boring 2400Mhz. But, it performed perfectly and benchmarked appropriately for those speeds when checked. It's not particularly cheap for ram, but with prices going up on everything, I'd say these are good sticks if you can get it for a good relative price. The boost in available ram is noticeable for performance.

title: Does not work with calls, but otherwise great!
text:
This is a great way to continue using your wired headphones without giving up your charging port. It is a little bulkier than a straight USB-to-3.5mm adapter, but that's just how it has to be in order to make room for two plugs on a dongle like this.
A couple of things to note: The USB cable does not support data, only charging. But that's expected since it says so on this listing.
The thing that DID surprise me, however, is that it does not support the inline mic for calls. During a test phone call, the audio was coming from the phone's mic and not the headset, which we confirmed by tapping on the mic and then again on the phone (only the phone tap sound was heard). It actually says for calls on the listing, which I believe is a mistake. I'm guessing this unit supports TRS and ignores the extra pin for TRRS, so it's great for listening to music only and this is why I'm removing one star.

title: Fantastic for editors on the go!
text:
If you're familiar with Samsung's other portable SSD drives (T5, regular T7, etc), you expect this to be a product that will deliver on speed and portability.
And it DOES.
Working with media production (video, photos, music, etc) on the go, having a super fast external drive is a necessity. I'm actually quite impressed at the speeds I'm getting off this. My office desktop workstation has a 14TB internal drive plugged directly into the motherboard for working on video edits, and this tiny marvel is almost 10x the speed, even as an external plugged into a petite USB-C port! That's incredible. And the new rugged design means I can slip it into a backpack or gear bag and know it will hold up.

Note for drive shuckers: Unlike the T5 and other older SSD offerings from Samsung, this does NOT have an mSATA inside anymore. It used to be worth it to buy an external drive on sale to strip for the SSD inside and upgrade your computer's internal drive with. Not with this product, the internal design is a single board with the memory chips, USB interface, etc, all on one board. But it's excellent at what it does!

title: Great hardware, terrible software. Come on Oneplus, you're better than this!
text:
[[VIDEOID:8bed6d79d90a43dd042702aefe52b20a]] I wanted to love this phone so badly. Now that LG has left the phone market, I wanted to know there are still flagship killers like Oneplus out there to take on the bullies of wireless phones. And on paper, there's a LOT to love about this phone. Let's mention the good things first:
- As a photographer, I really like the Hasselblad cameras that include a very capable manual mode. See the included photos taken with the phone, no fake bokeh effects. That's just the natural blurring DOF of the lens and sensor.
- As someone who is picky about user experience I absolutely LOVE the silent/vibrate/ring physical switch. All smartphones need that, in my opinion.
- CPU/GPU benchmarks are awesome, right up there with flagships that cost more.
- Coming from the Galaxy S10's terrible in-screen fingerprint reader, this one renews my faith in fp readers.
- Display is beautiful and crisp.
- Battery is surprisingly good.

In a nutshell, the hardware is great! If they just throw a stock Android OS on here, it would be perfect! But sadly, no... they didn't. And the software is TERRIBLE. Chock full of bugs.
Some examples (some of which I tried to capture on video):
1) Google Voice call redirects are broken.
I've been using GV as my phone number for nearly a decade and never had a single problem like this before. The stock dialer does not care what you set GV to, it will IGNORE your outgoing call redirect requests. No matter what you set it to, it uses the carrier number to call out. Even if you select "ask before each call", the phone is so excited to dial out it will show you the option to pick, but in the background IT STARTED CALLING ALREADY and clearly doesn't care what you want. To be fair, this started with the Android 12 update on the Oneplus 9 series as well, so it's a Oneplus problem in general, it seems.

2) Android Auto pop ups make no sense.
When you plug the phone into a USB port, it will prompt you with three options. Charge, Transfer Files / Android Auto, and Transfer Photos. When I plugged it into my car with AA, I see it starting on my car's display, but the pop up still appears on the phone. Naturally, I picked option 2, since it says android auto. It disconnects. So I unplug and try again, and leave it on charge, which seems to work. For the sake of testing, I also tried transfer photos, and it also worked. It seems that THE ONLY OPTION THAT DOESN'T WORK is the one that says Android Auto on it! Seriously?! Is it opposite day?! But that's ok, my car radio also supports wireless Android Auto (uses Wifi direct instead of a cable), so that should avoid the problem right?

3) Wireless Android Auto breaks Wifi's ability to reconnect to known networks.
I know what you're thinking... come on, right? How many Google features can Oneplus break at a time. Apparently a lot. When using Android Auto over the wireless connection, it actually works great, but then the phone seems to give up ever wanting to connect to my known wifi networks again. I get to work or return home and found out that I've been using cellular data the entire time, unless I manually go into Wifi settings and click join network. If I leave the coverage area or toggle wifi off/on, it won't reconnect. I have to manually connect it in settings each time or be stuck using my data plan. A reboot fixes the problem and the wifi reconnects as expected afterwards... until the next time I take the car somewhere and the problem comes back.

4) The 3.3x Telephoto camera has its own color science.
It doesn't match the others. The main camera is actually quite good, and the wide is decent as well. The telephoto is a bit less vibrant and noticeably more dull on warm color themes. I though these were Hasselblad tuned and calibrated to have professional color science and detail? This isn't a major issue, it just seems surprising. Especially when you point the camera at something that is too dark for the limited exposure capability of the 3.3x tele lens, and it jumps to a zoomed in version of the main camera lens instead. Seriously- see my video for a demonstration of that. You see the color suddenly shift into something that looks very different whenever it changes. The main zoomed in actually looks better, and it has enough native pixels to resolve a decent image... which then begs the question of why even have a dedicated 3.3x tele lens?

4) The notifications in the shade don't let you jump to the application... only individual messages. For example, if I have a bunch of Gmail messages, I can see them in the shade and click them individually to go to them each. But I can't just go to Gmail and see my inbox. Sometimes I want to see my inbox and decide what to respond to first. I have to either go to an individual message, or back out and find the Gmail icon to click it directly.

All in all, the phone is usable but I just can't shake the feeling that the OS is half baked and not ready for release yet. The Android Auto issues and Google Voice ones are so major to the way I use my phone on a daily basis, I might prefer to go back to a device from 3 years ago than continue using this one. It just feels unpredictable and unreliable in its current state. I really do hope Oneplus fixes those bugs soon, because the hardware really is nice. Or better yet, give us the option to run a stock Android without all this OOS nonsense. The customizations aren't a selling point, they are detrimental at best and downright BREAK CERTAIN FUNCTIONALITY at worst. I will gladly change my review and update the rating if an update that addresses these issues comes around. Come on, Oneplus. We know you can do better than this on a phone that costs this much.

title: Whoa- this is an upgraded mini PC! Twice the specs, and finally a USB type C!
text:
I love mini PCs. I use them for all kinds of projects, from digital signage to file servers and attached to TVs to make them media consumption units. Usually they are somewhat low powered, running a slightly older architecture chip like a Celeron J4125, and low ram/storage limits to the soldered on chips. For simple computing tasks, they do a good job as long as you don't expect too much of them.

But this one is SPECIAL! First of all, can I get an AMEN on finally recognizing the need to give us a USB type C port on one of these boxes? For specs, the N5095 is easily 30% faster in benchmarks to most of my other mini PCs, and has twice the ram and storage! At 16GB and a 512GB SSD, the specs are starting to look closer to my work laptop than a cheap media center box. This box also has the usual perks of a mini PC like a SATA port for an add-on drive, although with 512GB of storage you won't be needing it as often as those 128GB storage cheap boxes. I've used Beelink boxes before, and I've always found them to be decent quality, from their Android MXQ media boxes to these newer Mini PCs, I'm excited to see how far they've come in replacing the standard desktop for an ever expanding variety of users!

title: Efficient mini-PC, but still no USB-C
text:
I love mini PCs and I've collected a few of them for different projects. The Celeron chip isn't a speed demon, but combined with Intel's GPU it is fast enough to drive 2 HDMI displays quite well, and like most other mini PCs out there, it has enough RAM and storage for light media consumption and internet tasks.
But there are few things that stand out with this model:
- This one is FANLESS. Without moving parts whirring, this actually manages to stay completely quiet while running.
- Also since the body is the heat sink, it doesn't need space for airflow and is therefore more compact as well.
However, not all of those changes are positive:
- There is no upgrade option for the storage like other mini PCs. Some of the popular boxes out there have an access door to add your own sata SSD drive for additional storage. This does not.
- The fanless design also sometimes means that in hot environments (such as attached to the back of a large TV display sign), there is no way to cool itself off other than throttling the processor. Most of the time this doesn't mean anything, but like all fanless computer designs it is extremely possible the unit will need to slow itself down to prevent overheating if used for extended periods of time. A fan unit has alternative ways to cool itself off at least.

But the biggest disappointment to me personally, is the lack of USB type C ports. It looks like this has one, but that look is deceiving. The port is just a PD input to run the unit. I actually like that it is using a standard instead of the circular DC ports that other mini PCs use, the PD power port is plentiful these days and you can use most laptop and other standard PD chargers to run this device. However, it still does not work as a standard USB-C for peripherals that are compatible with one. To be fair, most of these mini PCs I've tried oddly lack a type C port as well. I can't really detract any stars for that, but I got excited for a moment that this would have one only to see it is the power port.

title: Mind blowing wifi coverage, but had some minor hardwire issues
text:
Honestly, I wish I had a tried a Wifi6 mesh system sooner. This is NIGHT AND DAY difference over my previous D-link router + extender. I thought that since both my router and extender were D-link and had the ability to "communicate" with each other, it would work pretty well, but honestly even when it "worked" it was pretty laggy, and outside on the porch it would drop to single digit speed tests, if anything at all (forget about streaming for backyard movie nights!).
This system, however, is incredible. I'm now getting nearly 200mbps outside where I used to have nothing, and in most of my house I'm hitting my maximum 250mbps that I'm paying for with my internet service. Everything responds quickly and smoothly, and I love the control that the TP link system gives over what devices are connected (it alerts me when a new device connects!) and being able to set restrictions and time limits as well!
The one downside, however, is the physical ports. For starters, there are only 3 of them per unit. If you use ethernet backbone to connect them, that leaves only one on the primary node (one for the internet connection to the modem, and the other going to the second node- only one available for anything else). In my case, I have an ethernet cable going to my desktop for work (the most reliable connection), and another going into a telephony system. The 3 port limitation would have been difficult if I hardwired the satellite, but thankfully I didn't have to. The wireless mesh over 6Ghz actually works quite well so far so I managed with only the 3 ports on the primary one.
That being said, at first I had a major issue with the speed on my hardwired connection. The desktop claimed to only connect at 100mbps. Meanwhile, if I turned on wifi I was pulling 250mbps. That can't be! Many chats to customer support and we couldn't figure it out until I switched ports on the Deco and now I'm getting the full 250 over ethernet. I don't know if it was the port having trouble or just reseating the wire that did it, but I never had that on my previous D-link router, and it had more ports too in case I needed them.

In a nutshell, I got it working, and for what it is supposed to do, I'm VERY very impressed at the performance. But the hardwire hiccup and limitation in number of ports available makes this a 4 instead of 5 star review.

title: Sounds great and super comfortable
text:
These are excellent for listening to audio in a noisy environment such as an airplane or bus. I wasn't expecting much out of the noise reduction system at this price point but it was pretty decent. Even more useful, however, is the ambient noise mode which will allow you to hear some of the background noise in case you need to be aware (someone talking to you or if you need to hear traffic on a bike, etc). I've used modes like that on modern Sony headphones, and was surprised to find it on something in this price range.

But above all else, I'm most impressed with the comfort of these. The cushion feels premium, I don't know how else to describe it, but it reminds me much more of headphones from brand names that cost several times what this does. The build quality looks much better than my cheap wireless headphones too. The only thing I wasn't impressed with is the call quality with the microphone. But that's sort of par for the course, as only the truly name brand higher end ones seem to get that right- putting a mic by your ears and still somehow picking up your voice over the background noise is a neat trick that isn't copied well by other brands.
Otherwise, for just music and audiobooks with some decent NR and comfort, this is a great value!

title: Tiny and speedy!
text:
The read speeds are pretty spot on in my testing, this approached 390+MB/s which is quite close to the 400 max written on the packaging. The write speeds were decent but I see others here have gotten faster speeds than I did on my HP Pavilion USBC port.
I love the size of this thing- it's smaller than a key fob and actually barely any bigger than a USBc to USB-A adapter would be. Speaking of which, this does not come with a A sized adapter so really this is for type-C devices ONLY.
That being said, modern laptops, macbooks, phones, etc, will be great with this!

title: It works, but odd design. Why front mic?
text:
The good news is that it DOES work, and sounds pretty decent for a cheap no-name brand. If you've installed a double din stereo before, it should be pretty familiar and straight forward.
But let's just jump right into the odd design. Why is there an "external mic" option that is RIGHT NEXT to the internal mic? Usually an external mic is supposed to be mounted somewhere closer to the driver's mouth (up by the visor or mirror, or over the dash by the steering wheel, etc). The purpose is to get better sound, and either having the internal one as a backup if you don't want to mount one, or using it to pick up ambient background noise for NR filtering. Having an external nub right next to the internal one makes ZERO sense at all! Why even have one?! If anything, making it lower than the internal one seems like it would get WORSE sound, and if the position were so good, why not make THAT where the internal one is? Not to mention it looks weird as heck.
The features seem to be functional at least, but it has a pretty noticeable lag to the user interface. If you're expecting an OEM style menu experience, you might be disappointed. This feels like an old-school web browser loading pages when you open up a feature. Compared to modern units like, for example an Atoto F7, this feels like something a generation older at least.
I want to give this at least 3 stars for functional purposes, but the truth is I know that you get a much better unit for not a lot of money more. I can't really recommend it unless it is on an extreme sale.

title: Move over, Sony!
text:
Technics is a brand well known in audio gear, originally a sort of higher-end branch of Panasonic. They are known for pro equipment like DJ turntables, however I haven't seen them in a while and surely never seen them trying to compete in the consumer wireless headphones space before!
I own various wireless headphones, from cheap brands to industry standard Sonys, and I have to say- I usually understand why Sony is considered the industry standard for prosumer headphones. Others come close, but I've never actually felt like a product in the same price range could surpass it, until now. This set of earphones actually has pretty remarkable ANR, and they are actually more comfortable than my Sony sets ever were (to my ears at least, I can't speak for others). The sound quality is no slouch either, which is, let's face it, the reason you'd be interested in this at all.
I can't say for certain that it is BETTER than the Sony in sound quality, but it is at least as good, yet more comfortable to wear and actually sports a longer running time. I have to admit, I was ready to come here and say that these are overpriced when I first saw it, but I'm pleasantly surprised at how good these are. I shouldn't have been, Technics are quality and always have been.

title: No dongle needed, pairs effortlessly!
text: I have used other wireless mice before, but something about this just feel PREMIUM. The build quality is excellent, and it feels sleek in your palm. At first I thought I wouldn't like it because it is too flat and I'm used to having something more ergonomic in my hand, but truth be told I adapted to it very quickly- by the next day it felt like I've been using this my whole life. No dongle is needed, which usually means a whole pairing session is necessary, but to my surprise as soon as I turned it on, my Windows 10 desktop perked up and said it detected a new peripheral and asked if I wanted to connect. I didn't even need to open the Bluetooth menu, it just knew and handled it automagically! Color me impressed, usually I like the dongle systems because I know I won't need to go into settings and find the Bluetooth menu. This was so simple and no dongle to lose! The entire top comes off to install the battery, which is kinda neat too. Oh, and it comes with a solid brand name battery, Energizer Max! No cheap junk "starter" disposable battery, this is the real deal out of the box! The whole thing just feels very premium compared to what I've used in the past, the price is justified in my opinion.

title: A must have for modern C-only laptops
text:
This thing is so practical to have theses days, unfortunately. My daughter has a Macbook Pro which offers only USB-C for all connections, and sometimes I really miss the older laptops that had ports built in for whatever you might need! I bought her a docking station which offers all kinds of connections, including USB and HDMI and charging all at once. The problem, however, is that it is HUGE and really not portable at all, which defeats the purpose of a hyper-portable laptop. Who cares if you have a super slim and light laptop if you need to run to your desk just to plug in something simple like a thumb drive with your homework?
That's where this comes in handy. This gives you the "big 2" missing ports, a full sized USB port and an HDMI port, all while still allowing PD charge in simultaneously. It is small enough to fit in a pocket, and easily travels around in a laptop bag along with your charger. No, you won't get a card reader or multiple USB ports or a network jack, etc... that's what the larger hub is for. But for 90% of the things you wish your USB-C only device had, this works!

title: Solid high end Android head unit, and WIRELESS ANDROID AUTO IS POSSIBLE (with beta firmware)!
text:
I bought an Atoto F7 standard last summer, and while I loved the features for the price, there were some shortcomings that made me want to try their higher end S8 editions instead. I got a chance to swap it out for an S8 Ultra, and I'm very impressed so far.
Let me tell you, I had my reservations about a phone/tablet OS running as a car stereo, but Atoto has done an incredible job making this as smooth and user friendly and FEATURE PACKED as you could ever imagine. Android Auto works of course, if you want to use your phone connected to the display. Even better, WIRELESS Android Auto works as well! They don't advertise this since it is in beta as of the time I'm writing this, but after asking Atoto customer support about it I was given access to the new test firmware and it works surprisingly well with my Galaxy S10 phone. All I have to do is press the Carlink button on the screen, my phone can stay in my pocket, and within 10-15 seconds the Android Auto connection is displayed on the car screen as if I had plugged it in. It also has an excellent Bluetooth audio input for the microphone, which is something I struggled with on the F7 I purchased previously. My car has a convertible roof that creates extra wind noise on the highway even closed, and callers can hear me just fine! But of course, the biggest pro is the ability to run Android apps directly on the head unit without needing to connect my phone.
I preloaded offline maps for most of NY/NJ in Google Maps, so wherever I end up I can navigate home (even if I don't have reception up in the mountains), all without needing my phone connected. I can also stream youtube and other apps (for the passengers, obviously!) as well as install all kinds of cool automation tools and car diagnostics thanks to a bluetooth OBDii plug I already owned.

It's not without a few caveats, however. Some things to be aware of:
1) The unit has a 5 minute delay when shutting off. This is apparently to avoid data corruption in case of a power cycle (key removed and restarted, such as for example if restarting the car). If you plug anything into the USB ports, you'll see them still on and drawing power for a solid 5 minutes after you've left the car. My wireless charger, for example, continues to be lit up and charging if I use the head unit's QuickCharge port built in. Any other peripherals such as remotes or volume knobs, etc, will remain illuminated for those few minutes. While most apps (built in music player, youtube, etc) are able to receive the signal to stop playing when the power is shut off right away, third party apps (such as some podcast or other streaming music players) actually CONTINUE TO PLAY during this 5 minute delay unless you paused/stopped them before removing the key. It's only a few minutes, and the truth is I usually play podcasts from my phone streaming, which DOES shut off right away since the Bluetooth connection is severed immediately when the key is removed. However I was surprised to find out it didn't stop everything immediately and they don't tell you this in the instructions at all.
2) If you are using Wireless Android Auto / Carplay, it creates a wifi ad-hoc connection that your phone connects to. With Android Auto, this can take a pretty big hit off your battery, but it is worth it to not pull your phone out on a small drive. However, due to the 5 minute delay I mentioned earlier, you might find that your phone is still connected to the car for a few minutes after you've left if you are in proximity of it. My car is parked just outside my office window, so I was surprised my phone wasn't connecting to my office wifi at first, then a few minutes later the car finally shut off the wifi and my phone was able to connect to the local network as expected. That delay, once again, was a little bit unexpected since at first I did not understand what was wrong.
3) Bluetooth and Android Auto volume are not consistent. For some reason, when connected with Android Auto, the volume is louder. So if you switch between them you'll have to adjust. Again, none of these are deal breakers, but things I found odd.
4) Bluetooth streaming has limited control over track. This is the one that surprised me the most since the less expensive F7 is superior in this regard. For those who know about Bluetooth profiles, there's the streaming stereo profile which gives you some ID tag metadata, and then there's AVRCP, which is the part used for remote controlling the playback. It seems that if you're playing audio from a phone, you are only getting the first profile, and not the AVRCP one. I've included a picture to illustrate the difference. With track control like you get on a dedicated bluetooth headunits, it shows the duration of the file being played, and you can even scrub through it by holding the forward and reverse buttons (like you would on an old school CD player). I listen to a lot of audiobooks so I like seeing how far into the file I am. But on the S8, it just shows the name of the file and artist/title, and then dancing lines to the audio levels. To be honest, the dancing lines are kind of distracting as well, but I can just hit home to go back to the main screen and not look at them. There's not much point in staying on that screen if I don't get track duration info anyway.

All in all, I think these setbacks are largely due to the way Android works and was designed as an OS. Atoto has had to customize a lot of things to make it work as a head unit, since things like receiving a Bluetooth stream (remember, phones and tablets running Android transmit to OTHER speaker systems, the system itself wasn't designed to be a receiver!) and going into a specialized "sleep" that shuts off all critical functions when you leave (all radios and apps running shut off) yet starts back up within 2 seconds when you turn it back on, etc (this is not regular sleep which still runs background operations- you don't want to come back to a dead battery! but powering off completely means you have to wait longer for bootup)... I think these limitations are reasonable. Atoto support has been amazing and incredibly responsive, whenever I had a question or concern, they got back to me within 24 hours which is more than I can say about radios I've owned from Pioneer and Sony in the past.
I think with time and software updates, they can eventually find clever ways around most of those caveats mentioned above, in which case I'd update this review to 5 stars. For now, I'd say this is a solid buy for what you get, I don't think a better iteration of this product with these features exists yet today. The sound quality is better than my stock Toyota ever was (even using the JBL amp it came with), and all in all I'm super happy with it so far.

title: Decent budget music player, with headphone jack!
text:
I know it sounds silly in this day and age, but sometimes we need to sing the praises of a music player that still gives you a traditional audio jack. That's where devices like these shine over using a modern cell phone- I like that this actually uses USB-C for charging so you can use a modern phone charging port but still use REAL headphones or your home stereo without an adapter.
This overall a good mp3 player. The headphone jack is a bit of a tight fit, and taking out the Micro SD can spring/project it a couple of inches if you don't take it out gently. The sound quality is good with a bit of extra reverb making a very open and uncondensed sound.
The user interface is a custom one, and you can find some that run modified versions of Android which feel a little bit more polished, but otherwise this does the job and seems pretty straight forward.

title: Sound is ok, controls are difficult
text:
This is a decent sounding pair of budget friendly wireless earbuds. They aren't the best for the price, but they aren't the worst either. They're about normal. But one of the big features of this set is supposed to be the touch controls, however my daughter found them completely unreliable. Sometimes she had to touch them 5x before they registered to pause the music, which made her more likely to pull out the player and pause it there instead.
I'd say these are 4 star headphones except for that selling point failure, if you are buying these because of the touch controls, I'd have to reduce the score to 3.

title: Cool for kids, but could be improved
text: My daughter loves these for the their fit and the concept overall. She has small ears and said this is one of the first comfortable earbuds she managed out of the box. The sound quality is ok, but she really likes the mirror functionality of the case. The problem with that feature, however, is that the display stays on for too long sometimes. It will show her the battery level when she closes it, but then you can't turn it off right away- you have to wait for the display to time out so that you can use the mirror again. Kind of silly for a case that advertises using it as a makeup mirror. But otherwise it's a pretty cool set of affordable earbuds.

title: Good for what they are, but there are better ones
text:
I love the concept of bone conducting headphones, and if you haven't tried a set before you really should! The sensation is a little unsettling at first but when you get used to it, you are rewarded with the ability to hear deep bass in your sounds without covering your ears completely the way ear buds and over-the-ear headphones require. They're not for everyone admittedly, but I love that I can feel/hear the sound and still be aware of my surroundings and able to respond if someone calls my name.
Good bone conducting headphones are easily 2x-3x the price of these, so keep that in mind. This is not going to be an alternative to a big name brand set. However, they aren't terrible either, and I kind of like them for the novelty of it at the price point.
If audio quality is your primary goal, understand that for the same money you can get a very decent pair of traditional headphones that will outshine this. But where's the fun in that?
4 stars for the novelty of it, but I give the sound quality and cost value only 3 stars.

title: Wireless, good looks, and TRUE stereo!
text:
I was skeptical because I've used multi-point bluetooth speaker arrays before that just sort of doubled-up a mono signal to different speakers. But this appears to be using the same Bluetooth 5 protocol that wireless earbuds utilize to send a proper dual-stream (left and right) channel for true stereo sound!
I did some sound tests that play only on each channel at a time, and it performed EXACTLY as intended! They look really cool and the lights add a lot of character to an evening garden party as well. The only issue however is that they don't get as loud as other speakers I've used. They are plenty loud for any sort of indoor space, but you can't really place these at either side of a backyard and expect to hear each other at maximum volume. You need bigger DJ-style speakers for that. But if you just want some background tunes to set the mood at a get-together on an average sized porch or deck, these are very nice and don't require any electrical outlet nearby.
I like them and intend to to use them more as the warm weather sets in.

title: Awesome for V-mount equipment
text: I have a rather large LED panel that I like using as a key light, however it supports only AC power or V-mount, and with this I can finally use it wirelessly on an impromptu setup without access to outlets. I've used other accessories from Neewer and on my camera equipment, from cages to adapters and mounts, and I've always been impressed with it for the asking price. I'm happy to say this is the same experience I was expecting from them. The product does what it is supposed to and at a price that seems more than reasonable. If you need an affordable V-mount battery and charger with D-tap support, it's hard to go wrong with this option. The USB is nice to have too, but I didn't really need or use that option.

title: Useful, but also MASSIVE power brick
text:
If you use a USB-C only laptop like a modern Mac, you need something like this to break out into display and USB A ports. I love how slim and functional the station itself is, it looks great on a desk next to a sleek laptop like a Macbook. However, it requires a large unsightly and clunky power brick to function. The brick is bigger than the whole docking hub!
You also can't use it without the brick, the unit needs its own power and does not get powered by the laptop. I understand the idea of a docking station is to charge the LAPTOP, but I've used smaller ones before that could either charge the laptop, or be used solo as just an adapter OTG for a USB stick to plug in. No such luck here, if the brick isn't plugged in, the hub won't turn on and none of the ports will work. For the price, I wasn't expecting that limitation.

title: Great for velcroing LARGE things!
text:
First, note that this isn't just a hoop-and-loop product. This is VELCRO, the brand name itself! So you know the expectations are set high. And they deliver.
I've owned similar products that are good for wrapping up cables I bring to jobs, but when I'm doing a live stream event and need to run hundreds of feet of CAT5 cable, you need a BIG strap to secure them up when wrapped up to go. These 30" straps are not only big, but they are stretchy as well, so I could easily make a bundle of very thick cable and hold it all together like a bow. This is exactly what I wanted and needed, thank you Velcro!

title: Good for media center or digital signage
text:
I love mini PCs. I've use a bunch of them to run kiosks at tradeshows and behind TVs to make them into smart TVs. Beelink's take on this is not only smaller and cuter than the others I've tried, it also looks the sleekest!
But here's the thing, it's actually one of the lower spec'ed mini PCs in this price range. Not by a lot, most of these are pretty slim on specs by nature honestly, but don't be fooled by the dual hdmi ports into thinking this is a graphics powerhouse. The CPU and GPU are underpowered for gaming unless you're sticking to retro emulator games (which are still fun, don't get me wrong! But even a Raspberry Pi can handle that with ease). The SSD is severely limited in space too, but that's OK. You are using this mostly as a gateway to other things usually. A streaming computer setup or HTPC most likely, so it won't need to host a lot of storage. And if you need to, thankfully there are plenty of USB ports available (take THAT, fire stick and Roku!).
However, oddly there is no USB C which I would have liked. I have a touch-screen display that can connect to a single USB-C cable for power, display port and touch input, so you need only one plug going to the mini PC to make it into a touch-screen kiosk... if that mini PC supports a proper USB-C. Sadly this does not, so I need to have three cables to make this work (USB touch input, hdmi, and another for power). Also on account of being so small and thin, it actually does not have a bay for additional HDDs/SSDs like other mini PCs do. One of my mini PCs actually had the hard-wired SSD drive go belly-up on me, so it was nice to know I could throw a cheap Kingston SSD into the bay inside and restore windows to it. But if this one ever goes, it's toast. There's no way I'd be able to replace anything inside something this tightly integrated.
For what it is, I'd say it works well. It's a marvel that a full desktop OS fits in something so tiny it can make any TV into a computer. It's fast enough for browsing and streaming. Just don't expect much more out of it, and you'll love it!

title: Great replacement for my 2017 Macbook!
text:
I got this to replace the original charger for my Macbook, and I couldn't be happier with it. It even looks kind of like an OEM Apple charger, complete with folding socket prongs! Charging speed seems pretty decent, and since it is a standard USBC PD charger, it works to quick charge other devices like Samsung phones or even standard USB devices (however if they don't support QC or PD, they will charge at the traditional slow 5v method).
It's everything I wanted and expected it to be, highly recommend.

title: Decent for TV, not great for PC
text:
I was looking for a simple keyboard/mouse combo to use with a Windows 10 htpc attached to a projector. Pairing was simple enough- unfortunately, I needed to dig up a real USB mouse in order to pair, but that's true of all Bluetooth input devices. Unlike a unit that uses a USB dongle, you need some other form of input to initiate the process first. On my fire stick, I was able to pair it using the remote pretty easily as well. Once paired, you are able to use it like a directly connected keyboard or mouse by just powering it on in the future.
The lights are cool looking (and very nice when using in the dark with a home theater setup), and the keyboard is nice and large, easy to type on. However, the mouse was little bit too jumpy for my taste. It was difficult to nail icons with accuracy due to how erratically it moved. On Windows, I'm sure I could have turned down the mouse speed to make it better, but on my fire stick there isn't that kind of control available. I definitely would not use this as a keyboard/mouse replacement for a desktop experience due to the mouse experience, however it is ok for a presentation control or htpc that doesn't require a lot of pointing or clicking.
The only thing is that I KNOW there are smaller keyboard-only devices on the market if you aren't going to need the mouse that much, and ones that can use a USB dongle to avoid the pairing process. And if you want to use this with something like a firestick or Roku, one could argue the mouse part (which takes up a significant amount of real estate on the bar) is superfluous and doesn't have such precision control even if you DO want it (using Silk browser, for example). I sort of feel like you can get better options in all those scenarios, but it is OK at what it does. So 4 stars at best.

title: Cool idea, but could use improvement
text:
This is a really solid idea for bloggers and others who want to mount camera and other recording equipment to their desk. I occasionally do video blog demonstrations and in my home office, that means setting up at least one light stand, a tripod with my camera, and a mic stand. Lots of stands on the floor taking up space.
With this, I can clamp the camera to my desk and use the crane arm to adjust- sounds great right?
Well- I'll be honest, this isn't designed to carry something like a DSLR or other ILC camera. Sure, I can get it to stay in place with some very delicate movements, but the slightest vibration and the camera wobbles which will show up in your video. I also am constantly afraid the balance will shift, I think this is better suited for a phone or gopro style camera.
In fact, I'm fairly certain this crane arm was NOT designed for this use at all. Something about it seemed familiar, and then I recognized it- it is the same desk clamp that came with one of my condenser mics, and I found it even has the 5/8" standard mic thread on the end! Basically, someone took a mass-produced microphone desk clamp and threw in some extra bits to adapt a tripod screw (1/4 20 thread) or phone holder mount to a microphone standard sized 5/8 end. That's it! This kit doesn't even come with instructions so you have to figure it out, but I could honestly have put this together with equipment I already owned if I knew that's all it was. I was hoping it would be a heavier duty product to hold my larger camera.

Oh well. It is still useful because I can mount a light to the 1/4" thread and use my other desk clamp to the hold the mic, thus leaving only my camera on the floor tripod. That's handy, but I can't give this more than 3 stars. I wish I could give 2.5, it's useful enough that it's not worth only 2 but 3 is being generous. Seems like a good idea that was thrown together without enough thought in the details.

title: Very similar to my favorite Logitech
text:
I've owned many different models of computer mouse over the years, and I have to admit I rather like this one. Your hand rests easy on it thanks to the subtle ergonomic curve, and it does exactly what you expect it to do and works as it should- no frills like extra mappable buttons that you forget exist and press accidentally (I'm looking at YOU, recently retired mouse that accidentally closed the page I was working on more than once and lost my work!). I like this exactly because it is a basic and professional feeling mouse without the bells and whistles that require a learning curve.

The ergonomic shape is much easier to palm and use comfortably than a flattened mouse, however it is clearly designed to be used in your right hand, so if you're a lefty-mouser, this might not be the right choice. It also reminds me heavily of my old favorite Logitech wireless mouse... I threw it away years ago because a corroded battery ruined the contacts inside, but it looked and felt almost exactly like this and was considered one of the best wireless mice for professional use at the time. Good job Amazon for making this one so affordable and keeping all the good stuff.

title: A solid option from a reputable brand
text:
[[VIDEOID:b45226034e07b4e60a830fa1a8bc9e15]] A few years ago, the only reliable option for this was an adapter from a brand called Magewell. It was expensive and overheated if you streamed for too long with it. Now, streaming is much more of a thing and the need for adapters like this have skyrocketed. There are dozens of cheap ones out there but most of them weren't great quality. This version is not only from a brand gamers know, but it actually supports 4k and it's REAL 2160p resolved resolution (not just downsampled to 1080 like cheap adapters).
No drivers or settings required, desktop OS sees it as a 4k webcam, really very much plug and play performance. I'm quite pleased with it and would totally recommend it. Glad there are better options these days than yesteryear.

title: Excellent value for headsets
text: Ok, first things first: Don't expect these to be great audiophile-sounding headphones. They are not. Can you listen to music with them? Sure. But at less than 7 bucks per set, set your expectations realistically. Then be pleasantly surprised when they are surprisingly decent for private listening on a budget. No, you won't get full symphony dynamic range response- Where they shine is in quantity and availability. If you've got a room of people having zoom meetings with clients or kids at home in online classrooms, these are invaluable. They have integrated microphones for 2-way communication, and GREAT for listening to movies / shows on a trip. We have a large family and on a recent plane ride, we were able to take these along for in-flight entertainment. Plenty for everyone plus some extras if anything breaks or gets lost. They are kind of large but at least the ear parts pivot 90 degrees flat so that they fit in a backpack with other things. The cords are also flat which is great for wrapping and avoiding tangles if they get thrown into a box together. The colors are fun, each of my kids could pick a different color to their liking. I highly recommend these for classrooms or large families on a budget.

title: Great to not lose stuff in your home!
text:
There are a lot of people in my house. Things like keys and remotes are ALWAYS getting lost, so a unit like this is very welcome!
We used to have a similar device over a decade ago that was much bulkier, mostly looked like an additional key fob on my keychain only bigger, and would chew through batteries quickly. I think we used it for only a month before just removing it from our car keys.
I like how much sleeker and slim looking this device is, a much more modern take on the item locator concept. The tags are actually so thin, it comes with adhesive hook-and-loop pads to attach to other non-keyring things as well, like the back of a remote control. The range is OK- unlike other products (such as Tile), the range seems to be only within a room or two away. From the front door, if my keys are in my bedroom, it would not ring. However as I passed from room to room, eventually when I get near the room they are in, it starts ringing. The flashlight feature is cute but not really useful.
Something to note: The fobs use watch batteries which are included, but the locator requires AAA cells, which are NOT. I actually didn't have any on hand and needed to go out and get some more to try this.

Otherwise, these are cheaper than a set of Tile or similar product locator fobs. And it doesn't require an app on your phone. I like it.

title: Great way to make power accessible.
text:
This is an excellent way to bring some power to a more accessible location. In my case, I have an electric piano that my kids use with an app to learn how to play, and this adapter clamps on to the piano's stand so I can plug the piano directly in, and have one of the included USB ports going to the tablet for the app, and still have another USB available for anyone who wants to plug in a phone or maybe a speaker to amp up the piano in the AC plug.
I can see this being great to clamp onto a desk or shelf to give easy access to outlet and USB power that might otherwise be obstructed by furniture or just hard to reach. I also love that the plug is flat so that it can easily hide behind other furniture if the outlet happens to be in a difficult location. So far so good, I highly recommend it!

title: This is so cool!
text:
What a cool camera! I have to admit I wasn't planning on enjoying this as much as I do. I have used cameras that "follow" your face before, but they were just software zooming on super wide angles (like the Facebook Portal, for example). But not this- this is actually a bonified motorized head that tracks and follows your face like a robot! The hand gestures are pretty cool too, you can easily zoom in and out, like being the director, actor AND camera operator of your own little set!
My wife even got freaked out because I asked her to come in and try it, then left the room and it rotated to follow her out the door! The quality of the lens and sensor are quite good as well. Not as good as my Sony Alpha camera in a HDMI capture card, but this is a fraction of the cost- more closely resembles a midrange phone camera or gopro in quality. But the big perk is that motorized AI head to follow your movements. This is excellent for giving a class or demonstration that would benefit from a camera operator to follow your movement. For the price, I think this is great!

title: Fun in and out of the water!
text:
[[VIDEOID:a9f2bbc3e1727a3fa67b3772039f007b]] This is a really fun camera that is basically an upgraded version of the classic waterproof point-and-shoot. If you've ever owned these cheap waterproof cameras before, you know they aren't the most user friendly buttons or the highest quality shooter- but they work and they take a beating and are fun to use in places you wouldn't use a bigger or more expensive camera.
This actually has some pretty nice upgrades over the others we've tried. For starters, DUAL SCREENS! That's awesome because now you can take selfies by using the screen button to swap to the front display. Unlike a phone that uses a subpar lens in front, the nice thing about this is that you get the same quality photo regardless of which screen you use, the only difference is that you can see it in the front when selfie is activated.
The photo quality is improved as well- Don't expect iPhone 13 or Google Pixel level HDR, and obviously not DSLR quality, but its as good as a basic phone if not better, definitely good enough to get the job done and take a decent picture. Close to GoPro quality in good lighting I'd say.
The video format is now offered in 4k 30p, which is a huge upgrade to the weak frame rame and size our old version of this offered (I think it maxed out at 720 and a very choppy 10fps). Great for kids or adults who want a throwaround camera they don't have to worry about compared to a phone or much more expensive camera. I'm including a clip and a photo taken in a local hotel pool we tried it in. A lot fun.

Note: The zoom is digital so you are better off just taking a full sized photo and then cropping it in post, no point in "zooming in".

title: Good on the cheap and kid friendly
text:
The good:
It's got an excellent case that will protect it through most of the abuse a kid will inflict on tech.
It's got Android 11, which is still pretty relevant and supported compared to other cheap Android devices that are a couple of versions behind.
Display is decent
Comes with kid friendly suite of games apps and tools with parental control.

The not as good:
It isn't going to win any speed tests. The CPU/gpu is ok for a small screen and for kids games, but you can get better hardware like an Amazon Fire for the money. Granted, it won't come with a cool kid friendly case at this price, but the case has caveats too: the buttons are a little hard for little fingers to reach in the cutouts. They will protect the device, so that's a decent tradeoff I guess. The display is ok, again you can get much better ones out there, but it works. The major thing I'm concerned about is the meager 2GB of ram. That's just not a lot for Android 11. You should be ok if you only run a single task at a time. It's a good value, just keep your expectations realistic.

title: Nice HTPC option, but listing is misleading
text:
First of all, don't trust the specs listed here. This is a great mini-PC, but the listing is confusing. I wouldn't say it's false as much as just sloppy. For starters, it says you get an 8 core i3. That's not true (and I'm not sure is even a thing to be honest). Don't expect desktop power and performance. In fact, this is an I3 8109U, which is a laptop-level CPU that has only 2 cores for efficiency. I think they meant to say GENERATION not core, since it is an 8th gen of the i3. But usually a desktop level i3 has 4 cores, and with hyperthreading you get 8 threads at a time. This has only 2, which gives you 4 with ht.
Either way, a far cry from the 8 in the title. Then there's the image comparing HDDs that tell you this has a 500gb Kingston SSD inside. That may be an option, but mine is configured 256. The picture on the listing still shows 500, which again... misleading.
Otherwise, I really do like this box. Confusing listing shouldn't take away from the experience if you know what you're getting. And you're getting an excellent device for a HTPC or digital signage / arcade box / etc. I'm actually a fan of Beelink's other products, having had one of their old Android TV boxes back in the day. This is great because it's smaller than even most mini-PCs that I've used, yet sports a mainstream Intel CPU with Windows 10, and a real kicker is that this one supports USBC. For some reason a lot of these mini PCs on the market have only traditional USB ports. A modern C port makes a lot of connections really simple and easy, using one port instead of many for the same things, and I'm so glad this has one.
All in all, I like it and would recommend it. It's great for light gaming (retro console / emulator), streaming media, and excellent as a desktop workstation for browsing / office documents. Not a powerhouse 8+ core machine that you might want for hardcore gaming or compiling code, video editing, etc. But good for most intermediate and under computing tasks. And did I mention it looks super cute?

title: Industrial grade PC!
text:
This is a very cool piece of computing hardware for specific uses. The fanless design means unlike other mini PCs that I've tried, this is actually silent! I'm surprised because the i5 CPU should generate more heat than the miserly Celeron that other mini PCs use, but the fins seems to dissipate heat rather well so far.
The 6 ethernet ports means this can make a pretty cool Windows-powered server for internet or file serving, and the fanless design means it can sit in a home users' closet and not make any audible noise either! While the CPU is pretty good, the GPU is pretty...not. If you look at the attached user benchmark, you'll see the CPU benched at about 74th percentile, but the GPU at a disappointing 4th percentile.
That means you won't really use this for things like games, not that anyone was expecting to. However, it does sort of limit this use for something like a media server using a platform such as Plex, as it would rely on the GPU for real-time media encoding.
For just playing back HD video it should be sufficient, and for other kinds of custom home server use and/or industrial use, this is a pretty interesting and useful product!

title: Amazfit is still the best value!
text:
I've owned and had the opportunity to try out many different brand of fitness tracker watch, from Fossil/Wear OS, to Fitbit, Apple, and many of the cheapo brands too. I've said this before, but generally you get what you pay for, aside from the Amazfit brand watches. These and the Xiaomi Mi band series always impressed me, punching way above their paygrade. This latest edition just continues that legacy.
To be clear- there are some pretty neat features and apps that Wear OS / Apple OS will offer that this won't, but for the money this is the best value and user experience.
For starters, everything about the user experience here feels premium for the money. The battery life on this is killer. I charge it about once a month, maybe 2x a month. Granted I turn off features like lift-to-wake, but my experience with Apple and Wear OS devices needed charging daily in comparison.
The display is beautiful- a very vivid OLED, with very responsive touch screen. The animations are fluid and feel premium, and the display is large enough to easily read notifications and even responses from Alexa! That being said, this model lacks the speaker that the Pro model does, so while I can ask Alexa questions, I have to read her answers. I also can't answer calls since there is no speakerphone, however I can silence the ringer if I don't want to take it.
The sensors are improved over the series 2, however the functionality is mostly the same. In fact, if you have a GTR or GTS2 already, one might argue that this is a lateral move and not necessarily an upgrade, aside from one major new feature: With the new Zepp OS, Amazfit is going to allow mini-apps that can be installed on the watch. THIS is the big thing that is missing compared to other name brand smartwatch devices. So far there are only a handful of mini apps in their "store" and arguably not anything I particularly was looking for, but there is talk of an API being released for third party developers. Who knows, maybe we'll even get some basic games or other nifty features coming soon. I still have my GTS2 which I love as well as this, but I'm holding on to this for the potential app development in the future. Can't wait to see what Amazfit does next!

title: Good concept, but bizarre bugs
text:
I've tried a similar box to this one, I'm familiar with the concept and I really REALLY wanted to like it. But sadly, it needs some more quality control.
I've always loved the idea of a Android powered head unit, I've seen aftermarket ones sold for popular car models, and I was hoping this would give me that functionality without having to replace my radio. But sadly, I can't use this.
For starters, it takes a long time to boot. That means you are first going to be greeted with your car's normal radio display, connected to my phone over bluetooth, and then once I've already pulled out of my driveway and started down the road, THEN it finally shows up on my display.
That is, if it displays at all. It seems to do this thing in which is boots up, checks for display info, then reboots in the proper resolution. The instructions even imply it does this. The problem is, most of the time my carplay radio will freeze up when it does this. Not only will it get stuck and not display anything, but my radio locks up and MY TIME RESETS. It's the strangest thing. After looking at reviews here, it seems at least one other reviewer said it make his car radio go crazy, so I don't really understand what this thing is doing that might cause that, but at least it isn't just me!
And even when it DOES work, it has a similar problem to other Android-powered adapters like this: it is a cold boot every time, with no idea what the time/date is. This is a major issue because if I don't supply an internet connection, the mini computer in this reverts to the wrong date/time on the display which is SUPER annoying. Ideally, they should design this to have a small battery to "sleep" like a phone, so it can retain time/date function and wake up faster than a complete boot. The way this is designed right now is really a subpar experience, assuming you can get it to boot up at all on your system.

title: Excellent and professional quality!
text:
I've been using prosumer video gear for decades, everything from the name brands like SmallHD to the cheapo no-name brands, and I have to admit: this impressed me. In my opinion, it is worth every penny of the asking price. It's a gorgeous display that also supports touch-screen controls with all the bells and whistles you could ask for... real time color info, graphs and LUTs? You got it! HDMI and/or SDI? Of course! These are features usually only found on highest end offerings. It even supports dual Sony NP style battery slots for hot swapping when needing to change.
Speaking of which, it includes a NP F750 style battery for that as well as a charger, and a barn-door style sun shade and carrying case. Really a very solid product that justifies the asking price.

title: Nice and FAST if you have UHS-II compatible gear!
text:
This is a great card if you have a reader and/or camera compatible with the newer UHS-II format. I shoot a lot of 4k video on Sony cameras, so I very much appreciate being able to copy lots of high bitrate footage after a shoot VERY quickly, which is exactly what this does!
You can always spot the UHS-II cards by their extra pins on the back. With a reader that can utilize them, I found this card performed pretty excellent in my benchmarks! 257MB/s read and a whopping 248MB/s write! That's incredible speed for write, I wasn't expecting it. On my other cards, UHS-II boosted the read times to similar proportions but write was similar to regular U3 class SDXC cards. That this Ritz card can produce similar write times as the boosted read is pretty incredible! This might be my new favorite media.

title: UPDATE: Huge design flaw, device is now a brick and zero options
text:
UPDATE 1/2/22:
I CANNOT RECOMMEND THIS PLAYER. My kid changed the password on the lock screen and then immediately forgot what it is, locking everyone out of the player. No big deal, right? Just hard reset the whole device and start over... except that there is NO WAY TO PERFORM A HARD RESET. You must be logged in and have access to the settings screen to reach the reset settings, if you are locked out you have exactly ZERO options.
I reached out to support, and they offered to send me files to flash and reset the device, but then realized there is no way to get into the bootloader for me. Rather than offer a replacement, they offered 40% off purchasing another. No thank you, that's a terrible design flaw. Avoid this product.

Original review:
This is a cute little media player that is clearly powered by Android under the hood. It is NOT a phone or tablet, it does NOT have the Play store... it is very much designed to be strictly a media player. However unlike other cheap mp3 devices which struggle to make their own UI, these guys took the short cut and decided not to re-invent the wheel, rather opting to use the open-source and readily available Android operating system to handle the interface. And let me tell you, that makes it GREAT!
No more struggling to find an archaic avi codec to make videos work like other players, no more learning how to navigate a backwards menu system, or finding out that certain bluetooth devices or wifi networks are incompatible... no, this has all the support that the Android platform does, and it does it smoothly and quite well! It even has one of my favorite mp3 playing apps, AIMP preinstalled! Nice!
If you wanted to use this for more than just the included functionality, you CAN side-load Android APK files to install new applications. I did that to put a few cute games on it, but major apps that are closely tied to Google services such as Youtube and Gmail will not work. But that shouldn't be expected, this is a media player after all that happens to run a popular OS under the hood. I really like it, and most importantly, so do my kids who I got it for!

title: Full keyboard and mouse, works well
text:
This is a great wireless mouse and keyboard set that frees you from cables. I just got a convertible standing desk, and knowing that I'm now able to easily convert without possible cable snag is exactly what I needed. The keyboard is actually really nice, it has a very comfortable click and is full sized with number pad, and even a dedicated calc button (something I was wary to give up on my full wired keyboard!).
The mouse is ok, but its going to take some getting used to compared to my old gaming-style mouse. There's a button to cycle through three options in dpi for speed selection, and the scroll wheel and clicking buttons work well enough, but I think I was spoiled by a very high end mouse before and this is just something I need to get used to. The movements feel a bit more muted than my old one. In no way is it BAD, believe me I tried a wireless mouse before this one that was just awful and would frequently disconnect and lag. This is consistent and works well enough for most things, I think the average user would be very happy with it.
The keyboard uses 2 AAA batteries and the mouse uses a single AA, both of which come included with the set (nice!). I like this pair and I'm happy with it so far!

title: Fun prints for kids!
text:
Let's get something straight- this is NOT a brand name instant like Polaroid or Fuji/Instax. Don't expect that level of quality in image or print.
But keep in mind that this is also a fraction of the cost and uses much cheaper standard thermal paper. Rather than have a printer that uses expensive instant film or toner/ink, this just uses the same technology that point-of-sale and store receipt paper uses (and old school fax machines, for those of us old enough to remember them!). That's great because the thermal paper is super cheap, you can buy any brand that fits physically in the machine- although this camera comes with plenty of rolls to get you started (which is more than some of the big brand insta-cams offer! My polaroid came with something like 5 sample photo prints, then I needed to spend more on a pack).
My kids have a blast snapping photos and printing them to hang on the fridge or their walls. Really cute! It supports printing from a phone or tablet via an app you can install if you'd rather use your phone's superior camera, but I didn't try that function. My kids were more interested in taking photos themselves and printing them.
One thing that is a little bit difficult, however, is navigating without the use of a display. There are some cool and fun options to tinker with, but it is very difficult to tell what it happening before it prints since there is no display to give you any feedback. To be fair, some of the other instant cameras also lack a display, but I wish the UI were a little bit more intuitive to make up for it.
Either way, it is still a very fun little camera for kids.

title: Great for music AND calls!
text:
I have been on the search for wireless earbuds that sound ok and can handle calls, yet don't cost as much as Apple's... and I think this is IT! I had tried cheap brands, and wasn't surprised that the sound wasn't good. I tried expensive brands (even those costing almost the same as airpods) and while they had some excellent sound quality and noise cancellation, the callers couldn't hear me! I sounded under water and very compressed.
I kept having to resort to an old-school wired headset for calls, or bigger over-the-ear headphones with a good mic. But this set is that perfect blend! Decent sound quality, pretty intuitive to use, and the mic actually works for calls! And on top of all that, they are pretty affordable and from a name brand I recognize!
My daughter isn't into the look of the hoop-over-ear design, but honestly they are comfortable to wear and work exactly as expected so I can't help recommending these and singing their praises. Well done Skullcandy!

title: Great hardware, could use some minor improvements
text:
This is a very cool digital art tool. It's a combination of wacom-style drawing surface and external monitor, so you can draw directly on the screen like paper instead of looking at the computer screen while you sketch.
Ideally, you can use a USB-C port on a device that supports it so that you can combine displayport and USB input device into one cable. However, it seems like you'd need an additional USB for power in many cases, and in my case I needed to use the three-wire solution: One HDMI out from the computer, one USB for the pen input signal, and the 3rd USB for power. Kind of a rats nest of wire and not very portable. It really makes me wish I had bought a Surface or Lenovo Yoga with the active Wacom pen built in so that I get this functionality in a much cleaner setup, but at least with this it is a pretty cool addition to my desktop without buying a separate computer. And now I can have something else on my PC screen while this operates as a drawing canvas screen #2. Cool for a desktop, not so much for a laptop, since there are 3 wires to connect at a minimum.
I've noticed that the driver is a little bit difficult to use sometimes- I've had to set up the drawing area in settings only to have it default when I reboot to the original drawing area and need to be set again. I'm still getting used to it. But when it works, it IS really cool. You need to find software that can support it properly, like Krita for example, if you want to get the full effect out of the pressure sensitive drawing.
