That being said, it feels kind of expensive and I wish it were a more straight forward and seamless experience for the money, but I don't think there's really a better way to do this with an existing PC.
If you want to add drawing capability to an existing computer instead of buying a Surface/Yoga/iPad Pro/etc, this is the way.

title: Microscope is ok, Telescope less
text:
This is a great toy for a kid who's interested in science! It's essentially a kid's digital camera that can record stills and FHD video onto a memory card, however you can pick either a macro lens (microscope) or telephoto (telescope) with the press of a button. I thought this would be more interesting than the stand-alone microscope option, however now that I've tried it, I think the microscope is a better product. The telescope isn't all that useful- for starters, at the sort of telephoto distance you'd use here, it's nearly impossible to hold the thing still enough to avoid a blurry photo or shaky video. Also, the white balance is ridiculous and seems to lock onto the K-value of sunlight only, making everything just look bad.
The macro Microscope, on the other hand, is really nice. The end of the lens barrel lights up with LEDs to illuminate your subject, and that ensures the color white is really white as well. Also at short distance, it is easier to hold it still and you can get some really interesting pictures and videos of things so magnified as to make it seem like something else entirely.
Switching between the modes isn't all that intuitive, my kids seem to have trouble swapping them every time. The unit also doesn't have the highest build quality, feels like a cheap plastic kids camera. For the price, I was hoping for something a little bit better.
That being said, my daughter loves the microscope part and wants to take it to school to show her teacher. She has thanked me multiple times for it. I can't complain too much, she has fun with it and it does work. I just know it COULD have been better.

title: Decent mini PC, but oddly hidden/gimped USBC. (and clone of ACEPC GK2)
text:
First the good- this is a decent mini computer that is useful for MANY things! It is not going to replace a gaming desktop for high end applications, but it is plenty powerful for running browsers or work applications on two displays simultaneously (even has 2x HDMI ports which claim to support up to 4k each!). It's also an excellent option for a streaming HTPC or digital signage, and can be mounted to the rear of a monitor or TV with a standard VESA mount. With this, you can basically make any screen into an AIO computer!
It is plenty fast to respond thanks to the SSD, and has enough RAM and CPU power to multitask through everyday tasks pretty effortlessly.
Here's the downsides though:
1) No USB-C port. Or at least, not a NORMAL one. Sure, you've got plenty of USB ports (some fast 3.0 as well as some regular 2.0), but the omission of such a useful all-in-one C connection in a modern tech device is just odd. For example, I have a touch screen monitor and tablet that can connect via a single USB-C connection - otherwise it requires three separate plugs for power, hdmi and USB input. On my laptop, I can use the USB-C port and it does everything with a single cable. I thought this would be a PERFECT use for such a mini PC, but I'm stuck doing it the messy 3-cable way since there is not a USB-C port available. Makes it much more of a hassle.
Meanwhile, underneath the spare HDD bay, there IS a hidden USB-C port inside! However it is not a fully functional one. Not only is it in a bizarre difficult-to-reach location, I tried connecting some USB-C devices to it and while the system indicated something was connected, it could not operate it. I'm guessing this is nothing more than a USB-A connection in a USB-C housing, or perhaps not a full USB3.1 standard, and this is why it is hidden. Or, perhaps saved for the manufacturer for updates, possibly why it is not accessible to the outside.
So, essentually, no USB-C on a PC in 2021.
2) This seems identical to another Mini-PC I owned once, the ACEPC GK2. Same specs, same housing, even same weird USB-C inside the spare hdd bay. This isn't necessarily a con since I loved that mini-PC, however it died an untimely death when the SSD kicked the bucket without warning a few months into owning it. I found a support forum of other users claiming the same problem, and their official support's answer was to buy a new 2.5" SSD to place in the bay, which we had to buy ourselves. Very upset about that, and the computer is no longer sold here, so I can't even complain to anyone about it. So far so good on this unit, but I'm wary that this appears to be the same computer rebranded under a different name. I hope this won't suffer the same face in a few months. I'll keep an eye on it and report back if there are any issues.

title: Voice calling is bordering on unsuable
text:
I'm very conflicted writing this review. As music listening and noise cancellation devices, they are wonderful! You can wear this in a noisy environment and get lost in your own tunes or just hear yourself think. Also, it has a similar functional design as Air Pods that allows air in to make it comfortable to wear without the vacuum "under water" seal effect that other ear buds have. So out of the box, color me impressed- comfortable and sounds great, what could be better, right?
Well, the reason I wanted to try Jabra over other brands is their commitment to call quality. Back in the early days of Bluetooth, Jabra was one of the kings if you wanted to ensure a clear 2-way conversation on a call. A lot of portable audio devices these days overlook mic quality and put all their effort into music / playback, with Apple, Sony, and some other big brands being the exception.
Sadly, these Jabras don't seem to deliver in that regard. People we call constantly complain they can't hear us, that we sound far away, under water or over-compressed / missing parts of our voice. In quiet environments it seems to work ok, but maybe the noise cancellation bit is working overtime? I don't know. All I know is I'm so disappointed with the call quality, I can't rely on these if I want the other party to hear me clearly. Yes, the ANC is awesome. Yes, the music sounds good. Yes they are comfortable. But if you need to switch to another headset to make a phone call, these are silly. I really wish it wasn't so.

title: A huge step up from the original Portal!
text:
We've been using an older first generation Portal and like it very much. I was not expecting to be so impressed with this one, but wow have they managed to improve almost everything about the original! It still has the very cool zoom-and-pan style camera feature that follows the subject, as well as all the fun filters and of course my kids' favorite, story time... but the polish and style of this unit is really premium. The speaker is fantastic and LOUD if you want it to be. The clarity and bass rivals my bookshelf speakers so well, sometimes the kids play music off it and I could have sworn they were using the speakers in the living room. But the biggest improvement over the previous generation is the ability to run off battery power and move around. The "portable portal" honestly makes so much sense, I wonder why the original stationary style ones came out first!
Make no mistake, it is NOT a tablet, it is not thin and won't fit in an attaché case nicely. It is wedge-shaped making it stand easily at an ideal angle, and even has a cut-out handle to pick it up and carry it to a better location for video chat. This is great for bringing it to wherever my kids happen to be congregating currently, and it can be put back up on the shelf when done to charge. Like the original Portals, it has Alexa built in and can act as an Echo for most things, however it is very tied into Facebook's ecosystem. That means that although it seems to run something akin to Android behind the scenes, this is NOT going to offer a standard App store, and even things like Youtube are not available for it (licensing issues with Google I'd suppose). However there is a browser, and you can navigate to YouTube and play it from the website just fine, although a proper app would be much easier to navigate. It does have Plex support, which I found interesting since I have a Plex server. I never thought I'd find Plex available where Youtube is not! Meanwhile, between Youtube in the browser, Amazon Music through Alexa and content on Plex, there are plenty of ways to make it a music streamer on that glorious better-than-it-should-sound speaker. And the camera works just as well if not better than the OG Portal!
Calls over FB Messenger or Whatsapp work well, and of course the camera / mic not only have a switch to toggle, but the camera has a physical cover that can slide over the lens in case you don't trust Facebook not to snoop. But that's another story.
All things considered, this is a solid product.

title: Great upgrade for old car, but caveats
text:
[[VIDEOID:39f57150f79275f153991c4d149bb17]] Ok, first the good things:
-This supports Android Auto and Apple Carplay (we only tested Android)
-It takes a measly single-DIN slot and gives you a fold out touch screen display to make things like the backup camera, phone UI, etc, possible which normally would not fit in a single DIN space.
-I can't stress this enough, but IT HAS A VOLUME KNOB. I can't even tell you how hard it is to find a modern radio with Android Auto / Car Play support that doesn't rely on touch screen buttons!

That being said, it has some issues. As you can see in the video attached, sometimes it takes more than one touch to navigate the touch screen options. A more annoying issue, however, is the AM radio. You can't pick a station that ends in a zero! So stations like 550 which we wanted to listen to, simply CAN'T be tuned in! Even if you try to manually type it in, for some reason the dial pad starts reducing available numbers as you pick, as if they don't WANT you to be able to pick a zero as the last digit. It's very strange!

I'd say for the user experience it should be 3 stars, but I'm adding a 4th because it's kind of rare to find a radio like this that fits in the space it does and offers these features. This Ford truck had a busted radio from the 90s, and this is a VERY welcome facelift and upgrade. I really like it and think for the price you're getting a lot of functionality. Of course you can't expect the polish or audiophile sound quality of a Pioneer or Alpine head unit, or even the mid-range quality of something like an Atoto, so for the price considering how unique of a product this is, plus the included camera, etc, I'd say it's a good value for a truck like this. I just wish the AM radio weren't so weird!

title: Solid and cost-effective, great as digital sign too!
text:
Let me start off by saying I've owned Kindles and other e-readers so I can say I'm already somewhat familiar with the concept. I really like what I'm seeing here for the price of this product! This is a small / affordable e-ink device that makes it ideal for all kinds of things.
Personally, I'm a big fan of Overdrive to take books out of our local libraries for free on readers. My biggest complaint on Kindle readers is that this was always a hassle - I needed to do it ON A DIFFERENT DEVICE. A laptop or phone with a browser was necessary because you could not access Overdrive to explore content directly. On the Kobo, like other non-Amazon devices, you are free to browse directly on the reader, find a title you like and click borrow, all for FREE and 100% legal! This is a huge selling point to me. My kids can browse the YA and children's' section and find all kinds of content right on the device using an account they made with their local library card.
The screen is great for little hands as well as big hands, it even looks great displaying some graphic novel pages (albeit in greyscale obviously). I found that I had zero problems connecting to my Wifi, and downloading books is fast and easy. Battery life is excellent as well! The only caveat is that when you DO need to charge it, it's the slightly-older micro-USB charging plug. I wish it would have been a USB-C as most of our micro USB cables are being replaced with the new standard, and in 2021 its a little weird to still have a new product use an old standard... but this is a minor issue at best.

Some really cool mentions:
1) There IS an experimental web browser function. It's very limited, mostly due to the limitations of using E-ink instead of a display that can be updated faster like LCD/OLED, but super cool for browsing websites for text articles!
2) You can manually load a document to use as a screensaver!! This was a very cool find for me. There's a folder on the device when you plug it into your computer called .screensaver , and if you place a document in there (jpg, pdf, whatever) it will display it when the device is powered off / sleep. I actually put our weekend calendar information on there so we can refer to times / reminders, and stuck some magnetic strips to the back of the reader. Now it sits on our fridge when no one is reading, displaying our calendar and saving us at least one sheet of paper to print per month! Then whenever someone wants to read, my kids (or me!) can take it off the fridge, read a few pages, then put it back there for the next person. Because the Nia is a small and light tablet, it stays on really easily! My old Kindle was too large and fragile for that.

Way to go, Kobo!

title: Pretty good and portable
text:
I wanted to use this to project sound at a small corporate gathering. Too small to use a full blown PA system, too big to use a standard bluetooth speaker. This is a really good in-between size! I was able to use the bluetooth mode to project music, as well as use a wireless mic system to project voice (using the hardwired receiver inputs on the back). The only thing is that the mic port on the back of this has some weird echo effect that I did not like. Thankfully the guitar port was very clean, so I switched the mic to that one.
It gets loud enough to get the job done, although I feel like I've gotten louder responses from other speakers this size before. It is still good enough for my intended purpose so I won't deduct any stars for that. The lights can be turned off if you don't like them, but they are pretty cool too. The only other caveat is that the buttons aren't easy to see. They are embossed rubber-on-rubber, and don't light up. So if you are in a dark room and trying to figure out which one is volume, it is more difficult than it should be to figure it out. I wish they had made those buttons more visible, either using a white text label or light up the buttons or something other than black-on-black buttons. But other than that, it's a great speaker, looks good and sounds pretty decent.
At 150 I'd argue there might be better options, but as of the time of this writing, the listing price is 99 dollars, which I think is worth it for a speaker with these features.

title: Works if you need, but jumpy
text:
I wanted to like this mouse. There are so many things I like about it better than my other wireless mouse- the design is more ergonomic and comfortable to hold, the buttons are easy to reach (if you're a righty at least!), and I like that it doesn't have a glowing red dot on the bottom, I'm assuming it uses IR or something invisible to humans. Although, to be fair, it does make it hard to determine if the thing is powered on or not!
At first I loved it, the scroll wheel is good, even the modes to control the dpi were a pleasure to cycle through. But then it got... jumpy. Like, sometimes I would move the mouse and it would feel like it paused and had to catch up all of the sudden. Movements didn't seem to mimic mine in real time. I do a lot of video editing and have to shuffle clips around with precise movements, I found this inconsistent behavior really unsettling to work with and needed to go back to me old boring flat mouse. If you don't have a mouse or just want to make browsing easier on a chromebook or something like that, it's good in a pinch, especially for the price. But sadly it is not reliable enough for moderate to heavy users in my opinion.

title: Excellent normal earphones! No frills, as there shouldn't be!
text: This is a great value for 2 "classic" wired earphones. They come with multiple tips so you can install ones that will fit your ears (we have small ear canals in my family), and they do a decent job blocking outside noise when properly fitted. They get plenty loud (like, loud enough that the warning on my phone makes sense to give), and the sound quality is fine. It's not audiophile quality, but I'm not expecting them to be. I'm expecting them to be functional at this price, and they definitely are that! I'm giving one to my daughter to use with her music player on the bus ride, and the other I'm using as a backup in my camera case for video gigs (I had my over-the-ear studio monitors die on a job once, so having a no-frills backup pair is welcome) and maybe to throw in a backpack when I don't want to charge my wireless earphones for my phone. Thank goodness some phones still have a standard 3.5mm jack! So glad they are still selling classic earbuds, and these are a great value at a great price!

title: It works, but I wish I had picked a different one
text:
I wanted to upgrade my 04 Solara stock radio to one with bluetooth and a backup camera, but the car has a JBL factory amp and I wanted to keep this install as simple as possible (especially including steering wheel controls). Crutchfield recommended this model to make that happen, but it was out of stock so I ordered it here instead.
Well, for starters it only supports control over L+R, fading from front front to rear isn't an option as it just sends both front and back speakers the same signal. That's fine for a limitation, I did read that from the description here so I wasn't surprised, but it was just the first sign of a product that seems half baked. Next up, the steering wheel controls DID NOT WORK. I have an Atoto head unit, and none of the dip switch SWC settings worked. You have to set the buttons on the Atoto, but no matter what switch settings I used, I only got SOME of the buttons working and not others. Like, sometimes only vol + but not vol -, or a different setting gave me just mode and track down, but never all of them at once. I reached out to customer support and it took several tries to get a response, after which they gave me a different set of switch settings to try (not one from the manual) which still didn't work.
In the end, I cut the SWC wires from the harness and fed them directly to SW1 and SW2 on the Atoto harness directly, and got them ALL to show up and set correctly! So basically, buying the model with SWC retention was a waste of extra money as it didn't even work.
Then I had some ground loop noise I was trying to troubleshoot. To be fair, it could have been the radio, so I tried wiring it directly to speakers to see if the output from the radio had it... it did not. Another weird issue is that I noticed a faint hiss coming from the speakers EVEN WHEN THE RADIO WAS POWERED OFF. As in, I'm not playing anything and want the car to be dead silent, but the adapter still turned on the amp even if the head unit is off! It was more pronounced when I had ground loop noise, but now that I've mostly fixed that, there is still an obvious hum like there is power going to the amp and it is waiting for sound. This should power it off if my radio is off, but that is not happening. I reached out to Crux again, multiple times, explaining the problem and got no response. I reached out again and asked if I could just buy another wire harness in case there is something wonky about the one I have (the swc issue I later realized might have been one of the wires not communicating to the adapter, since connecting only sw1 or sw2 at a time made it act the way it did before with only half the buttons working at a time- but obviously my wire to the car was working as was the headunit because different settings switched around which buttons were active... so the fault must have been in the adapter or harness). No response. It was too late to return it so I tried troubleshooting on my own.

I'm living with the faint hiss for now, when the car is on it isn't a big deal and usually I'm listening to something anyway so that's fine. The fade from front to back is fine because its a coupe and not like there's a lot of difference between the front and rear of the car. The SWC buttons are working because I bypassed the faulty operation of the Crux unit, so it's mostly fine now. But I feel like I overpaid for something that under delivered. I wish I had gone with a different interfacing adapter and/or bypassed my factory amp. This was supposed to make the installation EASY and it ended up causing me more grief instead.
Also? Crux customer support has been terrible. When they did finally respond, it seemed like they didn't want to help because I didn't buy it from one of their authorized retailers and I wasn't a professional installer. Their website also went down for weeks in the middle and I feared they went out of business due to the pandemic. They have since responded so I know they are still around, but were not really helpful. The technical team at Atoto was worlds more helpful (they wanted it to work and were trying everything to see if the problem was on their side). It seems the problem was with Crux's adapter and their lack of support.

title: Excellent for photogrammetry
text:
This is a great tool for 3D scanning via photogrammetry. I've been scanning models to 3D print, and making sure you get a perfect shot at every angle makes the process so much smoother and more accurate. This is also an excellent tool for product photography and doing 360 degree views for websites. The remote is really cool, although it does kind of remind me of my Android TV remote that has been repurposed.
I didn't use the cable to the camera, but it's nice that you have that option if you have a Canon camera (I shoot with Sony and didn't bother with any kind of remote). The app is a little bit finicky, I prefer to use a laptop to control it instead of installing a third party app on my personal cell phone. But it seems like it works if you'd prefer to control it that way. All in all, this is a very cool and useful product.

title: A great way to mount a USB port somewhere better.
text: I wanted to put a USB port in a cover for part of my desk, and this right here is the secret sauce to make it happen. Just print an appropriately sized face plate or cut a hole in whatever you want with the correct dimensions, and you can literally POP this into place. The plastic tabs that hold it in place aren't very generous so you need to make the hole precisely to get it to stay put. But, once connected the throughput is excellent, devices connect and transfer data / charge as expected at USB 3.0 speeds.

title: Bi-directional!
text:
They say this is for 2 computers sharing one USB device, but I found it works just as well in reverse! Let's say you have one source and want to switch between two peripherals... it works the other way around as well! Or at least, it does in my test.
I have a car with Android Auto / Apple Car Play and a single USB port to connect to them. I have two cables attached to that one port with this device- one cable goes to my Android phone, the other cable goes to an iPhone cable, and switching between the two is as simple as pressing the button on the unit! No more unplugging one and forgetting the put the other back in before my wife takes the car. Plug in the appropriate phone, and press the button if it doesn't start automatically. I'd imagine this would work well for all kinds of scenarios... if you have a computer with two different input devices (a mouse and trackpad, or 2 keyboards, etc) and want to switch between them without changing the plug as well. All kinds of uses come to mind for this very versatile switch!
And of course, having one device switching between two computers as the product advertising says obviously works too!

title: Very versatile bag
text:
I tried this out to keep some of my work equipment in (live production gear like adapters, laptop, cables), and I really like the different pockets inside to keep things organized, but most important to me is how it can be carried in 3 ways. It can be worn like a backpack, turned sideways like a briefcase, or put atop a rolling cargo suitcase / Pelican case, using the strap in the back to go over the handle of the case and hold it in place. If I'm traveling light, I can just carry it solo. Or wear it on my back. Or bundle it with my wheelie cases.
The lack of external pockets means you can really move this in any direction and things won't fall out, it's really well designed to be completely closed in any orientation. It's also evenly sized in all dimensions, unlike a bookbag or pack which gets wider in the bottom and thinner on top. This makes this bag a very useful companion for travelling with just about anything.

title: So much cooler than expected for the price!
text:
My son has been wanting a gaming monitor for higher refresh rates in his games for years now. Obviously we were excited to try this one out, and I have to tell you... I'm impressed.
I usually stick with name brands for my computer monitors, and for the retail price this is at, I wasn't expecting a whole lot. But the image quality is pretty sweet, the resolution at 2560 x 1440 is noticeably better than his old 1920x1080 one, and the 144hz refresh rate ain't bad either (a whooping jump over the 60hz his old one maxed out at, which is really what he wanted).
BUT WAIT, THERE'S MORE!

1) The monitor has SPEAKERS. He connected with the included display port cable and realized that a new audio device showed up on his desktop. I told him yeah, because DP and HDMI can carry audio so there's a 3.5mm jack on the back to plug in speakers. My LG computer monitors do that too, but they can't actually play sound. There's just a jack on the back to plug in speakers / headphones, and it just makes it easier to bring the plug closer than my desktop. But when he tried it, lo and behold, sound came out of the monitor like a TV! Holy cow, this could double as a media center for a fire stick or something because it has integrated sound! My son usually uses headphones for games and didn't like the look of speakers on his desk, so he's never had a way to play something out loud for another person to hear before. This is a VERY cool option to have!
2) There's an RGB strip on the rear of the monitor so it looks cool from behind! (see included photo).
3) There's a funky little projector circle that displays an image of a tiger head (seems to be the branding logo) on the wall behind the monitor. See included photo of wall to illustrate.

My son loved that projector thing and actually tried to find the logo online so he can make it his desktop background, but sadly the monitor doesn't seem to have any branding we can look up to find that logo, which is a shame. Otherwise, what an awesome product! More than I expected, so far we are very pleased with it!

title: Great kid friendly tablet, parent approved!
text:
I actually just had an opportunity to try the pink version of this tablet, which you can find under a different listing here. It's an identical tablet from the same brand with a different colored case outside. Which is a GOOD thing, because I actually really like the tablet underneath, and the case it comes in!
It's not cutting edge hardware, but its fast enough to do anything kid related easily. The cameras aren't great, but again- at this price you shouldn't expect them to be Galaxy S or iPad camera. But the actual user experience is pretty good despite the cheap price tag.
For starters you get Android 11 out of the box, which is pretty incredible to find on an inexpensive device. It also comes with some pretty excellent kid software that parents can use to control and offer fun, entertaining and educational games and apps.
The case is the best part, however, as it is thick and "kid proof", as they say on the box. There's a stand that be adjusted or used as a handle, and overall gives you something substantial to hold onto. The only thing I'm not crazy about is that the case makes the holes and buttons a little bit difficult to reach/line up. The case is very thick, as we already said, so sometimes plugging in, say, a USB OTG plug with a keyboard is a little difficult to line up in the hole. And the power button isn't in a great place for little fingers to find quickly. But these are minor details, it is still a pretty great tablet that will work well for kids.

title: Kid tested, parent approved!
text:
[[VIDEOID:ef18b2bc61d2bf43363a5f3d51e2b5d8]] This is a pretty great tablet geared for kids. Inside of the "kid-proof" case is an Android 11 powered tablet with a comfortable-to-read 10" display, much better than the 7" Kindle Fire tablet that my kids used to use before this. It has the standard Google play store, yet still comes with plenty of parental control tools and a pretty great suite of software for kid friendly use (something I really liked about the Kindle OS).
It even comes with a USB OTG plug so that you can plug in accessories like a USB sticks, a keyboard or barcode scanner, etc.
The only thing that bothered me a little bit is that the case makes the buttons and USB port a little bit difficult to line up. To turn on and off the power, for example, you need to find the on button next to the volume buttons, which isn't immediately easy for a kid to find. I can imagine younger ones especially hitting every other button first. And the OTG adapter had some trouble fitting in the hole cutaway since the port didn't sit exactly in the middle of the case. The cameras were also cheap-phone quality, but then again I never expect good camera performance at this price range.
That being said, it does an excellent job at what it is designed to do: Be a kind friendly tablet that parents will be happy about.

title: Excellent proof of concept, has some shortcomings in user experience
text:
[[VIDEOID:2212eb120f801d8851a76eb4e94985a0]] This is a really cool way to make your head unit act like a tablet. If you have Android Auto in your dash, you already know that it is pretty cool but a watered down experience of the full blown OS on your phone. It also relies on your phone being plugged in. This device eliminates that by having its own complete Android operating system on a stick that appears on your display, completely independent of your phone. Complete with play store and streaming apps! It is a very cool concept and pretty useful, but sadly I hit some snags along the user experience:
1) You have to wait 30 seconds for it to boot every time you start the car.
2) Unlike Android Auto on your phone, you need to supply an internet connection (you can use your phone as a hotspot if your plan allows and you have enough data, but it is extra steps involved every time you boot if you want to connect)
3) There is no shutdown/sleep. When you turn off the car, the device abruptly dies and has to start fresh again each time. Aside from the long boot up each time, this leads to two potential problems:
3a)The time/date resets every time you turn the ignition. If you don't have a network connection for it to grab the correct time, it will default to thinking it is Dec 31st and 7am. Every. Single. Boot.
3b) Anyone who knows how operating systems work can vouch that if you are in the middle of a write operation (saving a file, updating an app, etc) storage could become corrupted if power is immediately shut without warning to the device. There is no warning to the device, it's either on while the car is, or dead when the ignition is cut. Heck, even if you leave the ignition in the acc position so it remains powered on, if you turn to the ignition position, that momentary cut to the power while the car starts means another 30 second reboot and the time reset to 7am. Very annoying.
4) There is no pinch to zoom option, which some apps (like maps) assume is available for the user experience.
5) Bluetooth support from a phone is very poor. The unit can tell you that a call is coming in, but you can't answer or initiate the call without exiting the UI and either going back to the head unit menu, or controlling it from the phone. Also, no phone audio (A2DP) is played from the phone because the MStick is using the Bluetooth profile for its own audio.

In a nutshell, a lot of these caveats could be worked around with some design changes. The stick could be built with a small internal battery much like a phone or tablet, so that it can sleep when the power is shut off and wait for the user to turn the car back on without rebooting from scratch. This would also solve the time reset issue.
The same way that there is a button on the nav bar to pull down the notification shade, there could be a button to enable pinch zooming within apps that require it.

There could also be a built in way to attach another display, perhaps mirror to a phone or remote desktop in so that you can set up all your apps, etc, at home in the comfort of your wifi instead of doing all of this outside in the car. Everytime I wanted to try something, I had to tinker outside in my driveway and run down my car's battery and/or waste fuel keeping it running for no reason. Little things like that would make a HUGE difference in the end user experience. This product seems like more hassle than it is worth for the average user, but is an excellent proof of concept if you want to, for example, have Torque running on your car display but not upgrade the whole stereo to an Android powered one.
BUT, then again, it sort of begs to wonder why not just get an Android tablet or old phone and mount it on the dash and leave the radio to connect with your phone? The user experience might be better than working around the caveats that this introduces.

title: Its just OK, there are better
text:
I understand the need to have a dedicated media player at times. However, much like others I have used, this uses a very barebones UI that is laggy and feels very outdated compared to a smart device. The font has hard lines that are sometimes hard to read, and occasionally you'll even meet elements of the UI that have parts written in Chinese characters. And the video playback option is a joke- you can only play videos in a specific codec that is archaic and unreliable (and needs a bizarre app to encode to).
It has an Fm tuner which is nice, and the size is super portable and cute. And honestly, this would be a decent device if I didn't know that for around the same price you can get much more polished media players powered by a modified smartphone OS. For example, another media player that I recently tried actually had a linux/Android kernel running under the hood, but stripped of all the smartphone parts. It supported video playback of modern formats, had more more pleasing fonts and a UI that was fast and responsive. I mean, in this day and age, unless this were half the price, there's no excuse for a UI to feel so far behind.

title: Powered by Android!! NOTE: This model did NOT come with browser and FM radio
text:
Ok, first of all, I want to say I LOVE this player much more than others I've used. My kids are not allowed cell phones in school, but they are allowed music players- however most players that aren't smart devices are really janky with buggy/slow UIs and lots of impairments (I tried encoding a video for one and it wouldn't work unless I used a very archaic codec that required a suspicious Chinese desktop app). This, however, actually runs a stripped down version of Android under the hood. This is a GOOD thing! The UI is very polished and smooth thanks to open source mature OS, and features like video playback are much more robust with a wider variety of formats supported and compatible as a result as well!
The hardware is smooth and the menus are intuitive thanks to being familiar with the Android OS already. It's a very cute device!
So why only 3 stars? Well, the listing claims it has a web browser and FM radio. Both of those things are missing on this model. The truth is, I don't need my kids to have that anyway, but it feels weird that the listing advertises features which aren't there. I think I may have gotten a different model than the one advertised.
I considered side-loading a browser apk since it DOES run android, but the truth is this isn't designed for that sort of use and wouldn't make a difference for the purpose of this review. I'd imagine that there are a lot of possible hacks and modifications possible thanks to the operating system inside if someone wanted to tinker.

title: Great value, multiple ways to keep battery power!
text: [[VIDEOID:18cbb6e13742967cb26b9038231a3ac3]] At less than $15 per talkie, this is a great value. Multiple ways to charge, spare batteries come in the box which can be charged independently. See video for more details.

title: Compact yet powerful!
text:
I have a similar LED light with a Bowen's mount that is much bigger than this one, so I was a little bit hesitant to believe this would be as bright as they claim. However, they must have had some major progress in the field of LED brightness and/or cooling, because they somehow managed to shrink this thing down! The light by itself is going to be far too harsh since it is a tiny dot emitting all the light at once. With a good diffuser using the industry standard Bowen's bayonet, you're good to go!

Part of me still thinks perhaps this will overheat on account of being so compact without a big cooling system, but so far it is not failed me! I wish it would let me adjust the color, but it is permanently set at 5600k. That's ok as I'm used to similar lights in that range as well, and it is a good color to blend with natural light.

title: Improvement over the last GreenYi camera I tried!
text:
I like this style of camera very much. It mounts under the lip for the license plate on my vehicle and gives a very factory-looking installation, unlike the bracket mounted or license plate style ones I have been using previously. I had tried a different variation of this (also from GreenYi) before, however I had some difficulty with the product due to the way it worked on my head unit. The 170 degree view was only if using the AHD mode, which my unit did not support. In the lower CVBS resolution (compatible with more devices) it was cropped down to only something like 100 degrees, which was far too narrow to see around me in the back.
THIS product, however, seems to keep the full 170 degree view regardless of resolution supported! Just cut the green wire to set your own grid lines on the headunit (if supported), and good to go. My only reluctance to give this 5 stars is the fact that it is *just* that much tighter than my 175 degree bracket / license plate camera I was using until now. That extra 5 degrees doesn't sound like it would make a difference, but it does to me. I can see the borders of my bumper on the 175, but with 170 the edge is just out of view. This camera looks nicer and is clearer than my 175, but I think I need to stick with my 175 for practical useful reasons.
I'm waiting to see a wider angle from GreenYi, maybe they'll produce a 180!

title: Impressive value!
text:
[[VIDEOID:53ff6162ae211d5d47dd3aff908667ef]] I work with cameras on motorized gimbals at work, so I'm used to the expensive counterparts popularized by DJI and Zhiyun for larger cameras. Those models cost several times what this does, so to be honest I wasn't expecting a whole lot for the money. Especially if used with a wide angle action cam like a GoPro.
However, color me impressed! The quality of the machine as well as the functions and features are pretty respectable, I'd gladly recommend it. See video for demonstration.

title: Excellent for connecting sound
text: This is a great cable for use with my projector setup. I have a speaker tower that I use for sounds when watching a projected movie, but the trick is getting the speaker closer to the audience and away from the projector/laptop. This cable plugs right into the laptop and lets me put the speakers a healthy 15' away. It works perfectly for this, the sound is clear and the length is fantastic. I'm very happy with this product!

title: Seems like a good value
text: I don't know what the final price will be on this since it is not available at the time of my review, but you get 12 of them per pack which seems generous. I believe this will be priced competitively, but keep in mind many battery packs sell with only 8 (2x sets of 4), while this is 50% more. I have two high school aged kids that use TI 84 calculators, and wouldn't you know it, each needs 4 AAA batteries. And since apparently you can load games on these calculators, the batteries can be worn out quite quickly (and they do). Rechargeable AAA are the way to go, in my opinion! These seem to last a reasonably expected amount of time, and so far all of them have performed well in my Power2000 universal battery charger. No major heat issues, voltage seemed correct when tested with my meter, have only had positive experiences so far!

title: Good value for low-speed sticks
text:
These sticks are the ultimate no-frills portable storage. They have no branding on them, and are as generic as can be. This is actually great if you're going to deliver a file to a client with your own sticker on them, and the fact that you get five of them for the price is fantastic as far as value.
They won't win any speed awards, though. They're OK, and will definitely get the job done if you're just looking to deliver a final copy of a file. Don't expect any kind of impressive performance for the money.

title: This is HUGE and better than I expected
text: I have a kiddie inflatable bounce house with a similar blower system, so I was expecting this to be LOUD. Like, too loud for our usual outdoor sound system. But I'm pleasantly surprised to say the volume isn't all that bad... especially since you'll be sitting far enough away to see it that the sound becomes less and less of an issue. That being said, I think I didn't realize in my head just how HUGE this is! I have a large garage I wanted to test it out in first (big enough for a basketball hoop inside), and THIS WAS TALLER THAN THE GARAGE. It must be used outside, and they're not kidding about tying it down either! If there's wind, this thing will act like a sail and blow away. But when used correctly in the right setup, this is really an incredible screen. Much more fun that my old foldable or pull-down projector screen. You'll need a bright enough projector to present from far enough away, so I suggest using a real brand name high lumen one, the cheap made-in-china projectors tend to be optimistic about their brightness lumen rating, resulting in a picture that gets pretty dim when you're this far away. My trusty Viewsonic does a decent job, but I'd even try to get something rated for more light output if you can. The more the better. Great product, I recommend it!

title: This is AMAZING
text:
I've been hired to do a lot of live stream jobs since the pandemic, and that usually means my trusty laptop with OBS installed + Magewell HDMI to USB adapter + camera/tripod. If they need multiple cameras, I need to lug along my Blackmagic ATEM box and have that do camera switching before the Magewell. It's a lot of equipment to set up, worth a LOT of money, and that's not even counting the internet connection, which sometimes I need to supply via cellular hotspot device.
This unit replaces ALL OF THOSE. I can't even begin to accurately describe how incredibly versatile of a tool this is, but considering the price of all that equipment individually, this is a STEAL at the asking price. Sure, OBS might still be able to pull more complicated tricks that the UI here can't, and the ATEM switch can support more cameras (including SDI cables), but most of the time this is truly all you need and even then some! And there is so much value in the simplified hardware setup here.
The unit seems to run a customized UI over Android, and I was able to do some live multi-cam switching with minor effects on Youtube live using the built in Cat5 port. I am blown away with how capable this is. The only downside is there's a bit of a learning curve since it is a very niche product and offers a LOT of functionality, so you have to familiarize yourself with the features and how it works. But once you do? This is an excellent tool for any streamer. Highly recommended!

title: Its an OK tablet if you can get it cheap.
text:
There are dozens if not hundreds of off-brand Android tablets available these days. Some of them are impressive for the money, some of them have stand-out features like USB host ports, removable batteries or IR blasters... and some of them are just boring run-of-the-mill standard fare. This is one of the latter ones, unfortunately.
The screen size is nice at 10", but the resolution is a paltry 720p at that size, which makes the pixels more noticeable on fine text and graphics. If all you want is something to play games and watch videos on, the display is fine, but if you want the large screen for an e-reader or for pixel-peeping details in graphics, the resolution will quickly feel too low. The processor is not terribly fast, although it holds up decently if you're not multitasking a lot. That being said, the 2GB of RAM won't hold up to a lot of multitasking anyway. The cameras are pretty terrible, too. If you need a device for a zoom meeting and having good lighting, having a bad camera is better than no camera, but don't expect to take pictures worth keeping. Like, at all. Pictures look almost like old flip-phone era quality. And beyond that, there are no stand out features that add value to it. There's a TF slot, but that's not rare. Supposedly there is a SIM slot, however there is a lot of conflicting info in the paperwork re: whether this device is WiFi only, and I wasn't able to determine any cellular functionality.
At the end of the day, it's a good bargain tablet with a decent sized display. You can do basic Android tasks, play some light games, watch some videos, etc, and if that's all you want it for, it'll get the job done. BUT... keep in mind that there are alternatives like the Kindle Fire and brands like Lenovo's M10 which are pretty close to the asking price on this and have a far superior user experience. So it sort of makes one wonder why someone would choose this device over those. If you can get this for significantly less than those models (perhaps if it goes on sale), I'd recommend it as a toss around tablet. But the value is really hard to find at the moment.

title: Seems decent and legit!
text: This card is only rated for 10 MB/s write according to the packaging, normally I'd recommend something with faster rated sustained write times for recording UHD/4K video. However, upon benchmarking it with CrystalDiskMark, I found it surpassed both the 90MB/s read and 10MB/s write! Usually with brands I've never heard of, I'm worried about things being slower than rated, this was a pleasant surprise! So far, the card seems like the real deal and at an excellent price. Still wouldn't be my first choice for recording video as I can't vouch for long term reliability yet, but it's a good option for the money so far.

title: Amazing for the price!
text: Needed this for a job in a hurry as a backup and didn't want to spend a lot on it in case my setup didn't end up working. Turns out it worked better than I expected, had absolutely ZERO issues, everything worked exactly as it should. For the price compared to other options, I'm blown away!

title: Perfect for running my camera feed long distance
text: These are great for taking an HDMI output and converting it to a standard SDI cable, great for long distance or for inputs that require it. I used this recently for a live multi-cam concert stream to bring a small camera (Sony A7S) into my Blackmagic ATEM mixer over to mix with other SDI cameras. I ran it over 150' of SDI cable and it worked perfectly with no noticeable lag. For the price this costs, it's a no brainer to have on a job like this.

title: A good kit, nice and portable.
text:
[[VIDEOID:cc44ab885d67cee15f3444e8dd59fcb6]] I work with video for a living so I'm used to portable soft continuous lighting kits. This is more than decent for the money, I'm actually fairly impressed with how versatile and practical LED based bulbs have come. It's not the most high end kit I've used, but for the price I was expecting something subpar. This is very usable.
I did have an odd glitch when I first tested it however, in which the light did not respond to the remote or inline switch control. I had to pull the plug to reset it. I haven't have that happen since, but it is something I'm careful about now and would recommend a buyer keep an eye out for it. Otherwise, for the price, this is an excellent pair of softboxes.

title: Decent price for name brand, but USB2 speed
text:
I love and trust Lexar products for my work jobs (professional grade memory cards and other solid state storage), so I had high expectations for this product. I love the build quality of this material, it's a solid feeling metallic body instead of cheap plastic, and it gives the impression of a product that will hold up to the test of time.
The price is also impressive for a name brand product with this kind of build quality. However, I had almost forgotten how slow USB2.0 can be. I'm so used to USB3 storage speeds of easily over 150MB/s, that the benchmarks on this one seem almost painfully slow at around the 20MB/s mark. But, that's par for the course with the older standard, so I can't really fault the product for it. This is a great value but you could easily get a much faster storage stick for a bit more money. I could see this being useful for someone who wants to distribute a hard-copy of something by hand and would like to order a bulk supply of durable and fast-enough but still affordable media. Otherwise, I think I'd recommend one that is USB 3 compatible at least since you can always be backwards compatible with 2.0 if necessary, but have the increased speed when available.

title: Good value, comparable to big brand U3 speeds
text:
I have quite a few SDXC cards that I use for recording 4k, and I usually stick to trusted brands such as Sandisk and Lexar, and even some overpriced ones from Sony. After performing some tests, I believe that this Amazon Basics brand is comparable with those. The speeds are right where they should be for U3 rating, and it seems reliable and durable so far.
Interesting to see Amazon getting into the memory card business- so far this is promising!

title: Great replacement for my HP Pavilion
text: I'm always misplacing my laptop charger, so having a spare like this is a worthwhile investment. My HP Pavilion recognizes the charger and is able to charge up just as well as the OEM one. Cord is actually plenty long, which I appreciate as well. This is a good replacement or alternative to the original, I'd recommend it if you have an HP with one of the blue-tip chargers.

title: Useful for various laptops when away from outlets!
text:
This is a fantastic tool for people who need to work in remote locations with multiple kinds of computer. Not only does it work in the car for road warriors that need to meet a deadline or watch a lot of videos, but it makes it easy to power up off other DC sources without an additional inverter.
In my case, I do a lot of live streaming events and need to power a laptop for hours, usually too far away from a plug to be charged. So I carry around a portable power bank that offers 12v DC car outlets, and this is PERFECT for use with that!

Something to note: While my Lenovo and HP laptops were easy to identify the correct plug right away (yellow square and blue tip), my Acer was a little bit more difficult. Each plug tells you what voltage it is (printed on the plastic), and I found one that fit but was .5 volt lower than it needed to be. Usually if it is within range of the specifications it would work, but in this case it would power the laptop but not charge it. Only when I opened the booklet and saw there was a listing of different specific numbered tips with compatible models did I notice there was a better match, and upon switching to that one I'm happy to say my Acer was charging fine after that. I took a picture of the booklet for reference and am uploading it here.

Also interesting to note, I own both a MS Surface and older magsafe Macbook Pro, neither of which have tips included in this set. Strange as those are popular laptops. However those aren't ones that I use for live streaming, somehow all of the ones I DO have the included plugs here. But I feel like it is important to point out that certain popular models are omitted in case you are looking for support. If you have any of the laptops in the list shown, it's a great product!

title: Good batteries and adapter, not the most cost effective
text:
I happen to have bought light kits from GVM before and I've always been happy with their products, so I was excited to get a chance to try this kit out. I work with live production gear for a living, and these Sony NP-F batteries are like gold currency out on a gig. You can never have enough, especially considering how long they traditionally take to charge combined with how quickly a giant LED panel (such as GVM's own light panels) will deplete them.
I love that this comes with a dual charger instead of two single chargers like most third party battery packs do. Makes it easier to manage and keep organized. The V-mount adapter is pretty sweet too for some of my larger production gear rigs, I have a lot of gear that is compatible with V-mounts but far more Sony batteries than V-mount packs. Now I can use these for that.
The only reason I can't give this 5 stars is the price. These are good 6600Mah battery packs, but the kit is currently asking a hundred and thirty dollars, which is nearly double what a pair of third party F970s usually cost. These aren't OEM Sony and while I happen to really like GVM gear, I don't think they are particularly more reputable than other third parties to justify this price hike. Sure, the V-mount adapter is cool, as is the double charger. But the price is steep. I see there's a coupon at the time of this review that brings the price down to normal but I don't know if the plan is to eventually charge that much for this kit and not sure I'd recommend it for the price if they do.

title: These have come a long way since my first one!
text:
I've been working in video production for over 2 decades now, and bought my first teleprompter for infomercial style videos back in the early 2000s. Let's just say, much like camera tech has gotten smaller and more efficient, so has teleprompting!
The concept is pretty simple and hasn't changed- angle a piece of glass in front of the lens with a black drop material behind it to create a sort of 2-way-mirror, then reflect text in reverse (you know, because mirror?) and your subject appears to read their script off your lens while the camera doesn't see the text at all.
Things that are still true from back then:
- Your text has to be reversed. My old one came with PC software to do this, and since iPads weren't really a thing yet, we used laptops that could fold all the way backwards (Thinkpads mostly). This, surprisingly does not come with software. But no matter, there are some free ones out there, and my personal favorite is just using powerpoint. We reverse the images and make a slide show that the subject can advance with a standard presenter remote. None of those things are included with this set, but if you've been doing corporate and commercial video, you probably have access to this already.

- You will have some loss of exposure due to the mirror. This isn't a big deal, if you're lighting a scene properly you should be able to easily compensate for this, you just might need to hit that ISO or aperture to brighten it up a bit more. Just something to know.

- Your subject needs to be comfortable reading without his eyes darting around the camera. This is just standard teleprompter stuff.

Things that HAVE improved with this model:
- It now attaches to the tripod! In the old days, unless you had the budget for a proper display one that was embedded in front of the camera, you needed to do this with a stand for a laptop or monitor lying horizontal while the camera tripod was behind it. Not very portable, so it stayed in my studio. This one can be brought along to a location shoot and set up rather easily!

To be honest, that one improvement makes all the difference in the world. I barely used my old teleprompter because I couldn't take it out of my studio easily, and most of my gigs are on location shoots. This is going to make testimonial / narrated production videos SO much easier to shoot out in the field!

Just keep in mind you'll need to figure out the display mechanics (software, presentation, speed, remote, etc) on your own. This just gives you the physical hardware to get it done, the mechanics of it will need your own creativity. Would definitely recommend!

title: Works with Android Auto!
text:
I have an Android Auto head unit in my car, but it requires a direct connection to my phone to work. When I'm in a hurry, I usually throw my phone in the holster of the car and start driving... I don't have time to dig out the USB cable and carefully plug it in, it's an extra step that I often decide to skip and just stick with Bluetooth audio instead.
This cable changes everything! Now, the cable is magnetically hanging next to the phone already, all I need to do is wave it near the bottom of the phone and CLICK! It connects and starts Android Auto!
I had previously tried another similar magnetic cable, but it seemed to only work well as a charging device, it wouldn't send the data necessary for a connection like Android Auto over the USB cable. I'm happy to say, this one DOES, and it's every bit as wonderful as I hoped it would be! I can't speak yet for longevity, but so far I'm pleased with it. The unit comes with enough plugs and tips for my wife to have one in her phone as well, and of course enough cables for both of us to charge when not in the car as well. It IS a little bit of a finger magnet to have the little nub sticking out on the bottom of my phone, I wonder if eventually that will shorten the life of my USB port or the tip, but for now I'm very happy with it and would strongly recommend it for anyone in my position!

title: Works, but not the sturdiest
text:
I have another similar stand that I have used for my projector and laptop. I wanted a second one so I could both at the same time (projector mounted next to laptop, both on their own stand).
Compared to my other one, I liked that this could fold up smaller thanks to the top being able to fold in half, however I found the whole thing a little less sturdy overall. The center pole would wobble a little, and the top part that folds was actually really annoying to unfold to set up because the screws need to be removed and replaced. Sure, they are thumbscrews and you don't need tools, but I found it annoying as they would fall out as I was trying to hold it in place and decided it was better to just leave it assembled. Which begs the question, why even bother folding it? I also found that if I used it with the laptop and typed, the whole thing would shake with my typing. If you want to use it as only a projector stand where it won't get touched, I think that's fine and it will work well enough. But if you want equipment to not wobble if touched, I'd look for a different one.

title: Excellent mid-quality without breaking the bank
text:
These are very good mid-range headphones. They look cool, are comfortable to wear, and have much better sound quality than the cheapo headphones you find on Amazon. Sure, they're not Bang and Olufson, but you're not paying that insane premium price tag either.
For what these are, they are excellent quality. Has support for different types of cable connections, and when used with a proper Quad DAC audio player, the sound quality is impressive for the money!

title: I love that this has switches!
text:
This is great for my home office when I need to charge up a lot of gear before a camera shoot. I have lots of batteries and accessories, different chargers, some need USB and some need plug-in AC power, and this tower gives me everything I need, PLUS does it with a generous amount of space in between the plugs so that I can plug in lots of wall warts without blocking the ones next to it! That's awesome.
Meanwhile, even better, is the fact that the top has manual on/off buttons. Why is this a big deal? Because one thing I've always hated about leaving things plugged in is phantom drain. Many chargers and converters waste power even if you aren't actively charging anything by continuing to convert energy even when not being used. So, it's always best to unplug everything if you aren't using it. That's sometimes annoying, but with this, you can leave everything plugged in and just power off the outlets as needed!
The unit is split into two sections, the rear outlets and the front + USB ports. You can choose to keep one or the other or both on at a time. I really like that, and highly recommend this for people who need to charge up or power a lot of components at once!

title: Casts a nice large soft lighting circle
text:
Anyone in photography will tell you that the bigger the light source, the better the light. Hard small harsh lights are the worst in regards to shadows and contrast, and make terrible eye reflections of the light. Ring lights are popular because they spread a more even and therefore softer glow, and have those signature round eye catch lights. But a GIANT ring light like this one? Makes a good thing even better!
I was playing around with it tonight, but in the effort of keeping my family private, I used a Darth Vader helmet as my subject to share. Pictures are labelled, one without the ring light as a control, then using it to create a side light and then again as a front light, and then a practical example of using it to cast a soft light on a scene (my kid playing- face edited out obviously).
I like that this light comes with a camera mount as well as a cell phone holder, and especially that it can run on either battery OR plug in power. In fact, it even comes with 2 Sony camcorder batteries to power it! It only comes with one charger, so thankfully I already have other chargers for that type of battery around my house as it appears to require both to be used at once (so charging them one at a time is very annoying). I wasn't expecting the batteries so I'm pleasantly surprised and would not deduct any stars from an otherwise fantastic product!

title: A great way to keep classic Alpha and NEX cameras going longer
text:
[[VIDEOID:78f50a418bd0010e566249c53abbda3d]] If you've ever used a FW-50 battery powered camera, you know how weak they are, especially if used for video recording. The battery size may have been something that made sense for the original NEX E-mount cameras, but for something like the Sony A7S, they don't last more than about an hour of time at best.
For that, a Sony camcorder battery is a much better fit.
This isn't a new idea, in fact I actually built something almost exactly like this out of a Sony Camcorder battery charger years ago and shared it on Youtube and various camera forums. I'd like to say that this looks so much like my DIY adapter that I think it may have even been inspired by it! I explain more and compare it to the one I built in the video attached. Hope it helps someone!

NOTE: This is only for cameras that use the original FW-50 battery. Third generation A7 cameras now use a newer and larger capacity cell instead (thankfully), so you'd need a different adapter to interface with the battery cavity. In other words, This will work great with A7S mark I and II, but the III won't be compatible.

title: Excellent to attach accessories to light stand or tripid!
text:
I work in corporate video and photography for a living, and sometimes we need to rig up some bizarre camera setups to get the job done. Recently I needed a mini XLR mixer to feed into my camera but had to keep the controls accessible without putting the camera in a cage. Well, this little adapter worked PERFECTLY! I clamped it onto the the monopod leg securely, and attached the mini mixer to the 1/4 20 threading on the back.
Today, I attached a rigged battery bank to this to test power a camera for the duration of a concert unmanned. There are so many ways to attach and use accessories with it, I'd recommend this in the arsenal of anyone working with cameras that may need to rig up lights, monitors, audio equipment, or anything else in possibly non-conventional ways. I love it!

title: Great for adding a second screen + touch input!
text:
This is a fantastic IPS panel display that actually closely matches my laptop display in clarity, brightness and size/position. That makes it great for a quick "second screen" when I need to make a portable workstation on the go! Ideally, it should be possible to run the entire thing off a USB-C connection, so you don't need any additional power/hdmi/usb/etc connection. They advertise that this is possible.
However I was unable to get that to work. For some reason, my HP laptop, despite having a USB-C port, would not recognize this as a monitor. Neither would my phone which also supports display port over USB-C.
I needed to use the hdmi cable adapter, and then I was able to use the USB-C for power from my laptop. Interesting to note that if you want to use the display's touch screen capability, use the monitor in USB-C instead of the strictly powered one, and it will support full touch screen as well as power the unit. I was nervous when the single-cable setup didn't work that it would require all three plugs to be used in separate- power usb, usb for touch, and hdmi for video signal. 3 cables would have been too much and I'd just never use it. 2 cables are doable. I'd think a low powered unit such as a Raspberry Pi might require separate power since it likely can't supply enough power for the monitor, but the mini PC and laptop I tried it with seemed to do just fine running the monitor and using the same USB for touch-input support. I really wish it only required the single USB cable, however. I was unable to get that working no matter what I tried.
For what its worth, I'd give it 4 stars since it adds a touch enabled second screen to my laptop, and also makes my miniPC into a kiosk for interesting use at events. But I wish I could get it working with a single cable like it advertises. That would make it 5 stars.

title: Great for adding an angle
text: This is a great little adapter to help make your USB-C ports more accessible in tight spaces, or in my case make it easier to find. I have a wireless charger in my car that shares a plug with my Android Auto unit, and fishing around the back to plug it back in was always a pain. With this adapter, the plug now sits visible 90 degrees to the left of the charger making it very easy to find and plug back in. The charging speed and power seems unchanged, so I'd say it performs exactly as expected. A great product for anyone looking move their port at an angle!

title: Great power in a small package
text:
This is a great little mini computer that is only slightly larger than an external drive. It comes with a VESA mount so you can attach it to a screen or TV and use it for digital signage or a kiosk. I actually tested mine with a 15" touchscreen and was able to turn it into a touch screen windows desktop, which was pretty neat.
It has a healthy dose of RAM, but not a lot of storage. No matter, as you can actually easily add storage with the included empty SATA bay. If you don't want to use the additional storage, this bay can actually be removed completely, leaving you with a much thinner PC!
Here's the bit that's even more interesting: That additional bay appears to connect via a USB-C connection on the bottom of the unit. Oddly enough, this box does not have user-accessible USB-C ports, only standard full sized USB A. The only USB-C seems to be this "Secret" one found on the bottom and only accessible if you remove the additional storage bay. Strange design, but still very functional for my intended purposes.
As far as being a computer, it boots pretty quickly thanks to the SSD main storage, but don't expect this to be a speed demon or 3D gaming computer by any sorts. The CPU is actually not all that impressive, nor is the integrated Intel GPU that comes with it. However, in my benchmark test using the User Benchmarks website, it actually performed "better than expected" according to their expectations based on the specs. Here's the results I got:
UserBenchmarks: Game 3%, Desk 29%, Work 3%
CPU: Intel Celeron J3455 - 27.3%
GPU: Intel HD Graphics 500 - 2.6%
SSD: Kimtigo 128GB 128GB - 68.7%
RAM: ABCD 123456789012345678 4x1.5GB - 28%

The percentages are based out of all tested computers they have ranked. As you can see, for basic computing (Desk) it's decent, but for gaming or work (I'm guessing work means like compiling code or other heavy computational tasks), it's rated at 3% overall. But for light browsing, word processing, and running video (which it can do on dual monitors, thanks to the dual HDMI ports!), it's actually pretty good- much more capable and powerful than an Android based computer or Raspberry Pi, and runs the full desktop windows while at it!
Interested that the GPU is rated at 2.6%, the benchmarks claimed that this Intel HD 500 gpu is normally expected to perform around 1%, so the fact that it nailed a 2.6 percentile implies that this setup actually outperformed expectations for that chip.

All in all, for the price, it's a pretty neat little computer that can be used for all kinds of interesting things.

title: It works, but its not the best one.
text:
I wish I could give this 3.5 stars. It works, and helps in all the ways I didn't like my old one, so it is worth at least 4 stars. But there are some things about it that could really use improvement.
To explain, I had a nice backup camera that I installed previously which only ended up being about 100 degrees of view. This wasn't as wide as I hoped, and only showed me what was directly behind the car. THIS camera, however, is a full 170 degree wide, which even shows the edges of my bumper in the fisheye effect. I can see the space next to me, cars behind me, everything that I can't see well usually thanks to the cloth convertible rear view window I have. Thankfully they used the same wiring harness as my previous camera so I didn't need to re-run my power and reverse trigger from the rear light, all of that I could keep which made the wiring pretty painless.

But what I didn't like:
1) The camera is VERY noticeable and it sticks out pretty far. I found the license plate holder covered up the state label of my plate and stuck out too far (camera was beyond the frame of my car) so I used the 2nd mount it includes which can attach to the plastic area over my plate. But even that, because of the mounting bracket requiring space above and behind the camera, sticks out like a sore thumb and still sits the camera beyond the bumper. As in, if someone parallel parks and gives my car a "bumper kiss" (as they call it when parking here in NYC), I have no doubt it will damage the camera as it hits there before it touches my bumper. As you can see in the included picture, bumper kisses are common here.
I turned the camera down so it is at least not sticking out past the bumper, but more in line with it now. I still get a good enough view thanks to how wide the camera is, but I wish I could position the camera better with more choice. I'm forced to use it like this or risk damaging the camera.
2) The picture quality is just OK. The older camera I'm replacing may have only been 100 degrees and not wide enough, but the quality of the image was superior. This one looks more like an old cell phone in color reproduction and smoothness. That's ok, it does the job I guess, but the old one was more pleasant to look at, especially at night. This works well enough at night, but my old one spoiled me because I know it could be better.

All in all, its a decent product that honestly gets the job done. But I wish it had better ways to mount it directly to the car in a way that takes up less space / looks sleeker / doesn't protrude, and that the camera image quality was a little bit better, especially in low light. But it'll do the trick if you want a cheap wide angle.

title: Decent mid range USB 3 stick
text:
This seems like a decent mid-range USB stick. It's faster than some other USB 3 sticks, but not as fast as the NVME drive based ones. Speeds seem about what I expected for the price range and claims from the manufacturer.
It feels pretty solid too, metal body instead of cheap and plastic. The storage capacity is of a useful size, I'd say this is a recommendable product.

title: Really solid for the money, good value compared to Sony WH-1000
text:
There's a lot that I like about these Philips headphones. All the classic features you'd expect from a higher-end over-the-ear style wireless headset are there, including support for an optional 3.5mm jack with included cable in the box, and they even threw in an airplane adapter and carrying case.
It's got soft ear cups and padded head bar, and a pretty awesome NC system. Here's the thing: I own a pair of Sony WH-1000 headphones so I was expecting to be somewhat spoiled and biased about the sound quality and build. And I am. The Sonys are still some of the best and the standard by which I judge other headphones in this style. BUT... at the time of this review, the price of this Philips product is less than half of what I paid for my Sony. Are the Sonys better? A little. Are they twice the price better? NO WAY. This is far better quality in sound and build than the cheapo bluetooth headphones, and if I didn't try them side by side with my Sony, it'd be hard to tell them apart. The feature set are similar, including the app control which actually made the phone really easy to pair as well.
One thing I actually really like about these is that there are more buttons than the Sony alternative. A dedicated button for mute, a dedicated button for noise cancellation, and of course power/pairing. But there are also touch sensitive controls on the ear cups, which I did not realize at first. I have mixed feelings about touch controls, I feel like they are easy to accidentally trigger, but so far it's actually been pretty good.
I think for the current asking price of around 150, the pros are solid enough to be worth recommending.

title: Tiny sound, but convinient
text:
These are great for removing the clutter that comes from traditional PC speakers. Personally, I'm tired of the mess that my home editing/gaming PC speakers take: A right and left speaker with a cable connecting them, a cable with a 3.5mm jack to go into the back of the computer case, and then another cable to go into the outlet for power. It's just a mess of wires and really makes me miss my old Macintosh from the early 90s that had integrated speakers inside the case.
I was thinking about trying to wire up a DIY dynamic speaker inside my case, when I discovered this listing on Amazon. It essentially is a USB sound card built into a small stereo speaker array. All powered off the USB port. So you need one, single USB cable, no multiple wires back and forth, and no more giant wall adapter on my power strip! It actually is pretty cute on my desk, doesn't take up a lot of space, and has an integrated volume dial. Awesome!
The only catch? The sound isn't so great. And when that's the purpose of the product, you have to be a little upset about it. I have portable Bluetooth speakers that sound much clearer than this. It's not that it doesn't get loud (it totally can), but the clarity is lacking, as is the bass (in a major way). It's hard to describe- it's louder than a phone, but still has that tin sounding quality I'd expect from a speakerphone. Not exactly high quality. I wouldn't watch a movie or use it for atmospheric game soundscapes, but if you have a home PC and don't want to wear headphones or clutter up your desk with lots of wires, the single USB connection is pretty nice.

title: Stop shooting with umbrellas and get this!
text:
I have some studio strobes with standard mounts like this I set up for a client taking product photos, but when I was budgeting it out, all the money went into the backgrounds and strobes, so we have been using umbrella diffusers. I hate umbrellas as you can't really control light as well, but usually softboxes are pricey. Well, I'm happy to say there is a cheap alternative and this product is it! It works really well, attaches to the standard Bowens mount and gives me beautifully soft light without spill.
It also works great on my Godox video monolight (also with a Bowens mount). This is not the same build quality as a more expensive one, but I'm more than happy to recommend this to anyone still shooting with umbrellas.

title: Seems really cool, if it will fit your dashboard (MEASURE FIRST, from the MIDDLE!)
text:
[[VIDEOID:2e1e48afafe7261f888f4fa063c2dbdd]] I really like the fact that this is a larger display than the 7 inchers you usually find in car radio replacements. That's what initially attracted me to trying this unit, since my Toyota Solara's double din dash kit has tons of unused space to the right and left of the faceplate. The problem?
It's *slightly* too large vertically, and is centered instead of starting at the bottom. To explain: I measured my dashboard and realized it would stick up past the top and partially cover the bottom of my hazard button as well as the vents, but that's livable. I don't use the hazard button very often, and the vents can be adjusted away from it. The problem is, it sticks out both top AND bottom, with the middle double-din sized part being centered in the display. That downward part concerns me because of my ability to turn the knobs for the climate control underneath. I wish that the unit started at the bottom of the double-din space and only went UP only. That's what I was expecting it to do, the way modern car radios have displays that stick out vertically but are flush with the dash underneath. I'm not ok with it rubbing against the climate knobs.
I took a video of trying to install it on my dash kit before I gave up and put it back in the box. I DID hook it up to 12v power just to see it turn on and make sure everything works, and I have to say it's a shame because this LOOKS really cool. I love that it runs Android and has all the customization I'd crave from a system like that. Android Auto is a treat too. I didn't hook up any speakers so I can't vouch for sound quality and I can't vouch for the longevity of the unit since I didn't actually keep it in my car, but it looks like a pretty good value for the money if this fits your dash layout.
