I was hoping to consolidate all of those into one unit, and this really COULD have been the one to bring them all together if it was designed better.

title: Great for splitting a source to two monitors
text:
I'm occasionally asked to set up 2 projectors at small events (engagement parties, bar mitzvahs, guest speaker lectures, etc). This is a great and inexpensive little tool to take my media and duplicate it to two identical HDMI signals. The only issue is then that HDMI doesn't travel well beyond 25-50', but that's a limitation of the standard and cable, and not this adapter. If you're looking to use this for something like I describe, it definitely works and will do the trick, but do yourself a favor and also get either an HDMI-to-SDI adapter or HDMI-to-CAT5/6 adapter, as those will both allow much longer runs of cable without signal degradation.
If you just want to split into two signals in the same room (such as, projector and TV), this should work a treat.

title: Battery lasted 18 months, now swollen and dead.
text:
EDIT: Replacement battery went belly-up this June, about 18 months after installation. This was the second one the seller had given me. At least my daughter got a year and a half of use out of it before it stopped charging or turning on. I went to go remove it and oh my goodness, this battery was SWOLLEN. I'm glad I removed it when I did because I know what happens to Li-po batteries if this thing had burst. To be fair, she went away to camp and left it plugged in, so I'm not sure if this would have happened under normal usage. Be careful with your batteries and treat them well.
I don't think I can reach out to the seller now for a replacement 1.5 years later, but I wish I could say it lasted longer than that. Original review was 4 stars, reducing it now to 2 because the swollen part is alarming and I shouldn't have to swap batteries every other year like this.

ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW:
It seems that the battery I received was not actually the stated capacity, after a few charging cycles is claimed to only have around 79% of it's life remaining. The good news is that the seller is excellent and replaced it ASAP. The new I have is still around 85% capacity, but to be honest for the price I'm happy with it. My old battery was much worse, so this is a major improvement and I can't complain much for the price.
If you want something closer to the original battery, you'll have to easily pay twice as much if not more. This is a decent value for what it is, and customer support really stands behind the product.

title: Works well in my Mid size tower
text:
This fan is a pretty standard size and fits into the places it is meant to. It has directional arrows for rotation and air flow to make sure you install it correctly, and it comes with a metal grill to attach to the outside if desired. I wanted to use this as an intake fan behind the front grill so I didn't need that. It also comes with pass-through bolts to go through the fan and attach on the other side of the case with nuts. In my case, the front fans need a proprietary screw type so I had to find something else to secure it with.
After that, it seems to do what it is supposed to do as expected. The only caveat is that I wish the cable were a little bit longer. The front mounting brackets are a bit of a stretch to reach the motherboard's fan plugs, I had to unravel the wires from the side of the fan so that it came out of the middle in order to reach. If you have a smaller case or are using it near your motherboard, you should be fine.

title: Sounds and looks great, but defaults to bluetooth
text:
I wanted to use these to replace some older bookshelf speakers in our living room, currently connected to a streaming Alexa-enabled player. I like that these have two auxiliary inputs so technically I can attach it to our audio system and ALSO something like our home theater receiver, and occasionally use Bluetooth to connect to a phone when needed. These are much nicer looking and sound really good compared to my old speakers, however I'm rather annoyed that everytime they power up it defaults to Bluetooth again. My audio system gets shut off at night and turned back on in the morning via a switch. I really wish the speakers would go back to the last setting used, or perhaps have a way to change the default. As it is right now, every morning we have to find the remote and press Line 1 to hear the music, despite the player trying to play. Even worse, if we can't find the remote, there's NO WAY to change settings on speaker itself. This just seems like an unnecessary extra step and it has made some of my family members prefer the old speakers instead, sadly.
It is very unfortunate because these otherwise have the potential to be so incredible! But this is a usability fail. It should at the very least recall the last mode used.

title: Working great so far!
text: I used this on my first PC build in decades. I was a little nervous because last time I did this, cooling systems were a lot less complicated than they are now! I wasn't sure if the system I got would come with its own paste (turns out it does), but this brand came very highly recommended by master builders and for the price I figured I couldn't go wrong with it. I skipped the generic stuff that came in my cooler's packaging and used this instead. So far so good- I'm using this with an i7 9700k, and I'm slowly experimenting with overclocking. I haven't performed a high CPU stress test yet, but so far the system is running well and most importantly, running cool!

title: Great for adding more monitors to my setup
text:
I recently built a new PC and wanted to connect multiple monitors. this cable is great because it supports the DVI connection directly on the back of my 2nd monitor and the Display port on my graphics card without the need for any other adapters in the middle.
Previously I had looked into getting a display port to HDMI or display port to DVI and then running a cable from there, but this is just straight end-to-end exactly what I needed. Makes for a much cleaner setup with less connections to go wrong.
Very pleased with this cable and would recommend it!

title: Great way to connect to a TV
text:
I wanted to use a TV as a second monitor but only have display port connections available. This adapter worked perfectly, as it gave me access to the HDMI cable I needed coming from the back of the TV. Does exactly what I expect it to, no hassle no fuss.
I recommend it if you are looking to do the same or similar.

title: SLOG users, rejoice!
text:
This is more than just an external monitor, it is a near-essential piece of filmmaking gear, especially if shooting with small cameras like the Sony A7 series for video.
Not only can you pinch to zoom in/out in real time to check focus on a nice sized monitor (which is easier and better to judge focus than the camera), but it supports LUTS both built in and CUSTOM via an SD card. That means if you wanted to shoot in SLOG II or III, for example, you don't have to sit there staring at the flat image and wondering if the final will look good enough to use or not. This will show you a real time LUT application to judge your image with.
Granted, the color and quality might not be on the same scale as something like Small HD or a modern Atomos, but this is a literal fraction of the cost of those.
Also comes with an L bracket to mount from the side of the monitor instead of the bottom. Why? Because then you can rotate the display to see up or down for optimal viewing angles. Also supports power out which can feed into a dummy battery and power both your camera and the monitor on the same set of batteries.
Speaking of batteries, it works great with standard Sony camcorder style batteries. Note that it does not come with any, however if you work in freelance video you probably have NP-F style batteries lying around already for things like LED lights. Just be careful not to overload your hotshoe's weight capacity by using an F970 sized battery on this with the bracket and throwing it on top of your camera. Those mounts can break. I'd prefer to mount this to a cage or at least a flash bracket so that it is attached on the bottom instead of the top.

title: An excellent first generation product from Nikon
text:
Full disclosure: I'm a Sony E camera fan and use them for work, so giving this Nikon 5 stars means a LOT from me.
I was skeptical about Nikon's entry into the mirrorless camera world, since in the past they saved their higher end specs for DSLRs, and didn't take the mirrorless market seriously (*cough* Nikon 1 *cough*). However the full frame Z cameras got a lot of positive acclaim, and this Z50, their first APSC crop sized mirrorless, is a heck of a lot better than any first generation product has any business being!
First let's talk about ergonomics- the camera feels great, not point-and-shoot tiny in your hands. Definitely smaller and lighter than a DSLR, but more substantial than a phone, as a camera should be. It has a touch screen, which is AWESOME for touch-focus and really helps avoid the "how to I change that setting" learning curve- generally, just press on the icon and you can change the setting. Yet it doesn't RELY on the touch screen, there are plenty of physical buttons and dials, many of which are customizable and can be assigned to functions you need more often. Essentially, this is a camera that's got more than one way to do most things and therefore will adapt to YOUR workflow rather than force you to learn its own. The screen can also tilt up or down, and lets you flip it around on the bottom to see selfie-style if desired. This is one area that seems a little odd for me- other cameras like the Sony A5100 flip UPWARDS, so you can see over the camera if taking a self portrait. Or the Panasonic GH series articulates sideways. This, only flips DOWN. Which means if mounted to a tripod, you can't see the display at all. That is alright since honestly most of the higher end full frame cameras don't even let you flip the display around at all these days. The fact that you can, even if in a silly orientation, is better than nothing and a welcome feature.
Image quality seems pretty great, the kit lenses are adequate. I really liked the 50-250, as 16-50 with variable aperture feels very limited in creativity (however this lens is necessary as a "walkaround" standard zoom length). To be fair, I'm spoiled by my pro constant f-stop lenses that I use on my other cameras, so I'm rarely impressed by the performance of budget friendly kit options. I'll admit that for kit lenses these really perform remarkably well, but I'm hoping Nikon rolls out some awesome affordable Z-mount DX lenses soon. Cropping in to view pixels at 100% zoom size, the image holds up and seems reasonably sharp. Nikon colors are there as well, which are admittedly excellent. As with any new system, there aren't a lot of lenses available yet unless you adapt from other mounts. Nikon has F-mount adapters for native adaption, and I've read good things about third party adapters for other camera types as well (Canon, etc... I've even seen a Sony EF adapter for sale!). Sadly, I don't have access to any adapters at the moment, so I'm stuck judging imaging quality by the included kits for now.
Now for video, this gets even more interesting. Nikon has done a bang-up job supporting popular frame rates and resolutions (4k at 24p? Hello filmmakers!). In my tests, the quality of the video was very clean and sharp. I haven't noticed much in the way of moire or aliasing yet, and it has a clean HDMI out option as well if you want to record externally or view on a bigger monitor while filming. Unlike certain other cameras (like the Sony a6300), it is able to keep the rear display ON while also using the external monitor / recorder, and also recording internally at 4k. Other prosumer crop cameras have turned off the internal display when doing all of those things at once. It does support a microphone jack which means you can use this for recording interviews, however it is missing a headphone jack to monitor the audio levels. That's a huge omission if you wanted to use this as a semi-pro video making tool.
Thankfully, I found a workaround: If you get a cheap HDMI monitor (they have for around $100 that can attach to the hotshoe mount), they often have audio jacks. I happen to have a couple by Feelworld that do exactly that, and I was able to plug headphones in and hear the audio while in recording mode live. Well, semi-live at least. When recording 4k, there was a brief delay in the A/V playback, I'm guessing because the throughput required for 4K creates some latency. But the point is that you COULD hear it, and therefore make sure the volumes are appropriate and audible, and thereby making it possible to use the Z50 as a more pro level tool.
All in all, this is an excellent entry into the market by Nikon. Whether you are a beginner looking to eventually start using semi-pro tools or a seasoned pro looking for a budget friendly walkaround or B-cam, this is a very impressive value.

title: Better than Amazon Basics version!
text:
This works great to split the audio signal out of an HDMI feed- we use it to send audio to our surround sound system while using our home projector for an immersive theater experience. We used to have an Amazon Basics version of the same thing, but it did not work very well- sometimes the Amazon version would need to be set via a button to change 5.1 or 2 channel or passthrough sound since it wouldn't always remember the setting after a power down, but this unit has a physical switch so it will be hardcoded upon power on. Also sometimes with the Amazon version the sound wouldn't pass through to the video device (it would always send sound out the analog audio jacks, but only sometimes also out the HDMI- it is supposed to do both). This one seems to consistently do both, as it should.
I'd like to also add that THIS COMES WITH EVERYTHING! It has Two HDMI cables, a digital audio cable, an analog cable, etc, ALL IN THE BOX. A fantastic package that does exactly what you want.

title: It works- sorta
text:
I got this specifically to use with my Amazon Fire Stick 4k. I have a wireless media remote keyboard that I used to use with an HTPC that needs a USB dongle, and wanted to also take advantage of the wired Ethernet jack I had previously installed by my TV (wired is always more reliable for streaming in our experience). This device seemed perfect! It connects to the power socket of the Fire stick and offers a USB hub with ethernet jack.
The problem is, the ethernet jack doesn't seem to be recognized by the Firestick at all! I know what it is supposed to do when it recognizes a network jack, but the option to use the wired internet simply doesn't show up- it doesn't know or acknowledge it is there!
On the upside, at least the USB sockets work, so I was able to use my media remote keyboard. In fact, this device comes in two parts- one is a USB host plug that allows a single USB connection while passing power, and a standard USB hub + ethernet that attaches to that. In all honestly, if I just want to use the USB media remote, I don't need the hub... I can plug it directly into the host port without the hub attached. Its a shame because I really want ethernet. So it only half works.

title: Does the trick
text:
These are the large F960/970 size batteries, the biggest standard Sony NP sized batteries you can get them in. I use these extensively to power lights, recorders, monitors... they are the single most versatile sized battery a video freelancer can have on them.
I've used many brands of this battery, from Neewer, Wasabi, Power2000, Great Video Maker, etc, and they all seem pretty competitive to each other. Ironically, the only brand I HAVEN'T used is the authentic Sony batteries. This brand seems right up there with them so far. The batteries last a long time and are very large physically. On the flip side, they come with only a very basic charger, which anyone using these probably has plenty of already. So it shouldn't be any surprise that it takes hours to fully charge one of these (I usually leave them overnight, I don't know how long they actually take but it definitely seems to be more than a few). This is not the fault of the charger, this is normal for a battery this size.

title: It is OK for what it is.
text:
I got excited to see one of these small portable LED style ones that actually had a decent native resolution (most of them can accept 1080p, but are in reality only 800x600 resolution, or sometimes worse... 640x480!). This one is actually capable of displaying 720p of real dot resolution, which should make it at least as sharp as my Viewsonic and other traditional HD projectors. Ok, perhaps I'm spoiled, but I'm comparing this to our Viewsonic 720p projector that, to be fair cost me 3-4x as much.
And for the most part, it DOES work, however there are some caveats to its use. First of all, it doesn't seem as sharp as my 720p projector, even though it should have the requisite amount of dots. It's OK, its definitely better than the cheap 600p projectors, but something just isn't quite there when comparing side by side. It also doesn't get all that bright, but I suppose that's expected from the LED tech being used. You'll need black out shades or use it only during the night. Then there's the color- it isn't great. It works, but it has a cheap color reproduction that looks kind of flat and lifeless. Dark scenes sort of all blend together and become nearly impossible to see. It lacks the vibrancy of even an inexpensive television from decades ago. It gets the job done, but hardly the "theater experience" if you've been waiting to see that latest action/vfx film the way it was intended. It will look better on your TV at home, the only thing this has going for it is the large projection experience. For example, if you just want to give your kids a backyard movie night and don't care that the color and detail won't be as great as your indoor system, it will do the job on the cheap. I personally would not give up my mid-range projector for this one.
One thing that I found particularly annoying is that rather than the optical zoom and focus dials found on usual projectors, there is only a focus and tilt dial. No zoom. That means you have to physically move the projector closer or further to get it to reach the correct size you are shooting for. That actually got in the way of using it in a couple of specific places my other projectors can be used at optimal sizes.
That's not to say it gets everything wrong- I DO like that it is small and light and can even be turned on it's back to aim at the ceiling. That's something my big projector can't do, due to the airflow and cable management sticking out the rear. It also has a standard 1/4" 20 threaded tripod mounting point, so you can place this onto a tripod and get maximum mounting freedom. That will come in handy as I've always wanted to watch a movie in bed on the ceiling. But otherwise, don't think this projector will be as good as the other mid-rangers out there. This is still very much a low end projector. You'll have to spend at least 2-3x as much to get a decent home theater style experience, and much more if you want a high end one that will handle FHD/4k to get the real deal. This is more of a specialty use item.

title: Works great to connect my Macbook to my TV
text: I have a late 2011 Macbook pro that I'd like to occasionally use with a monitor/TV. Rather than getting a display port to HDMI adapter on the end of a plug, this is a straight male-to-male end 6 foot cable with display port on one side and HDMI on the other. So you can go straight from the laptop right into the TV. Worked perfectly, and couldn't be happier with it.

title: Great for adapting newer tech with analog displays
text: We have a minivan with a DVD entertainment system pre-installed. It predates the HDMI standard, so there are just RCA analog inputs in the back of the van. Since DVDs are pretty much obsolete, using this adapter we are able to plug in a laptop, raspberry pi or other digital video player to the car's system. I like that it is powered by USB, it is a convenient source of power especially when you don't have access to outlets (like in a car!). But you have to be careful about ground loop feedback. When powering it off a laptop, and the laptop is charging in the car, it can create either an audible hum and/or visual static distortion pattern on the video feed. This is common in DC circuits that share ground when working with analog equipment, unfortunately. I'm not sure if there's much that can be done about it other than try to run off batteries as often as possible (with this converter attached to a USB battery bank, the laptop on its own power, and the car running its own 12v DC). I have an older similar product looks almost identical that does the same thing so I'm guessing that's just a side effect of working with RCA inputs instead of digital ones.

title: Great for adapting HDMI out for professional runs
text:
This is a great tool for those who need to use prosumer equipment in more professional environments. HDMI is great at what it does, but it has limitations. Long cable runs and many professional live hubs and recorders require the more robust SDI cable format. I've found myself working live camera feeds, etc, more than once with prosumer grade cameras and laptops that needed to interface with our SDI equipment. Having these available means I can use SDI outputs even if my source doesn't have an SDI port. And while at first I wanted to remove a star for the lack of a proper power adapter (it just comes with a USB plug), I realize now this is a blessing. If I want to run it off a laptop, I have a power supply immediately available without another wall plug. If I need a wall plug, any standard USB charger will do, and those are plentiful.
Solid metal body seems durable, kudos to Amazon Basics for offering a good alternative for such a useful tool.

title: Very cool!! But not without caveats...
text:
The Portal is sort of like an Echo Show but with different strengths and weaknesses. There is SO MUCH I could say about this device, some good and some bad, but I'll try to stick to the more important points here.
The killer feature, as you may know from their ads, as the way it can automatically zoom in/out and follow faces in a video call. So essentially, you can move around a room hands-free and it will find you and make sure you're in the shot. It's like having your own personal camera man on call.
In my experience with it so far, this worked fairly well. Moving left or right, the camera followed me. If more people enter the shot, it will zoom out to get them all in. It isn't without limitations however, and sometimes you'll move too far and it can't see you. Other times it got confused and lost me (if I move out of the frame and back in, that usually fixed it). For the most part, it worked as expected.
The sound is actually EXCELLENT considering this is the Mini edition. I was expecting the sound to be more like the Echo Dot, but this has a very large speaker on the rear which is able to drive very impressively deep bass without even approaching max volume. So that was a pleasant surprise.
While it has its own "Hey Portal" voice commands, it ALSO comes with Amazon Alexa built in. That's where it sort of starts acting like a Facebook-branded Echo Show, playing music, announcements, showing you answers to questions, turning on/off digital things, etc. All the things you want Alexa to do. However, I was sad to find that it isn't considered an Echo device for certain Alexa features, such as multi-room music groups, the Ring doorbell, and probably other Alexa Skills that aren't supported on non-Amazon hardware. So you can't really replace an Alexa Show with this if you need those features.
Now, some things that are better than the Echo Show: PRIVACY. I know, this is Facebook we're talking about, but I really like that they included a tab to disable the camera (by covering it up, not just turning it off), microphone, or both. It's like they realized that someone was going to complain they don't want Facebook recording them in their living room and thought ahead to add that. The Amazon devices with cameras don't have a dedicated cover built in. Then there's video calling to people OTHER THAN OWNERS OF ANOTHER DEVICE. The latest Show devices from Amazon have cameras too, but you can only call other Echo Shows or phones with the Alexa app running. The Portal can call Facebook and Whatsapp users, which means I can actually reach other people I'd want to chat with. This isn't a perfect implementation either, however... For Whatsapp, it essentially uses Whatsapp's web functionality behind the scenes to connect to your account. If you use Whatsapp web on your computer, it will log you out of the Portal and you'll need to log back in again after using it. This is an unnecessarily silly extra step. I use Whatsapp web a lot, so we ended up using my wife's Whatsapp account on the Portal to call our family and friends so we wouldn't have to keep logging out and in.
Then there's media like Youtube- much like the Amazon Echo devices, Google has decided not to allow an official Youtube app for the Portal either. However, there IS a browser, and you can go to Youtube on it. This makes for an awkward user interface (and not just because you can't control it with your voice), but once the video is up it works fine. It not only plays beautifully full screen, but you can even go back to the home screen and it will continue playing as a picture-in-picture overlay which can be moved around the screen by dragging. That's pretty neat. It's almost like they tried to support Youtube as much as possible without actually having an official interface to abide by Google's rules.
Other fun features include Facebook games like Draw Something, Chess, Super Baseball Batting Derby, etc, which you can play against other friends on Facebook or Portal devices. Then there's a bunch of photo effects which are really fun Snapchat-style filters that follow your face in augmented reality-style real time. These features can be used not only in the Photobooth app, but also on ANY call with the device. Then there's my favorite fun feature: Story Time! This feature is sort of like the snapchat photobooth AR-style effects mentioned above, however you read a story and it will animate effects over your face to illustrate as you go. This can be done on the Story Time app on the device locally or in a call to another person. My kids actually really LOVE that feature, and my 2 year old likes to read along with me when we do it. I'll admit they are very cute and sometimes I've laughed out loud when I didn't expect what happens next in the animation being done to me.

Honestly, as an Alexa alternative to an Echo Show, it is close but not quite a replacement. As a video chat device, it is better but only if your contacts are on Facebook or Whatsapp. And even then, Whatsapp is only good if you don't use Whatsapp Web. I'd consider it a 3 star device for those caveats, however the Story Time feature as well as the camera that follows you is really quite cool. Add that they considered your privacy with the flap cover and I have to give this at least 4 stars. It really has so much going for it, and I'm hoping they can iron out some of the software kinks to make it even better in the future.

title: Great for hauling my gear around!
text:
Let me start off by saying I work in freelance video and I love how much I can fit inside this case! I've been using a Pelican 1510 as my go-to travel carrier, so that's mostly what I'm comparing this to. For starters, this is a longer case so in addition to my cameras, lenses, batteries and other accessories, it has a long open sleeve that can even fit a light stand or small tripod! For extra versatility, the whole interior can actually be pulled out (it has its own handle straps if you want to use it as its own carrier), which then frees up the ample storage space inside the case as a separate giant unit (see pictures to illustrate). There are also plenty of pockets on the inside, as well as the outside and front of the case. Of course, for a case this size there is the requisite wheels and carrying handle.
The only things I like better about my Pelican case, however, are the toughness and waterproofing. This bag comes with a rain cover which you can keep inside the case, however I don't like the idea of having to carry around a cover inside the bag, then take it out and put it on if it starts raining. The Pelican cases are air tight by simply closing them, no rain cover needed. The Pelican cases also are tough enough that they can be stacked under other equipment, thrown into a corner, sat on, stood on, etc, and 99% of the time come out unscathed. That's more than I can say for this bag. I bring this bag on gigs that I'm not worried about those things happening, because I can fit what I normally take in 3 separate bags into just this one. You could get a Pelican style case in this size, however it would cost quite a bit more than the asking price of this one. I think for the price this is a great tool to keep your stuff organized and ready to go whenever you are!

title: Does exactly what it is supposed to!
text:
I go through these quite often, sometimes attaching a laptop to a sound system for presentation, or when plugging in modern 3.5mm monitoring headphones to older mixer equipment. The ones I have tend to fall apart eventually after a lot of repeated use, but this seems to be holding up so far!
Sound transmission seems solid, and they have been holding up well so far, so I'd say this gets 5 stars for being exactly what it is supposed to be.

title: Fantastic, although the range might be a bit exaggerated
text:
So many things I love about these. These appear to be as rugged and well built as I'd expected from a brand name like Cobra. I love that they include a flashlight, and especially that the units are USB rechargeable! Such a convenient way to power things these days, I wish more electronics ditched the AAA batteries thing like this!
The range might be a bit exaggerated, but to be fair I live in a very wooded area surrounded by hills and valleys. I found that around my neighborhood it worked great but if I went a few miles away, the sound was mostly just unintelligible crackling. We could still hear that someone was trying to say something, but that's it.
On the flip side, we started hearing someone else's conversation the next day... we were just testing it so we didn't bother changing the default channel, and it turns out someone else must have gotten some talkies on the same default frequencies. I have no idea how close they were, but my kids pointed out that someone was talking and we didn't press any buttons and then we all heard it. "Dad? Do I need to come in? I'm playing outside", and then a few seconds later "ok, but don't ride into the street". Then some clicks of singing and other noises- clearly someone else communicating with THEIR kid was coming through to us. I pressed the talk button and said "Hi- this is the default frequency for these walkie talkies, so we should both probably change them!" and then promptly picked another channel. So, that's kind of neat because I have no idea where these other people were, we live in a pretty urban area with houses spread out and I know it wasn't someone from my block. Yet we heard them clear as day. So, I'd say these are pretty good at what they do, but maybe don't rely on the full extent of their listed range.

title: Looks nice, works well, but not full dual?
text:
I really like how well this fits in the the car's DC port- when pushed all the way in, it almost looks like a factory installed USB port that came with the vehicle. The USB type C port did a great job delivering power to devices that support rapid QC charging, however when I plugged a second cable into the USB A port, the second phone did not use Quick Charge. I'm guessing it can only support the high output on one port at a time, which is understandable but still somewhat disappointing.
Aside from that, I do like the way it glows and fits and it still works great especially if only using one plug at a time.

title: Great for video accessories, but not the camera
text: I wish I had gotten something like this sooner. I work in video and always find myself needing to carry around accessories like batteries and memory cards to easily swap out when covering live events. Rather than cram them into my pockets or wear a special cargo jacket, I can sling this attached to a shoulder strap and carry around plenty of batteries, memory cards, spare chargers, and even some smaller mirrorless lenses. Larger DSLR lenses would be tight and I'm not sure why they depict a full sized camera with lens attached- there's no way this is tall enough to fit that. When you see it in person, it's laughable that they implied you can. So removing  a star for being a little overambitious in their advertised capability. But for carrying around other accessories that I'd need WITH my camera, I love it!

title: So much better than my Ronin S!
text:
I own a DJI Ronin S which I use with my Sony A7 series cameras (an A7S and A7Rii). It worked well enough, but after trying this Crane 3 Lab, I'm blown away and ready to sell my Ronin for this.
For starters, I love the ergonomics of the extra handle. Being able to hold onto it with 2 hands and shift from the handle to the pistol grip makes using this thing far more stable than trying holding just the pistol with both hands. It also makes it easy to pass and shift to a low angle mode, as well as seamlessly pass it to another person easily for those really impossible looking tracking shots (thought a window, down a staircase, etc). I'm also really impressed with the buttons and controls- if you've got a USB cable controlling your camera, there's a lot more you can easily access right from the gimbal without touching the camera than you can with the DJI Ronin S. With the Sony cameras, unfortunately, you can't control the focus motor of an automatic lens with the follow focus wheel... that's a limitation of the camera since Sony doesn't have that protocol in their USB remote interface. Other features work perfectly, however, and I've been told that other cameras like Canon and Nikon work with the focus control as well (this is something I'm hoping Sony changes in the future, but for now I'll just rely on auto-focus during gimbal shots).
Another HUGE improvement over other stabilizers is the ability to LOCK the axis motors in place. This is a fantastic tool to help when balancing (you can lock the other 2 axis and work on balancing them one by one, rather than holding the other positions in place as you work backwards like on the Ronin), and its also great to lock it in place when you are powered down and carrying it around- I've found that when taking a break with my Ronin, it is always awkward to walk around with it since the camera can flop and swing around as I walk. The Crane 3 doesn't have that problem if you just lock the motors in place with a little red switch.
Honestly, I wish I would have waited just a little bit longer before buying my Ronin S so that I could see how much better this is. The app is honestly just OK, I've heard people say they like the DJI app better and I would probably have to agree with that, but this just does everything else so much better that it I'd still say it is worth it in the end. The crane 2 is easier to balance in my experience, more forgiving (less crazy vibrating when the gimbals shifts out of balance), has better features and ergonomics and overall just seems to do a better job.
I STRONGLY recommend it if you are shopping around between those two options.

title: Phenomenal cosmic powers, in an itty bitty living space.
text:
This little drive really impressed me. I work with large media files for broadcast, and always find myself looking for more hard drives to transport and backup. I usually get the larger desktop style drives because I was always under the impression that you get more capacity and speed for your money, with the caveat that you need additional sources of power (USB alone does not supply enough power to run a desktop drive motor reliably). But this little fellow not only looks like a shrunken version of one of my desktop profile Seagate drives (see picture, same pattern and everything), it offers the same 4TB capacity AND the ability to be powered directly from a USB port without additional power . And while the random access speeds aren't quite as zippy as a desktop one (see attached benchmark), the sequential speeds are actually HIGHER than my desktop sized equivalent. Thinking about the physics of it, that sorta makes sense- the physical bits of storage are closer together because it is a smaller sized platter, but the ability of the read head to move around and hit random access data points might be limited to a slower speed to fit this size.
If you're a numbers guy, here's the breakdown:
This drive:
Seq Read/Write: 144.2 / 101.2
512k: 66.86 / 66.46
4k: 1.069 / 5.596
4K QD32: 0.448 / 5.761

My older larger (but same capacity) desktop version:
seq: 98.83 / 77.26
512k: 157.9 / 51.31
4k: 1.489 / 6.422
4k QD32: 0.537 / 6.519

Obviously neither can compete with an SSD which easily smokes any of these drives in speed AND in energy efficiency, but this is an incredible bang-for-your-buck storage option if you need a lot of storage space, and it seems to compete fairly well with it's larger desktop sibling. And possibly best of all, it doesn't need another source of power off your outlets.

title: Love the built in USB
text: I'm tired of power strips that get filled needlessly with USB wall warts for all our 5V devices. This power strip offers the standard 6-outlet configuration but offers two 2.4a USB ports to free up more space on the 110v plugs for higher demand items. This is a great and efficient solution to a problem that is becoming more and more common as USB ports become standard. The build quality is great for the money, I'm very impressed with mine so far. Recommend it!

title: Great for hiding along baseboards!
text:
I built a home office a couple of years ago and ran a network cable during construction where I thought my desk would go. Turns out I like it better facing a different direction, so now I'm on a wall without an Ethernet jack. Well, that's where this fantastic flat Cat 7 rated cable comes in! I love that it is flat and white so it can be cleanly mounted along the baseboards. You can barely notice it if you don't already know it is there. I like that it also comes with mounting hardware (plastic clips with nails) to help hold the cable in place along its run, as well as a velcro strap if you want to use it as a portable cable and not permanently mount it somewhere.
Connection seems to work as expected, I don't have the equipment to test high LAN speeds or if it really lives up to the Cat 7 spec claims, but for regular networking use it seems great so far! I might try to get something similar to run behind our TV for a stronger steaming media connection.

title: Works well as a way to get analog out of your HDMI
text:
I'm running a 1080p projector for our home entertainment system, and have a high quality decades-old analog stereo system for sound. Without this Audio Extractor device, I used to be limited to source devices that let me separate the video from the audio (Fire TV box and other devices that offer both analog stereo and HDMI video simultaneously) since the sound has to go one way and the video feed another.
This device opens up possibilities such as more modern equipment that does away with analog connections entirely. A Fire TV Stick 4k for example, or Raspberry Pi board (yes, technically the Pi has analog outputs, but they are subpar and not recommended for high quality audio). I'm very happy with this device and the opportunities it opens for me. It works well for me with the 2ch setting and my equipment. I can't vouch for 5.1 as my system doesn't support that, nor can I vouch for 4k as my system doesn't handle that either. But so far it has worked well sending a stereo analog audio feed somewhere other than my projector when needed.

title: LOOKS LIKE NEW!
text:
I got mine from Omega Distribution USA, and I have to say, I'm IMPRESSED! This thing looks and acts like brand new. I've bought good condition "refurbished" handsets before, but this is something special. I don't know where they found a V20 in such condition, with a battery that seems to be holding its original charge like this. In fact, it even seems to come with the original Nougat firmware- usually a phone that has been used recently would have been upgraded to Oreo already.
Only problem is that I was looking for a version that would work with T-mobile, and while this handset is unlocked from Verizon, it doesn't work as well as an actual T-mobile branded would be (that's the H918 model). So sadly, I have to return this gem of a phone and get the one with the correct bands and software for my needs. Its a shame, I wish I could keep it. But if you're looking for a Verizon model to use with Verizon service, this is EXACTLY what you want for a great price!
As for the V20 as a phone- if you know what it is already, you don't need me to tell you. It's one of the last great super phones ever made. Built like a tank, this phone is easy to repair yourself if need be (no glue or heat gun needed to open it up and, say, slap on some thermal paste to keep the CPU cool under a load)- I've seen walkthroughs to replace cracked screens, camera backs, vibrating motors, etc, that require nothing more than a small screwdriver. If the battery starts to go or you need more power than a stock one offers, you can easily replace them and get BIGGER capacity ones. IR blaster, second screen display (which is really neat!) HDMI out via USB-c, pretty much everything and the kitchen sink is thrown in here. They don't make them like this anymore, folks. This was the last of the greats. That's why people still have and use them in 2019!

title: Gave an aging laptop new life
text:
I have an old latitude laptop from the windows Vista era that was pretty much considered useless. Someone recommended we try installing cloudready to turn it into a Chromebook, and now my kids use it as an internet machine (it's great for Google docs and YouTube as well as light chrome-based gaming).
Of course a machine that old had a battery dead as a doorknob, so they had to keep it plugged in 24/7. They were annoyed because the charging cable is actually quite short, so they were limited in where it could be used. When I saw how cheap this battery is, however, I decided why not splurge and make it into a portable machine again. They are SO happy now with it. If I had known how easy and inexpensive it would be to revive this old machine and make it useful again, I'd have done this a long time ago.
Note, the battery life isn't amazing. But to be fair, I don't recall how long the original would last either.

title: Very full sounding audio
text:
There's a lot I really like about these. Let me start off by pointing out, however, these are NOT USB SPEAKERS. They are simply powered off USB and use a standard headphone jack as the audio input. I have to admit, at first I was taken aback by how small they are, and assumed they must produce weak sound as a result (I'm used to a set of Harmon/Kardon speakers on my desktop which are bigger than these). But despite their size, they actually produce a really great and full sound, with an almost exaggerated stereo effect thanks to individual speakers pointing in different directions.
What I love most about it, however, is that it is USB powered. That means no additional plugs needed on my desktop, and in fact they are fantastic for boosting the audio on a laptop. In the included picture I'm posting with this, I have an old Dell Laptop that my kids use to watch things on, and these sound FAR better than the tiny built in laptop speaker. Since it is USB powered, it can be simply be run directly off the laptop itself, no additional wires or outlets necessary. Put one plug into an available USB slot, the other into the headphone jack. It makes a nice and neat looking portable setup. The thing is, I can't help but wonder why it isn't just a 100% USB sound system? I have a pair of headphones that I love using that are completely digital- it identifies as its own sound card when plugged in and requires only that one USB plug. I sort of assumed that this would be something similar to that and therefore require only that ONE plug to operate. In some cases, the digital sound systems are better than analog plug ones (interference, for example) anyway, so it seems strange to have an analog speaker system powered by a digital USB port. But I guess there can be interesting uses for this too.
For example, a device like an older phone with a headphone jack can connect to this which wouldn't work with USB. Or enhancing the speaker of an Echo Dot and powering it off a dual USB outlet (one for the Dot, the other for the speakers). It is definitely an interesting and useful thing to have around! And for the price, color me impressed!

title: Great for stills (just OK for video use)
text:
It should go without saying that a small tripod like this will hold your camera steady but likely won't be robust enough for use with a fluid head on a video job. I have to say, I was foolish enough to try just that.
I travel with my gear a lot doing video interviews for various projects on location, and a small lightweight tripod to replace my heavy Manfrotto one was a welcome experiment. The Carbon Fiber is really a remarkable material- it weighs almost a fraction of other materials yet is strong enough to support a healthy amount of load. The ball head on this is very easily removed (there is a hex screw holding it in place, once that is removed it is a standard twist-off), and just for kicks I replaced it with my Manfrotto 701 fluid head. It looks kind of funny and oddly out-of-place on such a svelt tripod, but I have to say it was somewhat functional in this setup. I wouldn't recommend it for regular video use, but if I applied some weight (either by holding down the tripod with my other hand or using the hook on the bottom to suspend some sand bags), it did allow the camera to smoothly pan and tilt without a lot of added movement from the legs.
But the strength in this tripod is using it with the included ball head for locked-off camera movement. In other words, when you don't want the camera to move at all. This is great for video interviews (as long as you don't touch the camera!) and especially great for stills, which it was clearly designed to do.
The legs are very easy to extend and fold up in a hurry, which I liked, and of course when completely taken down it is absurdly small. And like I said before, it weighs next to nothing compared to my other tripods. Even though it didn't exactly work the way I was (perhaps foolishly) wanting it to, I'm very pleased with the product otherwise and find myself wanting to take it with me on outings. A fantastic travel sized set of legs for most uses in my opinion.

title: Good if you like wear OS watches - but not a pedometer?
text:
This is a smartwatch running Google's Wear OS. My wife does love it, but we have some reservations with recommending it. Before we go any further, I'd like to point out that most of our qualms have to do with Wear OS itself, so it would be true of any smartwatch running that system.
Let me start off by saying this watch is really very pretty and my wife LOVES the styling of it. Before this she was using more utility-looking fitness bands like those from Xiaomi and FitBit. Her last band, a Mi Band 3, was great for functionality, but she found it ugly. This one she actually really likes, and features like apps, the full color touch screen, custom watch faces, programmable buttons, and dial to control menus really showcases the difference between a proper "smartwatch" and the cheaper activity trackers she is used to. It feels and looks undeniably cool.
But after a week or two of using it, there are some things that we really wish were different about it. For starters, the battery life is pretty terrible. On days that she uses it a lot (like when we first got it), it seems to need to be charged before the day is over. After settling into a routine and changing to a very basic watch face, and also turning off features like wake on wrist detection, we are able to last at least 24 hours to maybe a day-and-a-half on a charge. In other words, even with pretty conservative battery usage, you can easily make it the entire day but still need to charge it daily because it definitely won't make it through that second day. That means when we go away for a weekend, its another charger that has to come with us. I see that this is unfortunately normal for Wear OS devices, as 1-2 days of battery is the average even from other brands running Google's smartwatch OS. To contrast, my wife's Mi Band 3 went for nearly 3 weeks on a charge, which meant she could wear it 24-7 and get the benefits of things like sleep tracking with it. This can't really do that well. To be fair, my friends with other smartwatches (Apple, Samsung, etc) say they have to charge it daily as well, so perhaps this is an expected compromise for users preferring smartwatches to bands and other trackers.
The next thing, and this is sort of a recent sore point it seems, the pedometer and step goals have been replaced with "heart points" thanks to a very new partnership between Google and the American Heart Association. They decided that counting steps isn't good enough, and came up with a different calculation for activity and setting goals for it. This is all fine and good, except that they DON'T HAVE THE OPTION TO SET STEP GOALS. I guess in an effort to get everyone interested in the new system, they are almost trying to hide the pedometer functions of Google Fit. In order to get your steps you have to find them buried in a menu, and there's no current watch face that will show you real-time steps that I could find. Oh, and did I mention you can't set it as a goal anymore? This is very frustrating as my wife and I use steps competitively as do many work place initiatives and similar programs... this is a basic function that EVERY activity tracker lets you do! Everything from the cheapo Chinese trackers to the name brands, to the Apple watches, to even Google Fit as of a few months ago! I looked up ways to bring the pedometer functions back into front and center and found many tirades on the internet from disgruntled users who also wanted the feature back. I get it, the heart points is probably better, but at least let US, as users, choose!
At the end of the day, my wife and I find it very awkward that this higher priced smartwatch, with all of its high end features and wow factors, can't handle the simple things that her cheaper Mi Band did great- the old band showed us her steps on the main display with the time, in real time, and would need to be charged about once monthly. But to be fair, now that she's been spoiled by the style and ability to respond to text messages from the watch (the band only showed them, you couldn't respond to them), she's not planning on going back. I'm hoping that Google's Wear OS addresses some of these issues in the future and/or Fossil themselves address it. They could, for example, design a device with better battery and a custom Fossil watch face that still does step counting. But this doesn't. So for us, the experience doesn't seem to match the price point. IF you like Wear OS and are already aware of its limitations in battery and pedometer, this is a very nice option.

title: Works great to sync audio with DSLR
text:
My job has me working in video with small cameras, and sometimes I need to sync my audio recorder/receiver with a DSLR/DSLM. In my setup, this cable did an admirable job feeding clear audio to my camera from an external source. It seems to have a decent build quality, and the right angle is welcome because it makes it less likely to accidentally get pulled out by a cable tug.
My review is for the 4' length, which in my case is preferred to the longer cable. I'd honestly prefer even a 3' cable, not only is it less messy in my rig but less signal loss/noise attenuation on a shorter run is always preferable when working with recordings. Good value.

title: I like it better than my Logitech
text:
I'll be honest, I was expecting this to be another cheap off-brand mouse. I'm pleasantly surprised at how good it is- It looks pretty great, and rather than being covered in shiny fingerprint-magnet plastic like most cheap mice, a majority of the surface is textured (almost like a rubberized plastic). The USB receiver fits inside the body of the mouse for storage, which is great for travelling with it as I do. I've owned other mice that did that before too (an old Logitech), but unlike that old Logitech, this one uses a built-in rechargeable battery. To be honest, my Logitech mouse was great but after a couple of years the battery started making a bad connection inside (corroded contacts were keeping the battery from working), so I'd have to try to clean it off every few uses on the road to keep it working. With this product however, it seems less likely that will become a problem. Also, the ability to plug it in and charge it off the computer directly if it starts to die is a great plus!
My first impression was that the mouse was a little jumpier than I expected, but then I noticed the little button under the scroll wheel and discovered that it was for changing the DPI. Honestly, I'm not sure why they put it in such an easy to use spot, I feel like this isn't something that needs to change very often. But a couple of clicks on that button got me to about the mouse speed I like. I'm actually really happy with this product and although I was shopping around for a replacement Logitech, I think I'll keep this one in my travel bag instead!

title: Perfect for DSLR/DSLM video work!
text:
I work with video equipment for a living, and sometimes I need to wire up small cameras like DSLR/DSLMs to an external monitor or recorder on a job. Using a proper cable is important, especially one like this which goes from micro HDMI to full sized HDMI, rather than just using a regular HDMI and a micro-adapter on one end. Using adapters introduces more points of failure as well as distortion/possible signal loss at each connection point.
I used this on a job going from a Sony A7S to an Atmos Ninja recorder, directly from the camera to the recorder, no adapters needed, and it worked perfectly. Crisp clean signal as expected, and the setup was nice and neat looking.
If you need to connect a micro hdmi to a full sized port, you can't go wrong with Amazon Basics.

title: Great stabilizer, but poor experience
text:
[[VIDEOID:e88b9f67b8b32ec1c6281d91851e23f3]] After using a rented Crane 2 for a while, I decided to get something more robust for my own. I did a LOT of research, and all hands pointed to the DJI Ronin S being the best build quality for the money, and having owned DJI equipment before I knew it had a solid reputation already. It seemed a little more expensive than the ones I wanted to buy, but then I found this "essentials kit", which forgoes some of the bells and whistles and gives you just the stabilizer and battery for a price that made it VERY competitive!
So I got this thinking it's the deal of the year, until I had issues the first time using it on a job. One of the motors appears to be faulty and would vibrate like crazy at certain angles. I'm attaching the video I sent to DJI's tech support team to help troubleshoot the issue.
Initially I thought I had done something wrong, so I spent some time researching online and tried following some of the balance guides and firmware updates, etc, hoping something would solve the issue. But it remains. Then I found someone in a film making forum mention that he had to go through 3 or 4 Ronin S essential kits before getting one that worked... apparently the first 3 would all spaz out in what sounded similar to this one.
I got nervous and reached out to the seller wondering if there was just a bad batch of Ronin S essential kits out there. I was told to contact DJI because they might have a fix for it instead. Gullible me, I reached out to DJI who sort of gave me the run around trying different things again for them, and proving I had done them via photos and videos (they wanted to see a screenshot of what firmware, etc, what kind of vibrations, results of balance tests), and this back and forth went on for a while UNTIL I MISSED MY RETURN WINDOW ON THE UNIT. I shouldn't have listened, I should have just returned it and gotten another one hoping that wouldn't be a lemon, but I wanted to be courteous and try DJI in case the problem was actually me.
Thankfully, I'm under DJI's warranty so I can send it in for them to properly repair or replace. But to do that, I need to package it up and ship across the country, which could take up to a week, wait 1-2 weeks for the actual repair, then another week for it get back to me. That means close to another month of not having the stabilizer that never worked properly when I bought it over a month ago!
I've seen what it can do, and I'm confident that when I get the stabilizer back it will work better (and I intend to update my rating when that happens to reflect it working), but my experience with this thing so far has NOT been a positive one! There may be a quality control issue with some of the S essential kits, so be prepared to return them and/or deal with repair if it doesn't work right out of the box.

title: Wireless FHD video!
text:
I've always wanted a wireless off camera monitor for director/crew use on our freelance camera operator gigs, or for when mounting the camera somewhere difficult to see like the side of a car. A few years ago, a solution like this would have cost upwards of $2k, but now thanks to products like this one we can do it on a shoestring budget!
I attached the transmitter to a USB battery bank and used gaffer's tape to attach to my camera cage with my Sony A7S inside. On the other side, I took a flash bracket and mounted a 7" monitor, and once again used gaffer's tape to sandwich the receiver to another battery supply and secure to the handle of the bracket. Note that the receiver isn't designed to run off USB power like the transmitter is (why, I don't know), so I had to use a modified cable to make one end a USB - it is still only 5v, but I think it requires at least 2amps so it is pickier about what battery bank will work with it. My smaller battery supply didn't crank out enough power so it won't start (blue light would just blink), but a larger battery supply that I have did just fine.
Once the two were wired up, as a proof of concept I fired up the camera and had a live feed in full 1080p on the remote monitor, which worked fine as long as I was in the same room as the camera. Pretty useful! If you look at the included image, you can see both units on the floor working, but I'll need some shorter cables to clean it up in the future (didn't have any short cable available for this test, so it looks messy).
The only thing I wish Sabrent had done better is include a mount for the transmitter to attach to the camera hotshoe. They claim it comes with one in the box, and even show a picture of it mounted to a camera but it does NOT! It comes with a bracket that uses a thumb screw to attach to something, but it will only fit into a hotshoe if you have an adapter for your shoe mount that will accept a screw through it. The thumb screw and shoe mount that they show in the picture are not included in the box, which disappointed me. No matter, I'd still need a battery supply for this so I had to attach it to a cage anyway. But I felt like that picture was misleading in the product's image.
I also wish that they had made the receiver work off a standard USB plug as well so I wouldn't have to use a modified cable for it. It worked pretty well so I can't complain too much at the end of the day.
Although I was interested primarily in off camera monitoring, I discovered this device is very well suited to send your laptop's display to a TV. With the receiver on your TV wired up, the transmitter actually works like a dongle right out of the laptop's hdmi port, and just needs a short run of USB for power from the closest port. This is the cleanest use of this product that I can imagine, and it works well for that. Pretty amazing what it can do for the price these days!

title: Great color and affordable DSLR video monitor
text:
As a freelance camera operator, I'm no stranger to these. This is clearly designed for us low budget video shooters using small DSLR style cameras, which is why it uses a Sony camcorder battery plate and designed with a hood for outdoor viewing. It has some pretty great features for the price point, including crop mark overlays, peaking indicators, and individual color channels. That being said, it can be used for all sorts of things, such as a Raspberry Pi monitor, backup camera screen, or even a second monitor for your laptop (that's a fun one!). It even has included sound, something a lot of these monitors do not, more on that later.
This is really designed for video use, and for that it does a pretty great job for the price. It comes with a hotshoe mount adapter to put on top of your camera, and uses standard batteries (most LED lights and other accessories also use these batteries, so you probably have some already if you work in video). The colors are vivid and sharp, more accurate than my Atmost Ninja 2 recorder screen, and nice and big for focus checking.
The hood is a nice touch as well, but it requires the snap on frame to attach, and the frame has a weird problem in which it partially obstructs the HDMI port. Maybe I'm just doing it wrong, but I found I needed to leave that corner off the frame if I wanted to use the HDMI plug.
Speaking of the HDMI plug, it comes with one included which I thought was pretty rad of them, but it isn't the more modern micro HDMI type, but the slightly older MINI one. That's the outdated kind that older devices use (such as 3rd generation Intel laptops or cameras like the GH2), but pretty much everything made in the last few years has been using the newer micro one. So it seems weird that they included this one. Personally, it will come in handy because I DO have a laptop that still uses that plug, but I don't intend to use it with this monitor. All my cameras that use that plug are long gone at this point.
Another couple of things to note: The focus peaking is pretty much useless. It oversharpens the image and thinks high contrast parts of bokeh are "in focus", which is weird. Thankfully my Sony cameras have peaking built in so that isn't much of an issue. Also, the screen is large enough and is HD enough resolution (not full 1080 but more than 720) that you don't really need peaking to tell what's in focus. You can see it with your eyes. Also, if using with a camera that is outputting a 16:9 image, you have to change the screen size setting from the default, which is to maximize the screen. Everything looked a little stretched because the display is a little taller than the output of my camera until I turned that off.
As far as sound, I mentioned earlier that this monitor has a speaker. That's good for when you want to review footage on the monitor, and even better if using with a Raspberry Pi or monitor for other things where it might be your only source of sound. It is also really useful if shooting with a Sony A6000 or similar smaller camera that doesn't have a headphone jack... this offers a headphone jack so you can monitor off the HDMI feed. That's pretty useful right there! But don't forget, when you turn the live view back on, you are going to get major feedback from the mic to the speaker unless you quickly turn the volume all the way DOWN first! Or just leave headphones in if that's how you roll.

It is important to note however that it will not accept a 4k signal. The actual resolution is 1280x800, and it will accept up to 1080p as an input, but more than that fails. At the time I'm reviewing this, it seems that there are similar monitors that can accept a 4k input for around the same price. I'm guessing they are updated versions of the same design, as there are no monitors that actually have that resolution for this price, rather they just accept the feed and down-sample to 1280x800, just like this one. So at the end of the day, it probably won't matter if it accepts 4k or not. Some cameras don't like outputting a different resolution than they are recording, so if you are recording in 4k and outputting 1080p, that might be an issue. Otherwise, this is a solid value.

title: Very wide, and adhesive is STRONG
text:
This is a good product, but perhaps not exactly what I was expecting it to be. I was hoping to conceal two different things- a floor lamp cord, and a cat5 cable along a wall. In both cases, this cover is far wider than it needs to be. This is better suited for multiple cables, such as all the power/hdmi/composite/etc connections running down the back of a wall-mounted TV. For a single cable run like a power plug or a measly cat5 cable, it seems absurdly wider than the cable it is concealing.
That other thing I found interesting is that one of the walls I wanted to use it on isn't completely straight. A handyman had helped me repair a wall and paint it, and now I see it has a slight curve to it which I wasn't able to notice before. The covers don't sit entirely flat against the wall, which just sort of looks awkward around the ever-so-slightly-curved portion unless I fill it in with spackle. I could overlook all these things and say perhaps my test usage are uncommon scenarios, except for one final thing: the adhesive is TOO good!
If you decide you don't like it / want it, and used the adhesive instead of the screws, you are going to rip a lot of the wall off with the cover when you remove it. I wasn't sure if this was just me, but I see from other reviews that they claim pieces of the drywall were coming off with the paint, which is quite frankly somewhat horrifying if you didn't know it would do that. I still have the paint for this wall so I'm not concerned, but I'd strongly recommend using the screws if you have the option and don't want this to be a permanent fixture in your home.

title: Very limited use
text:
As someone who works with cameras for a living, I tend to occasionally misplace/lose my lens caps. Having a one-size-fits-all backup like this claims to be, is therefore intriguing to me.
What I found however, is that this fits alright for smaller sized primes (such as those with a front element of 52mm), but a lot of my zooms or larger primes with bigger front elements are difficult or impossible to fit over. Rear cap was also somewhat of a hit-or-miss; I own E-mount, EOS, Nikon F, Minolta A-mount and Micro4/3 lenses, and none of them are too large in their rear element, but some lenses get wide right after the mount and won't allow a cover like this to squeeze over easily. Some of the smaller primes, especially pancake lenses like the Canon 40mm STM, really can't fit both a front and rear "cap" like this since the entire lens would be engulfed in one end or the other.
On top of all that, even if it DOES fit over your lens, I'm cynical as to how how useful it really is. The purpose of a lens cap is to protect the glass from two things: getting dirty and getting damaged. For starters, the material is soft and won't prevent a hard object collision. I'm not exactly willing to test that theory but considering I can press in and feel the glass through the cover, I'm guessing a hard object in your camera bag could still hit it and crack/shatter/damage it. Perhaps the rubber would soften the blow, but a real lens cap would prevent any blow from happening in the first place!
For dust and debris protection, perhaps it is a little useful, however this sort of material tends to attract a lot of static cling. Just leaving it in my gear bag for a bit, I'm finding dust and hair clinging to it like a balloon. Now, it is possible that means the dust/debris will stick to the cap and not your lens, which is useful, however it doesn't give me a lot of confidence to see stuff stuck to the thing I'm about to use to protect my lens from more of that stuff.

I suppose it's good as a backup in my gearbag in case I lose another lens cap and want something to keep dust off it until I get a replacement, but otherwise I'd strongly recommend getting a proper front and end cap for your lenses.

title: The hardware is excellent
text:
From what I understand, the hardware here is the same no matter which model you buy- the different tiers are for licensing features of the software. I've seen some people complain that the software isn't very good, and they recommend you use the hardware with different software (some that might even be open source and free), in which case I would recommend getting the cheapest edition possible so that you can just get the hardware you need and figure out if the software is right for you or not.
The company allows you to pay a nominal upgrade free if you ever decide you want better features than the license it comes with, or you can always try some of the alternative options if you feel their software isn't a good fit for you. I have several computers ranging from Windows 7 to 10, and I can only say I've been trying the stock software for the sake of this review. It works a little bit different, arguably better on newer editions of windows, so keep that in mind. Perhaps the older editions of the software worked better on older Windows, I can't say for sure, but I did find it a little bit complicated to get the calibration to stick upon startup on some of my computers. That being said, as someone who works in video/photography, having a color calibrated display is very important and I strongly recommend at the least this hardware to anyone who wants to make sure their colors are accurate!

title: Not the old Lexar anymore, but still a good product
text:
Lexar used to be up there with Sandisk and other respected names in storage medium. These days the name was bought and rebranded, so I'm keeping my fingers crossed that this doesn't just kick the bucket one day!
So far so good, however. The drive is working, however I'm unable to get the full speed it claims due to my aging hardware requiring an adapter. I hope to test it on a newer computer I have in my office soon with a native NVMe slot and see if I can get it to reach the claimed speeds. With my adapted system, it is at least on par with the speeds I get out of my other internal SSD (SATA based), and with a USB3.1 enclosure, it makes a mean portable storage machine too that looks more like a USB stick on steroids than the bulky external HDs we used to rely on to carry information.
Hoping it holds up- for now I'm impressed with it.

title: Makes a great USB stick on steroids!
text:
I recently upgraded to a larger M.2 storage drive in my computer and was wondering what I should do with the older one. This makes it into an EXCELLENT high speed external storage drive! Unlike my other USB storage drives that are the size of traditional hard drives, this is a lot smaller yet has the capacity of a traditional drive and speed of an SSD. It supports USB-C and has an adapter to go back to traditional USB ports, and of course is backwards compatible with the older USB standard ports as well.
Sadly, on my computer, the drive doesn't live up to the potential speed it had when inside a computer, but that is largely due to the limitations of my USB ports (I don't have the 3.1 standard on this computer... yet). It is still faster than my other external drives, and a great deal faster than my internal storage HDD (just not as fast as my internal SSD).

title: Works great to send video feed across the room
text:
UPDATE: I noticed that my setup would start displaying an incorrectly sized and formatted hdmi feed (instead of 1920x1080, it was a squashed 960x1080 with incorrect colors). If I turned the whole system off and wait a few minutes before turning back on, it would sometimes go away but it is very strange. I thought it was either the player or projector connected to it for months now, but I just did some testing and realized it has been this HDMI extender! A monitor plugged into the source displayed fine, and plugged into this receiver had the same 960x1080 w/ mixed up colors that my projector did. The good news is that the transmitter has a reset button and that seems to fix it when it happens. But it sometimes comes back when I reboot or start up from everything being off. It is annoying that I have to go find the little reset button because the transmitter is hidden in a cabinet, and it seems like a completely unnecessary step to take every time I boot up. Hoping Sabrent can offer a solution- if so I'll update my review back to 5 stars because otherwise this is excellent.
These things are a great way to reliably reach farther than an HDMI cable, but you need to still understand the limitations. Video requires a lot of bandwidth, so the quality and length of your cable is directly related to how realistic it is to reach the maximum resolution and frame rate.
I already have an older one of these from a different brand, which I bought a couple of years ago for a projector in the back of the room (switch between TV and projector, but entertainment system is in front of room and projector is in back, hence the need for a long run of cable). That older one claimed to work at 1080/60p, and in my initial tests it did. But once I ran the long cable, I was able to only get 720/60p or 1080 at only 24p. 1080 at 60 was just too much bandwidth and the adapter just couldn't handle it over a longer cable run.
This adapter, however, is rated at a higher spec for 4K. Swapping my old one out with this one, I'm happy to report that now I can get 1080 even at 60p from point to point. Could I get 4k at that length? I don't know, my projector doesn't handle 4k, but I'm guessing as the length of cable increases, it will limit what spec you can reliably expect. But I am very pleased with finally getting 1080p at this length of cable, so 5 stars!

title: Fast ultraportable
text:
I transfer large video files to take home with me for work each day (cloud storage would take too long to transfer), and this is much nicer than the SATA-2.5" SSD drive I used to carry around with me. I love the size of it, its more like a USB stick on steroids in size and style, but has capacity and speed you'd expect from a larger hard drive. I also like the USB C functionality since my desktop at work has a modern USB C port built in.
Unfortunately, I can't get the full speed out of the USB interface on my home workstation. These NVMe SSDs are capable of going so fast, but my internal SATA SSD clocks higher in benchmarks than this one, and I'm pretty sure that's because of my older USB 3.0 ports. It goes about as fast as my other full sized SSD over USB, but is much smaller and future proof. I dig it.

title: Cute concept for kids!
text:
My daughter enjoys listening to music in bed and on car trips. The problem with traditional headphones are that they either fall our of her ears (earbuds) or are uncomfortable if she falls asleep (over the ear). This solves those issues. Although these are advertised as more of a eye mask with music, which I imagine would be a sensory experience to promote sleep, my daughter uses them more like a headband/sweatband to wear around the house. She just cleaned her room wearing them over her forehead and it reminded me of an 80's workout video. If it's cold outside, I think they'd make a pretty interesting alternative to keep your child's ears warm as well.
She says they are comfortable, and sound good, although I can't verify these claims since it doesn't really fit me. She likes them, so that's a win as far as I'm concerned!

title: High quality clips and lays flat
text: I used this to run an HDMI over Ethernet adapter to attach a projector on the other side of the room as my entertainment system. It is the perfect length for that, and thanks to the flat design of the cord and included mounting clips, I could run it along the baseboard and behind furniture without it being noticeable. I actually really like how rugged the clip on the end of the cable is. My old cable run for this was a standard blue cat5e and the plug wasn't so strong- more than once a component got moved and yanked the cable out. I just installed this new one to replace it and pulled on it, it seems to be staying put. Data throughput is handling my 1080p feed just fine.  I'm quite happy with it.

title: Perfect for minimalist installation
text:
My son wanted a computer for school work on his bedroom desk, but there isn't a lot of free space there. A wired mouse and keyboard looked very cluttered very quickly, so we looked for decent wireless options. I found some affordable Chinese ones, but my son wanted the ability to game every now and then and the cheap ones had reviews that claimed connection would sometimes die in the middle of use and require reconnect.
I found this one and remembered fondly that I used to use Logitech wireless equipment when I was in college and I always had a good experience with them. This model is no different, it handles his school work well and holds up to some light gaming without any noticeable hiccups or disconnects so far. And we can open the desk drawer and drop both the keyboard and mouse in when we are finished so he desk stays clean and uncluttered. I call this combo a win!

title: Great for holding diffuser on your lights.
text: If you have a flash or constant light on a stand and it doesn't support its own diffusion holder, this is the piece you need. I was working with hot tungsten lamps for a video job in a semi-permanent studio by one of my clients, and it was basically a 500 Watt bulb in a dish, which obviously casts a very harsh bright light with lots of shadow. I picked out some shoot-through umbrellas to get some basic diffusion of the light, and added this piece to go in between the light fixture and the stand to hold the umbrella rod. If you have worked with light setups like this before, you should be familiar as it is pretty standard/basic. Like other adapters of this sort, there is a hinge that lets you tilt the light to get a little extra control over where you are aiming. If you are using this with off camera flashes that use a shoe mount, it already comes with that preinstalled.  In my case, I didn't need the cold shoe mount (the video lights screw into a 1/4" 20 threaded bolt), so I just removed the shoe mount which revealed exactly the connection I needed underneath.  Very useful piece of kit for a simple setup.

title: Affordable diffuser for video lights
text: I needed something for a light setup I intend to leave in a studio I'm working in so I don't need to bring my lights every time to set up.
