text: I'm of the view that simple speaker cable, as long as it's 16-gauge or bigger, is just as good as fancy and pricey "interconnects". And this cable is very easy to use with a clear black stripe along one of the wires (I use that one for ground, and the unmarked wire for signal).

title: Best banana plugs
text: Very easy and sturdy wire connection, easiest I've ever used.

title: Amazing speakers
text:
Accuracy is amazing. Very clear with all types of music; I listen mostly to classical music but also some pop and jazz. Very excellent highs and mids, and bass response not boomy like some of the popular speakers today. The bass goes far enough down that you might not need a subwoofer -- you might consider trying these out first before getting a sub.

Unless I rearrange the room a lot, I don't have room for large floor-standing speakers. I'm very happy with these as my primary front L+R. I might get the center speaker in the same series at some point.

title: A bit pricey, but very good
text:
First impression is that it's physically beautiful, with the amazing piano black finish. It's fairly easy to set up, but I spent some time trying to figure out how to get it to turn on without an on-off switch. Turns out you just have to turn up your music to a respectable volume. After I figured that out, I'm pretty happy.

Oh, it sounds just great. :)

title: Supports a heavy graphics card
text:
And depending on your computer's configuration, it might support two graphics cards. This is a vertical stand that supports the end of your graphics card (the end without the video connectors).

You can also get a horizontal brace (a different product) but that would require available space below your graphics card.

title: Make sure it will fit in your case
text:
This is a horizontal brace that supports a graphics card. You'll want to use something like this for a very large and heavy graphics card, so that it doesn't pull so much on the PCI-e connector on your motherboard. The main issue I've encountered with this brace is that you need a couple of slots below your graphics card to accommodate this brace, and in a smaller case or with a smaller motherboard, you might not have that much space available.

You might look at another style of brace that's a vertical stand that supports the end corner of your graphics card. This might work better in a smaller case.

Note that this isn't going to work well for a build that has more than one graphics card.

title: Very full-featured
text:
I'll update this review as I get more experience with the radio, but my first impressions are very positive. It's an excellent value because of its huge number of useful features. However, some notable features are missing, especially SSB if that's important. Likewise, there's no connector for an external antenna. Other features, such as squelch, are shared with the numbered buttons, so they're hard to remember without referring to the (comprehensive) manual.

* AM, FM, and complete shortwave bands.
* Digital tuning, with fine tuning that's easy to use.
* Bandwidth selector that's amazingly effective. Strong AM stations sound amazingly good on the wide setting.
* It can charge rechargeable batteries. Or turn the charge switch off to use non-rechargeable batteries.
* AC power adaptor is included.
* Pretty nice leatherette padded case is included.
* Telescoping antenna is about 2 feet long.
* FM and AM work well. Not sure about SW yet. I need a directory, and I need to compare with better radios.
* Sound quality from the mono speaker is good at low volumes. At higher volumes, the 1 watt amplifier will start clipping. FM stereo is available when using earbuds.

More to come ...

title: Beware inadequate packaging for shipping
text:
This is a NAS drive, suitable for prosumer or professional NAS units. The concept of being a NAS drive is that if the drive encounters a read error (which happens every once in a while with any disk drive), you don't want the drive to take a possibly long detour into rereading the data and applying its error correction algorithms to recover the data correctly. Rather, you want the drive to give up quickly, and allow the remaining drives in the RAID array to reconstruct the data. So that means "fail early, fail often." The reason for this behavior is that if a drive in a RAID array takes too long to respond to a read request (while doing error correction), the NAS device might decide that the drive has failed, and fail it out of the RAID array, requiring a spare drive to be added needlessly to rebuild the RAID array.

However, my trouble was that Amazon's packaging was completely inadequate to protect the drive during shipment. I was astonished that anyone would ship anything like that, especially a delicate piece of machinery. The drive does seem to work, but I'll have a better idea of that over time.

There are two more considerations for NAS drives. You want to pay attention to whether the drive uses native 4k blocks, and probably all drives in your array should be the same in that respect. And some NAS devices are designed for one or the other. Seagate makes both conventional and 4k-native drives, and the product descriptions aren't clear in this respect. Do a search on the drive's model number and you can learn this information.

Also, consider whether the drive uses conventional magnetic recording (CMR) or shingled magnetic recording (SMR). For typical desktop use either is ok. For NAS use, you should always use CMR drives. Again, doing a search on the drive's model number should help you figure out what kind of recording method is used by each particular drive.

title: Hugs the wall
text: I got this power block to use in a hard-to-access location, and it's working out well. The plug doesn't stick out from the wall; rather, it hugs the wall so that my furniture cabinet can be pushed very close to the wall. The cord is on the shorter side, but that fits in my location just fine. So it's working out very well.

title: Easy to assemble, looks and works great
text: This is a beautiful all-metal case. I mounted my Blu-Ray internal optical drive in it -- took the drive out of an old computer so I could use it with my new computer that doesn't have a slot for an internal optical drive. The case is pretty heavy, very well built, stable, and it was very easy to mount the drive. All at a reasonable price. Highly recommended.

title: Very excellent
text:
I bought the ATH-A990Z as an upgrade from a previous pair of AT 700x headphones. These ATH-A990Z headphones are superb in many ways, and I often use them to listen to high resolution streaming audio from Qobuz (24 bits, 96 kHz). It's kind of like going from mono to stereo -- once you hear the difference that high resolution can provide, it's hard to go back to ordinary CDs or MP3s, even though those can sound very pleasant.

The fit of the earpads and headband is very good, and I often wear them for hours without any fatigue. In fact, the overall experience is so good that I look forward to my listening time. The substantial ear pads are very effective in blocking out noise from my surroundings, and create a zone where I can enjoy even quiet passages in my classical music favorites.

The sound is a little bass heavy, so those who like the Bose sound will probably be very happy. I prefer a flatter response, and it's actually pretty easy to accomplish that with the Windows equalizer for my Realtek hardware in the Sound control panel. The highs are very light and airy, beautiful. The net result is entirely excellent, with sound that is very smooth and open. Just fantastic. At the price, the ATH-A990Z headphones compare very well to much more expensive alternatives.

title: Almost ok
text: These were much less expensive than the OEM earpads, and you get what  you pay for. They almost work; hard to keep them connected to the headphones. (Maybe I'm not installing them correctly.) They include a plastic pry tool to remove the original worn earpads. These are considerably less comfortable than the original pads, and make the headphones somewhat uncomfortable to wear. Not horrible, just not as good. Someday I might splurge for the OEM pads.

title: Backup drive for all my stuff
text: I bought two of these for rotating my data backups. Very nice feeling to know that my data is safe. My NAS is 16 TB of RAID 6, but I'm using only 2 TB of it so this 8 TB drive easily accommodates everything I have. The plastic housing seems durable enough. I haven''t been very rough with this -- I think the 2.5 inch drives are built to take more physical punishment than the 3.5 inch drives like this one.

title: I really wanted to love these, but ...
text:
There are some very nice features to these buds, and I do intend to keep them. (Another reviewer was about to return them.) But there are some things that just aren't as good as I had hoped. I'll try to be as detailed as possible.

First, the out-of-box experience is kinda nice, but not fabuous. The smallish box presents the much smaller charger box that the buds live in, and a tiny box that contains a charger cable. Wait -- are there really no instructions? And I thought there were interchangable ear thingies to accommodate ears of different sizes. Ok, so the very brief instruction book clings to the top of the box because it's too big not to fall out on its own. And the ear thingies are hiding in the box where the charging cable is. I seem to be ok with the default ear thingies that are already installed on the buds. (Note, you have to use your own charger with the charging cable. You probably already have too many of those.)

You'll need to download and install the Galaxy Wearable app (on Android, a different one is available for iOS). The app helps you connect to the buds, pretty easy, and is reasonably fully functional. There are numerous options you can play with.

The fit -- quite comfortable actually. Looking at the peculiar shape, I wondered whether these would stay in my ears, and whether they would be uncomfortable. Yes, they stay put, even when walking around, and no, not uncomfortable. This was a pleasant surprise; Samsung really got this part right. I feel as though I could wear these at the office all day and not get ear fatigue. Much, much better than a clumsy pair of headphones slipping off my head when I'm walking around. When wearing the buds, you can hear outside sounds/conversations very well, and perhaps that's the whole idea of these buds. I like this.

There's an equalizer section on the app's main screen. The equalizer options are sort of ok, but not wonderful. I don't know why there's no option for a 10-band graphic equalizer. I just settled on the default after not liking the other choices any better.

You can turn on and off the ANC (active noise cancellation). I have a pair of conventional headphones (not Bose) with ANC that works really well. You feel like you're in a cocoon. These buds have ANC that you can barely tell is working. It sounds a little different, maybe even a little bit of an improvement, but it doesn't seem like it's getting rid of any particular noise. So the ANC is sort of a bust.

Now let's talk about sound quality. As I say, I really wanted to love these little guys. The sound quality is good but not great. Maybe I'm expecting too much. My pair of $250 conventional headphones sound spectacular, and I can listen to music for hours with them. These buds aren't that impressive. The sound quality is ok -- just ok. It's not "bad" in any way at all, but it's not great. I listened to an entire CD that I know well and like. The experience was pleasant, but at the end I really wanted to listen to it on the stereo instead. As I say, maybe I'm expecting too much. The sound quality is probably good enough to listen to at work all day. I had the volume up a little too high, and when my test CD was finished and I took the buds out of my ears, I felt that my ears were ringing a little bit. Next time I'll set the volume lower.

As an interesting aside, I'll compare the sound quality to another wearable that I just got, the Bose Frames (audio sunglasses, a weirdly interesting product). The sound from the Bose Frames is "smooth" in a very wonderful way -- much better than the buds. However, the Bose Frames have absolutely no lower end -- no bass sounds at all. The sounds they do have are great. By contrast, these buds are full range, with pretty good bass. But the sound just isn't smooth.

I didn't try to take a phone call., so I don't know how seamless this works. Considering it's Samsung, and I have a Galaxy S9, I bet this works well enough. I'm not very fussy about sound quality on calls -- I just need to be able to understand what's being said. So "good enough" for me is probably not hard to achieve.

There's a "button" on the buds that you press to skip a track, answer a call, etc. It's not a real button, it's just a touch-sensitive area on the outside of the bud. I haven't been able to get this touch point to work reliably. I don't think there's necessarily anything wrong with the bud, probably just my fat fingers.

Bottom line? I think I'll have a use for these, most likely when I want to listen to my own music without disturbing others, and without the very wonderful but cumbersome conventional earphones. When I'm walking out and about, the smooth sound from the Bose Frames is better. So it's a toss-up with the Galaxy Buds Live. They're good enough, but unfortunately not better than that.

title: Excellent quality
text:
This is a very well made dash cam. It doesn't come with a memory card (mini HDMI needed), but comes with a coupon where you can get a memory card if you write an Amazon review. There are numerous pieces in the kit:
- The camera itself, including night vision LEDs and viewing screen
- Suction cup holder for mounting to the interior of the windshield
- Power cable with cigarette lighter plug
- Cable to connect to the backup light to function as a backup camera (not quite sure how this works)
- Fairly comprehensive English-only instruction book

The instruction book says that it has an internal battery that's used only to write the video to the memory card. I'm not quite sure how this is supposed to work, but I think you need to have it powered while driving. And I don't see how to do that without the power cord dangling all over the place, or doing some awkward routing of the power cord to the vicinity of your 12v power jack. If the same company has a similar unit that can run for 4 hours or so on an internal battery, I would be likely to buy that version of the product.

title: Very good, not great
text: A very fine hybrid radio, especially if you have local HD radio stations that have different programs on the subchannels. Controls are very convenient. My only complaint is that it's not stereo sound, and kind of pleasant but only moderate sound quality. If you're ok with that, then you'll be fine with this radio.

title: Having the outlets on the side is a real space saver
text: I got a few of these for the new apartment, and they work great. Very convenient.

title: Easy to install, very good performer
text:
This isn't too hard to install -- you do it from both sides of the motherboard, after you install the CPU and BEFORE you install the motherboard in the case. Although it's big, it still left plenty of room for my GTX 970 video card and the DRAM sticks. This pulls a huge amount of heat away from the CPU. My 6700K is coasting with this, never breaks a sweat!

It doesn't come with the pre-applied goo that you'll need for a good thermal coupling between this and the CPU, so you need to squirt the goo from the little tube. (Sorry, I forgot whether the tube of goo came with the fan.)

title: Wow, this thing is fast!
text: I'm using this with a Sabertooth Z170 motherboard, and it works great. Blazing fast.

title: Gorgeous monitor, big wide viewing space
text: This is a beautiful, beautiful monitor. The colors pop. The curve of the screen might seem like a gimmick, but it's actually rather subtle and improves your view especially with a wide viewing space. There are *lots* of pixels on this monitor -- most newer video cards will be able to drive this, but you'll want to check first to make sure.

title: Good assortment
text: Beautiful cables, assorted lengths, bright colors. The ends are small enough to fit my Galaxy S7 through the case.

title: All the latest technology here
text:
This is the main board in my new rig, with Intel 6700K and Samsung 950 parts. It all works great, but the technology has changed so much over the last 18 months that I spent quite a while puzzling over everything. Here are some hints:

1. Read the very detailed instruction book before you begin. The second part of the instruction book covers the BIOS, which I found mostly self-explanatory. The first part of the instructions were indispensable. The instruction book for your case will probably be helpful too.

2. Look over all the parts that come in the box, and understand what they all do before assembling things.

3. Be aware that you'll need to install the standoffs in your case, and assemble whatever cooling solution you're using BEFORE mounting the motherboard in the case. I didn't do this, and I had to remove and reinstall (twice, sigh). Silly me.

4. There are lots of connector pins on the board for various things. They are labeled, but hard to read without a bright flashlight. The instruction book has a very good picture map of them all.

5. The package comes with *everything* that I needed, including the M.2 host adapter board, thermistors to monitor interior case temperatures. This package is loaded!

6. The two assist fans are hard to figure out. One goes on the top of the motherboard, in almost the exact center. You remove a metal cover that ends up being a keychain. That's what the little keychain cable was for! Told you it comes with everything. The other assist fan goes in the back, near the rear panel USB connectors. It's not hard at all to install, but neither is it obvious. I puzzled over this for a while before I figured out how to screw the fan to the plastic slider piece. Be sure to observe the airflow direction of the assist fans as you install them.

7. It comes with very competent on-board video, but of course you might want your own GTX 980 card instead!

8. With Windows installed on the M.2 drive, the thing boots up in like 4 seconds. Web pages appear instantly. This 6th generation technology is a huge step up from what we put up with only a year ago!

9. There are lots of options for overclocking, changing voltages, etc. BEWARE: If you don't know what you're doing here, you can do permanent damage. Best to work with someone who has done this before.

Hope you have fun building!

title: I love my Chromebook
text:
This is all the computer that most people will ever need. I've used computers for many years, and done software development on various different platforms. But now, I love my Chromebook. It's very simple, basically just web browsing, but also plays music. The only thing you can't really do is to install software. For many people, this will be just fine. (In all fairness, I also have a Windows laptop that I use for my more serious projects, like Adobe Photoshop and music production.)

Numerous companies make Chromebooks. This one is from HP, and it's a fine machine. Big bright screen, highest quality keyboard, fast Haswell processor. Some models have only WiFi, and some come with the free T-Mobile 4G service for connectivity on the go.

title: Cool sweep second hand
text:
The sweep second hand is cool -- no tick-tick-tick. And the clock is fairly attractive. It's medium sized -- not as tiny as a travel alarm clock, but not really large either. It's also extremely lightweight, which could be a good thing, but for me it's inconvenient because it slips around on the table quite a bit.

The styling is nice, but it's all plastic, including the lens. I wish it had a glass lens, as the plastic lens looks like it will scratch over time. The ring around the lens looks like it's calibrated, and maybe rotates, but it doesn't. It's just for show.

title: All in one box
text:
Everything you need, all in one small box. Pretty sweet. What you get is complete, but you'll be better off if you know something about Linux installation or software development, or have a friend who can help. The Raspberry Pi is a fun little device with enormous flexibility and can be the core of many interesting projects.

Build quality of all the included components is high.

title: Gigabit all the way
text:
Cosmetically, this looks identical to the industry-standard FS105 10/100 5-port switch. I like the fact that the cables plug into the same side of the unit as the status lights -- makes it easier to mount in tight spaces and still see what's going on. Lights show the link status for each port. One light glows for 10 Mbps, the other for 100 Mbps, and both glow for gigabit speed; the lights blink to show activity on that port. Very nicely designed, and it looks solid.

It does get a bit warm. I've been running this for a week, and it's fine so far. I can't evaluate some of the other comments indicating potentially premature failure.

It's easy to install -- just hook up your Ethernet cables, reboot your devices, and you're good to go. There's no installation software, drivers, or configuration needed. It just works. It's compatible with PC, Mac, Linux, DVD players, Playstations, etc.

I have a cable modem with about 25 Mbps downstream speed. I recently upgraded my home network to gigabit by getting this switch and a gigabit WiFi router. The laptop now "feels" snappier when accessing the Internet, but I can't tell if this is really true, or maybe just the fact the the 8-year-old WiFi router wasn't up to modern speeds.

title: Hardly more expensive than the relays themselves
text:
I bought this to use with the Raspberry Pi. It comes with absolutely no documentation at all, either in the package or on the manufacturer's Web site, and therefore it's taken me quite a while of puzzling through Google research to figure out how to use it. There are some answered questions in the Amazon product description that have been very helpful as well.

My configuration is that I use a 12v power supply to power the board (which powers the relay coils), and from that the board derives 5 volts to run its electronics. I am using this 5v to power the Raspberry Pi by connecting the 5v pin from the relay board's header to the 5v pin of the GPIO header on the Pi. I'm not using the standard Pi power connector. For each relay that I want to control, I'm using a 1K resistor between a GPIO pin on the Pi and one of the control pins on the relay board. When I turn the GPIO pin off, the board energizes the relay; turning the GPIO pin on releases the relay. (That seems a little backwards to me, but it works fine. I can control my load either way, because the relays have both NO and NC contacts.) I can control the GPIO, and thus the relays, from Python. I'm trying it control it from Java directly, but that's been hard for me to get working. The Python libraries have been easy for me to figure out. I'm hoping that eventually I'll figure out the Java as well.

The product design and build quality both seem to be first rate. The price is excellent -- you could scarcely buy the 16 bare relays for the cost of this board. But I have to knock off one star because of the complete lack of documentation.

title: Works very well, good price point
text:
First off, let's be clear that this isn't really a hi-fi speaker. With that out of the way, this is a very excellent speaker.

Pros
- Compact size, weighted well enough so that it won't scoot around on a table
- Very pleasing sound, even if it's not hi-fi
- Plays pretty loud for its size
- Small, throw it in a suitcase or travel bag easily -- ideal for use in a hotel room
- Speakerphone function is excellent
- Looks beautiful, build quality excellent
- Easy to pair with my phone, quickly restored when turning on
- Includes 3.5mm jack for connection to devices that don't use Bluetooth
- Sparse but logical controls
- Recharges with standard cell phone charger, charges quickly, and lasts plenty long on one charge (especially if you keep the volume down)

Cons
- I didn't hear any bass with this. I can be happy enough without bass at this price point.
- And the high treble is missing too. (However, the resulting sound is clear and pleasing.)
- It's not stereo. That was probably obvious from the shape of it. But just sayin'

I've found that placing the unit next to a wall makes the sound a bit fuller, even though there's still not any sign of what I would call bass. But the sound is very well engineered, so the sound that you end up with is exceptionally pleasing and clear.

I've also tried using this in the car, and it's good. My car is from the pre-Bluetooth era, so there's no way to hook up the phone to the stereo. I can listen to my tunes in the car with this. The sound doesn't rival the excellent sound from the car stereo, but it works just fine. I'm very happy with this.

title: Works fine in my Galaxy S5
text: It's hard for me to evaluate this product in detail, but I can report that it works just in my Samsung Galaxy S5. I turned the phone off (probably much better to insert/remove cards with the phone turned off) and then slid the card into the slot inside the back of the phone. When I turned the phone back on, there was no obvious indication that I had made any changes at all. However, when I started to take photos, the camera reported that it would now be storing pictures on the card instead of the phone's internal flash memory. So everything seems to work well.

title: Heavy weight, high quality
text: It's a cord, just a cord. If this is the style you'll need, you'll be happy. The quality of this cord is very high -- nothing at all to worry about. Recommended.

title: Pretty sweet
text:
It's small, smaller than I expected. The remote is small, light, and easy to handle. Picture quality is outstanding, as you would expect. The voice search feature works beautifully, and as of now has recognized perfectly everything I've said to it. Very nicely done, Amazon.

The out-of-box presentation is elegant. You have to connect the power adaptor, and the HDMI cable to your TV. (That means, your HDTV.) You have to put the 2 batteries (included) into the remote, and then turn it on. Configure it for your WiFi Internet connection, and you're good to go. Amazon has already thoughtfully registered the device to your Amazon account, so there's absolutely no additional setup necessary.

Why only 4 stars, and not 5? Well, the Roku gets 5 stars because of the many dozens of additional channel options with the Roku. However, all your favorites are here on the Amazon Fire, including Netflix, Hulu, Pandora, for example.

Should you get the Roku vs. the Amazon Fire? You'll probably be happy with either, especially if you don't think you would bother with all the additional channels available with Roku. For the usual things, the two are essentially identical. If you need a wired Ethernet network connection, there is a Roku model with that, and the Amazon Fire (like many other boxes) uses only WiFi. However, the Amazon has the nifty voice search feature, which is a clear improvement over Roku. (And I've been a Roku fan since it first came out.)

title: Very straightforward to configure, lots of features
text:
I got this on the strength of other reviews, and I'm not disappointed. Very polished administration interface, and it looks like it will be a solid upgrade from my 5-year-old WiFi router. It was an easy 15 minute process to install and configure this, including giving it the same WiFi SSID name and LAN address as my old router had. (That way, all my devices instantly recognize it as being the same as the old router, and the devices don't need to be reconfigured.)

The administration interface has lots more in the way of features than I expected. Check out the manual online before ordering if you want to be thorough. I've been doing network administration for years, and I think this router would be appropriate for nearly any home or small business application.

title: USB 3 is very fast!
text: I got this to connect my SDXC card, which needs special voltages. Bonus is that this operates as a USB 3 device, and I have a front-panel USB 3 port on my tower computer. I can copy files to the SDXC card at about 45 MB/s, pretty speedy. Not quite as fast as a modern hard drive, but certainly as fast as older hard drives. (And much faster than over a USB 2 interface.)

title: Very solid, old school
text:
This is a very traditional old school CD player. Aside from the gimmick of being able to vary the speed of the playback, this is as ordinary a CD player as you could imagine. It looks like it's built very robustly, which is why I bought it. It has a remote control, but nothing else at all that would qualify as a modern feature. (No bass boost, karaoke mic inputs, etc. Just playing ordinary CDs.) But it does know how to play MP3 CDs.

If that's what you want, I bet you'll be very happy with this.

You might also consider the more expensive CD-200i, which doesn't have the speed control, but does have an iPod dock. And there's the very much more expensive CD-500 CD player with many more features that are useful in a studio setting.

title: Great starter kit
text:
This review is for the Raspberry Pi Ultimate Kit. The assembled parts are all first-rate quality, and you get enough to get started and do a few simple projects. I had the basics assembled and working in about 20 minutes.

Here's a list of additional things you'll need:
Keyboard, mouse, monitor, Internet connection

The Model B board included here has the RJ-45 connection for wired LAN, or you can use the WiFi dongle that's included in the kit. A wireless keyboard/mouse will be handy if you get a keyboard/mouse pair that share a single USB dongle. (There are only 2 USB ports; of course you can attach a USB hub if you like.)

And here are some things you'll probably want to have:
1. Books on what to do with a Raspberry Pi. There are numerous inexpensive ones here on Amazon, covering things like the Python programming language to little projects you can create with the thing. Lots of information also for free on the Internet -- the Wikipedia is a fine place to start.
2. The camera module, if you want to experiment with that.
3. A clever idea of what you want to do with the thing. :-)

I've been playing with this all day, and haven't gotten bored yet. Fun stuff. If all you want to do is to learn about Linux, or do Internet surfing, this is all you need aside from the keyboard/mouse/monitor and Internet connection (wired Ethernet or WiFi). The speed is a little pokey (single core ARM CPU running at 0.7 GHz), so it's more or less the equivalent of high end computers of about 15 years ago. But it works well enough, and you can build a complete system for around $220 or maybe a bit less, including the monitor. Don't expect it to be the equivalent of a traditional desktop or laptop -- no CD/DVD drive, no easy way to copy files or make a backup, and you can't install any Windows application software, although there are lots of interesting and useful Linux applications that work fine. (Keep your data files in the cloud.) But consider the coolness factor, which it has quite a bit of.

title: Works good as a power strip
text: No lightning yet (thank goodness!), but seems to work well. The reset switch seems to be easy to accidently switch off, but it hasn't happened to me yet. The 6-foot cord is very handy to reach back to my power outlet behind the desk.

title: Difficult to uncoil
text: I had the same experience as other reviewers in trying to get the thing to lay flat on the carpet. I've almost got it, after heating the plastic (gently) a little bit. It comes tightly coiled in its package. Because I had to shorten it anyway, I cut off the end with the most curl.

title: Way overpriced
text: If you have TV Ears, you'll need to keep replacing the tips. These are the official tips, but the price is pretty steep for 10 little pieces of foam. I find the TV Ears product in general unsatisfying (mono sound, not very comfortable to wear), but my mom likes it pretty well.

title: Well-made cable
text: This cable is very well made, and includes labels on the RCA plugs to indicate tip and ring of the 1/8 inch plug. That's cool. My only problem is that the plastic end of the 1/8 inch plug is so thick that it doesn't easily fit my smartphone. I solved this by using a small knife to trim away a bit of the plastic. Not quite as pretty, but it works fine. Minus one star for that.

title: Excellent earbuds, with a few issues
text:
These are excellent earbuds. The sound is open, spacious, clear, and pleasant. I have listened to music for hours on these, and my ears don't get tired at all. Here's what I like and don't like.

The sound is open, with sparkling high frequencies and tight, precise lows. The highs sparkle so much that some listeners might think that the sound is too bright. I'm pretty happy with it. The midrange is clear, voices very easy to understand. The lows are not at all boomy, and not as powerful as earbuds that advertise things like "deep powerful bass." But the bass is solid, and for music that has lots of bass energy, these earbuds let it all come through. Overall I think the sound is very accurate, uncolored, and not at all leading to ear-fatigue. I'm very, very pleased with the sound. Pretty sweet.

The product packaging is pretty silly. It's completely overdesigned, with an outer box that separates to allow you to get to an inner tray. I puzzled over the package for about 3 minutes trying to figure out how to get into it, before I discovered a diagram on the side panel of the box. After I successfully extricated the earbuds ...

The plug has a novel oversized swivel that allows it to attach either straight or at right angles to your sound source. It's clever, but I prefer plugs that are visibly more protective of the cord. There's no bendy thing where the cord joins the oversized plug, so I'm concerned that over time the wire might break at the join. We'll see. Whether the swivel is straight or right angled, it's a large plug that I think might be uncomfortably large with some phones or MP3 players. I'm using it with a laptop computer, and it sometimes gets in the way a bit.

In the middle of the cable is a volume control barrel. Just like the plug, it's a classy-looking silvery metal color. But what it earns in form it loses in function, as the volume control slider is very difficult to operate. I have some earbuds that cost only 20% what these cost, and they have a volume control slider that very much easier to use than we have here. Nevertheless, the slider does a good job of controlling the volume when I can get my fingers to operate it.

The earbuds themselves are interesting because they have rather large metal pieces that support the part that fits in the ear. My first reaction was that they would be uncomfortably heavy, or that they might fall out of the ear, but they work remarkably well. I've listened for hours, and had to reposition the earbuds only occasionally.

The cable is typical plastic-coated cable that's heavier than some other earbuds have. It feels rugged, and it doesn't tangle easily. A cloth-wrapped cable would be much nicer still.

The earbuds come with a case that stores the earbuds and the included airplane adaptor. It's a rather large case -- it doesn't fit well into your pocket (for traveling), but does protect the earbuds very well. There's also a second very small drawstring bag, which I assume is for traveling, but it's just a bit too small and stiff to do that job well.

title: Good basic cable
text: The Amazon Basics cables are first-rate. This cable is well constructed from heavy cord. I'm using it simply to put my phone charger further from my desk, but it should work just fine for all USB 2.0 devices.

title: Works fine
text: This product holds the GPS securely, and fastens to the windshield easily. Not much else to say -- the product works well.

title: The cable guy likes it
text:
This is one of the modems that's on Comcast's recommended list for my cable system here in California. When the cable guy showed up to install my Internet service, he checked it out and said "It will work fine." After about an hour of pulling wires around my house, he hooked things up to the modem and I had very high speed Internet service. Pretty sweet.

I chose this model because its upload and download specs are well above what my cable Internet service needs, and because it has advanced features like IPv6. So I'm assuming they got the basic stuff right as well. Other reviewers have said this model runs hot, but I haven't observed that. I have it in my utility room which is in the basement where it's pretty cool to start with.

The lights on the front of the unit show what's going on, which is mostly useful as it boots up. They work well, and are also attractive to look at -- they had a good designer for that. The unit has only 3 connection ports on the back, one for power, one for the incoming cable, and one Ethernet RJ-45 out. If you want to hook up more than a single computer, you'll need to connect this single Ethernet port to a router, or wireless router. I have the cable modem connected into a 5-port NetGear switch downstairs, which is connected to an 8-port NetGear switch upstairs, which is then connected to my Linksys wireless router. My computers then use the IP addresses that the wireless router provides. (It won't work to plug additional computers into the switch that I connected directly to the cable modem because the cable company provides only one IP address. It's the wireless router that hands out additional IP addresses. Each computer that you're using requires its own IP address.) The wireless connection works well for my 2 computers and my Roku box for Netflix. (And the bandwidth available to Netflix is amazing. It spends virtually no time at all buffering before it starts streaming HD video.)

Oh, and of course I had to reboot everything (including the modem and the wireless router) for the new modem to be recognized. For now, I'm keeping my old DSL service as a backup Internet service. Not sure when I might decide to give that up.

title: Works great, adds good low end
text:
This is pretty heavy, but not so large that it's hard to position. I have it next to my computer that I use to listen to Amazon streaming MP3 music. My main speakers are NHT Model Twos, and this subwoofer supplies an excellent bottom end to the music. I haven't played it loud yet, but I'm looking forward to trying it out on a movie soundtrack.

The power switch has three positions -- Off, On, and Auto. In the Auto setting, it turns itself on if it senses an incoming signal. When I'm playing music softly, I'm finding that it takes a while to discover that it should turn on. In my case, the subwoofer is sitting next to my desk, and it's not hard to reach the power switch. But keep this in mind if you want to hide it somewhere that would make the power switch hard to reach. (It's near the top of the rear of the cabinet.) There's also a phase switch, with two positions. There's no magic to that; just set it to the position that sounds best. As with all subwoofers, the placement in your room isn't critical, although the subwoofer's sound can be somewhat amplified if you locate it in a corner.

Update: I've had time now to use this with lots of different types of music, as well as TV and movies. The bass is very solid and tight, with no boominess at all. It blends beautifully, with plenty of power for my medium-sized room. This is very musical, adding firm support that's more than just "punch". This is surely one of the best values in powered subwoofers, and I'd buy it again in a heartbeat.

title: Has some good points, but too many bad points
text:
I've used this touchpad off and on at work over the last few weeks. I really tried to like it, but it just doesn't work well enough for it to be my main pointing device. Here are the things that are issues for me:

* Tracking speed is very different from my mouse, which is a standard Dell mouse. This wouldn't be an issue if the touchpad could replace my mouse, but it really can't. So I'm switching back and forth between the touchpad and the mouse for different tasks. And I have to visit the Mouse Control Panel in between to change the tracking speed. This just takes way too much time.
* It's not as precise as my mouse (my standard Dell mouse). So it just always feels a bit clumsy.
* As other reviewers have noted, there's a margin of dead space around the trackpad, but no tactile way to sense this area. So I'm always getting to the edge without knowing, except seeing that the mouse suddenly stops moving. This is a continual annoyance.
* Sometimes the responsiveness isn't quite there -- I think maybe this is because it's wireless. Not sure. But I've never had this problem at all with my wired mouse.
* The multitouch gesture for scrolling does work, but it doesn't work well. It works poorly enough for me to prefer the scroll bar. The track wheel on my standard wired mouse is much better.

There are some good points:
* On-off switch on the underside is easy to see and use.
* Stays put on my desk -- doesn't slide around.
* Buttons are pretty easy to operate, with just the right amount of resistance.
* USB dongle is tiny, and it can stay in my laptop all the time.
* Other reviewers have commented that the plastic surface doesn't "glide" as well as other trackpads. But that part works fine for me.

title: Beautful
text: This is a beautiful e-reader. First of all, it's big. You can increase the font size to make books easier to read, and you can still fit most of a page on the screen even when the typesize is quite large. That's really nice. And it runs for weeks without recharging, so I'm not constantly trying to remember to charge it. Love it.

title: Good noise cancelling, sound pleasing but just ok
text:
You get two types of noise cancelling with this. First, there's some noise blocking just from having these stuck in your ears. Then the active noise cancelling works quite well. But you have to have them stuck in your ears really firmly, which isn't too easy for me. I suppose it all depends on the shape of your ears. You get several sets of tips, but none of them seem to fit me quite right.

The active noise cancelling works better than I expected. It does a better job with low rumbles, like aircraft noise. It's not so good with voices, but it does give you a little bit of reduction there too. I use them in my office, in a somewhat busy environment.

The sound quality is very pleasing, but it doesn't have the sparkling highs or very deep lows that you get with more expensive earphones or earbuds. Nevertheless, the sound is smooth and well balanced, so it's comfortable to listen to.

For the price, I'm pretty happy.

title: Disappointing
text:
From the many positive reviews, I had high hopes for this. There are a number of frustrating features with this. It does pick up good strong signals when it's aimed at a station's transmitter.

Good points
- Pretty good reception.
- It has dipoles too, which are good for VHF stations, if the stations are nearby.

Not so good points
- The whole thing is unstable, and keeps falling over. It should be weighted (heavier).
- When it does fall over, which is often, the metal antenna elements can bend easily. They're pretty easy to bend back into shape.
- The coax cable comes out of the bottom of the antenna, and it must be routed through the base. The cable doesn't want to stay put, making the antenna even more likely to tip over.
- The shape is unwieldy. That's a function of the antenna elements, inherent in the design. But it makes it awkward to rotate the antenna to point to different stations.
- When the dipole antennas are extended, the whole thing is very top-heavy. It's *really* easy to tip over.

The signal amplifier comes as a separate unit that you connect inline with the coax cable. I haven't found that it makes much difference in reception. If the station is too weak to pick up, the amplifier isn't likely to magically fix it.

title: Very good, but have reasonable expectations
text:
This actually works pretty well. How well it works for you is highly dependent on your car, and your car's FM radio. It's important to have reasonable expectations for this -- if you want to hook up your MP3 player to your car stereo, the best way is through an Aux input jack. Now, if your car stereo doesn't have an Aux input jack, that's where this product comes in handy. (Another way to hook up your MP3 player is using a cassette adaptor, if your car stereo can play cassette tapes. These also work pretty well, if you can deal with a wire hanging out from the slot where you insert tape cassettes.)

This unit is smaller than I expected, and hangs out of your cigarette lighter with a cord that plugs into your MP3 player. The reception quality over your FM radio depends quite a bit on the position of the unit and the wire. I've found it works best to position the unit somewhere that works, like in the ashtray, or wedged between the seats, rather than let it dangle. If you let it dangle, then its position relative to your FM radio will keep changing as you drive, and that can make the reception quality change. Even small changes in the the position of the unit, an inch to the right or left, can make a big difference in the sound. Sound quality will also vary depending on where your car's radio antenna is located, either in the back of the car or in the front. You need to experiment with this to find the best location.

There's a "Pro" button that cycles through 4 sound quality settings. You'll want to try all four to see how they work. Sometimes the type of music you're playing will sound better with one of those four settings.

Set your MP3 player's sound output as high as you can to overcome static on the FM radio. You need to set the unit and the FM radio to the same frequency. The unit's ClearScan button makes it easy to find an unused FM frequency in your area -- you then tune the car's FM radio to that frequency and you're good to go. As you drive, if you find that you get increasing noise combined with your music, that's often an indication that you've moved into an area with another station, possibly a weak station, on that same frequency. At that point, you'll need to retune the unit (and the car's FM radio) to a different unused frequency.

The part of the unit that plugs into the cigarette lighter also has a USB jack where you can plug in your MP3 player's charging cord, so you can charge your player while you're in the car listening to tunes. Pretty handy.

Considering that my car's stereo doesn't have an Aux input, and that I don't want to replace or upgrade my car's stereo right now, this unit works great. I'm not expecting perfection with the sound quality, but it's pretty good. Better than most FM stations on the dial. Certainly good enough to make me happy to enjoy my own tunes.

title: Above average
text:
This is a fine wireless router, well above average. It has a few shortcomings that I'll get to in a moment.

The good stuff: It's got lots of features -- wired ports, WiFi, VPN. It's pretty easy to configure, especially if you're familiar with networking.
The not-so-good stuff: The Web-based configuration utility is fine, but somewhat strangely laid out, especially for content filtering. The screens all work, but they are somewhat confusing. The content filtering works well, but it's not as flexible as I had hoped.

I bought this to keep the kids away from video games. The content filtering is sort of ok for that, but it's inflexible. You can permit access by time of day, and you can deny access to certain Web sites, but you can't deny access to certain sites at specific times of day. It's all or nothing. The content filtering works well, but if you have more than a few words you're trying to filter out, you'll find that Web pages load more slowly because the router has to scan them for your blocked words.

So in summary, for the price paid I'm happy. I wish it did a bit more for content filtering, but for the price this is a pretty good deal.

title: Very nice monitor
text:
This is the second of these monitors that I've bought. I've come to really like it. But there are some pros and cons. Here are my observations.

Pros:
Very nice colors
LED lighting is bright and even, and should last a long time
On-off button on the bottom of the bezel is easy to find and use
Easy to assemble monitor stand
VGA, DVI and HDMI connectors
Works well both as a TV and as a computer monitor. Large enough to be a TV, but not so large as to be unwieldy with the computer. (But for TV use, you'll need external speakers.)
Very light and portable -- easy to move from room to room

Cons:
Monitor stand is not adjustable, except for a narrow range of tilt
*Very* glossy surface, lots of reflections depending on how your room is lighted

I've used several types of monitors, and I'm very happy with this one. The glossy surface works especially well for watching movies. For the computer, I find I'm repositioning it sometimes to minimize reflections. This is a disadvantage of glossy screens, but I'm still very happy with this monitor overall.

title: Good value, and USB 3.0
text:
This is a standard portable external drive with a USB interface. It's small, easy to handle, and works well. Most external drives use the USB 2.0 interface. This has the newer, and much faster, USB 3.0 interface. (But it works just fine when connected to a computer that has USB 2.0. The speed in that case would be the slower USB 2.0 speed.)

USB 3.0 uses a different connector on the drive, so you need to use the USB 3.0 cable that comes with the drive. A standard USB 2.0 cable won't work because it has a different connector on the drive side. On the computer side, it's a standard USB plug, so it fits both USB 2.0 and USB 3.0 jacks on the computer.

I use this to move many GB's of data from my PC to my Mac laptop. The PC has USB 3.0, so it's blazing fast to move data from the PC to the external drive. My Mac laptop has USB 2.0, so it takes longer to move the data from the drive to the Mac. But it works. Drive capacities are now so large that USB 3.0 is a huge advantage. It takes quite a bit of time to move 1 TB of data at USB 2.0 speed.

title: Really easy to set up
text:
This device is a WiFi repeater. That means that it picks up your existing WiFi signal and rebroadcasts it to extend the reach of your network.

I got this (and the [[ASIN:B004WPUHXO Amped Wireless High Power Outdoor 14dBi Directional WiFi Antenna Kit (AD14EX)]]) to extend my wireless network to my workshop, at the back of the yard, about 250 feet from the house. This is far enough away that I don't get even the smallest amount of the WiFi signal from the house. I wanted to watch TV while I work, and I also needed to be able to use a phone there. I could run Cat-5e wiring underground, but that would require digging a trench across the yard, and also running the Ethernet cable from the router inside the house to a demarcation point at the exterior of the house, which would be quite a bit of work. Using this repeater and antenna--two pairs of them, actually, the pair in the house and the other pair in the workshop--I'm able to get a very strong and fast network link in the workshop.

It's incredibly easy to set up. The antenna is designed to be mounted outdoors, and they recommend using 25 feet of [[ASIN:B004WW5WAA Amped Wireless Premium Outdoor 25ft Antenna Extension Cable (APC25EX)]] to connect the antenna to the Smart Repeater. Instead, I connected the Smart Repeater directly to the antenna with the short cable that comes with the antenna, and both are sitting in a closet at the edge of the house. In the workshop, I have the Smart Repeater and antenna sitting on a shelf above my desk. I would probably get an even better signal if I mounted the antennas outside, but it works just fine for me with the antennas inside. In the workshop, I aimed the second antenna in the general direction of the one in the house, and it works great. There are a few trees between the buildings, and the signal still gets through.

You use a Web browser to set up the Smart Repeater, and it's incredibly easy. It automatically scans to find your existing wireless network, and then lets you choose a name for the new wireless network that connects to the first. It took me about 6 minutes to set up, including 3 minutes for the device to reboot after configuration.

Without doing anything to really optimize things, I'm getting 2.5 Mbps downlink, and about half that uplink. This is slower than my router's upstream connection, but it works just fine. For comparison, when I'm in the house connected directly to my WiFi router, I get 19 Mbps downlink, and 1 Mbps uplink. So I'm getting much less speed downlink, but all the available uplink bandwidth. I guess I'll go experiment with mounting and aiming the antennas better. But even with the reduced speed, I'm really enjoying having the network and phone in the workshop.

title: Excellent for long-range WiFi
text:
I got this (and the [[ASIN:B004NBL9WK Amped Wireless High Power Wireless-300N Smart Repeater (SR300)]]) to extend my wireless network to my workshop, at the back of the yard, about 250 feet from the house. title: USB 3.0 speed is great
text:
I bought this because of the USB 3.0 speed, to back up my music workstation. I have about 1.5 TB of active data, and I need to back this up in much less time than would be possible with USB 2.0. I'm using a new computer that comes with USB 3.0 ports, and it works great. Very speedy.

Some reviewers have commented on the proprietary software. You don't have to use this, and I don't. I just plug it in without doing any software installation, and it appears in Windows as an ordinary hard drive.

title: Works great with my Mac laptop
text: I bought this to do periodic backups of my Mac laptop. It works great -- it gets all the power it needs from the USB port. To copy my entire 500 GB hard drive using USB 2.0, it takes a while. For just a few files, it's very quick.

title: Works great!
text:
I had never before used a USB video adaptor, so I wasn't sure how well it would work with my large monitor. I have a 1920x1080 HDTV monitor, and this works just great. I use Microsoft office, and I put all my Word documents on the large monitor to work on them. The image is very crisp, and there's no problem with motion on the monitor when moving windows around.

I'm using this with a laptop computer that has only a VGA external monitor port. That worked ok, but I had some minor ghosting of the images using the VGA cable. I hoped that the digital interface of the DVI adaptor would cure this, and it does.

title: Good basic cable, works fine
text: Digital signals don't degrade when they get to the other end of a properly working cable. The Cables To Go cables are excellent quality, and work just as well as the much higher priced cables.

title: Great sound, good design, could be better
text:
This product and the similar [[ASIN:B004CQNTF6 Sennheiser CX 880i Premium Ear-Canal Headphones with Microphone & Smart Remote]] earbuds have great sound. The 880 has the integrated volume control, and the 880i has the iPhone/iPod compatible mic/volume attachment. (Even though that product is designed for iPhone/iPod, the mic and pause button -- but not the volume buttons -- work with my Blackberry Bold 9700.) There are numerous thoughtful details in this product, and a couple of significant shortcomings which I'll describe. Overall, this is a very excellent 4-star product.

Pros:
The sound is just great. You can get earbuds with better sound, but it won't be cheap. I listen to all kinds of music including many genres of popular music as well as classical, and the sound with all is very smooth. The highs are very open and clean. Some listeners may prefer to slightly boost the midrange. The bass, including the deep bass, is solid without using any bass boost. I hear a small peak in the mid-bass. I make very *slight* adjustments in my iTunes equalizer to make the already great sound a bit better.

The fit will depend on how well the included selection of tips fit your ears. In my case, I found tips that fit very well. They stay put very snugly, and they're very comfortable even for longer listening sessions. The shape of the ear pieces is angled, and that works out very well. The way the cord exits the ear pieces is also pretty good.

These are designed to be good for noise isolation, and Sennheiser pulls this off really well. Note that noise isolation is different from noise cancellation, but the end result is very similar. With both, you don't hear outside noises and you can play the sound at lower volumes (which helps to protect the ears). In my experience, noise isolation works better at higher frequencies, and noise cancellation works better at low frequencies (like airplane noise). I've already used these earbuds on one flight, and I'm happy enough that they'll find a home in my travel kit.

Speaking of the travel kit, the included case is surprisingly well designed. I love it. And the little cleaning tool really does help to keep the ear pieces clean, along with the well-designed diaphragm covers.

Cons:
As other reviewers have mentioned, there are significant microphonics issues with the cord. This is disappointing, since the sound is otherwise so excellent. I've found I can eliminate most of this problem by stuffing the middle of the cable inside my shirt a bit, so there's less loose cable to rub on my collar. That works pretty well. Still, a different material for the cord could solve this better.

Also, the cable feels a bit fragile, especially where it joins the earbuds themselves. I've been using this less than a month, so I don't know how this will fare in the long term.

On balance, these are easily the best earbuds I've ever had. I'm finding new joy in listening to music when I'm out and about, or late at night when I don't want to disturb the rest of the family.

*** UPDATE ***
Six months later, and I'm still very happy with these earbuds. There's one problem I've grown very tired of -- If you don't put them away properly in their case, the cord gets badly tangled. It takes much longer than it should to untangle these guys. Also, the plug end has become noisy where it attaches to my MP3 player. Same problem on 2 players, so it's the cord for sure. Not too bad yet that I want to return it; not sure if it will get worse over time.

title: Excellent carry-all with some quality issues
text:
I've used this bag for about two months. Basically, I like it pretty well. The interior is padded just about right, and there are lots of little compartments (which can be customized) that hold my camera, a few lenses and other assorted gizmos. The zippers work very smoothly, and it's very easy to pop my camera in and out whenever I need it.

But one of the straps has now started to come apart at the seam where it connects with the bag. I've filled the bag with gear, but certainly not overstuffed it. So it's disappointing that the manufacturing quality isn't what it should be. However, for the price I still think this is a decent choice.

title: Pretty good, and not expensive
text:
For moderate priced earbuds, these are pretty good. The sound quality is much better than average, with smooth response across the range. The highs are detailed, and not shrill. The midbass is clear, with no unnatural peak that sometimes passes for "bass boost". The deep bass is natural, and not artificially strong. Very easy to listen to for extended sessions.

For comfort, these are pretty average -- not the best comfort, but not bad either. There are interchangeable ear tips you can try out for the best fit. There's a lot of personal preference as to what's going to stay in the ear comfortably. The earbuds are angled, so you have to pay attention to the left/right orientation.

This is advertised as "iPhone compatible", meaning that there's a mic with tiny + and - buttons attached to the left ear piece. I'm a BlackBerry guy, and I'm happy to report that the mic works fine with my BlackBerry Bold 9700. But the + and - buttons don't have any effect (they don't raise or lower the volume). However, pressing the small button between the + and - buttons will either pause the song that's playing, or mute a phone call. Pretty handy.

Sound isolation is not a strong point of this set. I wasn't sure what to expect, so I guess I'm not disappointed. Probably you'd want to look elsewhere if sound isolation is important to you.

Durability may also be an issue. The wire is very thin, and it feels fragile, especially where it connects to the earbud. I'll know in 6 to 12 months whether these will stand up to regular use. The 90-degree plug will take wear better for many people, depending on how it connects to your phone, MP3 player or computer. Comes with a little storage pouch, which is good protection for the set when not in use.

title: Remote difficult to use
text:
This player has plusses and minuses. The player seems real nice. DVDs look good, and Netflix, Pandora and Vudu seem to work very well over my wireless Internet connection.

On the minus side, the remote is so annoying that gave serious thought to returning the player. The buttons on the remote are stiff, uncomfortably so. Not at all convenient to use, and sometimes painful on the fingers. Also, the player is not at all quick to start up, so you have to wait for a while before it will open its tray and accept a DVD.

title: Great sound, but design is a bit awkward
text:
First of all, these speakers sound just great, they really do. I'll echo the comments that the cords are an awkward design, depending on where you place them in relation to your sound source and listening position.

The power on-off button is on the top of the subwoofer, but the volume up-down control is on one of the satellites. And the sub's level control is on the sub itself. Aside from just plain being a bit weird, it means you're going to have to keep both the sub and one of the satellites within easy reach. Also, the cord that connects to your sound source is attached to the sub (as is the power cord); combined with the controls on the sub, this is just plain awkward. I'm using these speakers at work, and I have the sub on the floor under my desk. I'm controlling the volume from iTunes, so that's cool. But it would be very annoying if I had to be using the speaker's controls all the time.

A minor annoyance is the shape of the metal legs for the satellites. They are sturdy and look nice, but they take up much more space on my crowded desk than I'd like. Other speaker systems use more vertically shaped satellite stands, which take up half the space. These satellites are much more squat.

I also have one of the better Logitech 2.1 systems, which also sounds great. But Logitech puts all the controls on a little control unit that you can keep in easy reach. (And also has a headphone output too.) That's a much more convenient design. But between the two, the sound of these Altec Lansing speakers is superior.

Here's the dealmaker for me -- the bass control on the subwoofer can be turned all the way down, so the sub isn't putting out any sound at all. This is a great feature because it lets me play just the satellites late at night, and I'm not disturbing my housemate in the adjoining room.

title: Rotates pretty smoothly
text: This isn't the cheapest, and it's not the most expensive polarizer. I'm glad I got this one -- this filter rotates pretty smoothly, and it's not at all annoying in use. I'm using a Canon DSLR with auto focus lenses, and I've found that it's easier to switch the lens to manual focus while I'm rotating the polarizer, so I'm not rotating against the AF servos.

title: Direct equivalent for APC battery
text: This is the exact RBC7 equivalent battery that APC offers. It doesn't have the APC label, and as another reviewer has noticed, the sticky tab on the bottom of the battery comes mounted opposite where APC would mount it. Not really a problem.

title: Very good average keyboard
text: I researched keyboards before settling on this one. There's a lot of personal preference in how one is going to like a keyboard, and I've found I like the Logitech keyboards. This is several steps up from the cheapest keyboards, yet it's still modestly priced, and it works very well. Good level of comfort for the fingers typing, good positive action so I know when a key has been pressed. I'm a touch-typist, and I find I can type very quickly on it. But of course YMMV.

title: Good bargain tripod
text: This is a lightweight tripod. That's good in that it's real easy to carry around. That's bad in that it's real easy to tip over, or break. With my camera sitting on top of this, it just doesn't look or feel solid. However, for what you get, it's pretty good. Another reviewer warned of the quick release. It looks good to me, but it's very easy to not get the the latch mechanism all the way fully latched. You have to give it an extra push to get it to fully latch closed. Once you do that, I think it will stay latched. But why worry about the quick release coming loose when the entire tripod is so easy to knock over? Nevertheless, this is a good starter tripod. A pro will want something costing 3 or 4 times this one.

title: Really nice earbuds, and fantastic for the price

These earbuds come with a handy case, and are remarkably good and very easy to listen with. They've got a permanent home in my travel kit.

title: Nice webcam but overpriced for what you get.
text:
I ordered the "Yealink UVC30 Teams Certified Webcam 4k Web Camera 120 Degree View Desktop Webcam with Microphone 1080P HD Video Streaming Webcam with Windows Hello for Gaming and Recording (USB-A&C)" for review and would like to share my thoughts.

I was in need of a new Webcam and thought that the Yealink UVC30 camera would be the perfect replacement. It has been a good replacement for my 10 year old webcam however I would not say a perfect replacement. The build quality is good as is the quality of video and sound however for the price, I think there are better options on the market. My biggest disappointment was that there was no camera software included. I realize that it is totally plug and play and the fact that it works straight out of the box for Teams is great but I was hoping for some fun bells and whistles as far as software goes. Unfortunately there was no software included. I am not even sure if there is a way to upgrade the firmware for that matter. With that out of the way, the camera is good and the build quality is also good. It mounts fine to my Asus 27" monitor with no issues. I do like that it comes with a lens cover which just slides over the front of the lens. It's nice and compact and not distracting. Overall I do think it is a good camera but I just feel that it is a bit overpriced for what it is.

It has become my go-to gimbal for my Canon 90D DSLR. It handles the weight much better although the 90D is not all that heavy to begin with. I love how the handle can be placed below or above for easy handling. The handle placed above makes for smooth low to the ground perspective shooting which has become my favorite way to shoot video.

The Filmtacy C1 comes with several different cable connectors which should fit most cameras but most importantly (for me) was that it had the connector that I needed for the 90D. The Filmtacy C1 is well built and does not feel cheap in any way shape or form. Overall I think that this is one of the best gimbals out there at this particular price point.

title: Great for basic use.....
text:
I ordered 'Lenovo IdeaPad 3 14" Laptop, 14.0" FHD 1920 x 1080 Display, AMD Ryzen 5 3500U Processor, 8GB DDR4 RAM, 256GB SSD, AMD Radeon Vega 8 Graphics, Narrow Bezel, Windows 10, 81W0003QUS, Abyss Blue' for review and would like to share my thoughts.

First off if you are looking for a gaming beast of a laptop, this is not it. However if you are looking for a laptop that will mainly be used for web browsing, Netflix streaming, office document creating and some light gaming, this laptop does great. The only game that I have tried with this, (besides Solitaire) is Diablo lll and it did just fine. With that said, I would not recommend using this for gaming as it just does not have the hardware to support it. There seems to only be one RAM slot and no other hard drive slots to upgrade for more internal storage as you can see in the attached images.

Now with that out of the way, I will list some of the features I really like.
It's light weight and small enough to fit in most backpacks.
It has a built in privacy slider for the built in camera.
It is a solid build quality.
It runs Windows 10 very well and has been stable with every windows update so far.
It has an HDMI port.
It has a good amount of USB A ports (3).
It has a built in SD card reader slot.

Overall this has been a great little laptop for my use and I think it has good value if you understand the limitations. One thing that I do wish it had was a USB C port. Other than that it has been solid and reliable laptop that I mainly use for browsing the web, video chat, streaming movies and very light gaming.

title: Overall nice system.
text:
[[VIDEOID:5b880a1d8f11ab783ee7340a330164be]] I ordered the ‘CTVISION 4K 8MP Home Business Wired Security Camera Systems,8-Channel 4K 8MP PoE Network Video Recorder(4TB HDD),8pc 4K (4X1080P) Outdoor Dome PoE IP Camera,Free App,P2P Cloud,Onvif,Video Surveillance’ for review and would like to share my thoughts.

I will lay this out as pros and cons and give some final thoughts.

Pros: The kit as a whole is well made.
Cameras are well made.
The 4tb hard drive is a good name brand and seems to be performing quite well.
The video quality is good.
The kit comes with 8X good quality 50 foot CAT5 cables (more on this in the cons)

Cons: The included cables are only 50 feet each. In a home install, if you are trying to run cameras to all corners of your house, 50 feet is not long enough in my case. I only used three of these cables. I had to buy more cable (CAT6) for the longer runs.
Although the cameras are well made, because they are of the Dome type, if you adjust the cameras to point at much of an angle, you run into issues at night when the IR lights turn on. This causes the IR lights to reflect back at the cameras (See attached video) The best angle for the cameras are to point straight down or at a very slight angle.
Speaking of angles, these cameras only have a 90 degree diagonal viewing angle which was a little disappointing.
When viewing the live feed, sometimes the video feed gets distorted for a couple of seconds.
The software of the NVR is a little overwhelming and hard to navigate. This is probably due to the fact that I have never used this type of system before. There are a lot of options in the Software which does not work with these specific cameras, such as Human Detection or PTZ (Pan Tilt Zoom). Not having the PTZ is really no big deal but it would have been nice to have the Human Detection so that the cameras don’t alarm when the wind blows the trees and shrubs.
There is an option to send an email when there is motion detected on the cameras but I was never able to get that to work.
Although there is an email option, I would have liked to see a text option.

Overall I am actually happy with this kit. It at least provides peace-of-mind knowing that the cameras are always recording and with the included 4tb hard drive in this kit, it provides many hours of footage. I hope that this was somewhat helpful.

title: Nice, but not amazing for the price.
text:
I ordered the 'Malektronic Interstellar Premium Wireless Noise Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones' for review and would like to share my thoughts.

So I am no audiophile, but I do love a good quality headphone that is built well and sound good. Sounding good or even great is really subjective depending on personal preference. For the going retail price of these Malektronic Interstellar Premium Wireless Noise Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones, I really expected much more than what I personally find these to be. I'll break my experience and thoughts into a few main points that stood out to me.

Comfort - These are comfortable but they don't fit as snug as I would have liked. I have a small head for a 54yro male, and even on the smallest adjustment setting, they just don't hug my ears like I would have hoped for such an expensive set of headphones.

Noise Cancelling - yea this is a big one for me right hear (see what I did there). I am not at all impressed with the Noise Cancelling in these headphones for the price. I mean it's OK, but I have ANC wireless earbuds that do a much better job for about the same price. There are only two settings. ANC On and ANC Off. For me, It's really hard to tell whether I've turned it on or off. There is no indicator like others I have that would either beep or greet you with some kind of prompt letting you know which mode you are in (there are voice prompts when you turn them on or off so why not anything for ANC modes). In fact the only way I can truly tell that it's on or off, is to pause the song and push the ANC button at which point it's pretty clear. However, and with that said, I do notice that when it's on, the music almost sounds more heavy on the Bass. It's almost like the Bass is supposed to give that "ANC" feel. Remember, I am no audiophile but this is just my observation.

Sound - Now I can say this, and that is that these do sound good until you get close to max volume. At which point they just don't hold up to the volume. Not that they get really loud but if you have the ANC on and you are listening to a heavy Bass song, they tend to bottom out just a tad. It's not bad but again for this price point, I would have expected better. The highs are nice but even better when ANC is off. Mids are there and probably sound good in either mode really. Another thing I noticed is that if you take these off while the music is still playing at full volume, they sound like they are rattling and sound a bit distorted. However when you put them back on, there is no distortion like I noticed with them off. That was kind of strange.

Micro USB charging - I always have to point this out. It's 2020 companies and USB C should be the standard any more in my opinion. Just saying.

Build Quality - They aren't the worst I have seen or tried but at this price point they are not the best either. They are pretty much plastic although fairly solid.

Buttons - The buttons are hidden/covered near the edge of the ear pads and they took me a while to figure out where they are, but after using them for a while, I actually like the fact that they look to be buttonless.

Looks/design - These really do look nice both on and off. They don't look cheap which is nice, as I have some others that just look ugly and I refuse to wear haha. The design is well thought out and I do love how they fold flat and compact into the very nice hard case.

So with all that said, I do like these headphones. They sound pretty good. The ANC is meh but they are comfortable besides not fitting as snug as I would prefer. Build quality is decent and I do love they way they fold up and store nicely into the included hard case. Thank you for including this Maletronics! Micro USB charging is a bummer but they also can be used wired with the included cable if you forget to get them charged up. Battery life is not bad. 30hrs might be pushing it if you like to listen to them loud and are always using the ANC. I have yet to test that fully as the longest I generally go is maybe an hour at a time. So for me the battery life is fine.

Overall, I really want to love these, and I actually do like them a lot, but I am just not that "Wowed" at this price point. I have other brands at or around this price point that I like better. Now maybe I got a dud pair and that very well could be, but I don't dislike them. They are nice and I plan to keep them around as a back-up pair. I hope that this was helpful.
