title: Near-invisible protection!  And quieter too
text:
Fits perfectly on my new, "mid-2017" 15-inch MacBook Pro. Like others here, I have not needed to use the little pieces of stickum tape. It's really precision-crafted and fits flawlessly. It also seems to quiet the clacky butterfly switches a bit! With this in place, they make a nicely damped thumping sound.

I'm happy.

UPDATE: Just thought of something. This latest (2016/2017/2018) MacBook Pro generation has a reputation for unreliable keywords. In fact, Apple just announced an extended warranty. What actually happens is that tiny bits of debris get into the key mechanisms, which are exquisitely engineered and miniaturized... to the point that small pieces of dust can cause the keys to malfunction. This keyboard cover should really help that!

title: Problematic so far.  Haven't given up quite yet...
text:
One star until I get this thing running. I've provisioned multiple Raspberry Pis since the original model. This thing... so far no joy.

Part of the problem is the chaotic Libre Computer website, which is a marvel of broken links and broken promises. For example, the preferred SD card burner application is shown as available for Mac, Linux and Windows, but when you get to the actual download page it's Windows-only. Oh, there's a series of links that you can wade through (mislabeled Google Drive but actually leading to a Baidu page) that yields to a page in Chinese that suggests there's a macOS download, but clicking through that yields a download of a Baidu NetDisk, a Dropbox-wannabe that I would really not want to install on my computer! Meanwhile the "official" download button yields an error.

Fortunately there's a second application, Etcher, which works well on my Mac. It does, however, require that you download the firmware separately. No problem, there's a link for that, right? ...Except that Etcher won't recognize the download. Etcher requires certain file extensions and the download doesn't have any of them. Appending .img to the filename let Etcher proceed, but attempting to boot the Renegade using the resulting SD card spits a "Error -110 whilst initializing" issue and freezes the Renegade. Most typically with small ARM-based computers like this, that seems to indicate a card incompatibility due to timing or something. But I've tried this with known-good 8GB and 32GB cards originally used in Raspberry Pis and the failure is consistent. Perhaps the .img extension I appended is not the correct one? Who knows. I asked on the "support" forum and it's been a couple days with no replies.

I really hope I can get this working, because I need the higher Ethernet I/O throughput that it promises vs. the sadly bottlenecked Ethernet-over-USB2 architecture of the Raspberry Pi. But first the thing needs to boot!

UPDATE:

I finally got the preferred "SDCard Installer" utility downloaded, after extracting the link from the inscrutable Chinese website's source HTML code (!). This allowed the utility to download and install directly without attempting to install the Baidu NetDisk thing, which I would not trust. It took a really long time to download, though... close to an hour for 58MB.

So, the SDCard Installer utility incorporates an automatic download feature. Unfortunately the Debian option does not appear. So, I tried the Ubuntu option. Suspiciously, the download is shown as 100% complete in a couple of seconds. Can't be right. And sure enough, the flash process fails, with a nonsensical error message. I tried with all the other download options with identical results. Unimpressive.

So I went back to the downloads page and downloaded the Ubuntu image directly. This download failed midway about a dozen times but could be re-started. Once complete, I then checked the MD5 checksum... and it didn't match. Either the repeated broken downloads resulted in a corrupt file, or the published checksum is incorrect. Nevertheless, I tried installing using the SDCard Installer utility, and the flash completed without error (using the known-good 8GB SD card from a Raspberry Pi). ...But the card still won't boot, still reports that "-110 whilst initializing" error and freezes in the boot process.

title: Works well and will satisfy even the pickiest reader
text:
I love to read but held off buying a Kindle until now because I could not abide the resolution of early generations' screens. The fonts used to look penciled-in, jagged and coarse to my eye. Plus, I travel frequently and would need a backlight for reading on long flights, and the earliest Kindles lacked a backlight option.

Times change, and when I finally succumbed to the Kindle's siren call just ahead of a sun-drenched holiday where there'd be zero hope of reading poolside on my iPad or iPhone, I was happy to see that the Paperwhite model now comes with a high-resolution display and a backlight at a reasonable price.

Reading Experience

The fonts do look pretty nice now. There are about six or eight font choices you can apply, and you can choose their size and weight easily from a menu. I'm still experimenting to find a favorite. I'm a bit of a font snob but have no serious criticisms of the kerning and justification options (I prefer ragged right formatting to fully-justified, and most books allow this).

The backlight works well, is fully adjustable, and is nice and even save for a bit of faint scalloping at the far bottom edge.

Glare has been no problem at all.

Images look pretty terrible, but that's not what this device is for. It's a single-purpose tool for consuming textual books in any environment, and at that it excels.

There are lots of reader tools, such as word lookup and things like that. I haven't explored most of those options.

User Interface

I have a passcode set, and entering the passcode is weirdly slow; you must pause significantly between characters.

The touch interface works well, but there are some drawbacks to it. Mostly, it can be annoying to fumble the device and find you've lost your place in the process of grabbing it. That's less of a problem with the dedicated buttons on some other models.

I do wish the Goodreads option were removable from the menu as I have no interest in it and have accidentally tapped it a few times.

The single ads you see on waking the device don't bother me. They're static and inoffensive and go away with a swipe. I'm unmotivated to spend the $20 to eliminate them, but that option is there if they bug you.

Slightly more concerning is that occasionally the text has lacked contrast. But I've found that going into and out of a menu, which forces a screen refresh, can help that. (I have Page Refresh turned off to minimize the blinking effect that otherwise accompanies most page turns, limiting the blinks to chapter transitions. This may be the cause of the occasional contrast loss. Now that I've found what seems to be a work-around, I'll leave Page Refresh off.)

Connectivity

Both the WiFi and mostly-free 3G connectivity work well. So far I've tested the 3G in five countries with no problem. WiFi has worked well and I've had no problem connecting to hotel WiFi that requires browser input-- the Kindle's "experimental browser" has worked sufficiently well for that.

My understanding is that Amazon-purchased book downloads, syncing and updates are free over 3G even if you are roaming internationally. But, if you're roaming internationally, you will be charged a small amount for downloading documents other than Amazon-sold books. By the way, that downloading capability is a really cool feature (you can email .pdfs and non-Amazon ebooks in certain formats to your Kindle via a special Kindle email address Amazon automatically sets up for you) but one that I'd wager 99% of Kindle users don't use or even know about, much less use internationally.

Battery & Charging

Note that the vaunted Kindle battery life of umpty-ump weeks is based on benchmarking with an estimated usage of only 30 minutes per day, and I believe it includes Airplane Mode being enabled. But after my 12-hour flight that I mostly spent reading with the backlight on and Airplane Mode enabled, the device still has about 65% battery charge. Not bad!

I did not purchase a charger. I pack an Anker 10-port USB charger (which works off of any national voltage and frequency and is highly recommended!) to keep all my gizmos charged when I travel, and the Paperwhite has had no objection to that.

Bottom line

I'm liking my Kindle Paperwhite a lot. There has been no problem reading in the bright poolside sun or on darkened transoceanic flights, and the touch user interface works well enough for me. The unit seem solidly built and is a great bargain for serious readers.

UPDATE: I totally neglected to note how delightful it was to order this from Amazon and have it arrive fully configured and personalized for my account. This made the unboxing experience the rival of Apple's! Special kudos to Amazon for that.

UPDATE: I did the Kindle a disservice by calling its built-in illumination a "backlight". It's actually a "front light"-- the white LEDs shine along the front faceplate and their light is directed down towards the screen by a nano-machined pattern embossed into the back side of the faceplate. So, the light is reflected off the e-ink screen (just as ambient light is), rather than shining through the display as is the case with smartphones and tablets.

title: Very happy with this so far.  One dongle to rule them all!
text:
18 MONTH UPDATE: This continues to travel with me (in a little zippered hard-case) and so far, knock wood, no problems. It remains the only unit I've found with all the ports I need, including SD, VGA and HDMI. Five star review renewed.

UPDATE: I had an issue with data throughput to which the seller responded quickly. They documented a similar test that showed no problem and suggested I try connecting my Sandisk SSD to the BC (higher-power) USB3 port. I'd done that, but trying it again the performance is excellent (see photo). So who knows what was going on-- my Mac has been rebooted many times by now and perhaps some app was causing an issue. So I'm happily underscoring this review as five stars for the manufacturer's responsive support and willingness to work with me as a customer. The product continues to perform well in my first international trip with it, and it is very nice to have all the necessary ports in one USB-3.1 compact accessory.

Original five star review:

This is a nice companion to my wonderful new MacBook Pro. So far I've used it to run the super-slick Migration Assistant to pull my entire previous MacBook Pro over to the new machine over Ethernet. That worked flawlessly, and speeds exceeded my expectations for Gigabit Ethernet, faultlessly completing the whole 1-terabyte process in about three hours. No driver-download was required. The USB 3 ports work well with both the USB 3 and USB 2 peripherals that I've tried so far. They work fine when passed through to a Windows virtual machine too. I haven't tried the HDMI and VGA ports yet, which is surprising as they were what I was primarily looking for when I selected this product. Based on everything else, I'd be surprised if they don't work perfectly too.

Pros: Functional and speedy. Everything you're likely to need in one nice-looking, briefcase-compatible, USB-C-powered dongle that won't embarrass your gorgeous Mac. Lots of ports. Great for road-warriors who need fast Ethernet access, old-timey USB 3 and 2 connectivity, and display compatibility with HDMI and VGA projectors and monitors. One tidy gizmo to carry instead of a multitude. Way cheaper than the multi-dongle approach! For my purchase I selected the "Space Grey" option-- it is a pleasing metal finish, like Apple's Space Grey but with a slight rosy tinge that gives it a bit of uniqueness, yet it still complements the lovely Mac design. Don't worry, the "rosy tinge" isn't feminine in the least.

Cons: The USB-C cable is non-replaceable and, inevitably, will eventually fray and break. We'll see if that happens within the warranty period. The whole item might be a tad large-- almost as big as the trackpad on my new laptop. But that means the ports are nicely separated and easy to work with. No Thunderbolt 3 port, but that might not be a limitation since all Mac notebooks have more than one and this potentially replaces several separate port-consuming dongles. The USB-C power-in port works fine, so you don't need to consume a port on your Mac just to charge it.

It's early in my ownership of this, so I'll update this review if anything happens with it. But so far, so good. Happy purchase so far.

title: You get what you pay for: safety, lack of interference, computer lifetime...
text:
The internet is full of off-brand power adaptors marketed as alternatives to costlier OEM chargers from major brands like Apple, Samsung and HP. But if you do a quick search you'll find teardowns from people like Ken Shirriff that show exactly why cheaper chargers are cheaper: hasty design, risky safety engineering, marginal components, interference-inducing layouts, equipment-endangering outputs.

The safety issues Shirriff identifies should be enough to convince any sensible consumer that their lives aren't worth a savings of a few dollars.

Name brands became name brands by doing several things right, starting with not electrocuting their customers. Think about that as you shop!

title: Surprisingly good functionality for the money
text:
UPDATE: Six months in, this router has been flawless. AND I've discovered it has its own dynamic DNS support capability. That's a nice feature if you run any sort of server application. So, I continue to be impressed with this product.

---

I will be keeping a close eye on this router, which I just purchased yesterday, because it seems too good to be true. So far, in my 24 hours of usage since purchasing it for $29 at Walmart (sorry, Amazon, I was in a hurry) I have found it to be flexible and powerful in my unusual application, which is remote and requires 100% uptime with occasional bursts of heavy usage. Mine is a factory-fresh rather than refurb unit, incidentally.

I'll admit I had some trouble believing a router this cheap could be as good as this one turned out to be (assuming it stays reliable-- but, the one I bought trumpets a lifetime guarantee on the box). I expected something dumbed-down, with seriously constrained functionality and annoying firmware. (This model's v3 hardware, although Broadcom BCM5356-based, is not compatible with alternative firmware such as DD-WRT due to its problematic NVRAM size.) It's a single-stream design, with an internalized antenna, potentially suggesting performance limitations. And it's from Netgear, which I've frankly not had great luck with before... but it's been years since I've tried one of their products, and the reviews here are generally good. Most of the negative reviews here relate to support experiences, but my networking knowledge-level is expert, so ...what the heck, did I mention it was $29? An easy roll of the dice.

Though my application requires custom configuration, I initially started the unit using its web-based wizard, which you access by connecting your computer (via cable or WiFi) and pointing your browser to 192.168.1.1. With the unit connected to my cable modem, it set itself up quickly and voila, Internet. For most people this would be good enough and the job would be done. Kudos to Netgear for delivering the product with WPA-2 encryption enabled! They provide a SSID and password on a printed label. So, you're good to go. And its default configuration is just fine for most folks' usage.

For my application, however, I needed to cable several devices including a VoIP adaptor (a la [...] and a server with several ports exposed to the Internet. The unit needed to be set to a specific IP address scheme, SSID and password. And a dynamic-DNS utility on the server needed to communicate with my DNS provider. ...To accomplish these and other advanced tasks, the browser-based configurator at 192.168.1.1 has an Advanced tab. Proceeding through the settings is straightforward and similar to other reasonably-configurable routers. The default settings established earlier by the wizard remain intact in the Advanced panes so you are starting from a known-operable configuration. All good.

So I proceeded through each of my customizations, taking care to click the Apply button after modifying any pane. Usually there's a ten-second delay during which the unit sets up the new settings; a few necessitate that the router reboot itself. Everything went smoothly.

So, for $29 I'd replicated an unusual configuration and everything was working. But how well?

Okay so my wife had to take an important international FaceTime call as I was finishing up. So, for a while there the server was downloading some massive updates, two ssh clients were talking to the server, VoIP was in use, six WiFi clients were doing whatever they were doing, a 3G microcell tower was initializing and downloading firmware updates to itself ...and FaceTime was running smoothly with a high frame-rate on her third-gen iPad. A nice acid test!

In particular, I did not feel the need to mess with the unit's default QoS settings... and additional props to Netgear for including QoS in a router this inexpensive!

So far, I'm impressed. It's hard to imagine a better value in a router. I'll update this review if there are any reliability issues, but so far, so good. So excellent, in fact.

title: Serious documentation, feature and firmware issues
text:
I purchased this router to upgrade my home network based on excellent user reviews. My own home network situation includes VoIP, and since my family does a lot of video streaming, QoS is a necessary feature to ensure our phone connections don't stutter. My previous router, a D-Link DIR-655, served us ably for a long time until it started showing signs of age. So I got this one, set it up, and ensured it was running the latest official Asus firmware (3.0.0.3.178, downloaded 23 August 2012).

But: The new Asus router's QoS standard settings do not prioritize VoIP! Amazing. In fact, it's as if Asus has never heard of VoIP, and their documentation is barely comprehensible (and incorrect) on the topic of QoS in general. There is no VoIP-related setting to select in the QoS setup panel; you must manually specify the ports your VoIP provider uses. The documentation is no help, as it is maddeningly bad: for example, the router's online documentation contains such pearls of wisdom as "There are two kinds of packek, web packets(use HTTP at 80 port) and P2P packets(use other port) which want to go to the WAN" --see for yourself, that's a direct quote, typos and all, from [...] --the page you are directed to when you click the "QoS FAQ" link in the router's setup page. Two kinds of packek? Web and P2P? What nonsense is this?

Worse, enabling the QoS brought the throughput of the router to its knees. Various online speed tests showed my download throughput plummeted from the 20Mbps typical of my ISP to 0.2Mbps after enabling the QoS, and latencies went from typically less than 4msec to 40-50msec. Unfortunately, disabling QoS didn't fix the problem. Rebooting the router turned out to be the cure. As in: the thing must be rebooted EVERY time I attempt to modify the QoS settings. The behavior is very repeatable, and the QoS engine in this router causes serious throughput reduction even after rebooting and even with just a single entry to prioritize my VoIP traffic.

On the plus side, the built-in PPTP VPN server works very well and is easy to set up (although Asus' free dynamic DNS service is not documented at all: there is no sign-up, just type in a unique name and you're done).

There are enough positive reviews of this router that I'm not quite to the point of giving up on it quite yet. I hope to find some combination of settings that might work for me and be stable. But the crappy documentation and reboot-hungry firmware are not encouraging. I'd say there's an 80% chance that I'll be returning this for another D-Link.

UPDATE: I gave up on this unit. The firmware is just too terrible. Back it goes.

title: Can no longer recommend
text:
We are very satisfied with the two DIR-655s that we have (at two sites). They hold up well and cause no problems. They're fast and stable; they run cool and basically require little or no attention.

Two router features that deserve much more discussion than they usually get are the unit's firewall (if any) and its Quality-of-Service (QoS) engine (if any).

o The firewall keeps external probes and hack-attempts out of your network. You'd be amazed how many probes a home or business broadband connection gets every hour from places like China, Eastern Europe and the Middle East. They're looking for ways in so they can infect your machines and steal your information. A router with a good firewall implemented in its firmware is increasingly essential. Firewalls let internal users establish connections with remote machines, not the other way around. And the DIR-655's firewall is excellent, a stateful-packet-inspection implementation that is truly industrial-class. Frankly, I didn't know this when I bought my first unit but was delighted to discover it once I brought it home. Good stuff. And, it's compatible with my company's virtual-private-network (VPN) approaches, which can be a real problem for firewalls to accommodate. My company has used two VPN approaches in the time I've had our DIR-655s, and there have been no issues.

o A good QoS engine prioritizes time-critical Internet traffic such as voice-over-Internet (VoIP). I did not fully appreciate this until we pulled the plug on our landline and implemented "roll-your-own VoIP", saving 90% off our monthly phone costs (see [...] for details). Only a router with good QoS capabilities will allow phone calls to be clear, crisp and smooth in the face of other Internet traffic. And the DIR-655 turns out to have a very good QoS engine. It automatically prioritizes the standard VoIP ports so our phone calls sound as good as a landline even with two teenagers streaming video, cruising Facebook, listening to Pandora, Skyping and FaceTime-ing, etc. Unfortunately, the marketplace is not yet fully aware of the benefits of a good QoS engine in routers, so it's not a given. Even Apple's well-regarded and excellent Time Capsule and Airport/Airport Extreme routers don't have it, for example. But DIR-655 does.

The only issue we've ever experienced with the DIR-655s in our years of usage was once when a cell phone got into a conniption loop that had it disassociate and reassociate with the router over and over and over again, many times per minute. This caused the router to bog down and reboot itself (and who could blame it). The DIR-655's informative logs helped me diagnose what was going on. Eventually the phone got straightened out, and the problem went away.

UPDATE: I can no longer recommend this router. The latest firmware is abysmal and ruins what was formerly a good product.

title: Was A 1 Star Until I Adjusted It, Makes It 4 Stars
text:
I received this mouse on September 17th. It is now December 19th, so I have given it three months of use before writing this review. Before purchasing this 3M mouse, I was using just your average, typical, mouse with a scrolling wheel in the center. For work I am on the computer around 13 hours a day. Recently my right wrist, forearm, and shoulder started to ache and eventually became very painful because of the unnatural position my mouse held my hand/arm in. Also I use the scrolling wheel very often and my middle finger (which I used to scroll with), started to swell and experience pain in the joints, with a hard, painful bone-like spur on the underside.
After using the 3M Ergonomic mouse, the swelling/pain in my finger joint went away immediately, and the bone spur also dissipated.
However, while it did alleviate the pain in my wrist, it actually caused more pain in my forearm and shoulder, and now the bonus of the entire thumb area of the hand - from the wrist up to the tip of my thumb. After a week of looking at the design and messing around with folded towels under my arm, it finally dawned on me why this mouse caused so much pain....

Though I purchased the 'small', the hand shaft is still too long, and with the toggle button at the top of it, it holds the thumb in an unnatural upward position thereby putting strain on that entire bone. When you lay your arm down on a table, with palm facing inward, in the relaxed position a thumb is NOT sticking upwards, but instead it naturally lays level with the index finger. Hence the hand shaft is too tall.

The shaft cannot be cut down obviously, so the 'deck', the part that the hand rests upon, had to be raised. To to do this I took a few sheets of paper towels, folded them to the thickness that would give the best height for my hand, then wrapped sturdy packing tape around it, to keep it folded (and makes it easy to wipe clean). Then I made a 'collar' out of paper towel to go around the base of the hand shaft, to which I taped the front part of the folded paper towels to, it helps keep it from shifting. I then put a large piece of rolled tape on the rest of the 'deck' which holds the rest of the folded towels onto the deck.
Did it work?
Yes, it did. The paper towels have conformed perfectly to the shape of my hand, and is very comfortable. It stays rather clean because of being wrapped in packing tape, which I periodically wipe clean with rubbing alcohol. More importantly, it has elevated all pain in my arm, shoulder, and thumb area. It holds my hand and fingers in a very natural position.

So while it is not perfect, and I shouldn't have to make padding for it, I gave this mouse 4 stars because I do like it, even though I had to make adjustments to make it work. It glides smoothly on a mouse pad. The toggle button is smooth, as is the scroll button. It does take some time getting used to scrolling this way, but once I got the hang of it, it's second nature to me now.

Some tips:
* I found myself 'gripping' the mouse like a joy stick because I was so not used to a mouse of this shape, which makes the four fingers hurt after a while and would make me hit the scroll button inadvertently. I had to keep reminding myself to relax my hand. No need to 'grip' it, it's not going to take you on a 'white knuckle' ride!

* Does not move well on thin or hard surfaces. I had a very, very thin mouse pad and it would not glide well on it. I purchased a thicker pad and now it moves smoothly.

* Because the hand shaft stands so far up, I have knocked this mouse right off my desk a number of times, my arm would hit it, or walking past my desk my sweater would catch it. So when not in use keep it away from the edge of the desk. At least I know that this mouse can take a beating!

title: Great idea but too many variables affect reliability
text:
I was researching the best way to get high speed NETWORK speeds to a downstairs room. The cable modem was installed into an upstairs room (left side of house) and the WIFI speed in the first floor room (right side of house) was sufficient for most internet streaming services (about 60Mbps) However I needed higher network bandwidth for accessing a NAS.

I sought out solutions that could avoid having to run an ethernet cable from the first floor to the second floor. First I tried ethernet over AC PWR. I received the same speeds as WIFI. Then I found these MOCA adapters, once installed they appeared to work great. I got sufficient speeds but not quite as fast I wanted (about 100Mbps) But once they were installed I would experience constant drops in connection across all devices. It would go out for anywhere from 30 seconds to 10 minutes.

Customer service was great and responsive via email. We verified my setup and hardware were all compatible with the MOCA adapters but the only thing that could cause issues was interference in the coax cables. Since those cables are all inside the walls already, there really wasn't anything else I could do unless I wanted to run new coax.

Ultimately I decided to run CAT8 ethernet upstairs.

title: Fabulous 1080 Ti System + PassMark Benchmark
text:
Purchased this system because, at the time, it was the only way to obtain a 1080 Ti next day, but received a fabulous overall system which far exceeded my expectations.

For background, I usually prefer to build my own computers, but would have incurred a ~$500 penalty if I took that path this time because of the ridiculously inflated 1080 Ti prices.

Per the attached photo, my system is benchmarking at the 99th percentile for CPU (holding stable overclocked to 4.9+ ghz using the automated bios tool), and 99th percentile for GPU (slight factory overclocked MSI Aero, but haven’t tweaked further yet).

It’s a bit funny that the system only scored 98th percentile in the 2d benchmark. My guess is that the test isn’t taxing enough to bump the GPU out of power saver mode (some of the compute 2d tests later on run at over 1600 FPS). Note that with regards to these benchmarks, the system hardware was tested “as is” apart from the CPU overclock.

My only concern is not terribly substantial, because I had already planned to replace the HD before I placed the order on Amazon. The HD is only benchmarking at the 69th percentile. It’s actually benchmarking pretty far below average for the WD blue 250 gb ssd, but I’m not overly concerned because it will soon be replaced. You shouldn’t be concerned either because you’re buying this system for the 1080 Ti, not the starter hd.

The keyboard and mouse are acceptable starters. I’ll be replacing these soon as well (as almost everyone buying a $2000 system will be) but they were actually better quality than I expected. Phrased another way, I’m prioritizing the new SSD over new keyboard and mouse.

Overall build quality is good - the system runs fairly quiet (though not as quiet as an iMac, but to be expected with this kind of gpu power), and looks beautiful. It’s a bit time consuming to open the case, but one does so infrequently to the extent it’s a non-concern.

In terms of gaming performance, this system is overkill for playing anything at 1080p - you should expect performance close to 150-200 FPS at 1080p.

Have been playing on a 4K gsync monitor. Witcher 3 and AC Origins performance has typically been 40-45+ fps, with all settings maxed. Sometimes it will run surprisingly close to 55-60fps. Suffice it to say 4K ultra is a stunning experience for a (former) console peasant like me.

In summary, highly recommended. Definitely choose this system if considering versus an off the shelf model. You’ll probably receive this system before a competitor starts building an alternative box. Note, this system has increased in price since my purchase, but it’s not unexpected given current ram and GPU availability constraints.

Side note: almost as bad as the poor audio quality, the sound bar's remote signal interfered with my TV. Some of the functionality appeared to be coded with the same wireless channel, such that I could press one button on the sound-bar remote, and the TV would pick it up as a completely unrelated input. Sometimes both devices would accept an input, when I was standing up. While sitting down, the sound-bar completely blocked all input from my TV's remote.

Perhaps some of the reviews for these speakers are fake, though I can't be certain.

text:

The hood is made of steel, so I used the magnets to attach the main unit under the hood and then wrapped the cable sensor unit through the steering wheel and around the pedals. Set up was pretty easy once I watched the online videos. I have it set up so I use my phone to text to the unit to arm and disarm it. When I am using the tractor, I take the cable off and wrap it around the roll bar for storage.

So far I have tested cable alarms, and starting the tractor creates a vibration alarm. It is to early to tell about battery life but so far after a week I have a very good level. I have tried the GPS location and it worked great and showed the location within about 10 feet on a map.

My original plan was to only use it when the tractor sits outside but now that I see how well it works, I may buy the DS525 equipment power adapter so it can be permanently installed and charged from the tractor battery.

title: Works great, but not the radius advertised.
text:
REVISED to 4 Star review: After using the antenna a week, I re-ran the channel search--which I should have done after installing it. I am able to pick up 38 of the 45 channels within a 60 mile radius of my house. They all come in very clearly. The amplifier wasn't working at all, and we determined that the brick was defective. Plugging it into another USB brick didn't really improve the signal by much, but it at least worked.

All-in-all, I'm glad I bought it. I'm able to clearly receive: 4 PBS stations; 3 CBS stations; 1 each NBC and ABC; plus FOX, CW, and an assortment of crap (TCT, HSN, QVC) networks. Enough to make me happy to leave TWC and in the dust.

UPDATE: 8/2/2016 What I have found is that the signals from channels with transmitters within 10 miles are not being up, while those 12 miles and beyond are coming in clearly. I suspect this is due to my location and not the antenna. Still, the amplifier causes the entire thing to not work, so I don't know what's up with that thing.

This antenna arrived as indicated. However, instead of the nearly 45 channels within a 60 mile radius of my home, I'm only able to get about 15. I installed it on the roof, and the direction did not seem to make a difference. NOTES:

Originally, I hooked this up and leaned it against the back of the TV before I had someone install it. I got no more channels installing it on the roof than I did that way.

The amplifier which comes in the box with this antenna actually made the signal worse--not better, so I disconnected that.

Give the few number of channels that actually come through, on hindsight, I would have bought a much cheaper antenna. It does not pull in channels more than about 20 miles away. Even channels 20 miles away aren't received.

Otherwise, the reception on the channels that do come through is great.

All of this may be because I am in an old, downtown neighborhood, with close houses and lots of trees. Although I installed it in an area of the roof free of trees.

title: BluRay player won't play DVDs
text: We got the LG BD300 for Christmas.  It worked fine for two months, but after a firmware update for streaming YouTube videos it would not play DVDs anymore. title: This wasted my time and created anxiety
text:
I can't tell you if the Garmin product is good or not. This "Refurbished" item was worthless. It worked when I received it, and I was able to download Birdseye imagery for a backpacking trip. Then, the morning I was leaving for my trip, the refurbished unit wouldn't turn on. I tried three different sets of batteries and various USB cables -- nothing. It wouldn't even blink. I had to leave on my trip with it not turning on. It never turned on since.

I've seen through hikers on the PCT with similar devices (been hiking the Sierra since before GPS myself). I would have counted on this for a risky trip deep beyond the wilderness boundary in a flyover state. I mean, I wouldn't have planned on this being necessary for my survival, but there is a risk that it could have been. Well, this one let me down. Now I'm unlikely to try any Garmin/DeLorme product out of fear for the same result.

For the brief period that it did work, this navigator seemed to have a fine GPS function. The maps were underwhelming. While I'm ok with just basic 24K USGS topo maps, the detail available on Keyhole (Google Maps/Earth) is far better. The Garmin unit seems to just use Open Street Maps and is missing most of the labels for National Forest service roads. A lot of the roads are just totally missing. The Birdseye aerial imagery would show them, but unless I buy them on an SD card for ninety more dollars, the device only lets me download a tiny 2.7 mile radius of imagery at a time and it takes too many key clicks and minutes to download what should only take seconds.

title: No handle
text:
This is a big slippery case and it has no handle. It does come with a shoulder strap, but it would be better with a handle.

As other reviewers have pointed out, if the case is overstuffed, it will bow out and fail to seal on the edges. If water-proofness is critical, it must not be over-loaded so that the single clamp at the front of the case will hold the seals together.

title: DOES NOT work with ACRA standard plates
text:
Got this to carry a big film SLR while backpacking. I was tired of the camera on my neck strap bouncing or if I put an arm through it, cranking on my neck.

This thing seems to fit a thin strap ideally but it will fit fatter, padded straps just not as well. It hold my SLR just like the camera in the picture. It's easy to unclip and clip back. It feels secure.

Unfortunately, I misplaced the plate. I went to buy another one and found that Peak Design does not appear to sell the plates only. No problem, right? Because it's claimed to be compatible with the ACRA standard. I tried another brand ACRA standard plate and it DOES NOT FIT.

Apparently, the Peak Design plates might fit an ACRA tripod, but an ACRA plate will not fit the Peak Design Capture because it does not have the proprietary slot of the lock pin.

THIS IS INCREDIBLY LAME!

There are ENOUGH tripod base plate standards out there already. Peak Design could have made their Capture compatible with any of the great ones that have been proven to work for decades. Instead, they introduced yet another new, INCOMPATIBLE plate. Do they really think I'm going to buy a whole collection of their plates for their Capture clip while disregarding all my other tripod heads and mounts? This is stupid and insulting, and I resent it.

title: Requires a smartphone or it won't work
text:
There is no web interface to configure or manage this via your PC. I contacted tech support and they confirmed a smartphone and their "app" is required to configure and manage the router. To use this, you have to buy into owning an abusive smartphone.

When I did try the smartphone app, the first thing I was requested to do was to create an account with Gryphon. I didn't want to create an account or send anything to Gryphon, so I contacted their support. They advised me that it required an account to work. I asked, "why?" Their response was, "That's the way it's designed." "No account, no work."

I created an account and the next thing the app demanded was my phone's GPS location. I attempted to deny it, but the configuration would not proceed without it. The app then requested permission to my photos and files and I denied it. I was able to proceed that way.

Once I had the network parameters configured to establish basic connectivity on the Gryphonhome network, I used the default "family" user to configure the filtering level. I tried elementary, middle-school, high-school, and adult. Note that even "adult" is supposed to filter undressed people.

I used a Windows PC on the Gryphon network to test -- not the smartphone I was using to manage/configure. I put the PC into the "managed devices" group. I confirmed that on the school-level settings, it would force Google's "safe search." If I searched Youtube, those videos of people shooting watermelons on the most popular shooter channels would be blocked. So would searches for boobies and stuff like that. That's all attributed to Google safe search. However, if I tried to browse the URL of the two most famous naked people magazines (that's what I could think of to test), they came right up. Even on "Elementary" level, I could see in Gryphon on the browsing history that the PC in "Elementary" category had browsed those famous magazine sites and they were not blocked but allowed.

I didn't feel like testing the malware function since my eyes were already burning. Total failure on so many levels.

title: Field of View
text:
These binoculars are all about quality in the largest field of view. If you want to see a wide expanse of nature or the heavens downrange from your position, these are the way to go. I got them specifically to frame smaller constellations and asterisms, the detail of which can be further examined with a scope. They help tremendously to put the object in the scope into context. Ordinarily, observing half a degree of field tends to abstract objects almost entirely from their surrounding. Since it's not practical to really "zoom" in using a single optical instrument, using these in combination with something of higher power is ideal. Don't get me wrong, I do have a zoom on the scope... it zooms from 25x to 50x -- amazing but you have to understand that this is a field of view of 2.4 to 1.5 degrees -- essentially like looking through a pipe to a drinkstraw. These Nikons however, show over 9 degrees field of view -- something which is unsurpassed in the highest-end binocular out there.

There are compromises necessitated by the optical principles used to make these function. They do not have a very flat field of view, meaning objects in the center of the field (circle) can be focused, but objects nearer the edge of the field are out of focus. This is because the focused field is curved not flat. This problem is also evident in most 10x50's for example. It's less of a problem in good quality 8x42's like Nikon's Monarch for example, and obviously the high end Swarovski, Leica, Zeiss etc. This problem matters more when you have a narrow field and highly magnified image where the subject tends to fill the field of view. It matters less when the subject is focused in the center of the field and the background surrounding it is slightly out of focus.

Still, even if you pay the biggest bucks for bright, flat, and sharp images from the top of the line binoculars, you'll still only see about 8 degrees true field of view, whereas these give you over 9 degrees. Furthermore, they give an apparent field of view of over 59 degrees, rivaling the top-of-the-line binoculars.

If you're looking for a handy, all-purpose binocular, the roof-prism 8x42's are proven to be far more popular for a number of good reasons (more compact, more magnification while not yet needing a tripod or IS like 10x does, more competition and choices etc.) But if you're looking for the best field of view with high quality optics, this is it, and fortunately it comes at a very reasonable cost. I don't know what other 7x35's are out there, but I can tell you this is far better than Celestron or Bushnell.

title: speedy
text: I bought this to replace a WD 750GB Black that had a SMART predictive failure after about 2 years use.  I have about equal appreciation for both these drives.  The WD was cheap and served well.  I've replaced many hundreds of drives in my career so I don't particularly get upset about the occasional failure and wouldn't characterize the product by a single experience.  Obviously in the case of the Seagate I haven't owned it long enough to know whether it will last longer or not.  It's worked for almost a month now and seems similar in performance which is quite high for a laptop drive.  I also have a SanDisk SSD which I am a little disappointed in simply because for practical purposes there is no performance advantage compared to these much less expensive and much higher capacity hard drives.  For a tablet or ultrabook I would go SSD, but for a mostly desk-bound laptop, these 750GB drives seem to work great.

title: performance not better despite high cost
text: I bought this to replace a 750GB WD Black hard drive in my older T61 Thinkpad.  That hard drive was fairly fast (2nd place in Toms Hardware tests of HD's).  Obviously this is lower capacity so I also bought a Seagate 750 HD for data storage (another fairly fast one).  I was hoping that the SSD would provide a performance advantage, faster boots, and faster response times in day-to-day desktop tasks.  It does not.  If there is any advantage in performance it is only visible in rigorous benchmark testing or atypical massive throughput tests.  In everyday desktop tasks, there is just no perceptible advantage.  I can see a non-speed-performance related advantage for other uses (tablets and ultrabooks), but for my use this just hasn't proven to be worth it for double the cost of a hard drive that is 3 times greater capacity and for practical purposes just as fast.

title: inexpensive, functional
text:
This is a great, inexpensive little webcam for personal video conferencing (Skype). The picture quality is not incredible, but still far better than what most people you'll chat with have with their iPad, phone, or the camera built into their laptop.

I've been doing videoconferencing and webcasts for some twenty years -- in the early days it was mostly Polycom units, but lately Cisco Telepresence. With Telepresence you have three 1080p 60" big screens. The monthly cost is enormous but often justified by savings in travel costs (if you say so). Personal IP services like skype aren't as dependable or as rich in quality but they're outstanding on a cost basis, especially if the DSL or cable ISP fee is sunk.

I was tempted to step up to the 1080 (C920) camera but I've resisted because already nobody that I conference with (for personal use) has anything near as good as this, and they may also have trouble receiving or displaying 1080 video. Some of them even have monthly byte transfer limits from their ISP. So I see the 1080 HD services as better if it's really going to work out on all ends. Short of that, the autofocus this camera has is great especially when it's going to be more than a face-cam. I use mine to conference a whole room with a family of four. The kids are walking back and forth, to and from the camera and focus stays good. Its reasonably wide-angle is good too -- wide enough to see the room at some distance, but not so wide it distorts faces badly in closeup. I need to test the audio more at the longer ranges. It has an auto-gain feature that seems to be working well. Again, unfortunately, even if I get great audio at the source, it ends up going through someone's laptop speakers or an iPad on the other end.

The most important and biggest improvements to video conferencing to make once you have an adaquate camera like this is in lighting and acoustics in the room. It's real common to see people on camera that are back-lit, with their faces in darkness and a room full of echoes, reverb and weird modes.

Put a little thought into the whole audio-video scene of the conference from end-to-end and this camera/mic combination can be made to perform very well for quite a low cost.

title: excellent
text: I have used it to blow potentially abrasive dust off lenses before swabbing them with alcohol q-tips to clean them.  I also used it to blow a speck of steel stuck on my eye.  It wouldn't flush out with water but this puffer had enough force to blow it off the cornea.  In other words, it's great for blowing off delicate lenses!

title: Not convinced about USB connection
text:
The sound is fine. It's what I would expect from quality tweeters and a reasonable size woofer with a decent driver. It does not compare to a decent set of bookshelf type monitors like the JBL LSR series but the price is far lower so I guess they're ok for PC speakers.

But the excellence ends at the sound. The speakers do not have an analog signal input from the computer (there is one at the puck for a MP3 player or whatever). Instead, the signal comes via USB. The problem is the speakers do not come with any drivers. Bose assumes you have the drivers already on your Windows installation. That's a very bad assumption as many people do not have the drivers (just do a google search on Bose Companion 5 drivers to see). There's no help from Bose here. The drivers cannot be downloaded from their web site. I called Bose's tech support and after half and hour they were not able to solve the problem. I eventually solved the problem myself on my Windows 7 Pro 64-bit install but I think it's terribly lame that Bose cannot provide the driver for their product. If I wasn't using the pre-load install of Windows they assume everyone uses, then I would be screwed.

So exactly what do I get for this odd USB input in lieu of a standard audio input? Nothing except incompatibility and the inability to use the speakers apart from a full blown PC. The audio quality and features are not improved by USB audio input. Period.

Room mode correction should be a straightforward feaure on speakers like these. It is not. Although my sound card supports it, the Bose speakers do not have the DSP to do it independently. The lack of sound-card independent RMC doesn't justify the high cost of these speakers. If it were included, the price would look a little better.

I installed the Companion 5 system on an Ergotron cart. The two speakers fit perfectly under the monitor the way I wanted (I removed the stands). The acoustimass is bulkier than I would have liked but I think it's fair to say a smaller module would not perform as well and for most under-desk installs it would be fine. What I do think it's fair to complain about is the poor design of the acoustimass module case. Despite being very heavy, it features a plastic rear end-cap that is fragile. Come-on. For the price, give me painted steel not brittle plastic. The case is also oddly shaped with curves that prevent anything but a bottom-down mount position. The case is not designed to be mounted in a down-firing position, up-firing or on it's side or upside down. The case is also not equipped or rated to be flown or ceiling mounted (it could fall apart and drop parts on people below). Bose should know these are all viable positions. Not everyone can have this thing on the floor with like six wires running out for people to trip over -- seriously, that is totally not acceptable in a public space.

Bose has a habit of not publishing Watts RMS specifications for their amplifiers or speaker handling abilities. I sort of understand not wanting to confuse consumers who don't understand driver efficiencies, but at least give us some max. 1 meter SPL's so we have some clue how loud these things are. As it is, the Companion 5 is loud enough for a PC system in a fairly live medium-sized residential room. It's much louder than my Wave system which proved way more anemic than it was made out to be. The Wave is useless except in the smallest bedroom. I use the Companion 5 primarily in my kitchen (on the Ergotron cart). The kitchen is fairly live but has some acoustic paneling to tame some of the reverberations. If I were putting this system in a small classroom, I would think twice. As a PC system for someone who sits right in front of it, it's obviously perfectly good. I probably wouldn't even use it at half-volume sitting that close.

title: too much stiction
text: The head when fully unlocked has too much stiction and causes bending and spring-back of the instrument.  I was using it with a 80mm Swarovski spotting scope.  With the head unlocked, I could center an object in the FOV.  Then I would attempt to move the object to the edge of the field.  I push on the scope or handle and the head resists this movement until I give enough pressure to overcome and it moves.  Once the object is on the edge of the field, I release the scope or handle and the object bounces out of the field -- because to overcome the stiction in the head, I was using enough force to bend (elastic deformation) the scope/mount combination so when I release it, it springs back.  This is annoying at high magnifications where even a slight amount of elasticity will mess up your field position.  It's totally worthless for video where fluid movement is critical but this head is not for video anyway.  It would be adaquate for low magnification (20-30x) wide-angle spotting of terrestrial subjects where framing does not need to be precise.  For my purposes, Gitzo's ball head worked far better.  A geared head also works ok for me.  This one just didn't work like I expected with smooth pan and tilt.  It was jerky and sprang back too much.

title: Average
text:
I bought these at the same time as a Steiner 7x50 Commander XP model. The Commander XP's use the same case but for triple the price have better eyepieces, coatings and optical specifications and a few additional or better accessories than the Marine model.

I compared them in terrestrial and celestial viewing but the easiest comparison is done with astronomical subjects since they really define performance clearly. The images in the Marine model merged effortless. In the Commander XP, I have difficulty merging the images. The XP's are obviously badly out of collimation. I don't care to fix this myself on binos in this price range but I was pleased that the much less costly Marine's appear to be flawless in this respect.

I evaluated the real and apparent fields of view as well as the sharpness near the edge of the field.

In the Marine model, the real field of view is reasonably wide but apparent field is quite narrow. It's not bad but it's not a spectacular vista either. In the Commander XP, the real FOV is only barely perceptibly wider. Steiner's website lists the specifications. The apparent field, which is not specified is about the same for both. The almost indiscernable extra width of real FOV does not contribute much to the value of the XP's for triple the price.

On the Marine model, I put Sirius and Jupiter in the center of the field. They each looked nice. Moving the binoculars so that the objects were farther from the center of the field I could see the image degraded about half-way to the edge of the field of view. Near the very edge, the image was appalling. Much more than half-way out of the center of the field of view, the star or planet turns from a bright point to just a smear. Near the very edge it's a dim smudge. I tried the same with the Commander XP. It was every bit as bad. I could have probably improved things a little by refocusing but that only means that the field isn't flat either.

Are the XP's better on dim objects? The optics are supposed to transmit 96% light compared to the Commander V's 95% and the Marine's 90%. I saw very little difference on dim objects like the Orion nebula or the background of the Pleides or Jupiter's moons. Again, I can't see the justification for triple the price, so I commend these Marine models over their far more costly cousins.

Both have generious eye-relief, 20mm for the Marine and 22mm for these XP's. They also have the same weight and dimensions. They're heavy but still reasonable if you're wearing a thick coat to pad your chest and a harness to keep them from swinging all over if you're moving. Also, at 7x they're reasonable for handholding. For me, 7x50 is about the limit for handholding. Heavier or higher power would be too shakey. 6x56 might be nicer if they were more common.

Where the XP is clearly better is with small details like the click-loc strap attachments (for use with Steiner straps and harnesses only), the better eyepiece covers, lens covers, focuser grips, shading eye-cups, and various doo-dads that come in the case. It comes with a flotation strap which the Marine doesn't, but I would still rather prefer a harness which neither comes with.

I bought these Porro prism binos because I thought for the high price, particularly the XP's, they should be outstanding. While roof prism binos might require fifteen hundred dollars or more to achieve optical exellence (or so I've heard), it should be easier with porros. With these, the optical quality is lacking nontheless. To be honest, I have nothing to compare them to. I've never seen better, but I was still totally underwhelmed by the performance which was only slightly better than I would expect from binoculars in the hundred dollar range. In the case of the XP's, it's a rip-off, no question. In the case of the Marine model, the value is closer to reasonable because of the far lower price. I didn't compare them to other binos in their price range. The Fujinon line would be the most similar but it would also be worthwhile to compare Nikons, even the well-regarded Monarch roof prism models which are in this price category but are totally different.

title: Great lens and sensor, bad shutter lag, audio and switches
text:
The wide angle lens is wonderful. The field of view and the speed (light gathering ability) of the lens can only be rivaled by high end camera and lens combinations costing six to ten times as much (admittedly those are superior in many other ways as well). Still, the point is that no other compact point and shoot camera can rival the field of view and speed of this one. Nevertheless, some things come up short of fair on the LX3.

The shutter lag is terrible. I am a very instinctive shooter that is quite capable in photojournalist style candids but I am almost always defeated by this camera.

I am not a photophile or electronic gadget spec sheet bench racer. I've done wonderful 8x10 prints with a 6MP camera and 10MP is enough to get prints after substantial cropping. I have huge film scans when I need them but I cannot realistically show dozens of megapixels on screen or in print for more than a handful of images. I also shoot in .jpg and it's great. I can't imagine the agony of terabytes of raw data jamming my PC.

I love the LX3 video quality for movies. It's ideal for Youtube and even Youtube HD. I do not like the Quicktime .MOV format or the weak compression algorithm. I wish it had H.264 and wrote an .MPG type format. It still beats the data format from a DVD camcorder though.

The audio quality for movies is terrible. Again, I'm not talking audiophile critique here. For comparison, my Sony DSC T9 (ultra compact point and shoot) has far better sound.

I hate the manual aspect ratio slider. If I shoot movies I want 16:9 but for stills I want 3:2 (of course). The LX3 requires that I remember to both turn the dial and slide the switch or I will end up shooting 16:9 stills.

Overall, it's a great camera. I hope they get the rest sorted out by the time I expect to buy another one in about 3 or 4 years.

title: Very light and convenient
text: I love these! I wanted something that wasn’t bulky and had no wires. I also did NOT want noise cancellation because I use it for walks around town and want to hear if there’s something approaching, a car horn, etc. And unlike earbuds, they don’t fall out and get lost. For the price these are great! I listen to podcasts, so I can’t speak to the music fidelity.

title: Working fine, so far
text: Using it with my Roku Ultra.  Seems to work just fine.

title: Works for me! And really cute!
text: I just got it so I don't know how durable it is, but it feels pretty well made and looks just like the photos.  My 9.7" 6th gen iPad fits very snugly in the semi-rigid case (it isn't as bendy as their photo makes it out to be).  Also, unlike the standard Apple iphone magnetic covers, this one opens and closes like a book and to prop it up you just rest the edge on one of the slight grooves on the inside cover.  It works for me but, some might find it too easy to knock over compared to the usual way that iPad covers fold up to prop up the iPad. I love the cat design, and the plastic is lightly textured so it isn't too slippery.  It does add quite a bit of weight to my iPad, but I needed the protection, so I don't mind the extra few ounces.  The magnets in the cover work well to put the iPad to sleep when the cover is closed.

title: Will not charge my iPad. Works fine with cellphones.
text: Meh. Too expensive for what you get which is mediocre sound and mediocre charging ability. However, living in San Francisco I bought it for an earthquake kit. I use it to listen to podcasts and it's fine for that and it does charge my cellphone, but is not powerful enough to charge an iPad. It isn't exactly light either so not something I'd want to take backpacking.

title: OK. But they squish your ears....
text: OK for the discounted price. They squish my ears because the earpad is too small.  After a couple of hours it's pretty uncomfortable and yor ears get sweaty.  These are fine for plugging in at work and working for shorter periods of time. The ear cushion area would fit an elf but not an adult of any kind. I'm a 5 foot 3 female and was hoping these would cover my ears more rather than sit ON them.  Perhaps I'll get used to them and for watching a movie on an airplane for a couple hours they are fine but I'm not sure I can stand to wear them too long.  The sound is decent, and they were only $23, which is the only reason I gave them 3 stars.

title: I received a defective set
text:
I was very excited to receive this! It was easy to charge and set up. I was also able to connect it via Bluetooth to my iphone. BUT, the left side speaker does not work at all. I tried jiggling it. Adjusted the volume. Turned it off and on again. Nothing. Item is going back.
The sound out of the right side is decent. Not super loud but that is good as I don't want to go deaf anyway. They are also pretty comfortable for a woman with an average sized head but I think they may be a little small for some guys. The dials feel like cheap plastic but given the price I guess it's to be expected.

title: Unreliable!!  DO not buy.
text: Bought this in January 2014.  Worked fine for a few months.  Then started dropping intermittently.  I blamed my ISP at first and we were able to test and figured out it was the wireless router!  I could spend hours trying to troubleshoot this and perhaps squeak out a few more months, or I can just spend more money on a better device made by someone else...

title: Like these so much I bought 3 pairs
text:
These are the only earbuds that actually fit in my ear comfortably and don't fall out when I move my head.
I still like the kind that have a behind the ear clip if I run but it isn't convenient if you are taking them on and off alot. These are perfect inexpensive earbuds for everyday use. Fun colors too!

title: I'll definitely read alot more now!
text:
I am so glad I waited for the Kindle 2. It took me only about 5 minutes to figure out how to use most of the buttons and within 10 minutes I had downloaded a couple books! Downloading is so fast it is hard to believe - just think the COMPLETE works of Charles Dickens in 30 seconds? Crazy!

I don't read alot of books and newspapers because my eyes get tired, but now with the adjustable font, and the gray scale, I don't have that problem. However, I still need my reading glasses as the font is not adjustable on my homepage menu and the popup menu. And I have NO idea why they couldn't make the teeny letters on the keyboard either darker or slightly larger, as I can't read those either. At least it's a qwerty keyboard so I know where all the letters are.

The text to speech is surprisingly good. Not perfect but certainly tolerable. I am an iPhone user, so I wish there was touch-screen and I also wish I could make calls on it. I also wish there was a rubbery area on the back to help me grip the device, the way there is on the Kindle 1.

But all in all, a lovely, cool, amazing machine!

title: Great headset  for the price...IF THEY DON'T BREAK
text:
NOTE - I've had these for just a month and they just broke. No sound comes out of the right side at all. Very frustrating. I only used them a few times each week, so I would say they are not well made. I returned them to Amazon for a refund.

ORIGINAL REVIEW - I needed these because the stupid white bud earphones that come with iPhone kept falling out of my ears and there was way too much ambient sound. These are exactly as described, they come with nice adjustable foam plugs so the buds will fit in your ear and now I only have to listen to my iPhone at half volume rather than cranked all the way up. The sound is good. I don't think the sound is incredible, but I don't really care about that, as I didn't feel like spending $100 on something that I will probably lose or break in a year. I wanted to spend even less, but couldn't find anything that wasn't cheap feeling. This is a nice middle ground. They also look nice, the silver/black matches the iPhone.

title: Cool and convenient!
text:
I LOVE my new camera! It can go with me anywhere because it is thin and light and oh so attractive. It also is easy to use and takes great photos. The basic functions are well laid out and intuitive to learn but there are alot of subtle features that take some figuring out. I wish the complete user manual was actually printed and not provided on a DVD. You may want to print out the darn thing so you can study it at leisure.

The screen is hard to see in bright sun but that is true of all cameras. I was also impressed how much I was able to capture using the low light setting and NO flssh. Am still playing with the "best shot" features and some of the options like Sepia and Black and White. The nice thing about that it shows the image with the tint or in black and white.

All in all, I am a happy camper, this camera is all that I need for a long while!

title: NOT unlocked, locked to Xfinity
text: Ordered because it was 5g and unlocked. Received it today, started it, and find that it's locked to the Xfinity network and the bootloader CAN'T be unlocked (tried). So, if you are looking to root this to remove the factory loaded 16gigs (yes, from the factory!) of memory hogging bloatware, well...,  you can't. Pass this phone up.

title: This really is the only way to feed your dashcam
text: Just take the plunge, feed this properly under covers, headliner, etc., and be done with it. Only have to do once, but well worth not having wires dangling or losing a cig lighter port. Works flawlessly, has for almost a year. Won't hesitate to buy again.

title: Great system to install a new stereo!
text: Super easy to crimp to new radio pigtail and is a perfect match for car. Just crimp up using their instructions and the instructions from new radio pigtail (thank goodness most have gone to standardized colors for power, ground, speakers, etc.). Worth every penny to save the total headache it is to put in a new stereo!

title: Not even close to 1amp output...
text: Using meters, then a scope, the most I can get is 4milliamps, not 400, FOUR! Not sure what's up, but the output on this is nothing near what's claimed. Might return for replacement, see if there's maybe a QC issue or just a fluke, either way, it's not working for me as-is.

title: Fit as it should and keeps the water out
text: These are a must to keep around, for sealing against water and other environmental contaminants. Lube the threads with vaseline or dielectric grease. Fit perfectly and works well.

title: Flimsy plastic bracket assembly, but LED's and OK camera/night vision
text: I returned this to keep a cheaper, but higher quality unit, the "Boss" backup camera (with integrated metal bracket). Seemed just too flimsy and like anything that might hit it (say, while loading up a trailer, or the bed of the pickup with lumber) would break it in pieces. It does have LED illumination and good picture quality, but that would only last a few days around here, till it was hanging by its wires...

title: Metal mounting bracket (not plastic like others) and seems really solid
text: Camera is kind of low-res, nothing to write home about, but the overall quality seems very high compared to others I've seen and one other I ordered (and returned because of the flimsy plastic bracket). The bracket for this, the complete outer assy is metal. Probably zinc casting, but still, way less likely to break than the flimsy plastic of the (more expensive!) other one I looked at. Happy with purchase, night vision is lacking and it's a bit blurry, but gets the job done and will clearly find the zombies you'll surely need to back over (remember, use the rear bumper, not the front, a zombie body can easily take out the radiator of your vehicle.

title: Really, REALLY big and heavy (that's a good thing for keeping it on your vehicle)!
text: Didn't even open, went with a through-mount for my HAM antenna. But..., this was way larger and heavier than I expected and for the price? Damn, seems like a deal if you're stuck on magnet mount (no pun). This one WILL stay put, no matter what the wind load you see. Good deal and Tram products have always been top-notch.

title: First one that actually fit the UV-5R, out of half-dozen ordered
text: By "fit," I mean the plastic base matches the Baofeng and isn't huge, or too small or seats 1/8" above the base ring on the UV case. This one comes with a washer, but there's no need, it seats down snugly into the UV-5R and looks like it was made for this radio. I have tried (and returned) at least six other antenna's that said they were for the UV-5R, but stood up off the case when fully tightened (too much for a washer to take up) or had bases so large they would snag on anything and made it look like a toy. Even tried a $26 Mirkit antenna (think what came was a knock-off) and prices all across the board. This one, one of the cheapest of the foldable antenna's, is the first to fit and show a 1:1.2 SWR. Excellent antenna and excellent fit with an even better price!

title: NOT 8w, barely 6w TX on High power
text: This is not what's advertised. I've tested this on four different meters, all show about 6w max power. 2.5w for low and right at 5w for Med power. If you're looking for truly 8w power, look elsewhere. This comes as a nice kit with lots of cool gadgets, but if the radio doesn't perform as-stated, then all the "stuff" is pointless unless you're happy with a 5w radio!

title: NOT advertised brand, this is a Nissei
text: Afraid of other's experiences with inaccuracy, I tested this extensively against four different calibrated radios and compared to an old Japanese-made meter from the 1980's, so far, it's dead-on accurate (enough for a small, hand-held meter anyway). Not happy that it's a different brand than advertised, but happy with accuracy so far (I reserve the right to amend this review if I find accuracy issues in the future!)

title: Counterfeit, same as $12 HYS antenna, NOT a Mirkit
text: See pics and pics in ad. The numbers molded into this antenna are the exact same as a $12 HYS antenna (https://www.amazon.com/Bingfu-136-520MHz-Foldable-Tactical-Handheld/dp/B07TYBX86D/ref=sr_1_6?dchild=1&keywords=foldable+antenna+uv-5r&qid=1589643418&sr=8-6), only difference is the HYS doesn't have a peeling "mirkit" sticker on it. Haven't tested the cheap HYS, but I'll bet it has the same mediocre TX/RX as this fake Mirkit. Save your $26 and get the HYS (link above) for half the price!

title: Installed and worked (just as RAM should!)
text: Fairly fast RAM and reliable (this was bought to complement another pair I have, to bring everything up to 32gb). Never had issue with Kingston RAM. Install it. It works.

title: Fits well, OK TX/RX, but gooseneck connection gets in way
text: See pics. Gooseneck fits the UV-5R radios really nicely (the Abbree tactical antenna's are WAY to large at the base), but where the flex part screws into the gooseneck is NOT a good fit at all, hangs on stuff (again, see pics, you'll see what I mean) - I went with the Mirkit tac antenna for the Baofeng.

title: Identical to what came with a Yaesu mobile unit
text: This was used to install a duplicate mount in another vehicle. It's the exact cable that comes with new Yaesu radios. Good quality, same fit/function as stock.

title: Runs cool, precisely adjustable and rock solid with voltage
text: So far, has been solid and reliable. Once adjusted to a certain voltage, say 13.6v, it stays there, no matter the power out requirements. Overall, excellent value for a good power supply.

title: High SWR, not the best RX or TX either one
text: Seems a quality made product, but SWR tests super high (~4:1). Skip this one and get something else. It is cheap, but not good RX or TX with this antenna. Little difference between this and the stock Baofeng rubber ducky

title: Hoping for lower SWR, but it works
text: This tests about on-par with an HYS 771N (copy of the Nagoya, but in BNC config). But at least this is foldable/shorter when need be. Haven't tested SWR with it folded, but it tests out the same as the 771 for SWR. OK, nothing to write home about, but OK. I can reach a local repeater.

title: Very high SWR from this antenna, I'd pass
text: Tested this as soon as it arrived and the SWR was 4.2 at best. Tried many things to try to get the SWR down, changing adapter on radio, different patch cable on meter, etc., nothing helped, it's an honest 4+SWR. Unusable.

title: No way to tell if it's a new battery, but it stopped clock errors, so a thumbs-up
text: Works to stop clock errors in thinkpads. Seems to work like a new battery, so I'll assume it is (leads are too tiny for me to accurately get a voltmeter reading, but it "fixed" the constant start up error saying bios clock needs to be reset.

title: Good quality, worked flawless as a portable HD
text: Used this as a backup HD (with a 1tb M.2 SATA drive in it) for a backpacking/photography trip around Europe and the ME. Light, solid, protective and made the cheapest, lightest, smallest portable HD I could come up with. Housing worked great, wouldn't hesitate to buy again.

title: -UPDATE: a few months later and less than ten writes, it doesn't see any discs
text:
Works fine for me, not loud when running, took a few restarts to get it working (drivers loaded, seen by windoze, etc.), but works fine now. Cheap and appears good quality. Will update review if I have problems w/it in future.

UPDATE 14 May 2020: Literally less than ten discs through this writer and now it just doesn't see NEW writable discs as new, constantly says, "No compatible drives" or "disc not writable" - with BRAND NEW discs. Sigh..., gotta say, this unit is a POS. Prob should avoid this one...

title: Seems non-OEM, but fit and looks perfect. Good deal.
text: Came fast, fit just like the OEM and looks right (matches the rest of the plastic on the X230). Overall, a good deal. Time will tell and I'll update this review if a problem comes up, but so far, no issues (was replaced to fix a cracked OEM outer shell).

title: Kinda chintzy, but overall has been working 24/7 for weeks now, so can't beat that
text: Using this to power a parking heater in the garage. has worked without issue for almost a month (a feat for most cheap Chinese electronics!).  stays pretty solid at 24v and fan rarely comes on (doesn't heat up much).

title: Screws were correct and exact match to factory, driver fit well
text: the screws perfectly match the apple factory screws for late 2017-18 macbook pro. Worked fine. A bit hard to turn, but I realized that was because of the locktite/glue on the threads to keep them from loosening. The driver isn't a Snap-On, but it's strong enough and fit the apple pentalobe screws perfectly.

title: Worked, but Sony recognizes as aftermarket and you have to "OK" use in-camera.
text: These worked, fine batteries, but the camera sees them as non-OEM and an error pops up on-screen. You have to agree to the use of the batteries in your camera before you can use it. Pain each time you turn camera on, but otherwise, the batts were fine.

title: Used to love Meike quality, now it's same garbage as rest (see review)
text: I've tried many of the non-OEM grips, in the past, the Meike's were the only ones that lasted and didn't start having connection issues. Bought a new 80D last fall, so I bought this (after, again, trying a lesser brand non-OEM grip). Now, six-months later (started a few months ago) it fails to connect to camera about 25% of the time. Drill is, turn on camera, nothing, pull battery tray, re-install, sometimes works. If that doesn't work, pull grip and re-insert, THEN the camera has power. Always fakes me into thinking batts are gone, but I put in Canon 100% charge batts and operates camera fine without grip, shows 100%. Install grip with same battery in tray, nothing. Pull grip, re-install again, tighten as tight as you possibly can and then it might have power. Lost a few ops because of this POS grip. NOT happy that I paid twice what a cheapo non-OEM grip costs and STILL have the same problem the cheaper grips have. Avoid this. Find a Canon one used or do without, but you'll end up tossing the rig in the rubbish tin using this grip!

title: Very high quality, lives up to Sony's rep, but had front-focus issues no one could figure out?
text: When you're talking mirrorless and everything's on the sensor, there shouldn't be back or front-focus issues, all on the sensor. But I could manually adjust or auto adjust to the center of a camera target and the focus point would be forward of that, with center a bit defocused. Doesn't make sense, but the Sony equiv to Canon's nifty-fifty is spot-on with the same setup (tripod, dead-level, camera target distance, etc.). Not sure if I should just capitulate and do the Sigma with an adapter...??

title: So far, this thing actually seems to be working really well!
text: So far, I haven't been able to tell from a native lens. I have tried face tracking yet though, so, YMMV.

title: Not the quality Meike has come to be known for, but it's OK
text: Meike commands a bit more cash than other cheapo grips, it's a bit better quality, but not much. They used to be the best of the knock-off grips, now they're just ahead of the cheapest of the cheapo's, not worth what they ask, but worth something more than getting the cheapest. Too bad, used to depend on quality when you bought this brand (previously used on Canon's, this is for a Sony)

title: Fits perfectly and entire EVF is clearly visible, keeps out ambient light.
text: This fits and works perfectly on a Sony A7R III. Doesn't block the EVF, but does block out ambient light. Works as it should and is one of the cheapest eye cups out there.

title: Batteries are good, grip has QC issues
text: I've used "Neewer" products before, including grips for Canon's, but this one has the casting flash that's sharp as a razor and the holes to hold the door pins for the stock battery door storage are not centered, so no matter how you try to force the door into it while holding the pin-retractor lever, one of the pins will never line up and find its way in, so you have to hold the door while installing the grip or the door falls out. And remember to grab the falling door when you take the grip off again. PITA. The Meike's are higher quality, but don't come with a battery bundle...

title: Procedure to initialize is a pain, once connected though, actually works!
text: I look at these kinds of things as "snake-oil," but this actually works. Boosted signal where it wasn't getting any to three to four bars. Worth the money. Just follow the setup procedure and blinking lights and all to make sure it's connected to your wifi. Takes a bit, but worth the effort.

title: Looked fine, good quality, like a genuine Nagoya, but reception sucked
text: No quantifiable evidence here, but compared it to a $7 knock off and the knock off won each time. For TX/RX both. Disappointed w/this particular antenna.

title: Very well made, but a b*tch to get in and out!
