Update-Bought the 3 pack in January, but they all stopped working by June. That's about 2 months from each cable. Not worth the money.

title: Minolta Dimage 7i personal review
text:
I researched many cameras in stores and on line. I wanted high pixel, lots of zoom and movie with sound. Nikon 5700 with 8x zoom is more expensive and was not available. Nikon 5000 does not compare in the zoom.
I was sold on the Minolta. I am still experimenting with all the amazing features. Automatic does a great job. I recommend reading the manual several times,,,, actually I study the manual and then practice on the actual camera. I bought an AC adapter and run an extension cord and practice on that and not use up the batteries,plus walk around the rooms taking pictures connected to the AC adapter...
This camera is like buying a small computer. I love it. It is the best buy out there for a 5+ pixel with the 60 second movie with sound. I love the macro switch for close up work! There is even a menu to shoot black and white if you need to do some art work. You can change so many variables and even label your files that will come up on the PC when you download. In the LDC screen there is a small keyboard that shows up so you type in your own name to a photo file. I also bought a compact flash reader that connects to your USB and I don't even have to download from the camera. Plus with my printer I can just put in the card and print directly. I also bought a compact flash card with more MB. It comes with Sanyo rechargeable batteries and the recharger. I can't say enough about how please I was to find this camera. And actually a review like this about a Dimage 7 helped me realize the Dimage 7i is the newer model with sound for the movie! The investment of $1000 is worth it. This camera's technology will be around for a long time. Have fun !!!

title: If You Own a Kindle, You Need a Cover!
text: I've had my Kindle Fire for about a year now, and love, love, love it!!  I received a cover as a gift, and it changed my world!  It was a Vera Bradley cover, and that's why I bought the one shown, because it was the style and Vera Bradley workmanship which is wonderful as well as the varied choices of cover patterns.  The Kindle is held within the cover by a strip of elastic at each of the four corners.  They hold the Kindle very securely and it doesn't move around at all.  The cover allows me to hold the Kindle in a much more relaxing fashion, and works so much better for me when I am reading a book from it.  I prefer using a stylus with my Kindle and there is not a place built into the cover to hold a pen or stylus.  There is space between where the Kindle attaches to the right cover and the left side of the cover, however.  I merely took a small piece of velcro which was pre-pasted, and inserted it along the left side of the Kindle onto the cover near the "spine" of the cover, and attached second small piece onto the stylus -  it works beautifully and I now can keep the stylus right inside the cover next to the Kindle, it is where I need it to be, and it doesn't fall out!  Oh, and BTW, the cover really helps in keeping your Kindle clean, and adds a great extra level of protection for it.

title: I know I'm going to be unpopular for this...
text:
...but when I write a review I consider the value for money, in addition to the quality of the item.

The 10x30cl Swarovski is a good pair of binoculars. They feel good in the hand, are relatively light, and are easy to use. I do find it very tricky to manage the separate right eye adjustment with this model - the twist part is very very tight and impossible to manage when the binoculars are on your face. Other Swarovski models have a 'pull-out to release mechanism' before you adjust which makes the adjustment very easy when the binoculars are on the eye.

The 10x eyepiece lens makes holding a steady image a bit tough when birding. I thought that the light weight of the binoculars overall would counteract that - but I still find it hard to keep them steady.

I would suggest that if you want super lovely Swarovskis you try these AND the 8x32EL model. To me the 8x32 is way better (and I wish I had saved the money for them instead of these...)

There are bins from other manufacturers like Nikon and Olympus that are half the price of these 10x30 CLs - and just as good. Time will tell whether the famous durability of the Swarovskis will convince me that this purchase was money well spent

title: Great Garmin spoiled by advertising
text:
The nuvi 1370T is (currently) the only model that comes with available maps for Europe, so if that is what you want or need then stop prevaricating and buy it.

Maps available actually means setting up an account with Garmin, registering the product, locating the maps you need and downloading them. With a solid high-speed connection this took me no more than one and half hours, but it would be a disappointment if you attempted to use the device without first going through the updates.

Advantages over the old models:

1) Screen resists reflection better
2) Looks more up to date
3) Traffic alerts and alternative routes to avoid traffic seem to be much more 'real time' than before and have been useful to me -- my old model would have me take alternative routes late morning because of traffic from the morning rush hour.
4) The unit shows which lane to use on freeways, which is useful

Disadvantages over the old model:
1) The power cord is much thicker and harder to hide
2) MAJOR DISADVANTAGE - the unit uses an obtrusive 1/8th of its screen for unsolicited advertising that Garmin call 'Offers'. These are in the form of exhortations to go one second rate chain of restaurants or another and 'eat all you can for $15'. Or stay at some random hotels chain and 'get x thousand points in their loyalty programs'. I have not been able to turn this off - if anyone knows how to, please leave a comment below for the benefit of our collective sanity.

In short, a major upgrade on the old models and worth purchasing rather than pay for up-dating maps, but the advertising cheapens it. To me the advertising is completely unacceptable.

title: Great product OK sound
text:
I have had my cherry M50s for a little over a year and use them extensively for listening to radio, music from CD and iPod and movies.

In a nutshell these are beautiful furniture quality speakers that pass that most important 'will my wife like to have them in the living room' test, however the sound is not what it could be for a large floor speaker. The sound is actually pretty good, but tolerable is the word I would prefer. I found them to be a bit harsh in the highs and lacking depth until I bi-wired them. They are hungry for power and bi-wired with 105 watts per channel watts they sound better, but still lack crispness and punch.

The point is that the case and build quality suggests that these are going to be in my living room for a good ten years, during which they will look nice but I will also feel like I compromised on having just 'OK' sound. Go ahead and buy them as your first set of floor speakers - but know that you will likely want to upgrade in the future. But I strongly suggest that you not upgrade to these, hold on to what you have and save a few more bucks for a pair of RTi A5, A7 or A9s.

For me I will buy a pair of cherry RTi A7s to match (when they come down in price) and use the M50s as rears. Like I said, I'm sure that these will be in my living room for a good ten years...

title: Simply superb - but don't bother with the Push-to-hear
text:
I use these headphones on long intercontinental air flights (from the West Coast to Africa several times a year) so they are often in my ears for hours on end. I find them very very comfortable and beautiful to listen to. They are so good at isolating and amplifying sound that when I plug them into the in-flight entertainment systems I usually have the volume at the lowest setting.

I am not a techno-phile and use these with my iPod to listen to various 1970s rock bands, audio books and 'sounds of the wild' ambiance. Admitting this probably labels me a nerd, but it is useful to consider what these headphones do. Listen to Boston, Hendrix or Led Zepellin and it is as though you have never heard your favorite music before - it is that good. Listen to spoken word and the quality becomes a problem - unless the production is perfect you can hear each breath of the reader and even the pages turn (I'm not kidding), which is a distraction. For the hippy-esque relaxation sounds of nature I like, these are again superb - every drop of rain in a shower and each bird call is crisp and clear to take you away from it all.

I bought the (push-To-Hear) PTH option as well. It works very well indeed and the little microphone picks up speech with amazing clarity. Problem is that the headphones are still jammed in your ears and the smiling flight attendant doesn't know that you can hear him perfectly as he yells 'chicken or fish' at you. Basically I feel embarrassed to talk to people with the earphones in so don't use the feature.

These replace a pair of Bose QC2 which fell apart (literally) after a couple of years of gentle use. I wouldn't ever consider going back.

These are expensive to be sure, but worth saving for. Anything else would just disappoint in comparison. In fact the quality of this product continues to cost me more and more as I now have to systematically upgrade my radios, home Hi-Fi, the sound system for my TV, and even the Harmon Kardon stereo in the car sounds hollow now I'm used to my little shures.

title: Hang on to your old XP notebook
text:
I can't begin to say how disappointed I am with this product having had it for about a year. I bought it to replace an 8 year-old Compaq Presario that had finally gone to the great junk yard in the sky. I spent a long time researching options on this and other makes before finally going for this one.

The big problem is of course Vista. My 8-year old notebook took less than 10 seconds to boot up when new and was still getting there in under 30 8 years later. This one? Well over a minute just to get going, and if you need to restart you had go put a pot of coffee to brew because you'll be enjoying a cup before the computer has finished. This extends to every operation you do, what used to take a blink of an eye takes a long yawn. And that makes it impossible to enjoy.

The screen is excellent, the speakers are good, the keyboard is a keyboard. I optimistically tried to return it after a month but 'its not very good' was not sufficient grounds for a refund.

Honestly if your old XP computer is still working - hang on to it or buy a mac, just don't bother with one of these. The problem is not with the HP product which seems robust - its the operating system. Would you trade in your 2000 BMW because its old and be happy to have a brand new 1985 Buick LeSabre given to you? Thats what this feels like

title: Good idea, great price, okay execution
text:
I really want to like the Co-Star, but it's just not there yet.

Pros
* Simple - Easy to set up and use.
* Remote - Other than the delay mentioned in cons, the remote performs beautifully.
* UI - Vizio did a great job altering the stock Google TV UI.

Cons
* Connectivity - The device doesn't seem to want to stay connected to my WiFi. It also doesn't always auto-reconnect when it loses the signal. It's worked great ever since I started using a Cat5 cable instead.
* Apps - The App store is filled with mostly terrible apps at the moment. I was excited about the Amazon app, but it literally just launches the Amazon webpage. Really Amazon!?!?!
* Blocked content - This isn't an issue with the device, as much as content providers' reaction to it. Major content sites like Comedy Central and Hulu have blocked Google-TV. This can be fixed by altering the user-agent in advanced Chrome settings, but 1) that leads to a desktop site that's harder to navigate and 2) most people won't know to do that.
* Flash player - Again, this isn't necessarily an issue with the device, but Flash tends to crash or run very slowly on it.
* Delayed input - The remote seems to have a 0-1 second processing delay (normally closer to 0), but this leads to you double pressing buttons and ending up in the wrong place.

I would rate the experience much lower than my media center PC and about on par with Roku II (which I also think is flawed).

title: CAUTION:  Does NOT work with Surface Pro
text: This may be an eminently useful connector when used with the Surface RT - I simply don't know - however, I can attest that it does not work with the Surface Pro.  For reasons which elude logic, the two tablets require signficantly different connectors: the Surface RT's looks like a mini USB and has an angled connection base; the Surface Pro's is apparently a much larger, proprietary design.  Don't be misled by the photographs of the two products on Microsoft's own website which make it appear that the two are identical.  They're most definitely not, which Microsoft customer support acknowledges with an apology for being so vague on this point.  The front of Microsoft's packaging of both units states simply "SURFACE - VGA Adaptor."  Only on the back cover will you find in 6pt type that it's for an RT (or presumably for a Pro).  The major retailers selling the Surface Pro (Staples, Best Buy) both seem confused--though as nearly as I can tell their websites only stock the RT version adaptors.  Pro owners proceed with great caution - it may well be for the moment that the Microsoft Store is the only sure source of the right adaptor. And in any event, the SRP of the adaptor, in either version, is forty percent less than what is being offered on Amazon on 3/1.

title: An Excellent Touchpad
text:
I am loving the Logitech Rechargeable Touchpad T650 with its user-friendly ease of use and many great features. The small size of 5 1/4" width x 5" length, smooth surface, rechargeable battery, very responsive with light-touch to activate gestures, on/off switch, place anywhere to use and sturdy design makes this the perfect touchpad for me. I got this touchpad as my computer mouse stopped working. I thought about a touchscreen monitor, but opted for this touchpad instead as it would be so nice to not have to stretch and fatigue my arm with the actions needed with a touchscreen monitor. The touchpad only needs a very light touch of the fingers to click, slide and navigate the gestures to activate the product features, which is most excellent to keep stress off the fingers. I have a desktop computer with Windows 7 right now, but this touchpad supports Windows 8 when I make the change which is another plus for me. Note a gesture not listed on the Logitech site that I just happen to notice worked to activate the right mouse click is a very light tap of two fingers in the middle of the touchpad. Also, note that a two-handed gesture not listed on the Logitech site that I found useful to highlight is to apply pressure to the left-hand bottom corner of the touchpad with the other hand lightly touch the touchpad with a smooth move of the cursor to highlight, then release the pressure on the touchpad to end highlighting-- after you have finished with copy and paste or drag and drop, to release the highlighted text--place the cursor on the highlighted area then lightly tap anywhere on the touchpad with one finger. Make sure to download the latest version of software for this touchpad to avoid possible glitches. It took me less than a day to get used to using this touchpad, and I find this touchpad superior to a mouse. I highly recommend this rechargeable touchpad and hope this review is helpful to others.

Tips for this touchpad's gestures (includes some that I wrote above):

(1.) To activate the right mouse click is a very light tap of two fingers in the middle of the touchpad.

(2.) A two-handed gesture to highlight is to apply pressure to the left-hand bottom corner of the touchpad and with the other hand lightly touch the touchpad with a smooth move of the cursor to highlight, then release the pressure on the touchpad to end highlighting-- after you have finished with copy and paste or drag and drop, to release the highlighted text--place the cursor on the highlighted area then lightly tap anywhere on the touchpad with one finger.

(3.) Download the latest version of software for this touchpad to avoid possible glitches.

(4.) Use the on/off switch on the top right side of touchpad to turn off when not in use for a long period of time to save the rechargeable battery.

This one has side bins that do not add to the bulk, and a drawer that has room on either side for other desk items, like staplers, tape, etc.  The height is perfect for me.  Assembling it took less than 5 minutes.  We bought multiple ones  for our office.  Great price and arrived quickly to Alaska.

title: Great Gift
text: This was a gift for our exchange student who loves photography.  We don't know much about cameras so we relied on reviews and asking friends.  This was an excellent choice.  She loves it and the color is a nice deep burgundy red (not a bright shiny red).  Great price and fast shipping.

title: Highly recommended!
text: With Just Netflix and no Cable -> This works REALLY good at getting Great reception for Channels we thought we'd never see again!

title: Great for the price!
text: Excellent tablet!  I love watching movies on because of the clarity.

title: Cd
text: I put lots of cds in it the side flap makes them easy to get out

title: Music
text: My husband could use it easily and our CD player hooked up well

title: Element remote
text: [[VIDEOID:a3afd51f05171aeef80915a77b74d53]] It worked on the tv right away. Mom could turn it on and off with ease. Mute button and volume worked.

title: Cd player
text: It is very compact and I can use it anywhere

title: Fits tightly into Shure SE215, light, flexible, good quality, great sound
text:
I needed a cable for my SE215 earbuds, and after looking at what was available, decided to get these. I'm quite happy I did: the fit into the SE215 is nice and snug, the 3.5mm is also good, and the cable appears to be well-constructed. The sound is excellent. (The sound source is VLC Player rendering FLAC and MP3 audio files, coming through my computer's usb port via a FiiO BTR30Pro in DAC mode.)

I'm not convinced that for the low currents needed for earbuds all this 6-core/8-core stuff makes a difference, so I think any good quality cables would be fine. But the MMCX fit matters a lot: I had a cable that didn't fit tightly into the SE215, and that meant I had problems whenever my head moved ... ugh! So just for that reason I'd pay up for a decent cable.

title: Does what it says, works without any trouble at all.
text:
I was a little doubtful about this product because of some of the negative reviews, but decided to try it out anyway. I needed something like this because although my Samsung TV is supposed to be able to play MP4 files off a USB stick, it doesn't work too well, and sometimes just trashes (erases & reformats) the drive. And I desperately wanted to play some very precious old home movies stored as MP4, so this product looked like a viable option.

I was expecting more difficulty than I had, tbh. I unpacked the item, read the instructions about updating the firmware, and followed them (after connecting to power & TV, obviously). Firmware update went without a hitch (make sure you're downloading the right firmware!!). Then I plugged in a small USB stick with some test videos, and read the manual about the controls (for example, pause/resume using the OK button). Zero problems so far, and I hadn't spent that much time on the whole thing.

After that I was ready to roll. I was able to walk through my folder hierarchy, scroll through the file list, and play what I wanted. I set up the auto-resume in the settings (I think it's the default), and adjusted the screen zoom to make sure the entire picture was in the frame. That was it.

So based on my experience, I have no trouble recommending this product. Read the manuals carefully (they are pretty clear, despite the reviews that claim they're not), and follow the instructions exactly (they're not complicated). Enjoy your success.

If for some reason you have trouble, even after doing everything by the book, it's possible you got a bad one -- it happens. I would suggest first trying out a replacement (since Amazon makes that super-easy) before concluding the product is bad.

title: Excellent NAS drive, good performance, large app library
text:
I needed to replace my aging WD NAS, which was struggling to keep up with my needs. After quite a bit of research and product comparisons, I decided to go with the market leader, and bought a NAS that seemed likely to be able to support my needs for several years, and offered some options for expanding the ways I use a NAS.

For context, I mainly use my NAS as "network-attached storage": I back up files, and I share files for use on our multiple home computers. I don't use it for remote access (security concern: I'd rather use cloud storage services for that), and I don't use it as a repository for a media server, or anything else like that.

I decided to use WD "Red" drives for this unit: based on specs and user and professional reviews, they seemed most likely to run reliably for as long as I needed. My previous experience with WD black, blue, and red drives has been consistently positive, whereas other vendors have let me down.

Installation and setup was very easy: I had the unit up and running within a few minutes. Copying files over from my old NAS took some time, but the performance of this Synology unit exceeded my expectations. I was also pleased with how much faster my backup jobs were. I was especially pleased when apps that use network files began running much faster: so clearly both read and write performance were much improved in comparion with the old system.

I also set up a USB backup. It took a little bit of reading in the Synology KB to learn how to do it right, but after that it was a breeze. I plugged in a USB hard drive in the back port (the front port can be configured for use with the USB Copy button), opened up the Hyper Backup app, and ran the initial backup to copy the entire NAS contents to the USB drive. Then I scheduled it to run incremental jobs every day, so now my paranoid backup demon is happy. (I save backup drives in a secure location to provide "disaster recovery"; overkill perhaps, but it buys peace of mind.)

One criticism: the unit came with only 2GB memory, which seems cheesy. And what makes is super-cheesy is the way they price their branded "compatible memory" at ridiculous multiples of the market price. I was able to buy a 4GB Samsung memory card for under $15, and it worked just fine. You can do a web search and see that others have upgraded using larger memory cards.

The Synology KB website is very good: it's well written and comprehensive. There's also an active user community, so there is a ton of information easily available. Overall I'm very happy with my Synology purchase, and would buy their NAS products again without hesitation.

title: Ok, but thinner and flimsier than the usual cd case
text:
These will do the job, but it's immediately obvious how much thinner and flimsier these are than the usual cd cases you get with audio or software cds. I very carefully opened the back on one just to try it, and was worried that it would break something during this process. It didn't, but I wasn't left with a great feeling of comfort, either.

So I think they're ok for a cheap replacement case, but if you want something sturdy, keep looking.

The one good thing is that they were packed nicely in a robust cardboard box, and were not at all damaged in transit.

title: Excellent card to add USB3 ports, includes internal header
text: Despite using a 7-port hub, I was running out of USB ports on my computer, and also needed an internal header for a front USB-C port that didn't have a suitable connector on my older motherboard.  After a lot of searching I found this product, which had what I needed, and at a very reasonable price.  Installation was easy (if you're used to installing cards in a computer), and everything worked without any trouble.  The results are satisfactory.  (USB products are labeled in a really confusing way: do a web search to make sure you understand the various USB3 standards, including "USB 3.2 Gen 2".)

title: Delivers what it promises
text: This is an excellent reader for SD/microSD cards, and I found the USB-A/C option quite useful, especially since some laptops come only with C ports now.  It works well, delivers the speed promised, and is a great value for the price.  I've found Ugreen items to be of good quality in the past, and I'd expect the same here.  They have several card readers, but if you're mainly dealing with the now-standard SD/microSD cards, why pay for features you don't need?  This one fits the need perfectly.

title: Works well for separating audio out from HDMI
text: I'm using this simply as an audio extractor, so can't review the video capabilities.  I have a Chromecast v3, and wanted to use it simply to stream Youtube music or recorded (FLAC/MP3) music from my library, and feed it into a DAC connected to my stereo amp.  I hooked it up, used a fiber cable to connect the audio into the DAC, and the results are quite satisfactory: the sound quality is very good, and I'm not experiencing any problems.  No issues with distortion or noise.

title: Very good DAC, but read the specs carefully
text:
I needed a decent DAC to stream music into my stereo amp (a very good one, but old enough not to have an internal DAC), both from my MP3/FLAC library, as well as online sources. (If you're an "audiophile", you can stop reading now.) So I'm using optical (or coax) in, not USB. The headline specs are 768kHz/32bit max, but read carefully, that's for USB in. With coax/optical in you get 192kHz/24bit max. All I care about is CD quality or better, since like most people I can't hear the difference with anything higher, so these specs more than meet my need.

Specs aside, how does it actually sound? Very good indeed. The sound is perhaps just slightly different (wee bit brighter) from my very good CD player (with Wolfson DAC) -- but I'm not sure I could tell which is which with a blind test. I'm quite happy with it, even when I'm streaming FLAC-source classical music that I'm fussy about.

I think 100-150 is the sweet spot for DACs: if you choose carefully you can get a very good one for the money, and paying more isn't necessarily going to give you better sound. Do your research carefully, and enjoy!

title: Excellent memory expansion option for Synology DS220+
text:
I wasn't willing to pay the ridiculous Synology price for the official memory expansion card, so I looked at the specs, and decided that this Samsung 4GB card would meet my needs nicely, while still staying within the official 6GB maximum.

Installation is quite easy: you shutdown and disconnect the box, take out one of the drives (on the side with the memory card slot), carefully insert the new card at a slight angle, then press down gently until it clicks into place with the retaining clips. Then restart, and check the system info to confirm that you have 6GB memory. I experienced no problems throughout this process.

Note: if you do a web search, you'll see various sites discussing the addition of an 8GB or 16GB chip, supposedly this works because the system board supports it. I didn't go there because my system isn't going to be heavily loaded (I use it as a NAS, that's it), so it wasn't worthwhile for me. I seem to have sufficient headroom for all my anticipated needs, and the system performance is more than adequate.

title: Works like a charm with Chromecast, no setup needed.
text:
I bought two of these, one to use with a Chromecast Audio, another with a Chromecast video (Gen 3, I think). In both cases this gizmo worked flawlessly: all I did was plug the USB-A end into a charger, an ethernet cable (from a switch) into that port, and finally the micro-usb end into the Chromecast. In both cases the connection just took a few seconds (the Chromcast light went white), and the Chromecast worked as it had been working before on wifi, but with a wired connection. (I verified on my wifi controller and my router that the connection was now wired.)

The price was just a tad higher than for some competing products, but I've bought Ugreen devices before, and they've been reliable. So I paid slightly more for peace of mind, and I'm quite happy with the product and the decision.

If you're looking to connect your Chromecast to your wired network, I can recommend this product without hesitation.

title: Very good optical cable for audio connections
text:
I compared this cable with the optical cable I got with a SoundBlaster sound card, that I've been using to connect a Chromecast Audio to an external DAC, which pipes the sound into a stereo amp. I played a Scarlatti sonata with this cable and the other cable, and can detect no difference with my ears. (I don't claim this is a lab test, but with optical fiber at these short lengths and this limited frequency range, there really ought to be no measurable difference that would matter to human ears.)

So I'd say these cables are just fine, and they're sufficiently well made that I'd have no qualms about using them. I have to say though that I disliked the thick wrapping they gave this cable, as if the fiber were extra thick (that's a joke), or needed extra protection (it shouldn't need this much). And this heavy braided wrapping makes the cable heavier and less flexible (as well as uglier!), so I'm taking off a point for it, since I can find other such cables that are superior.

title: The sound is excellent, the features are convenient, but I found it not too comfortable to wear
text:
I really like these headphones at first: the Soundcore app made them easy to configure and update, and in LDAC mode the sound was very very good. So that was great. But then I found that I couldn't wear them for long periods, and this might just be me, your mileage will definitely vary. I wear glasses, and after a while over-the-ear headphones can make my outer ears hurt, and can make them hot. (I have a pair of gaming headphones that I use for conference calls, that are a bit more comfortable, but even those I can wear for about an hour at most.)

So I'm rating these 4 stars, giving them full credit for sound and convenience, and taking a point off for discomfort, although that might just be a personal thing.

title: Great cable for connecting computer to 4K tv/monitor, it just works
text:
I tested this by connecting it from a Windows laptop to a large 4K tv. I hooked it up, and within a few seconds Windows had found the new display. I clicked on the option to extend the display, and in another few seconds was able to watch a 4K video in full resolution. No messing around, it just worked.

Physically the cable seems well constructed: the tips fit nicely, and the fabric-covered cable is sufficiently flexible.

Overall just what I'd want in a cable of this type.

title: Good optical audio cable
text:
I had to laugh when I saw the gold tips on this cable: while gold connectors might make sense on cables that carry electrical signals (analog or digital), they're irrelevant for optical cables, the tips are just the mechanical connection into the socket which aligns the optical fiber-ends. So there's no difference between this tip and the black tip of other cables like this (such as the Amazon Basics one).

That said, this cable does fit into the proper sockets just fine, and works as well as the other such cables I've tried. I used it to connect my SBX4 sound card with an Fiio BTA30Pro DAC, and listened to it with earbuds as well as external speakers, didn't experience any problems. I didn't expect, and didn't perceive, any audio superiority to the Amz Basics optical cable I had been using, so there's no reason there to prefer one over the other. Physically though this one is just a bit more stiff, so I tend to prefer the more pliable Amz cable. If that's not a concern, I would recommend buying whichever is available and cheaper.

title: Nice little USB3 hub with A/C adapter
text:
I got this to carry with my laptop, which has just the two USB-A ports one of which has my mouse dongle. So clearly not enough sometimes. This is nice little adapter supporting USB3 speeds, and the compact size makes it particularly good to throw into the laptop bag. The A/C adapter is also handy since my work laptop has an available C port, but no open A port.

I tested this with large file transfers on my Windows 10 desktop, copying files from an SSD to a USB3 drive. I consistently got about 45MB/s (bytes, not bits), which is what I would expect for this kind of transfer -- and I confirmed that it's the same whether I use the hub or plug the drive in directly.

So if you're looking for a handy and versatile little 4-port USB3 hub, this one should be high on your shortlist.

title: Excellent sound (with LDAC)
text:
I like the sound of these earbuds way more than I expected: they're clean and clear through my hearing range, and I didn't even have to fiddle with the EQ settings to get there. I also have the Liberty 2 Upgraded version, and while those are very good, these are clearly superior.

I did use the Soundcore app to update the firmware and enable LDAC: you'll definitely want to do this before you begin using them. Also, there are other settings on the app you might find useful.

They are also very comfortable to wear for long periods (I use them at my desk while working), and even using LDAC (which uses a lot more power) the battery lasts as long as I've needed so far. The case is nice and compact, and of course charges the earbuds quickly. The only thing I would grumble about (and now I'm being very fussy) is that I have to turn the earbuds over to get them into the right position for the case.

Another note: Anker was offering a "used like new" item for a much lower price, so I decided to try them. I'm very happy I did, since they really were just like a new product, seemed unused (probably a quick return). All the earpiece bits were new, of course.

Highly recommended for excellent sound and comfort at a very affordable price (new or used).

title: Works well, easy way to connect 3.5mm connector to RCA stereo connectors
text:
I needed to connect my desktop speakers (with the usual 3.5mm audio plug) to a DAC's RCA connectors, and this little product worked perfectly. It's hard to get picky about the sound from your basic desktop speakers but these work as well as I would expect: certainly the improved sound I get from my Sound Blaster X4 carries through just fine.

An alert reader would note that I could have connected the 3.5mm plug directly to the SBX4, and I did do that at first, but there were convenience reasons for me to move the plug to the DAC: this way I can just use one device to determine whether I'm listening to my headphone or letting the sound go to the speakers. (TMI for more people, I think.)

title: Nice little hub for external drives or other peripherals
text:
I used this hub to attach a couple of external drives (for backup) to my computer, and am quite satisfied. Performance is as expected: note that to get full speed your computer has to support 3.2G2, otherwise you might get 5GB or less.

Overall a good product for a fair price.

title: Decent set of screws for attaching fans to a case
text:
I used these screws to attach a couple of fans to a computer case -- the fans didn't come with screws, and were radiator fans so the usual screws didn't work. They worked nicely for the job, and I ended up not using the tiny little disk magnets, they're just cosmetic, which I didn't care about, and have the risk of falling somewhere, which I didn't want.

Overall a good set for my purposes and similar jobs.

title: Works fine, but fits inconsistently
text:
Monoprice products are usually good value for the money, but this one falls a bit short because of subpar manufacture. I have a 3 ft version of this cable that works fine, fits tightly on both ends. I decided to move to a 6ft cable to support a slightly longer connection, and found that the cable kept slipping off the connection at one end. I was going to return it, but just for kicks decided to try reversing the cable: and that worked better. Although the looseness is still there, it's not quite as bad on the other side and I can keep it more stable.

So buyer beware: check the cable thoroughly and test the connections as soon as you get it, and return if needed. Or avoid this and get some other brand.

title: Very nice product, but documentation is pretty limited
text:
This is a very nice package, containing a decent DAC with a bluetooth receive/transmit capability (supporting AptX HD and LDAC). Now that I have it set up and connected, I'm very happy with the sound quality, both through the stereo amp to speakers, and through bluetooth headphones using LDAC. For the price, this is really an excellent value, I haven't found anything else nearly as good for this price.

Setup is a bit involved and tricky, and the documentation is quite poor. (Fiio has this reputation.) I hooked it up to my computer using USB, to update the bluetooth & DAC firmware. Then I used the Fiio Control app on my phone to complete the setup, choosing the desired EQ settings and BT codecs. Pairing the headphones was a bit tricky: I found very sketchy instructions on their forum (there's also a Youtube video), which worked after several tries.

But the end result is that I have excellent results for a very moderate price. So if you're a bit technically inclined and not afraid of doing some digging and figuring things out, check this product out. I would recommend it highly.

title: Decent internet radio, with Chromecast, but limits digital output quality
text:
(Revised & re-rated.)

I wanted to upgrade my office music setup: I had a Chromecast Audio connected (through a line booster) to a stereo amp playing to a nice pair of Aperion "bookshelf" (medium size) speakers. I decided to replace the Chromecast with this Grace Link player, hooked up to an external DAC, with output going into the stereo amp.

The problem is this: the Grace Link limits the digital output to 48kb, which doesn't support the "high quality" from streaming music services like Youtube Music and Amazon Music, let alone the high-resolution streams you can get (if you pay more). The old Chromecast Audio does better, especially if you use an optical cable and pipe it through a decent DAC.

I returned it, and am kicking myself for not reading the fine print more closely. I'll look for a better streaming audio receiver (which will of course cost more), but until I find something I'll go back to my Chromecast Audio.

title: Nice low-priced graphics card
text:
I used this in a very nice daily-use computer I recently put together, combined with an MSI mobo and a Ryzen 5700 processor. I use it with a dual 4k monitor setup, and use the rig more than 12 hours/day most days. I don't do much heavy-duty gaming, but I do like my graphics clear and responsive, and want my video playback to be as good as possible. This graphics card serves perfectly for all my needs: it runs cool, shows no glitches, and I'm completely satisfied.

If you're looking for something modestly priced for modest needs, this is an excellent product to consider. I've been buying MSI motherboards and graphics cards for more than 10 years, and have never been disappointed.

title: Very nice sound after proper settings, comfortable to wear, great for the price
text:
Overall rating 4.5, rounded up to 5. I don't think there's anything better for this price.

I wanted a "better" set of wireless earbuds for casual music listening: I wanted either AptX HD or LDAC, good battery life, and comfortable to wear for at least an hour or two. (I specifically ruled out over-the-ear headphones because I can't wear them very long, and ruled out wired earbuds for convenience. To me these are acceptable compromises.)

I was considering the Sony WF-1000XM4, but didn't want to pay that much for casual listening. I was also considering the new Soundcore Liberty 4, which on paper seems to be a great product. But I decided to try this "Liberty 2 Pro Upgraded" pair to see if was good enough for a lot less money.

So far I'm really very pleased: the sound is excellent for all my favorite music genres: classical, country, pop, rock, and latin pop, and after replacing the earpiece flaps and cushions I'm finding them very comfortable to wear as I work at my desk.

Important: to get the sound right, I had to do several things. First, I downloaded the Soundcore app, connected the earbuds, set the audio quality to LDAC (in settings). Then on my Android phone (Pixel), I went to the bluetooth advanced settings (usually hidden under developer options: do a web search for more details), and set the Audio Codec to LDAP, the LDAC quality to 900kbps, and made sure that the other BT settings (such as sample rate, bits per sample) were at the highest for good audio. Finally, I went back to the Soundcore app and played with the equalizer settings until I had what sounded best to my ears. The app has a neat little personal-hearing tester, which is worth a try, especially if your ears are getting older. After all this I had nice clean well-balanced sound. You might try different EQ settings for different music genres if you like, it does make a difference, but perhaps not huge enough to matter.

I've read many grumbles about LDAC, but I wonder if those are based on using the default settings: in my experience getting the settings right makes a very big difference.

PS It seems that the LDAC settings on Android go back to "best efforts" everytime the earbuds are disconnected. Quite annoying: I have to set them back to 900kbps every time. The other settings are stable.

title: Misleading product description (for 1TB USB stick)
text:
I don't know whose fault it is, but the product description for the 1TB USB stick is incorrect, and the error is significant: says "USB 3.2 Gen 2" (10GB spec), but the package is clearly labeled "USB 3.2 Gen 1" (5GB spec). Now of course the USB labeling was invented by some gnome with a bad sense of humor, but if you're going to use the labels, you have to get it right. (To be fair, the "upto 600MB/s" is a clue that should have raised my suspicions, but unfortunately I wasn't really paying attention to that.)

This might still be a reasonable product for the price, but not what I'm looking for. Caveat emptor.

title: connectors aren't right, fit is too loose
text: Useless item I'll just have to throw away.  The connectors aren't good, they don't fit standard TS-9 ends properly (too loose, no way to get a proper connection).

title: Excellent motherboard for a mid-level computer build
text:
I wanted to build a relatively inexpensive computer to replace my 7-year old machine (also custom built), and after looking at various options I opted for this MSI mobo. I'd used MSI several times in the past, and was happy with their product quality and their support. (BTW, I use pcpartpicker to assemble my components, I recommend the site.)

After putting everything together and running it, I'm very happy with my choice. The mobo physical layout is excellent, installation of the cpu and cooler and graphics card was easy, and all those fiddly connectors were not too hard to identify and access (needed a flashlight sometimes, and younger eyes would have helped). The firmware settings interface is decently designed and easy to use: I particularly liked the fan speed controls.

The Bios flash is easy to do with the firmware file loaded onto a USB key. (I didn't try the funky flash button, did it from the interface.) I wish MSI provided a Windows app to download and update the Bios, as some other brands do, but this is a minor thing.

For the price paid, the value of this mobo is excellent. I highly recommend considering it for a mid-priced Ryzen build.

title: M.2 SSD is the way to go for the boot drive, and this is good value
text:
For building a custom computer, I wouldn't consider anything other than an M.2 SSD chip for the boot drive: they're easy to install, and much faster than SATA drives. While you can pay almost as much as you want for these drives, I don't see the point in going overboard when a decent drive like this one will get you more than 90% there: the returns from spending more dollars are not going to be noticeable for most people (who aren't building special-purpose and very expensive gaming/computing rigs).

This one is definitely worth considering: I'm quite happy with it, and expect that it will work error-free for a sufficient number of years.

title: Seems to work ok, but you do have to set 3200 in bios.
text:
I bought this pair for a new "how cheap can I make it" build (on MSI mobo). So far all seems ok. As others have reported, the board initially runs these at 2666MHz, you have to change your settings on the mobo (enable XMP, set speed to 3200) to get the rated speed. Although technically this is "overclocking", it's one of the more safe things you can do. How much difference will you see in performance with the 20% improvement? My guess is not that much in most cases.

Anyway, if cost is a factor in your decision, this 2x16GB pair is worth considering. If you want the comfort of going with a more proven brand, consider Corsair and G.Skill among others.

title: Excellent case, fits new Kindle PW nicely, works as promised
text:
This is an excellent case for the new Kindle Paperwhite. It fits nicely, looks attractive (see the Green Datura style), and works just as promised. Yes, contrary to some confused reviewers, it does have a magnetic closure (light but definite stickiness, not some undesirable 20lb force), and yes, sleep/wake on the Kindle works with the cover closing and opening.

What's left to say? If you're looking for a nice cover, put this one on top of your shortlist.

BTW, if you do happen to get a defective unit (it can sometimes happen), instead of rushing to write a nasty review, try contacting Amazon for an exchange, they're always happy to do it in my experience.

title: Convenient design, but seriously underpowered
text:
The design concept is great: six widely spaced power outlets, plus six usb charge ports in a compact, lightweight brick. And with the limited tryout I gave it, I can say that it works at least partially. The problem I have is with the ratings. The total current rating is 10 amp (or 1200 watt if you prefer to think that way), so don't be planning to plug in six power-demanding devices. (Six laptops, or three laptops plus three displays, would probably be fine.) The USB power rating is even worse: the max per port is 2.4A, and the total over all six ports is 3.4A (no, I'm not kidding), or 17W. So if you use all the ports to charge your phone, kindle, tablet, earbud, etc., don't expect fast charging. A good multiport USB power brick should give you roughly 10W per port, so for six ports it should have been 60 or more watts. (There are 65W chargers on Amazon.)

So overall recommendation is to give this a pass: you can do better by buying a decent power strip to meet your power distribution needs, and a separate USB power brick to cover those needs.

title: Sharp and bright image, decent software, but make sure it works for you
text:
I liked this camera quite a lot, at least on initial evaluation. It was easy to set up, and downloading the Konnect software enabled good camera control. Overall, it was somewhat superior to the Logitech c922 camera I normally use.

However, one big miss that kept me from switching to this camera as my primary: I didn't find a way to control the picture when using Google Meet, which is what I use for work (and sometimes for personal meetings as well). The Konnect software couldn't change what I was seeing on Meet (note that the Logitech Camera Settings app does do this), in particular the zoom level and camera angle.

I did not test the camera with Zoom or other video meeting applications, since I don't use them much.

Overall it's a fine camera, and may suit your needs, but you just need to be aware of the limitations if you use Meet.

title: Does the job, but has large footprint
text:
I needed a stand for a single 27 inch monitor that is going to live in basement storage as a "guest spare", and bought this because it was the cheapest one available that could do the job. It's sturdy enough, and easy to assemble: it's very similar to other stands of this type I've bought at Amazon. So it serves my purpose. I found the base footprint rather too large for a single monitor stand: I suspect they have just the one size they use for singles and doubles. I also found that the swivel for tilting the monitor forward and back was just a tad hard to tighten sufficiently so the monitor wouldn't sag forward.

But overall this does the job it was hired for, and the price was right, so I'm giving it 4 stars. Maybe take it down to 3 or 3.5 if the footprint matters a lot to you.

title: Works like a charm (when used correctly)
text:
I have an HP Omen with an Nvidia RTX 2060 graphics card providing HDMI, DP, and DVI ports. Based on the specs, the DP supports DisplayPort 1.4 (8K @ 60Hz). I got an active DP-HDMI adapter from Amz that turned out to be unreliable, so I decided to get this passive adapter that promised to support 4K @ 60Hz. (As I understand it, I don't need an active adapter with this graphics card.)

I connected this up to the monitor using an HDMI cable, and it works flawlessly. No weirdness when starting up, turning the screen on/off, recovering from sleep, or anything else that I've noticed so far.

I think the negative reviews are from situations where this adapter isn't the right solution, for whatever reasons. When used appropriately this is a great product.

title: Perfect stand if you want to stand your laptop on its edge!
text:
I use my work laptop with an external monitor & keyboard, so I was attracted by the idea of getting a stand to save some desk space. After some looking, I decided that this product was likely to be sturdy enough and easy to use. I've been very pleased with it: it was easy to adjust to the right width (there are adjustment bolts underneath you can tighten with your fingers), and proved to be as stable as I had wanted and expected.

Note: I have a 15" laptop: I think the stand would be fine with a normal 17" machine, unless of course it's unusually heavy.

Overall I can comfortably recommend this stand.

title: Doesn't work: disconnects the monitor and doesn't reconnect on its own
text:
TLDR: don't bother, this doesn't work. Find a different product.

This was great, until it wasn't. I was using this to connect a second monitor to a video card with a DisplayPort port (in addition to HDMI & DVI ports). New computer, good graphics card, all drivers current, no other issues with the computer. With a different DP-HDMI adapter it works fine, no glitches, no blackouts. With this one, every so often the monitor this was connected to would go dark, and wouldn't reconnect on its own. This happened repeatedly, until I was able to conclude that this adapter was the problem.

title: Excellent hardware at a great price, but configuration is too complicated.
text:
This is a superb piece of hardware at a great price. In my initial testing I was really pleased and impressed with the performance. So if you're a professional with deep understanding of how to set this up, go for it. (But read the rest of my comments here first.)

If you're not a pro, or at least someone with extensive network management expertise, you might wish to consider something with an easier management interface.

The basic configuration was simple enough. But I wanted to set up WAN failover. And I wanted to set up basic security stuff, including setting it to disable pings and connection attempts from the WAN side. I hadn't even gotten to the advanced capabilities. But it was frankly just a giant pain. The website guide and the forum were barely helpful, especially when professionals argued with one another about how to best do something. (Not a confidence builder.) This took hours of trial and error. And just resetting the router is a pain, you have to hold the button for 30 seconds, after which it might or might not reset.

Finally, I thought I had it all done right, and was happily running tests. And then I found out that I had somehow managed to disable the ability of my wifi access points to connect to the network. At this point I decided to accept defeat, rather than spend another day trying to figure it all out. I sent it back, thank goodness for Amazon's excellent return policy.

I wish Mikrotik would invest in a really nice GUI, and a small set of config wizards: yes, that would add cost, because good software costs money. But I think it would greatly increase the appeal of their products. Even pros like "ease of use", because it saves time and hassle and reduces chances of error.

title: Feature-rich but easy to configure through GUI, impressive performance
text:
This is a really great prosumer/SOHO router, from a brand that deserves to be much better known in the US. I found it very easy to configure through the Web GUI, and there are tons of easy-to-follow instructions on the Draytek website. You can also just try out the GUI for any of their routers right there on the website in what appears to be a live demo of each of their devices.

I was looking for a dual-WAN high-performance router with strong security features, high throughput with security capabilities turned on, and, most importantly, easy to configure through a GUI. I considered Unifi, but the user experience with their more recent product leaves me very sceptical about giving them my business. I tried out Mikrotik, which sells excellent hardware at very reasonable prices, but proper configuration required way too much time and effort (and trial & error), so I gave that up. Finally I learned about Draytek through a review from a UK-based site, and decided to check them out.

So far I've been very pleased. It took me about an hour to update the firmware and set up the router to be a secure gateway, and the throughput for my CenturyLink gigabit connection has been consistently impressive. I've searched the Draytek website for various recipes, and have tried them out: each one has been fairly simple and easy to follow.

The WAN failover is very simple to configure, but I haven't yet tested the functioning. I don't expect a problem with it, based on the "it does what it says" experience I've had so far.

All that said, this is by no means an inexpensive router. If you want the features, and you don't mind paying a little extra for ease-of-use, then you might want to give this one a serious look.

title: Works as required for Lumix DMC-LX10 battery
text:
This charger fits the battery for the LX10 without any trouble, and charges it to full charge (LED indicator turns green) without any hassle. A bit more convenient in my view than plugging a cable into the camera. The charger itself is lightweight and should be easy to pack for a trip.

I just received it, so can't offer any comments on how long it will last, etc. Based on my experience so far, I'm happy to recommend this to charge a compatible battery.

title: Good but not wonderful sound, improves a bit on the tv.
text:
I don't care to create a "home theatre experience", I just want to have very good picture quality with decent sound. Also, I wanted to keep things simple, didn't want multiple units which I'd have to place somewhere. So I ended up with this soundbar, which fits nicely in front of the big Samsung QN90A tv, without obscuring anything or needing a lot of space.

I connected it using a good HDMI cable to the tv's ARC port, and went through the basic settings: not much complexity or hassle. Then I watched a few minutes of several different blu-ray discs, some with big orchestral sound. I did A-B comparison with the tv, and also asked a family member to opine.

Result: the soundbar was clearly better, producing a deeper richer sound with nice but not overwhelming bass (to me this is a good thing). Overall I was happy to keep it to enhance my AV entertainment.

Now, is it worth about $150? Probably. If I were to rethink the decision, would I have paid more for a soundbar with better sound? Maybe. I'd have to do side-by-side comparisons to be persuaded, since the many reviews I read weren't all that convincing, until I got into the much more expensive products.

title: Probably the best non-OLED tv you can buy right now.
text:
I'd been looking to upgrade my tv to a bigger (75in) and better one. After doing some reading, I narrowed my choices down to this newer Samsung Q90A and the LG OLED C1, and then decided I'd stick with the non-OLED tech to get the higher brightness, and of course the somewhat lower price. (I've read that OLEDs aren't made as bright because of burn-in concerns.)

So far I'm very pleased with my choice. The picture is wonderful: my usual test is a 4K nature documentary, and I think Blue Planet 2 looks just amazingly good, although I've seen it before on a slightly older 4K Samsung tv. The brightness is great, which I needed for an open living room with big windows.

I like to turn off the Samsung "smart hub" thing, which I find intrusive and annoying, so I can't review any of that for those who are interested. Amazon, Disney+, and Netflix streaming content looks great (through a Fire TV cube), so I'm perfectly happy.

As for other features, the 4 HDMI inputs is nice, and just adequate for my current needs. I do think these bigger tvs should come with something like 6 or 8 (why not?) HDMI input ports so that you can have multiple players and game consoles hooked up without having to get a separate switch.

The sound from the multiple speakers is very good, probably as good as you can get from a modern tv. I'm considering getting a decent (but not overly expensive) soundbar to try, see if it makes the sound noticeably better.

title: Excellent HDMI cable, at least for UHD (not tested at "8K")
text:
Note: the 4K term is marketing, just about all consumer devices are UHD (2160p). So I'm going to use the UHD term, feel free to translate to "format commonly referred to as 4K" if you prefer.

I tested this cable on my newest UHD tv, with streaming UHD video from multiple sources, and then with a UHD nature documentary on a bluray player. I'd been using a very good 18Gb ("4K") cable before, so possibly a side-by-side test wouldn't show any difference. But I did immediately notice how sharp and bright the picture was in both cases, so I can at least say that this makes a very good video cable for UHD.

The cable is well made and feels sturdy, with a nice grab handle at each end, and inserts just the way it should into HDMI ports, with neither wiggle nor overmuch tightness. I didn't notice any minor flaws that might make me concerned about build quality, and I would expect it to last, at least until it becomes obsolete.

What should you buy if you don't have any so-called 8K media or devices, like most of us, and don't see them in your immediate future? In that case I'd just go with very good "4K" or "8K" cables, but without paying premium prices. The product description might say "Premium High Speed HDMI Cable" (18Gbps) or "Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable" (48Gbps). The first corresponds to the HDMI 2.0b standard, the second to HDMI 2.1.

title: Works as advertised, with newer and older BD players
text:
I have a Sony UHD (non-HDR) bluray player, and an older Panasonic bluray player, that I wanted to hook up through a switch to my 4K tv (so I'd be using only one HDMI port). I also wanted at least one spare port on the switch to use with a computer or tablet or whatever. I was a little wary of buying a no-name product, but the description and the more knowledgable reviews convinced me to give this a try. (This is where Amazon's great return policy comes in: I figured I'd just return it if it didn't work as expected.)

I just plugged it all in today, and my conclusion is that you can pretty much ignore the most negative reviews: this works, and works well. The connection to the tv is trouble-free and glitch-free, with image quality being what you'd expect. (Make sure you're using good HDMI cables meeting the required spec, of course.) I didn't even bother using the remote: the auto-switch function works just as it should: when I turned a player on, the switch selected the right input port, the tv responded as you'd expect (also switching input as it should), and all was merry. No hasssle, just as you'd want. Recommended.

title: Didn't work with Sony BD player as one input
text: I wanted to use this to hook up two BD players to my tv: a Samsung model, and a Sony model.  The Sony just didn't work, it showed something, glitched, lost connection, etc.  I tried all the usual: change the port, change the cable, turn everything off and try again, etc. etc.  The Samsung worked perfectly, but the Sony didn't.  I couldn't figure it out, it might have something to do with the HDMI standard the player is using, or just possibly it's a defective unit.  But bottom line, this was useless for my purpose.  (It does advertise that it works with pretty much anything, so it's failing to meet its claimed capability.)

title: Works as well as the original TCL Roku tv remote (or actually, better)
text:
The remote that came with my TCL Roku tv (bought early 2018) was defective from the beginning: it kept draining the battery within weeks, despite very low usage. And recently it became even more erratic, working in a hit-or-miss fashion. So I was glad to see this replacement available on Amazon, for a great price. I received it today, inserted two AAA batteries, and it worked perfectly right from the beginning. I was able to use all the functions with the tv, including some editing of the home page shortcuts, didn't run into any problems at all. (I didn't try the streaming-channel buttons, have no plans to use them.)

So if you have a TCL tv on the list for this remote (see product name & description), and need a replacement remote, this will do the trick, and be very easy on your wallet too!

title: Died after about two years, no battery backup now
text:
I was quite pleased with this UPS when I received it, and bought a couple more in different sizes. I used this with my desktop computer, to bridge the 2-3 minutes it takes between the main power going off and my generator kicking on automatically. It did that job perfectly for about two years, but recently just stopped providing backup power. The computer thinks the battery is fine, and is charging, but with any loss of supply power, this thing just fails to provide the backup power and the computer essentially crashes. I suspect that either the battery isn't good or (more likely) the cutover circuitry isn't functioning properly.

I decided to switch to a TrippLite UPS instead (the AVR series): it gives you a much better system for just a few extra bucks.

title: Excellent earbuds, great sound
text:
These earbuds are really very good. The sound is balanced and clear, and it's a pleasure to use them to listen to all kinds of music, from classical to rock/pop to country. They're more than adequate for phone calls and online conferences. They're pretty comfortable to wear: I have a difficult time with most earbuds, especially with the ones that need a large hard object sitting inside the earlobe, so I might wish these were a tad softer, but really I haven't had any trouble wearing them for an hour or so.

The little charge case is nicely made, and very easy to use. I use it for more than an hour or two per day, and at that level I think the box only would need charging every few days, making it pretty convenient.

Are they worth the price? I got these from the VIne program, so price wasn't a consideration for me, and I haven't compared these with other items in a similar price range. The sound is better than some very nice earbuds I have that cost quite a bit less, so at least I can say that they're delivering some value for the extra money.

title: Well made sturdy lightning cable, works perfectly
text:
This is a very good cable: it's well made, looks like it will last as long as it needs to. The ends plug in firmly and securely to the charger and the Apple device (e.g., iPad), respectively. There's no problem with charging, it all works as you'd expect.

BTW, the cable comes with a little velcro strap for holding it together when coiled. Nice touch.

I got this with the Vine program, and there's no product page up yet, so I don't know the price. But it's Amazon Basics, so it's probably very competitive -- assuming that, this is definitely a cable I'd buy if I were looking for another one.

title: Nice wireless headset for use with a phone (NOT a computer)
text:
This is a very comfortable headset, I can wear it for hours without any discomfort. The sound is clear and well-balanced, good for music, voice calls, podcasts, and audiobooks. The active noise cancellation is quite good, it does cut out background noise effectively, without any unpleasant side-effects.

The headset comes with a nice carrying case, a useful aux cord, and a 2-prong adapter for airplanes.

The only way to control the settings is with the mobile app, which is easy to use. However, pairing it to and using it with a laptop (for example) is quite difficult, and you cannot (yes, that's right) adjust the settings when paired to a computer. (And no, you can't pair it to two devices at once.)

The sleep timer default is annoyingly short, and even with the mobile app you can only set it to a max of 1 hour.

There is an auto play/pause function, activated by placing the headset on/off: this is a good idea in theory, but in practice is frustrating. For example, when I put it on while using my Mac, the Apple music app is automatically started -- NOT what I wanted, people!

Overall: a nice headset which is comfortable and has very good sound, but comes with some quirks and limitations.

title: A surprisingly good laptop at a very affordable price
text:
I was expecting this laptop to be a bit under-powered, and not quite up to the mark in video and audio. I was completely wrong: this machine blew past my expectations. For a general use laptop, used for web browsing, word processing, and similar purposes, this is more than an adequate machine, this is really very good. The performance is more than acceptable: I haven't noticed anything being unusually slow or erratic, it just runs smoothly and fast. The display is 1920x1080 (so HD but not 4K), and clear and crisp for watching online video (for example). The audio too is surprisingly good: you can play music on it and enjoy the well-balanced sound, no cringing necessary.

Notes: 8GB memory, 256GB SSD. HDMI, USB-A, USB-C ports, SD card slot, and 2.5mm audio jack. Bluetooth & Wifi. No ethernet jack, you would need a USB-A or USB-C ethernet adapter if you wanted to use a wired connection. The wifi works quite well, so it's not a major concern.

For this price you're not getting a powerful workstation or a gaming machine, obviously. And you're not getting 4K video or tons of memory or disk storage. But if you're looking for a very good "normal user" laptop for yourself or a family member, this is definitely one to put on your shortlist. If you want to compare, I've also been pleased with the similarly priced Asus laptops.

title: Well made sturdy lightning cable, works perfectly
text:
This is a very good cable: it's well made, looks like it will last as long as it needs to. The ends plug in firmly and securely to the charger and the Apple device (e.g., iPad), respectively. There's no problem with charging, it all works as you'd expect.

BTW, the cable comes with a little velcro strap for holding it together when coiled. Nice touch.

I got this with the Vine program, and there's no product page up yet, so I don't know the price. But it's Amazon Basics, so it's probably very competitive -- assuming that, this is definitely a cable I'd buy if I were looking for another one.

title: Waste of money: poor sound, controls are difficult to use, lacks mute function
text:
This was a mistake. It's a pretty bad headset overall. Despite adjustment, the sound is poor, and makes it really hard to carry on a conversation with the echoing hollow sound effects. The controls are, at least for me, nearly impossible to use while wearing the headset, and not all that good even when it's off. And, to add a last kick, it lacks a convenient mute function: this is just absurd to me.

I recommend going quickly past this one and considering other headsets instead.

title: Useful and convenient adapters for all those micro-usb cables
text:
I have a large collection of micro-usb cables accumulated over the years, but although I need them for the older devices, they're not useful for the new phones. These adapters fill that little short-term need, allowing me to be cheap for now and continue to use the old cables when that's convenient, and carry just one cable for multiple devices when desired.

They work quite well: each adapter comes with it's little clip & chain, fits neatly on the micro-usb tip, and works as expected for usb-c charging. Since it does make the cable tip rather long, it's important to be careful about avoiding stress on that tip, to avoid the risk of breaking it and/or damaging the device charge port.

title: Good cables, can charge as well as handle data transfer.  (No PD charging, USB2.)
text:
These cables are well made, and work quite well as promised. I've used them for charging my Pixel 3, and for data transfer to the phone from a Windows 10 computer, had no trouble with either. For the price, they're great.

Do note however that (as described on the product page), these are USB2 cables, so don't expect USB3 speeds. Also, they don't support Power Delivery (PD) fast charging. I think the latter is a minor issue, and the former is acceptable for moderate data transfers (for example I did a 10gb transfer today, and just walked away for a few minutes while it ran). I'll get a USB3 cable when I start needing to transfer a lot of photos or other bulky data like that.

Note on data transfer, in case it helps anyone else:
I was having trouble with the data transfer when I tried connecting through a USB3 hub I have on my computer, the phone wouldn't connect in data transfer mode. When I connected the cable from the phone to a computer USB3 port directly, it worked without any fuss. Something to do with drivers or connector cables, I guess, but it's too hard to figure out exactly what's wrong.

title: good cables, but they're not PD and not USB3
text:
Good USB2 cables for charging or data xfer, working just fine with my Pixel3. They seem well-made, and sturdy without being too bulky.

But do note that they're not USB3 (max data speed is 480Mbps or USB2), and don't support "Power Delivery", which is the Pixel fast-charge protocol. I charge my phone overnight using an old 5v charge adapter (Pixel's OEM adapter is 9v 2A), so it works fine for my needs.

title: Nice SSD at a reasonable price
text:
I was looking for a 1TB SSD to upgrade the storage in my computer. Background: I have a tower computer I built about 3 years ago, and at that time I used a 500GB SSD for the system drive, and two 1TB hard drives for pretty much everything that didn't have to be on the system drive. Since SSD prices have fallen so much, I decided to replace one of the 2 hard drives with an SSD and use the remaining HD mostly for less frequently used files.

After reading a few professional reviews, I decided on the WD Blue, because it seemed to offer the best combination of adequate performance, reliability, and competitive price. I skipped on some cheaper options because of suspect reliability.

I'm quite satisfied with this drive: the performance is very good, as promised. I haven't run into any problems with the drive, and my experience with WD & SanDisk storage products has been generally positive.

Caveats: (1) Of course I can't predict how well it will do over the longer haul, that's where I relied on reviews and brand experience. (2) Yes, one can get more speed for more money, but for my normal use it wouldn't make any practical difference in overall performance.

Note: If I were building a new computer today I'd use an M.2 SSD for the main drive. In fact that's what I did in the new computer I recently built for my son.

title: You get what you pay for with this one, it's ok for infrequent use
text:
This is what it promises to be: a reasonable quality low-priced monitor that won't dazzle or delight you, but is quite acceptable if you want to spend as little as possible. I bought it to use as a spare monitor for setting up a new computer or reconfiguring an older one. And it's completely acceptable for that purpose, although it's cheaply made and has a lackluster display.

If I were buying one to use daily, I'd spend a little more and get a model with higher resolution and better display, and a larger screen, perhaps 22 inches or more.

title: excellent enclosure for SSD drives
text: I upgraded a computer's drive, so had a spare 256GB SSD.  I popped it into this Orico enclosure (took about 15 seconds), and I had myself a nice external drive for fast backups or extra storage.  R/W performance is as you'd expect with USB3, I've had no problems.  Recommended.

title: Incorrect description: does not work with DMW-BLH7PP (Lumix LX10 battery)
text: The product was a little shoddy in construction: the cover for the LCD screen was falling out when I received the package.  I put it back on, but then found that the battery doesn't fit, so I can't actually use this thing as claimed.  Returned.

title: Easy to use, excellent video quality: this is the best streaming box available
text:
I needed to retire an old tv, and bought myself a Fire TV cube and a 4K tv. The combination is absolutely terrific. The setup is so easy that it doesn't require discussion. The speech recognition (Alexa) works smoothly out of the box, and can do more things than I care to try out. 4K video from Amazon or Netflix or my streaming package (PS Vue) looks very very good.

I should mention that I have a high bandwidth (1 gigabit) network connection, and a gigabit wired network at home, and use an ethernet cable to connect the Fire TV. If you have a good wifi setup you can use that, but I much prefer wired connections for most things, especially streaming video.

If you're looking for the best streaming box available right now, I think the Fire TV Cube is it. Highly recommended.

title: works well as USB3 speeds
text: This a nicely sized and well made short adapter cable, and in my tests it worked well at USB3 speeds.  Not much else to say, it's a simple product that does what it promises.

title: they work, but they're skinny
text: These are cheap, but not a great bargain.  They're thin cables, not copper (says "copper-clad aluminium"), and the plugs aren't quite as nice as some of my other cables (from various vendors).  I was in a rush, but I'll slowly replace these with cables I make myself at home, and then give these away. So if you're trying to save money they're ok, but don't expect anything superior.

title: it works, but hard to configure, and pretty expensive for an unremarkable router
text:
I was hoping for better. I have gigabit fiber internet, and wanted to upgrade from the Actiontec router that I bought from the ISP. Unfortunately, this ER4 doesn't cut it as an upgrade.

It is a pain to configure: the web gui is clunky at best, and advanced options require using a command-line interface through SSH. Even updating the firmware is more pain than it should be (you have to download from web and upload from computer).

But all that would have been acceptable if I'd seen any significant advantage over the decent-but-not-stellar router I've been using. There isn't any. For my home office & home streaming/voip/web needs the Actiontec is a tad unsatisfactory but just as good as this one, at less than half the price. And it doesn't seem to be all that great for the next level up either: if I wanted a true small-business router I'd look for something more capable (and easier to manage!).

Ubiquiti seems to be letting the USG/ER product line languish, at least at the lower end. Maybe they've decided that it's not a profitable segment for them.

title: excellent hdmi cables, does improve 4k picture, works well with fire tv
text:
All HDMI cables are the same, except they aren't. Firstly, some of them have quality problems, so that they don't quite work right. Secondly, some older or cheaper cables don't meet the new specs for 4k/HDR video, and you can see the difference.

I first used one of these cables with a Fire TV connected to a non-4k TV. (It's a good TV, and there's not that much 4k content where the difference matters to me.) I'd been having regular problems with this setup: I'd turn on the tv and wake up the FireTV, and get a gray screen until I fiddled with the controls for a couple of minutes. After some experimentation I concluded that the problem was the cable. I swapped in the new cable, and look at that, no more connection problems between the boxes. It works now consistently without any problems.

Then I decided to swap in another of these cables on my 4k setup which has a Fire TV Cube. I watched a 4K video stream for a few minutes, then paused and swapped in the new cable. Yup, the picture was definitely brighter and sharper. I'd deliberately paused at a good comparison point to be able to tell, and I'm satisfied that I'm not fooling myself. (Yes, a double-blind controlled experiment would be better, but I'm not running a lab.)

For the price these are a great buy, even if all you're thinking of is "good-enough HDMI cables". I'm thinking of replacing a couple of my other old ones with these.

title: not good enough: picture is blue-ish and fuzzy, there's no controller software
text:
I was hoping that this might be an alternative to the Logitech webcams I've been using for some time. In particular, I'm comparing this product with my Logitech c922 for picture quality.

Firstly, the picture is sharp enough, but not quite as clear and sharp as the Logitech picture. It has an odd fuzziness that I can't quite diagnose, and what's worse is the slightly blue tint I'm seeing. Even the cheap Logitech c270 doesn't do this.

Secondly, there's no controller software: I want to be able to zoom in at the very least, and ideally control the angle a bit. (No, it doesn't work to move the camera in closer, because then it's at the wrong angle, and in front of my monitors.) So that makes it much less useful for me, especially compared to the Logitech.

For the relatively high price for this product, I should really rate it 2.5 stars. My recommendations: if you're looking for relatively inexpensive, no frills, get the Logitech c270; if you want something a bit nicer, get the c920 (not the c922 unless you really need its features). You'll save money and be a lot happier.

title: Very well designed, but a bit small and rather expensive
text:
