This is a very well-designed and well-made lightweight backpack. (But what makes it a women's backpack? That designation is dumb and a bit insulting.) If you're looking for a smaller backpack to carry the minimal set of things you need: small laptop or tablet, plus a Kindle and/or book, then this might fit the bill. I particularly liked the strap in the back for fitting over the pull handles of a wheeled carryon, the little pocket in front for the phone, and the multiple zippered compartments for easier organization of all the stuff that creeps into a backpack.

But really, it's too small to be versatile: I'd only take this if I really wanted a small pack, otherwise a normal sized backpack is way more convenient. And given the price you'd pay for this, it might not be where you want to spend your luggage money. If you really want a small backpack, you spend less than half of the price of this and get a pretty decent one that meets the need.

title: Very useful converter & power strip for travel
text:
For many electronic items you just need plug adapters for international travel, you don't need a voltage converter because the chargers accept 110-240v and 50/60hz. But there are a few items that don't fit that profile: my electric toothbrush for instance. For some years I've been carrying a clunky voltage converter, but this power strip style really is more convenient: you can plug in several items, and also use the USB ports to charge the phone/tablet/Kindle trio that seems to be a must-have for most of us. (In fact, this is so handy that I'm planning to carry it even for domestic trips.)

The power cable for this item has a Euro plug, so you need an adapter for non-Euro countries including the US. They provide several of them (see product description): US, UK, Australia, Italy, Israel. (Note however that they erroneously say the UK plug works in India: it doesn't, you need to get yourself a separate one for that part of the world.)

I'm not travelling yet, so can't confirm that it does work for step-down operation in 220-240v countries. I've tested it here, and it works just fine. The USB charging ports are particularly satisfactory, they clearly put out the advertised power for fast charging.

Overall an excellent and very useful product.

title: excellent POE switch, full gigabit throughput
text:
So far I've just done my initial testing with this switch, and it passed with flying colors. I hooked up a Unifi wifi access point to test the POE function, and that worked without any hitch. The acccess point powered up quickly, and had no problems with bandwidth or anything else. I then hooked up a computer to another port, and ran some bandwidth tests. I have a gigabit fiber service, and was able to get full throughput with no problems detected.

I haven't done any kind of load test or hooked up multiple POE devices (like the rest of my Unifi APs), or multiple computers running big downloads. So I can't attest to the behavior of this switch under load. However, I really don't expect any problems for my home networking needs: I have perhaps a larger than average networking demand with multiple computers and multiple wifi points and several streaming devices, but based on the specs I'm expecting that when I install this switch as the main distribution switch (after the ISP gateway) it won't limit me in any way.

If you're looking for a decent POE switch with 16 ports, this is definitely worth considering.

title: excellent for network and usb connections, hdmi port work work unless you have a newer USB-C device
text:
Update: I corrected this review, since it seems that the HDMI not working is a limitation on my Asus computer (the USB-C device doesn't support the HDMI video transmission, and apparently Asus has no plans to update).

I needed this adapter for my new Asus laptop (Win10), which came without an ethernet port or an hdmi port. The ethernet connection worked really well, I was getting full gigabit connectivity, with no detectable difference from a direct RJ45 connection.

The USB3 worked very well too: I hooked up an external SSD and was able to get high speed file transfers without any problems.

However, I was not able to get the HDMI connector to work at all. I looked for a missing driver on the TrippLite website, but didn't find anything. Without that, the device just didn't detect the monitor plugged into the HDMI port. Just to make sure, I tested the setup using another computer, and everything worked immediately, so I though the problem was this adapter. Turns out that it's actually a limitation on my Asus laptop's USB-C port. I fault TrippLite for making this a bit obscure and not being clear about the requirements, but that's all.

I did not test the charge port.

Given that an important feature doesn't work, I can't justify giving this adapter more than 3 stars. It's excellent (5 stars) for the two ports that I used and did work.

title: A MUST-HAVE for anyone with RF-blocking coated car windows
text:
Before:
I drive a car with the coating that blocks RF (and UV), so my (Android) phone kept losing its GPS reception. It was sometimes hilarious: Google Maps would think I was on the wrong side of the highway, and would give me directions for a u-turn, then would think I was on a side road, and get thoroughly confused. Sometimes it was frustrating, especially when I'd be looking for a detour around heavy traffic for instance.

After:
I installed the Bluetooth GPS app (it's excellent), paired the GLO, turned on the mock GPS provider, and ta-da! No more GPS tracking problems. Zip, nada. Travelling hundreds of miles up and down the East Coast, through the boonies, etc., no GPS problems. (It sometimes helps to download offline maps and directions, but that's easy.)

I was considering drastic solutions, but for what I consider a very reasonable price, I have a painless solution.

If you have an RF coated car, and like to use your phone for navigation, this is simply a must-have. Easy recommendation.

title: Excellent WAPs, but designed for technically sophisticated users
text:
For background: I don't have any affiliation with Ubiquiti, and I'm not a network engineer with inbuilt preferences or dislikes of networking equipment. I do have a lot of experience with all kinds of computing and networking technology.

For my relatively large house I've needed multiple wireless routers set up as wireless access points (WAPs), but over the years have gotten more and more frustrated with the limitations of this kind of setup. I could solve the signal distribution problem by setting up many WAPs, but I still had the problem that my devices wouldn't roam seamlessly from WAP to WAP as I moved around the house.

So this year I decided to look into a better solution. One option is a "mesh" solution like Eero, Orbi, or Google Home. Another option was to go with
wired WAPs, like these Unifi devices. After quite a bit of research, I decided to put my nickels down and try these "Pro" units. Why? Because I wanted (1) very strong wireless signals; (2) commercial grade manageability; (3) products already proved in the market, and favored by many experts; (4) products priced competitively.

I'm happy to report that after much tinkering and experimenting I'm absolutely delighted with these devices. I have three of them spread around the house, with a "Cloud Key" controller device (highly recommended) giving me management access from computer, tablet, or phone. I'm getting excellent bandwidth (usually at the max my phone/tablet will support), and trouble-free roaming. I'm able to see all relevant information, including interference information (from the pesky neighbors!) in the "console". I'm able to easily configure the networks, and updating the software and firmware is painlessly easy.

This is good stuff. Not for everyone, since you do have to be comfortable with technical details that would daunt the less experienced. But if you know how to set up your router/WAP, and either understand or are willing to learn about various networking details, then you might want to seriously consider Unifi access points.

I'm trying to decide whether I should buy two more AP-AC-PROs, or should save a bit of money and go with the Lites.

title: Excellent SSD for your PC
text:
SSD makers give us these benchmark numbers that aren't all that useful for most of us not using well-equipped computer labs. I mean, how would I even verify that an SSD can achieve 500+MB/s read/write speeds anyway? I'd be using a test program that does a lot of intensive (and synthetic i/o), perhaps? I don't see the point in that, I want to make sure it serves my usual purposes. That means fast bootup times, fast operation when running my usual programs (including especially web browsers), and so on.

Some background ... I've been using SSDs on my family's several computers for some years now, and have built a few computers using SSDs as the system drive. The performance improvement is quite dramatic, even a bit amazing at first. It helps a lot when doing local network file transfers or cloud uploads/downloads, and also helps with normal everyday use, especially game playing.

For this drive ... I had a 250GB Samsung 850EVO SSD in my computer, and had no problems with it. When I received this 500GB SanDisk SSD from the Vine program, I thought it might be handy to get a bit more space on the system drive, put some more frequently used files there, and so on. I used a handy USB3 to SATA adapter, plugged into the computer, then used Macrium Reflect Free to clone the C drive to the USB drive. (This will take some time, dependent on how much data you have, and the overall performance of your system.) Then I swapped the new drive in for the old one.

Result: I now had a larger C drive. Performance? About the same as with the Samsung SSD, no surprise. Here are some numbers: HD to SSD copy ~145MB/s; SSD to HD copy ~85MB/s; SSD internal file copy 100-170MB/s (varied widely probably because of other system load). What about those 500+MB/s numbers? I suspect I could get closer to those if I were writing to/from system memory, but I don't care. It's the real world performance that matters to me.

The SanDisk management software (SSDdashboard) is easy to find on their website, and easy to use. It checked and told me my firmware was upto date, and told me my drive was connecting optimally to my system. It didn't mention anything about my AHCI setting (which is important), where the Samsung Magician software tells you clearly whether AHCI is activated.

So overall a fine SSD for the money, does the job, makes no noise :-)

Final word: I don't know any reason, other than price, to pick a SanDisk over a Samsung. In fact, I don't know for sure that you lose much by going to the less expensive brands like Crucial and PNY. Read the "expert" reviews on the web and judge for yourself.

title: excellent wifi router, but AP mode has limitations
text:
This is an excellent wifi router, with good range and excellent connectivity. If I'm relatively near the router, my Samsung tablet will connect at 800+ Mbps. Even if I'm further away, with a couple of walls & rooms in-between, I get 200+. So all in all pretty good.

The user interface is clean, and easy to use. I find it better than that on an Asus router, and perhaps about as good as on a TPLink router. I had no trouble at all with the setup (except, see below about AP mode). Even if you're relatively new to router config, if you follow the instructions carefully you shouldn't have trouble.

The firmware update actually works (first router I can say that about!!), and does what it's supposed to, without hitch.

One note: they add an "AP mode" in the latest firmware, which didn't show up the documentation I was able to get from the Tenda website. Nice, I thought. The idea is that you're using the unit simply as a wifi broadcaster (i.e., a WAP, not a full router. However, in this mode much of the configuration vanishes, including the ability to specify a LAN IP address. I like to set a fixed address so that I can find the device on my networ easily, and log on from any computer. I think this is a design mistake. Anyway, I use it as a WAP, simply by not using the WAN port: I connect the wire from the main router to one of the LAN ports, use the other LAN ports for connecting other devices to the network, and everything's just fine. (The UI will warn you that the router isn't connected to the WAN, but you can ignore that in this mode of use.)

title: Mediocre: you can get better, much better, for your money
text:
This is an unremarkable USB drive, with unexciting performance, for an unattractive price. (That's pretty much it for the substance of the review.)

I do my tests on a pretty fast computer with tons of memory, and an SSD system drive, while I'm doing nothing else on the computer, so no system resource constraints should affect the results. I test writes from SSD to USB, and reads in the other direction. I also use a set of 2GB test files, so that I get true results (small files can give misleading results).

I saw writes to the USB drive going between 4.5 and 8 MB/s, which is really pretty slow. I can get 16+ consistently on a little Lexar 32GB drive I have lying around. And a quick look in Amazon shows that I can find much faster USB3 drives for a bit less or a bit more, promising about 5x the write performance.

Finally, the form factor is terrible. This is a big fat ugly drive, you can get higher capacity and much better performance in slim little drives, including nano-drive size products.

Bottom line, it's ok, but I can't recommend it.

title: Well-designed, easy to use, but no wired network
text:
The Roku Premiere player is easy to set up and has a well-designed user interface that requires no reference to a user manual. I connected it to the tv (using an HDMI cable), plugged it in, turned on the tv and selected the appropriate source. I was disappointed that there was no option to plug in a network cable for a wired connection (like there is for the Fire TV box; you have to go up to the Premiere+ to get that port). This might be a concern for anyone with a weak or problematic wifi signal.

The initialization was fairly simple: language selection, wifi connection (it supports AC as well as N), automatic detection of the tv display type, automatic software update, then a separate session on the computer to register the device and create a Roku account. I had another disappointment here: the account creation requires the entry of payment info, either credit card or Paypal. If I want to use the box just to watch my subscribed services, such as Netflix and Amazon, there's no reason for me to give Roku any payment information at all, it just increases the risk of malicious use. (If you really don't like this, you can sign up using a Paypal account, then go back into your Paypal account and rescind the Roku permissions.)

After that it was all plain sailing, and I had no complaints: streaming video was clear and glitch-free, the sound was good. All in all, a very nice streaming box for a reasonable price. For my money, however, I would consider upgrading to the Premiere+. Or, the Fire TV box, which is what I normally use at home.

title: Excellent 4-port USB3 hub, high data transfer rates.  Also charges, but with lower current.
text:
This is an excellent 4-port USB3 hub. I tested it with a couple of USB3 flash drives (sticks), and saw data transfers (from/to main SSD drive) in both directions to the limit of the drives (60-90 MB/s). I also tested with an external USB3 SSD drive, and saw transfers to the limit of that drive (150 MB/s write, 350MB/s read). Needless to say, I used good USB3 cables to connect.

I also tested charging my phone with the hub. This worked, but I did get a notification on the phone that it was charging slower than normal. I don't find this surprising, I think you'd charge directly from an outlet or from your computer, you wouldn't use the hub unless you really needed to do so. So ok for an emergency bit of charging.

I've used other StarTech hubs (and various other products), and have not been disappointed. If you need a solid USB3 hub, this one deserves consideration. But I always do price comparisons, since there are competitive products that are sometimes cheaper.

title: Very good 7-port USB 3.0 hub, works without problems
text:
This hub works quite well: I tested it with an external 1TB hard drive, as well as a 256GB flash drive. Using the flash drive, write speeds (from SSD out through USB) were about 170MB/s, read speeds were about twice that. I did have a little trouble at first, where the flash drive wasn't being recognized by Windows, but that cleared up, so perhaps was a transient driver issue.

I also tested whether I could charge my phone and my TomTom fitness watch, and both were successful, I didn't see any problems. The TomTom application on my computer also was triggered as expected.

Overall, I have no problems with the device, and can recommend it. I would however look at the price (it seems a bit high to me), and consider competitive products that might be available for less.

title: Excellent high performance high capacity flash drive
text:
This is a pretty amazing product: as much storage as a mid-sized SSD, in a compact usb drive. Even better, the read/write performance in my testing was much higher than I expected: doing SSD to/from USB3 file transfers on my computer, I saw 180MB/s write speeds to the stick, and read speeds of 375MB/s from the stick. That's way better than I've seen from my other USB3 flash drives.

Note however that the 256GB is a "marketing number" (probably obtained by using an incorrect definition of GB). My drive manager (on Windows) reports 235GB formatted (or 253.2 billion bytes if you want to count that way).

All in all, a really nice product that allows you to carry a small SSD in your pocket. I'd readily buy another if I could invent a need for it. (For this one, I'm thinking I'll encrypt the whole drive and carry all my important data when I'm travelling.)

title: Very nice bluetooth speaker that is really waterproof
text:
Summary: Very good waterproof bluetooth speakers that work as advertised, and better.

Firstly the sound is really very good, considering the size of this unit. It's loud enough, without distortion or other oddness -- quite suitable for using outdoors, at the beach, or even on a boat.

It really is waterproof, and does float without any trouble. After trying it out on the beach, I was confident enough to take it sailing (with the phone in a waterproof bag, of course), which was novel and amusing.

Charges fast, pairs easily, comes with a carabiner clip.

If you're looking for a small bt speaker to use with phone or tablet, and use near or in the water is important to you, this is definitely one to consider seriously.

title: Excellent sound, good in-ear fit (but not ideal comfort)
text:
Summary: Overall this is an excellent bluetooth headset for music and calls, with excellent sound. It's reasonably comfortable to wear, but I find the weighted behind-the-neck loose cord troublesome and leading to ear discomfort after some time.

Some specifics:
(1) Charges using a now-standard micro-usb port, makes it easy. Charges pretty quickly for hours of use.
(2) The sound is excellent for all kinds of music, including classical and rock. I've been using it to listen to music from my phone, and have really enjoyed the clear, undistorted and well-balanced sound. Definitely the best headset I've owned, except perhaps for my old pair of corded Sennheiser headphones.
(3) I found that the earbuds and retainers that came attached weren't quite right for me, but they thoughtfully include 3 sets of each. After a little trial and error, I was able to find the combination that worked well for me.
(4) I find that the control near the right ear are a bit harder to use than I like: I sometimes find myself taking the right earbud off to do something. They could have been positioned a bit further down, perhaps.
(5) There is a cylindrical weight in the middle of the cord, that I gather is supposed to go behind the neck. Except it's really annoying, keeps falling to one side or the other, pulling at one of the earbuds. When sitting I found it better to let it hang in front of me. This is the kind of design you get when you have a "great idea" and fail to test it thoroughly with a number of users.

So, while I do like these earbuds, I recommend them only with some reservations about the comfort and the fit.

title: Very good lower-priced SSD, but don't get the combo
text:
This is a great low-priced SSD option for upgrading a computer, or making a fast external usb drive. I did some performance testing using it as an external drive (I intend to use it as an upgrade drive for a family computer), and found the performance more than satisfactory. Using a USB3 adapter, the read-write performance with large files was comparable to my Samsung SSD (at probably half the price). Yes, the life is likely to be a bit lower, but should be good enough for normal household use. I have of course not had the time nor the resources to do extensive reliability testing.

The combo was initially nice to get, and it's a pleasure to see thoughtful inclusions like usb and sata cables. However, I think making the enclosure USB2 rather than USB3 was just a dumb idea (just to cut the price a few $). Might as well not bother, sell a good enclosure separately at a fair price, or let consumers get their own. Using it to transfer 150-200GB of data from a computer hard drive just became painfully long. I recommend getting just the drive and getting a competitor's USB3 enclosure or adapter.

title: Very well-made cable, works well for all the usual purposes
text:
Very well-made cable, works without problems. Slightly thicker than some others I have, but coils and uncoils nicely anyway.

The 10ft length is great for use in a car, and also for when you're on a couch with the power outlet at the other end.

The only minor criticism (or caution) I have is that the micro-usb end has a bulky housing. Makes it easier to handle, but also can get in the way with some phone/tablet cases that have only a small aperture for the socket.

title: Well made & sturdy, great product for reasonable price
text: Well made and sturdy bracket to install 2.5 inch drive (e.g., SSD) in a 3.5 inch bay -- I needed this to replace a hard drive with an SSD.  Great product for a very reasonable price -- they even included extra mounting screws, so the whole thing was very easy.  Can easily recommend if you need an adapter bracket.

title: Pretty good miniature flash drive, with useful free encryption program
text:
It's pretty amazing to me that you can pack so much data now in such a tiny drive. It's about the same size as my Logitech mouse "nano" receiver.

The drive capacity is almost exactly 32 billion bytes (that's really 29.8GB, not 32GB, but the marketers have defeated the engineers on this). For some reason it was connecting at USB2 on my front port, where other USB3 drives connect just fine. Once I got it connected on another port at USB3, I did see better behavior. However, file transfer speeds are limited by Windows (and perhaps my computer hardware) more than anything else. Even transferring to/from an internal SSD drive I didn't get sustained speeds over about 38MB/s (that's megabytes, not megabits). I've read tech journals that say that the smaller USB3 drives can't transfer at the same speeds as the super-duper larger ones, but for real-world file transfer (as opposed to lab benchmarks) it doesn't seem to matter. Suffice it to say that I get about 10x speeds on USB3 drives vs. USB2 drives, and this one works as well as my other USB3 drives.

The drive came with a basic file encryption program (you can download it from the Lexar website as well). This easy-to-use program encrypts files using AES-256 (more detail wasn't given); you can buy an upgraded version which allows upto AES-1024, and has a few other features. Each file you encrypt is stored in a separate folder hierarchy (labeled the Vault), there isn't a separate encrypted file system. It's probably secure enough for general consumer use, and is certainly a convenience making it easy to protect your data. There was a Windows version and an Apple version of the program, so I think it means that encrypted files can be shared with either type of system. Not being a Mac user, I couldn't verify this.

Overall, this is a very nice product for an attractively low price. There are 64GB and 128GB versions as well for those who need more storage.

title: Bad.  Unacceptably bad.
text:
Unacceptably bad. I rarely give 1-star reviews, I think the product has to fail basic function to deserve that. This one does.

I plugged it in to my laptop (which has tinny built-in speakers, as is rather common). I played a few pieces of music, and found the reproduction ok, but a bit scratchy, cloudy, and flat. (Yes, all three together.) The volume was weak, even when turned up to max. Then as I was looking for more music to try, I heard an ugly scratchy hiss, and thought my laptop's fan was acting up. Nope, it was the speakers. Yes, they produce a nasty noise when idle, and it doesn't go away, stays there so you can hear it under the music if you listen carefully.

To me that makes these speakers fail the basic test. Especially when you consider that you can get better speakers for about half the money, and a whole lot better for similar money, these are just unacceptable. Therefore the 1star rating.

(In case you would like a recommendation: I have a pair of Altec Lansing speakers that I think are really very good for desktop computer speakers, with rich clear well-balanced sound.)

title: Pretty nice, but low-powered, so make sure it fits your needs
text:
This is a nice little kit for a rather low-end computer. USB3 ports, and great wired/wireless networking built in, easy to set up, at a great price point. But be aware that it doesn't have a lot of horsepower, it'll run out of oomph pretty quickly. Some details to explain what I mean ...

I put mine together with an 8GB memory card and a 120GB SSD, to use as a low-end streaming/playing device to play music from the web (e.g., Amazon & Google music) on my stereo. Installed Ubuntu 15.10 (beta for now, to be released in about a week), so not a lot of OS overhead (compared to Windows). Playing music from mp3 files (using Audacious) works just fine. Playing music from Amazon Prime uses a bit more juice, but still well within the system's capabilities (around 40% cpu). Now if I run TeamViewer to do a bit of remote control, that pushes the cpu to its limits, we're now at around 90%. (Memory use still low, no swapping, no other issues.)

So I'd definitely go with the Core-i3 version (or better), for about a $100 more, if I were planning to do more on the box. But this is certainly more than good enough for lightweight computing tasks -- heck, it's better than the overheating 8-year old Pentium-powered laptop it replaced!

title: Doesn't quite do the job (doesn't fit TabS)
text:
Nah, doesn't really fit the Tab S. Not even with vigorous stretching of the corners. (Reminds me of the story of Procrustes.) Since I got it for my TabS, I obviously can't recommend it. It might work for the TabS2, which is slightly shorter than the TabS. But even today the headline on the product page says "Compatible with Galaxy Tab S 8.4" -- compatible how, exactly?

It seems well made. That's about it. I don't like the design of the cover too much. Basically your tablet is held by four elastic straps at the corners, with a stiff short brace on the right. It's hard to get it in (not impossible if it's a bit shorter than a TabS perhaps), hard to get it out, and after all that it's not all that comfortable to hold.

The one I'm using (from Wawo on Amazon) holds the tablet securely, has a strap in the back for holding while you're using the tablet, as well as notches for propping up on the table in front if you so desire. It's well-designed, but somewhat sloppy in construction, which is why I was looking for an alternative. Sadly, this Belkin isn't a good one for the purpose.

title: ok, but consider other options
text:
It does the job, and I have a fairly powerful and functional computer, but on consideration I think I should have considered some of the alternatives instead.

The most frustrating problem has been unaccounted for behavior with Windows 7, apparently related to the mobo. For instance, wake from sleep consistently crashes the computer (I checked the dumps to verify that it was definitely a wake-related crash), and there is (as yet) no bios or driver update to fix it. Ok, sleep isn't that important, I can live without it. But sometimes a simple reboot will hang, apparently in the same place, right when Windows should be booting up. A forced shutdown (holding the power button for several seconds) and restart fixes that problem. But neither of these is really expected, or acceptable.

A lesser problem is the sound -- somehow it's tinny, sounds worse than the audio on my 5-year old mid-range computer. I'm probably going to buy an audio card, which shouldn't have been necessary.

The onboard networking is just fine, I haven't had any problems with it. The onboard video is ok as well, but I didn't test that too much since I added a separate video card.

I think I should have gone with MSI or Asus instead, and that's what I'm going to look at when my son & I build a mid-price gaming rig for him later this fall.

title: does the job but isn't spectacular
text:
This case was recommended in several build guides, and seemed to be highly rated on Amazon, but I must say I'm quite disappointed.

Pros:
(1) It does the job. It's roomy -- in fact, it's really big. There's room for a really big graphics card without taking out any drive cages.
(2) Comes with four quiet fans (2 intakes in front, one large intake on the side, one exhaust on the back), and room to add more on the top.
(3) Having a couple of usb3 ports and audio/mike ports in the front is very convenient. Having the power supply at the bottom (in the back) also worked well for me.
(4) All the bits come apart and back together without too much trouble.

Cons:
(1) I had a lot of trouble getting my EVGA power supply to install, because the screw holes didn't line up nicely. Finally managed it by using a combination of power and adapting to what the case gave me.
(2) The 5.25 drive bays go in the conventional way, with the backs near the mobo for easy connections. But the 2.5/3.5 drive bays go in sideways, which might seem convenient at first, but now you have their connectors on the other side of the box -- so you're threading your power and sata cables around, and creating a bulge of cables etc. And that extra wiring room that the case promises? It doesn't extend all the way to the front, apparently the artists overcame the engineers (or they fought and the users lost). This arrangement also means that it's harder to share your sata power cables, depending on what you're trying to do with your setup.
(3) As others have pointed out, those nice intake fans aren't standard, they would be hard to replace individually. I'd have to replace all of them with standard case fans, I think.
(4) I wasn't as impressed with the cable management as many others were -- while it was useful to be able to run some wires on the back, that also made some of the shorter ones trickier to connect. Also, I find it easiest to place the box down on the side to work on the inside. Having to flip it over or keep it standing vertical wasn't my idea of convenience during assembly, and it made things really tricky when I wanted to add another hdd.

Neutral:
(1) An inexpensive mini-speaker (for POST beeps) would have been a good idea to include with the box.

All in all, I'm not unhappy enough to curse it, but I'm also far from recommending it. I'd look around more the next time, so 3* seems about right.

title: Useful backup power for phones/tablets and such
text:
This is a handy little item if you need power backup for a phone or tablet, when you expect to have an extended period away from a power source. I'm planning to carry it with me when travelling, for example, and it might be handy on a hike as well.

I plugged in my regular micro-usb phone charger (the specs call for 2.1A at 5V) to fully charge it. Then I tested it on a phone (Samsung S4) and a tablet (Tab S), and found the results quite satisfactory. The specs say that the two USB ports will provide 2.4A at 5V simultaneously, and I was certainly able to charge my two devices at the same time without problems.

There's some discussion in the instructions about "smart charging", but I can't verify if that makes any real difference. (The idea seems to be that you can tell the charger to dialog with your device to select an optimal charge profile. Nice idea, but I didn't see a difference after I did what they asked. Maybe it was optimal already ...)

The flashlight is a nice touch, but I don't know that I'd ever use it. I'd carry a flashlight if I think I might one, rather than depending on one charger to provide backup power as well as a light source.

Finally, the charger is well-made, and compact in design. Easy to slip into a backpack for instance. One important limitation to keep in mind: you will probably need to carry a separate USB-microUSB cord (I have a 1 foot cord I use), because the cord that comes with it has a fat rubberized head, making it impossible to fit into some recessed charging slots (such as my tablet when it's inside a case).

title: Nice case, but not a clear winner
text:
Here's the bottom line: I compared this case with the Amazon Basics case, and frankly found the latter to be comparable or even slightly better (at a much lower price).

This is a pretty nice case for a DSLR wearing a zoom lens. I have a Nikon D5300 which I usually pack with a 18-200mm zoom lens on it, and have found the Amazon case to be satisfactory for holding the camera+zoom and the lens hood in the main compartment, and the battery charger and of course a spare chip in the side pckets. There's room in a side pocket to carry a small card reader if I want to bring that as well.

The Case Logic case is very similar, and if I had gotten it first I would probably have been quite satisfied. However, I found that the suspension "hammock" for the camera didn't work quite as well in practice as it does in theory. The camera isn't symmetric of course, and more of it seems to slip through the hole than is intended, and it lies in it at an angle. I also found that I couldn't quite as easily put the lens hood on top as I have gotten used to doing with the Amazon case.

Otherwise, this is well made, with sturdy looking and smoothly functioning zippers, robust strap & handle, and functional side pockets. Certainly a good product, you won't regret buying this case, other than possible regret over the price paid. (Note that I haven't owned the cases long enough to comment on any durability differences.)

title: Ok, but tinny sounding, which becomes annoying quickly
text: They're ok for basic use perhaps.  Perhaps.  But they're really quite tinny sounding, and I quickly find it painful to listen to music playing through these speakers. To be clear, I'm not expecting the performance of my home stereo, I'm just comparing them to my other computer speakers -- they're much better.  So if you have a sensitive ear, you might wish to spend a bit more money and get a nicer pair.

title: Nice case for a 7 inch Garmin GPS  (and similar items)
text: Very nice case for a large Garmin GPS -- well padded, well constructed, handy outside pocket.  Good to have when you want to carry your GPS unit around -- I do that when I rent a car, for instance, saves me a lot of hassle.

title: a very nice option for the ipad air 2 if you want an always-attached keyboard
text:
I've been using this keyboard for about a week now, and haven't found any flaws yet. It just works as expected. I can imagine a few improvements, but this is really a 4.5+ star product.

Pairing was dead simple. The ipad was simple to fit in to the back, and stays securely inside. Folding in and out (or z-fold) is also about what you'd expect, no nasty surprises. And when you're typing, you once again get just what you expect from a keyboard. I find the touch and responsiveness to be pretty good -- the only trouble I have is adjusting to such a small keyboard, but that's also to be expected, it's not a flaw in the product. The various function keys at the top of the keyboard are pretty handy as well.

I haven't tried the feature that allows you to charge your phone from the keyboard's battery, I don't need it. But it's a nice idea.

Very minor criticisms: (1) It should have come with its own charge adapter, not just cables. (2) A way to carry a stylus might have been nice. (3) A visual charge level indicator would be helpful (not just the led). (4) In the z-fold mode, it's not the most comfortable thing to hold in your hands -- maybe a way to detach the top would have been better.

title: Very nice SSD at reasonable price, but for a bit more you can get better
text:
This is a very good lower-end SSD, with basic capabilities and in-range performance, but for just a few dollars more you can get the MX100, and for a bit more than that you can get the Samsung 850 EVO, which are a bit better. Not that there's anything wrong with this one: I found that this drive performs as advertised, and if you don't need drive encryption or the "write acceleration" (cache-based performance improvement), this might be just the thing you need if you don't want to pay any more than you have to. I've used the Samsung drives in the past, and have found the management software (Samsung Magician) to be very useful. Crucial's Storage Executive doesn't really come close.

Quick background: Converting your computer to run from an SSD instead of a normal rotating hard-drive will definitely give you a Wow! level performance improvement. If you're reasonably technical, there are several guides to be found on the web that will help. I would recommend using Macrium Reflect to do the drive cloning (much better than Samsung's software for this purpose), and Defraggler to defrag your hard drive before cloning if needed.

title: very nice option for an ipad air 2, at a reasonable price
text:
I've been pleased with the CaseCrown cases for the various Kindles I own, so decided to get this one for my iPad Air 2. It's well made, and fits the ipad very nicely. I had a little trouble with the little flap that needs to fold under the ipad (after it's been inserted) and then be attached to the bottom with velcro -- but with a bit of trial and error I got it in snugly, and have had no problem since.

It's nearly perfect for my daily use, and I have only two minor criticisms.
(1) The case looks a little askew, as if the pieces weren't cut exactly right. Makes finding the power button a teeny bit more work. But it's a minor defect. No other problems with the various ports and buttons, they're all easily accessible.
(2) The triangle "stand" position I make with the front folded back and pushed into a little flap on the back, requires a little fiddling, and doesn't always sit quite right. Making the flap a bit wider & deeper might have helped.

Finally, the wakeup/sleep function for the ipad works just fine, I've not had any problems with it.

Unless you're willing to pay up a lot more (I wasn't), this is a very fine option.

title: ok, but not really a tablet case
text:
Reasonably well-constructed, multiple slanted pockets for gadgets & "stuff". Apparently sized for paper files/folders, not for tablets -- I suspect that some re-labeling is going on here. It's not particularly well-suited to anything: it's too big for a tablet, there aren't any slots for pens, no hook for keys, no nicely-sized and placed pocket for a phone. And no strap at all, where a hand-strap might have been useful. The padding could have been better. Also, somewhat cheap look and feel.

I don't think I'd buy one of these: I'd either get an Amazon Basics tablet case if I were looking for something inexpensive (I have one of those, and use it all the time), or I'd pay up and get a nicer case to fit exactly what I need.

title: Quite good, but not perfect
text:
(Note: this review is the the enclosure specifically for the 7mm drives.)

I wish it had screws to hold the drive firmly, and insertion was a bit easier. But it does work, and seems to hold the slim drive securely. After that, connection/operation with the computer is as expected, nothing much to report there.

title: It works, but loose drive is unacceptable
text:
Unfortunately, the weakest part of this enclosure is the drive housing: it's a (relatively flimsy) open plastic box-frame, without any screws or other way of holding a drive firmly. So you slide your drive's contacts into the drive socket, then let the drive drop into the frame. Now you slide the frame into the cover, and you have a nice rattling portable drive. Just not acceptable in my view: I've used many 2.5in drive enclosures for drives recovered from retired computers, and not a single one of them is like this.

Mine is going back, and I don't recommend a purchase. Guess Sabrent is going on my "don't buy" brand list.

title: good hardware, terrible migration software
text:
The drive delivers on the SSD promise: very fast access times, even on an older computer supporting SATA1 only. The computer boots up so fast it reminds me of old days before operating systems became so bloated. (Yes, I'm talking pre-history.)

However, as others have noted, the software supplied with it for migration is just terrible, it only works if everything is perfect. And the instructions and error messages are completely inadequate (mostly missing, really).

I wanted to do more than complain, however. I figured I'd share some experience and some tips, that might help another user.

My existing disk was a 1TB hard drive that had some bad sectors (hence my desire to replace). I removed enough data from it to reduce the usage down to about 160GB, figuring that was good for a 250MB destination disk. Then I tried the Samsung cloning software. Many times. It kept failing, sometimes early, often after a few hours. With no useful information (unless you count obscure error codes that are not documented to be information). I tried running disk defrag, achieved no useful result, other than a failure after the cloning reported 100% complete. Deeply frustrating.

I couldn't do a system image restore, because Windows (Microsoft is another producer of dumb and unfriendly software) will only do a restore to a disk of the same configuration. (Here the message is simply that it "can't find a suitable disk", you have to hunt to figure out why.) And I wasn't about to buy a 1TB flash drive.

And I wanted to give it one good try before settling for reinstalling from scratch, because I didn't want to spend several more days getting my computer back to where it was.

Solution: I highly recommend using defraggler (from Piriform) to clean up your disk. You might also find it useful to shrink your partition to the minimum possible, using the WIndows disk management tool. Then I highly recommend using the Macrium Reflect Free Edition to do an "intelligent" clone of your OS volume to the SSD.

After I did this, everything worked perfectly, no problems. Wish I'd known about these tools and all the gotchas ahead of time.

Another tip: If you want to set AHCI in the BIOS (yes, now I'm getting to advanced users), you may need to first enable the AHCI drivers, otherwise Windows will not boot up (you'll get a BSOD). Do a search for this, there's a Microsoft KB article.

Good luck!

title: works like a charm
text: Works well with Lenovo W-series laptop (to Samsung monitor, but that shouldn't matter), no issues at all.  Fits snugly in computer port, HDMI cable fits fine into the adapter.  Will also use for connecting to tv, will report if any problems, but I'm not expecting any.

title: good design, but looks and feels cheap
text:
My first impressions of this are captured in the headline, and further investigation reinforced that impression. The design is good, similar to other backpacks of this type: several commodious compartments, including a padded laptop compartment. There are outside mesh pockets for water bottles, a top pocket for a phone or ipod, many-pocketed front compartment for pens and cards and such. All good.

However, in comparison with a backpack that I would say is "nearly perfect" (for example, an LLBean backpack I bought some years ago), this just fails to meet the mark, even making some allowances for the lower price. The back feels like it's stiffened with cardboard, and sounds that way too. The inner material rustles like paper (it really does), which I find oddly unpleasant. The whole thing has this "cheapo backpack" look and feel, and reduces both my liking of and my trust in it. I think Amazon would have done better charging $10-15 more and delivering a much nicer pack.

I'd use it if I were desperate, but I'll probably keep it as a spare (and eventually give it away), and continue using my old one for a while longer.

title: excellent fire case for small money (and no smell)
text:
I didn't like the idea of spending $45 or more for a kindle fire case, so looked for casecrown, since their case for the old kindle was good value for the money. I was a little wary because of several reviews reporting a problem with the chemical smell that you get from certain plastics.

However, I'm delighted with the case. There was no stink at all, not even the moderate one that I might have expected to last a few hours. The case fits well, appears to be constructed properly, and works just as described.

If you're looking for something inexpensive to protect your fire, this is definitely something you ought to consider.

title: great monitor, but HDMI-HDMI connection didn't work for me
text:
I like ViewSonic monitors, and have been very pleased with the 2431 I've been using. So I decided to get a larger one, and opted for the 2730mh, in order to get the hdmi input (the similar 2703 has only dvi).

However, I found that with my Windows7x64 machine, the display just didn't work right when using hdmi-hdmi, the display was fuzzy and the screen didn't fully cover the lcd panel.

It looks wonderful with dvi input (hdmi-dvi or dvi-dvi worked equally well), so I'm inclined to think that it's a driver problem. The latest driver didn't make any difference. (However, if the hdmi input worked for some people on Windows 7x64, then of course I must have received a defective item.)

Given that I paid about $30 extra just for the HDMI input, which apparently hasn't been well tested, I'm not delighted. I'll still consider other VS monitors, since they often represent good value for money, but perhaps avoiding the newest products is wise.

title: excellent cooling pad with large quiet fan
text:
I've tried many similar products, and most of them range from bad to horrible. In fact I recently returned one that had fallen apart during shipping (although it had been well-packaged). I have another one from a different brand (Monoprice), that has been quite satisfactory, having kept a hot-running notebook in good shape for more than a year.

Having had to "borrow" that one for another feverish computer, I needed another one, and after some hunting found this on Amazon. It has now been running for 10 days or so under an older 13 inch notebook that runs really hot, and has been doing a great job.

The pad appears to be solidly made, with no rattles or squeaks. The metal mesh top and well-vented plastic bottom provides plenty of ventilation -- it might actually do a great job even without a fan -- which is what you want to see. The large fan runs silently but moves quite a good volume of air (you can check the specs if you care about numbers).

Note that the USB plug provides a USB port, so you don't lose one by using this. Doesn't matter to me, but might to some users.

All in all, a good product I can happily recommend.

title: very nice headset, excellent sound
text:
I've used this headset quite a bit over the last few weeks, for work-related conference calls. Although I really like my tiny BlueAnt headset for casual use, I find myself reaching for this one for the ease-of-use convenience and better sound.

Firstly, the setup and the usage is quite well designed, as simple as it could be. I was suspicious of the voice prompts & messages ("phone connected", "answering call", etc.), but have found them quite useful and not at all intrusive.

I find the cord attaching the control pod (has on/off, volume control, and mute button) is a bit too long for my tastes, but some might need a longer one, so can't complain. The controls themselves are very useful to have where you can see them, you don't have to try to find something behind your ear to manipulate while you're on a call.

The sound is excellent: what I hear is always very clear. What others hear, whether I'm in a somewhat noisy room, or in a car, is also reported to be very clear, I've never had to raise my voice or repeat myself. BTW, the mic boom swivels out of the way easily when needed.

I'd give it 4.5 stars perhaps, with half a star off for my personal discomfort with a large-ish earpad (makes my ear hot after a while). But that's nit-picking, and probably won't bother many people.

title: well-made, attractive case, suitable for travel or everyday use
text:
This is a well-designed case, with the kind of detail that reflects attention to how someone might actually use it. For instance, there's an outside sleeve on the back, where I might stow a paperback or kindle and my boarding pass or train ticket. There's a small zippered pocket on the front flap where I might stow my phone or my subway pass. Inside, there's a padded compartment (10in wide), designed for a tablet, and a larger compartment (12in wide) for other items (such as books). Under the flap there's a zippered comparment which can hold pens, cards, a phone, and other items of similar size.

Note the size, however: this isn't a briefcase, or even a larger messenger bag. If you're looking for something to carry several accessories (such as a power cable with a brick, or even the iPad extender cable), then this might not be what you want, I'd suggest something more like a small laptop bag or backpack.

But if you want something relatively small to carry your tablet or ebook reader, and a few personal items, then you might find this just what you need. I have another small messenger bag that I've found very useful when I've wanted something bigger than my pockets but smaller than my briefcase.

Finally, the case appears to be well-constructed, of a durable material. I've had good results with Case Logic products in the past.

title: good cable, reasonable price
text:
Well-made audio cable with gold contacts, does improve the sound over cheaper cables. I used it to connect a computer to my stereo (e.g., to listen to Pandora), and the sound was definitely clearer and brighter with this one than with the cheaper cable I'd used before (because that's what I had on hand).

One thing to note: my RCA plugs had very tight sleeves, so I was having trouble getting them on/off, and was worried about breaking the ports on the amp. I took a pair of small needlenose pliers, and gently stretched out the insides just a tad (there are six segments on the circular sleeve, so you need to do this in 3 places around the circle). After that it still fit snugly, but was no longer an effort needing a lot of muscle.

As others have pointed out, paying ridiculous prices for such cables is silly, they're mostly the same quality hardware with a lot more marketing. This price point is just about right in my opinion.

title: great cable, but you can get them elsewhere for less (maybe)
text:
These are really great cables. I used one to connect from the analog audio output of the tv to a stereo amp, to get better sound out of much better speakers. And the results were really good. So if you need a 3.5 to RCA cable, these are among the best you'll find (I've tried others).

HOWEVER ...

The manufacturer name on the packaging was Monoprice -- in case you don't know them they're well known for low-priced good cabling and electronic components. I often buy direct from Monoprice, so went there to check on the price, and of course it's a lot less. But their shipping cost can be high, so depending on how much you're buying, it might be cheaper to get free shipping from Amazon, or pay Monoprice for shipping.

It pays to shop around, but also keep in mind that Amazon's service is excellent, even when you're buying from a third party.

title: the best mouse & keyboard for the money
text:
I have several of the Logitech M510, and think this is the best general purpose mouse you can buy. It's comfortable in the hand -- I have a large hand, some in the family have larger hands, some have smaller hands, but everyone finds the mouse comfortable to use. It's precise, easy to configure, and I'm very fond of the tiny usb adapter.

I particularly like the fact that you only need use one usb adapter for multiple devices (the "unifying receiver"). In fact you can switch between different Logitech mice if you need to do so (e.g., for a portable).

As for the keyboard, I was a little wary of the "wave" shape, not having used one before, and having some mild carpal tunnel issues. But to my relief, the keyboard is really comfortable to use, the wrist rest is well placed, provides support just where I need it. The keys have a nice touch, not too light, not too heavy, so perfect for me. There are a number of programmable buttons on the keyboard, most of which I tend to use only occasionally, mostly because I forget I have them. But the volume control is very useful, as is the button to bring up the calculator.

Do make sure you install the Logitech SetPoint software (you can download from their website) to properly configure the devices. You'll need that to make good use of the unifying receiver, among other things.

So if you're looking for a good mouse keyboard combo, I can happily recommend this set. If you just want one or the other, I still recommend the M510 mouse, and one of the many Logitech wireless keyboards that you can buy separately. (For instance, I also have the K270 keyboard, and find it to be quite good.)

title: Excellent BD player, no frills
text:
If you're looking for a BluRay player, and don't need 3D capabilities or a web browser, then this just might be the best buy available. As another reviewer has observed, it's the best player in this price range. I'm giving it 5* because picking some nits for something this good at this price just seems unreasonable.

I've been very pleased with my Samsung TVs and BD players, they have proved to be excellent in video and sound quality (which to me is 90% of the evaluation). I bought this one to replace an older Sony BD player that was getting cranky with newer disks (even after updating). With this unit after I plugged in HDMI, ethernet cable, and power, it automatically turned itself (& the tv) on, and presented a simple configuration screen, and followed with an online update. After that, it was a pleasure to sit back and enjoy a movie.

I cannot honestly tell you that the picture from this was better than the one from my 2 year old Samsung BD-C6500 player, If there were any differences, they didn't jump out at me. The box itself is smaller and lighter, and instead of LED controls, this one has little buttons. Although those LED controls are cool-looking, I have to admit that these clunky buttons are a lot easier to find and use. The remote is smaller as well, and comes with Netflix & Pandora buttons (I don't like that, but others might).

I didn't test the streaming features, and probably never will, since my TV has streaming capability as well, and I tend not to use streaming that much.

I like the way the Samsung BD players integrate with the Samsung TVs, automatically turning on/off, and setting the optimal picture settings. I wouldn't buy them just for that, but it's a nice plus.

title: excellent wireless keyboard, Unifying nano receiver is wonderful
text:
Firstly, unless you care about the design, look for other versions of the K360 -- I saw another one on Amazon for quite a bit less. If you're like me, you care about the electronics and the functional quality, not the "skin". That said, the "ink gear" design is just fine.

Anyway, if you're looking for a good, inexpensive wireless keyboard, I'd suggest that you look at Logitech. I've learned over the years to rely on the Logitech mice and keyboards, and have never been disappointed. (Yes, I mean "never".)

This keyboard is a reasonable size, comfortable for a touch typist. It has a light touch with good tactile feedback. Both my wife and I find it very easy to use, so it does seem to suit our different hand sizes and preferences.

Finally, I do like the Logitech "nano" receiver, tiny enough to leave on a laptop when packed. And the "Unifying" nano receiver is even better, since you need just one of them to connect with your mouse and your keyboard.

Technical Note: I already had a mouse with the Unifying receiver, on a Windows Vista machine. After connecting the keyboard I was able to use it, but needed to recycle the SetPoint app (icon shows in the Windows notification area) to see the keyboard control panel in the app and adjust the settings.

title: works the way intended, great solution
text:
This is an excellent solution for sharing a single 8-wire ethernet cable for two 100 megabit ethernet connections. (Note: Does NOT work for gigabit, see below !!) If you use this correctly, it works just fine. My minor complaint is the price: $10 each seems high, makes a single application $20. Now you're getting in the range of a basic ethernet switch. So I took off one star for that.

Admittedly, the description here, and the lack of documentation with the product, makes it hard for the less technical person to figure out how to use it. So I'll repeat the explanation some others have provided. Hope this helps.

An ethernet cable (cat5, cat5e, cat6, etc.) has 8 wires. For a 100 megabit connection (normal "fast ethernet"), only 4 of the 8 wires are used, in a specific pattern. Therefore it is possible for a special device to take an incoming 2nd signal and re-route it to run on the unused 4 wires, but at the receiving end this 2nd signal needs to be re-connected in reverse to go to the right pattern in a jack, in order for it to be received correctly. This splitter combiner does exactly this, so you need two of them. You get one of these devices, connect two separate 100Mb lines in to the two female sockets on the sending side, then plug in the male end into the wall, so both signals are travelling on the single cable, side by side. (For example, the two incoming cables could be coming out of two separate ports on your ethernet switch/router.) At the other end, you connect the male end of another of these devices to the wall, and connect two separate cables to the two female sockets, and now you have a single cable in the wall doing the job of two 100Mb cables.

If you run into a problem, patiently check to make sure that your connections are all correct, don't immediately blame the devices. For example, make sure that the connections work when you're not using the splitters.

I used these to connect a tv and a bluray player to my switch, through a single cable in the wall. The alternative I considered was to place an ethernet switch to connect the two, but that seemed overkill, since these probably don't have gigabit ports, and streaming throughput is limited by the ISP bandwidth anyway.

title: be wary of this one
text:
I had trouble with this chip in a Lenovo X220i -- the specs say it's a compatible chip (Kingston says it's equivalent to the item Lenovo will sell you). However, the OS became unstable, kept crashing with memory errors in different places. Probably a defective chip, but that might say something about Kingston's quality control.

I've replaced or added memory chips many times in the last decade or so, using chips from different manufacturers. Never had a problem until now, so I am now wary of Kingston. Might have been a random event, perhaps it could have happened with any other brand. But now I'm going to avoid buying Kingston chips.

(In case it matters: I bought the item through Amazon, but from another seller, AntOnline.)

title: excellent sound
text:
4.5 stars -- see below.

These headphones have excellent sound, as good as or better than a more expensive headset I have. If you line in-ear headphones, these are definitely worth your consideration. I use them with my computer and my ipod and my Droid, find them quite satisfactory -- I've stopped using my other headphone.

The reason I docked a star (should really be half) is that the default earpieces were not comfortable for me. I don't know if that's just my ear -- but they just felt wrong, even apart from the size. I changed them out for another pair (several are provided), and happiness was restored.

title: very useful device for backing up data (or taking it with you)
text:
Although USB3 devices are not common, that's no reason to avoid this little gadget. Firstly, you can use it directly with a USB2 port, you'll get USB2 speeds. But even better, it comes with a y-cable for use with a pair of USB2 ports, which gives you much higher speeds. They advertise 30MB, but the best I saw was 21MB. Still, very good when you're copying tons of data.

Only concern I have is that it seems to get very warm, so I worry about leaving it plugged in for a long period.

title: best non-3D LCD HDTV on the market now
text:
As others have observed, the picture quality is stunningly good. I watched a BluRay disk of "Life" (which I also highly recommend), and was surprised by the quality of the picture, it was just that good. I think you'd have to pay at least 2x to get a comparable value in a 3D tv.

I also use the tv to watch Netflix streaming video, and find it quite satisfactory.

However, I can cavil about the too-many Samsung apps, and the visual clutter of the presentation. The user interface with the clumsily-designed remote is not what you expect in 2010, but tv makers seem to have gotten stuck in a rut there.

Further, I suspect that setting everything up correctly can be a challenge for the less technically inclined (suggest you get some help, you will enjoy the tv more).

But my rating is about my expectations and my experience, and so far I have nothing to complain about. Hence the highest rating.

[...]

title: excellent LCD tv for a great price
text:
I expected good, but this tv is astoundingly good. especially for something in this price range. It's way better than my old Sony Bravia -- beautiful clear & bright picture and good sound.

I was considering a new LED TV, but decided they were overpriced right now, looked for a very good LCD tv that had decent internet capabilities. When considering price-to-value, I don't think you can do better than this model. Whether watching DVD (with upconverting player to get 1080p), BluRay, or streaming video, I am very pleased with what I get on the screen.

I would highly recommend this tv if you're looking to upgrade but want to stay away from the multiple $1000 range.

title: good memory unit for Brother MFC-9120CN printer
text:
The Brother printer is shipped with 64MB memory, and has a slot for additional memory (make sure you check the specs carefully for your printer). Adding memory can help avoid problems with large & complex documents, and in most cases will also speed up the printing. I chose to add 256MB rather than 512MB, since my guess is that 256MB is sufficient for the kinds of things I'm likely to do at home, and it saves me a few dollars. Also, the spec asks for CL2, and the 512MB was CL3 (slightly slower).

I chose Crucial because I've been happy with their memory cards in previous uses, and I'm suspicious of the cheaper no-brand parts. It's a fair price for a good product.

Installing the memory was easy, and the printer recognized it immediately. Not much more to say, since I didn't go through detailed performance comparisons with & without the memory, etc.

title: good replacement psu, but may need sata cable extender
text:
I got this to replace the PSU for a Dell E521 (about 3 years old, psu started making a nasty noise). The power rating for the original is 305W, so this one at 460W is more than adequate. (An online calculator suggested that I needed 365W.)

I would describe myself as relatively inexperienced at doing this sort of thing: I've replaced cards & memory & floppy/cd drives, but this was the first time replacing a PSU.

Removing the old unit and attaching this one inside the box was easy (just needed a philips screwdriver). The connections were mostly easy, but presented two challenges, one minor, one major: (1) The motherboard connector (P1) for the old one was a one piece unit, this one had two pieces, so I had to make sure I was connecting them correctly. (2) There is a single SATA cable, with three connectors, but my cd drive and hard drive were far enough apart in the box that I could not connect them both. Solution I'm going to try is a SATA y-cable (essentially an extender) from monoprice.com. I'll post an update about this once it's done. (BTW, I highly recommend monoprice for anything they carry: ethernet cables/connectors, parts, network adapters, etc. etc.)

Once I had it all in there, I plugged the computer in and started it up: everything worked fine, and the PSU was delightfully quiet. So far so good -- I'll post updates if I run into any problems over the next year.

title: excellent and compact usb drive
text:
You get 320GB of storage in something roughly the size of a trifold wallet (actually, my wallet is thicker). Comes in a rubber cover that feels quite durable -- but I didn't test by dropping it ... :-)

Copy-in speed from my laptop was about 18MB/sec; copy-out speed was about 26MB/sec. I find both quite satisfactory.

Also comes with some software, which I don't care about, and did not use.

I also did not test the Turbo USB software; some reviews I've read say that the speed increase can be abour 25%. But there wasn't enough technical information provided about compatibility for me to feel comfortable installing it. I think this is a deficiency, but I'm not rating the software, just rating the drive as an external drive, so not docking any points for this.

I like this enough that I might get another, I can think of many uses. I have other external drives, but the compact size is the winner here.

title: updated: works well, no problems
text:
I got the newer variant of this (last 3 characters in model name are 20U not 10U), which is supposed to be the same except for more power for the T5xx series. (Lenovo website says both are compatible with my Lenovo T410 computer.)

I thought I had a serious problem because the ethernet port simply would not connect. But I've since figured out that it had to do with some configuration problems on our office network (I won't go into details here, but they were obscure).

The minor problem I find is that the sound seems muted, but I am not worrying too much about that.

So no issues: buy one if you have a compatible system. (Check compatibility on the Lenovo website.)

title: excellent basic keyboard
text:
Especially for this price, this is an excellent keyboard. (I don't get what some of the negative reviewers are complaining about, unless their reviews are misplaced, are really for a different product.)

It's quiet, it has a good feel, is easy to use. You plug it in, Windows & Logitech do the rest. You type away happily. I don't expect much more from a basic keyboard.

No it doesn't make the coffee or automatically type my thoughts for me. So maybe I should dock it a few stars.

title: excellent bluetooth headset, good sound, nice multi-phone feature
text:
This is an excellent headset -- I have to say that I'm puzzled by all the negative reviews. (Which did make me hesitate for a bit.)

The pairing works, and easily, and the first time. I paired it with my Samsung Renown, and my iPhone GS, and now when I turn on the headset, it pairs up with both phones (as promised), answers whichever one is ringing or connects with the one being used for a call.

The sound is clear at both ends, without any of the ugly distortions you sometimes get with such devices.

I like it, am happy with the purchase, and consider it a great value at under $40. I continue to be happy with every BlueAnt product I've acquired.

title: ridiculous price for such a limited product
text:
This is best thought of as a very limited small computer with restricted functionality. You can use it to get news, see photo slideshows, some webcams (National Zoo was fun for a few minutes), or listen to mp3 music.

BUT, I don't recommend it.

There are many things wrong with it: (1) Comes with 128MB memory, you have to use an add-on memory card to do anything useful with pictures or music. 128MB?! Might have cost them $4 extra to add about 4GB. (I bought an 8GB sd chip(2) The screen is surprisingly poor -- pictures that look bright and sharp on a good LCD look fuzzy and dull on this. (3) The speakers are simply horrible, no other word for it. They sound harsh, distorted, and range-limited.

So save the money, put it towards a nice basic notebook, you'll get something 100x better for about 3x the price.

title: surprisingly quiet, and also surprisingly effective
text:
I had low expectations for this, since I haven't had great experience with cooling pads. They only sort-of work in terms of heat dissipation, and tend to be noisy (or become noisy as the parts wear in).

This one has so far been a very surprising change from the past. It's very quiet, I'm not sure if what I hear is just my notebook, or the pad as well. So I was even more sceptical about the cooling, but it fooled me. So far, my hot-running Dell XPS has been running much cooler, even when I'm doing something cpu-intensive like playing chess.

So try it, you might really like it! (The price is a bit steep, in my view, but I guess you get what you pay for.)

Note on size: this is about 14.25 x 11 inches, large enough for a 17-inch laptop perhaps.

title: easy -- just connect it, that's all
text:
A good switch should require no real thought to install. You plug in, connect cat5e cables, and you're done. After that, it should work invisibly, giving you good throughput and no concerns whatsoever.

This one does that. If you need a modest-cost 5-port gigabit switch, I can recommend this one without reservation.

Notes: (1) If you don't need gigabit, you can get 100mb equipment pretty cheap right now. (2) Keep in mind that you use 1 port in a switch for the incoming cable, so a 5-port gives you connection to 4 devices, 8-port allows for 7 devices, etc. (Yeah, I know, it's dumb, but that's the way techies think.) (3) If you think you might need a couple more ports later, then definitely get the 8-port switch, since you don't pay that much more for the extra ports.

If you're concerned about expectations for the brand -- I am generally pretty happy with DLink products. I certainly haven't had any breaking right after 1 year of use, as I have had for some other brands.

title: excellent product at a great price
text:
This is an excellent HDMI cable, at a very good price.

Although certain vendors will urge you to spend large amounts on audio/video cables, all reliable and independent experts will tell you that the expensive cables don't give you anything extra (other than satisfaction of having spent more than your neighbor, perhaps). You should certainly get good quality cables -- but paying more than around $10 for a 6/8 foot HDMI cable is definitely not necessary!

This one might be just a wee bit better than other cables in this price range. I replaced the cable I had been using with this one (using Sony BluRay player with Sony LCD HDTV), and found that although the difference was slight, the colors were just a bit richer and the picture perhaps very slightly sharper. I wouldn't have paid more for that difference, but it's certainly pleasing to get it without having to pay more.

I've used other products with this brand, and have generally been quite satisfied.

title: Excellent gigabit + wireless-n router
text:
No need to look further, this is it. This router has all the features and the performance one could want (at a reasonable price). Gives you a gigabit router/switch (the WAN port is also gigabit, unlike some other similar products), and trouble-free wireless-n as well.

I always use the "manual" configuration modes, so cannot comment on the wizards etc. But I found the setup well organized and easy to follow. The advanced config stuff is separated, so you don't have to go there if you don't want/need to do so.

Oh and by the way, you can also use this as a wireless access point if you want to, although the documentation doesn't say anything. Just make sure you do this: (1) turn off UPnP; (2) give it a fixed IP address and turn off DHCP; (3) connect to the main router through a LAN port, don't use the WAN port.

One minor cavil: the MAC address filtering (i.e., selectively allowing known pcs only to connect) apparently applies to wired and wireless connections, which seems overkill.

One plus: DLink tech support is very good. I sent an email with a technical question about the WAP config, and received a clear and concise response within a day.

title: excellent dvd player at a very low price
text:
I compared this player to my Oppo 980 (which costs about twice as much), connecting both to a Sony LCD HDTV, and I have to say that there was very little difference in the image quality between the two players. I happen to think that the Oppo has excellent picture quality, so it's worth noting that if I were trying to choose between them, and going only by the picture quality (that's about 90% of how I'd choose), I'd have a hard time making a decision.

On the other hand, in some ways this is a pretty basic dvd player. The remote is quite limited (it's not programmable for your tv, for instance), and there are few meaningful adjustments you can make to the settings. One big objection I had is that all pictures are stretched into 16:9, there is no option (that I found) to force a 4:3 display for the standard format recordings.

So if all you want is a decent dvd player that will do a pretty good job doing what a dvd player should do, then for the money this is a pretty good option. One thing to consider: given the move to BluRay (and the fact that BluRay players will play old format dvds), it might not make sense to spend a lot on a dvd player right now.

title: very nice pc speakers, price is a concern
text:
I'm not going to compare these speakers with my Aperions, I'm going to compare them with my old pair of HK speakers that they replaced, and with other decent pc speakers we have in the house. I have to say that I'm a bit surprised by the other reviews -- judging by what I consider appropriate standards, these are really excellent speakers, with clear bright sound, reasonable bass (for their size), and surprisingly good stereo separation. Much better than the others I mentioned -- so much better that I was honestly impressed.

Whether they are worth $80 is more a matter of personal choice than anything else. I haven't compared a range of speakers between $50 and $100 to see if you get a lot more for a bit more money, or almost as good for a bit less money. If a credible reviewer has done that, great, use that info to make up your own mind.

title: excellent mouse, precise and comfortable
text:
In my opinion, the key features of a mouse are precision, ease of use, and comfort. This mouse satisfies all three of these criteria as well as I could possibly expect.

Beyond this, the feature set is quite complete enough for most users (I'm not a gamer, so can't comment on that kind of usage). You ought to use the Logitech SetPoint software (download from logitech.com) to be able to use all the features and customize the mouse to your liking.

I am using this with Vista, having acquired it to replace a dead rollerball mouse. Since I already had SetPoint installed, all I had to do was to plug it in, and it picked up all my previous settings without trouble and began to work well.

I also like the power-saving feature (automatically goes to standby), and the power switch (useful if you're packing the mouse for travel, or if you're going away for a few days without the mouse).

I myself wouldn't use this mouse for travelling; for that I prefer a smaller Logitech mouse which allows the usb key to be inserted into the mouse. (See the V450 for example.)

Check the Logitech website for driver support for other operating systems.

title: fairly comprehensive backup & copy utility
text:
If what you're looking for is a complete backup utility, that's reasonably easy to use, this one might suit your purpose.

Installation, update, and activation are easy, similar to other Symantec programs. (This one also uses Live Update.) I do have an objection to the fact that Symantec never does a full uninstall -- they leave around stuff in the registry, as well as LiveUpdate, and it requires extra work (and some technical skill) to remove everything. I take off one star for that.

The setup is quite simple, especially if you follow their procedures. A full system backup is recommended, and the program will nag you about your system being "at risk" if you don't set up the full backup. You can in addition set up backup jobs for selectively backing up some of your files and folders. So for instance you might want to do nightly backup of your key folders, and weekly or monthly backup of the full system.

I would recommend that you use a network disk (NAS) for your backup -- there are many not-too-expensive products available, and I've been quite happy with the Buffalo products.

You can also use this program to do remote management of other computers on your network, but be aware that each computer needs its own license for the program.

One thing I don't like is that the backup files are not copies, they are in a compressed format. For daily backups I prefer to be able to make normal copies of files, so that I can go quickly to the backup folder and find a backup copy I might want. This optimizes my time and convenience over computer time and disk space, and this is how it should be. Or at least, this should at least be an option.

I take off another star for the nagging about full system backup, and the unavailability of a simple file backup or file sync (backup by copying selected files/folders directly from one disk to another).

But overall a solid program that does what it says, and does it competently. Just make sure what you want is what it wants to do. :-)

title: careful, this one may interfere with HD signals
text:
Unfortunately, not all coax cable splitters are the same. The frequency range supported does matter, since cable companies are now using higher frequencies in their signals.
