title: Respectable fiber paper for rewinding a motor
text:
I used this paper inside of an electric motor I was re-winding, in order to protect the coils from the edges of the stator. For this purpose, it worked quite well. I was able to cut it to dimension, fit it into the stator, wrap the windings around it. It took the Super Corona Dope resin I used to secure the coils without any issue, and survived the baking process (at an admittedly modest 220F) without undergoing any changes.

I can see now why some of fish paper has adhesive backing - that would have been helpful here. I ended up using spray adhesive, which worked, but I think I would have preferred it the adhesive was just part of the paper instead. Depending on what you are using this for, that may not be of interest.

So, basically, would recommend for re-winding a small motor, you get plenty for what you pay and its tough enough to survive the winding with minimum tearing.

title: Works on plug-in with Manjaro KDE and Bose Soundsport Free
text:
I use this to stream audio to my TWS headphones so I can listen to music, videos, and audio books while working out or doing projects around the house. I've been using it for about a month now, and I'm pretty satisfied with it.

It worked on plug-in with Manjaro KDE, and integrated with the OS without any additional configuration. It reliably auto-connects and the system even routes audio to it while it is connected, and then restores it to my main headphones when it is not.

Audio quality is decent, about what you would expect from something like this. Not as good as a direct connection obviously, but for most non-critical listening this is perfectly sufficient. Just make sure your headphones support the higher bitrate codecs - I knew mine didn't, but double check to be sure. I have some Bose Soundsport Free headphones which are vented, which is great because I can hear what's going on around the house, but they don't support any advanced codec at all. So I end up with about a 500ms delay on the audio. That's fine for me - if I'm at my desk, I'm using my main headphones anyway, but just be aware.

Range is tricky. With the Soundsports, it's pretty bad, maybe twenty feet in open air, ten feet if there's any obstruction. I have some Sony WF-1000XM4 TWS earbuds and they do better, but only by about 50%. If you are going more than 15ft from the source, you may have issues. However, my system is close to a wireless router and a UPS, so that may be interfering in my case.

Broadly, for this price, I'd recommend this. Sure you can look for higher quality transmitters that go for $50-$100, but until you pull the trigger on that, this should serve your purposes fine.

title: Useful pair of cables

text:

The plug snaps securely into both 3.5mm ports; the cable and strain relief both seem to be of sufficient quality.

Would recommend for the purposes described

title: Great right-angle adapter for phones and MP3 players
text:
I purchased this for my Sansa Clip+, which I keep in my pocket when running and hiking. I specifically needed the relatively low-profile right-angle plug, since this greatly reduces the strain put on both the MP3 player's jack and the headphone's plug, the latter of which would otherwise function as a lever and apply constant torque to the connection.

I previously had the Seadream right-angle adapters (ASIN: B01DCBJ51I) which is about the lowest profile I've seen, but that one cable became stiff over the next two/three years, which eventually torqued it's own internal wires so much that it stopped working. If you really need as low-profile as possible, that's the better choice, just keep that in mind. It's also a bit shorter, so you don't end up with extra cable on your headphones, but the difference is only 3", so not a big deal.

This adapter is far more flexible, seems better built in general, and has a standoff only 50%-ish greater than the Seadream, minimizing additional torque. I was leery of this at first, but having used it a few times now I'm happy with the outcome. I intend to continue using this one indefinitely into the future, and would recommend to others.

title: Cuts out the ground loop
text:
I used this as an interm solution in my car while I attempted to identify the source/character of a ground loop I was experiencing. It worked well for this purpose, cutting out the ground loop/alternator whine entirely, it was quite satisfactory. I might have just left it in place - however, the proper way of resolving a ground loop buzz is to fix the underlying issue, and as I have identified the cause - a potential difference between two cigarette lighter sockets - I will resolve that instead.

Still, if you cannot or are disinclined to address the source of the buzz, this will suit your purposes well.

title: Solid USB panel connector, but you'll have to find your own way of securing it
text:
I purchased this to install in the center console of my '05 Subaru Outback, connected to a pair of 12V USB buck converters which were tied into the cigarette lighter there.

The unit has a very solid build, thick cables which are not too stiff, and an attractive finish on the front. I was quite happy with the general appearance and make. The design is mostly good, except for the tabs that are intended to lock it to the panel. For me, the plastic of the center console was too thick to accommodate them, and attempting to make them fit resulted in their breaking off entirely. I was able to find a different way to secure the connector, but the design doesn't seem to be a very good one. Other than that, both plugs work as anticipated, for charging anyway.

For notes on the install - I measured 1.9cm to a side on the main body of the connector, but you will probably need 2cm or a bit more to allow the support tabs to lock in place. The front panel has enough margin that even if you are off by a bit, it shouldn't be visible from the front. In my case, I removed the center console entirely from the car, measured and scored the wall of it where I wanted the panel, ensuring it would fit when installed back in the car. Then I used a drill to remove most of the material from the panel wall, and an exacto knife to make it square. After I broke the tabs while trying to secure the connector, I ended up removing them entirely and supergluing a small rectangle of kydex in their place - this made the connector snug. After this, I used a conservative bead of JB Weld around the connector to secure it permanently. Not my favorite solution, I like to leave things in a state where they can be disassembled if needed, but I saw no other obvious means of going about it. After that I reassembled everything and installed it back in the car. I had a lot of cable left over, so it'd be nice if it was available in a 1ft length rather than 3ft, but I suppose extra is better than not enough.

Generally speaking, would recommend as a USB panel connector.

title: Durable, attractive braided cable for external drives, though not as flexible as it could be
text:
I purchased this as an add-on to a portable HDD I was giving to a family member as a gift, both to class it up a bit and to make it easier to connect the drive to a USB port. USB 3.0 cables can be quite stiff, and while this isn't an issue with heavier devices, portable drives are lightweight and can be "pulled around" by their cable, sitting at odd angles on the desk as a result.

This sort of works. It is more flexible than a standard USB 3.0 cable, and largely avoids the issue described above. However, it could be a bit more flexible. The feel of the cable is so-so, but the appearance is premium - it doesn't kink like rubber sheathed cables and has a pleasing texture. So if most of your cables are braided, this will fit right in.

Build quality is solid, and data transfers are to spec.

Would recommend for an external portable HDD, or other electronic device, permanently or occasionally connected to a computer.

title: Feels a bit flimsy, a bit cheap, but very compact
text:
So this is a low-profile 3.5mm cable, to be used in situations where space is at a high premium. The cable is thin and very flexible along its wide face, and the 3.5mm plugs are about as low profile as possible. They are a bit long, which is a same, but can be trimmed a bit if you are willing to sacrifice the strain relief.

Quality of materials seems iffy - I would not use this in any situation where I'd expect high wear and tear. Finishing is similarly lackluster, and there's no shielding of course. However, audio quality seems fine and it is very compact. I use this in the center console of my car, joining a 3.5mm jack to a BT transmitter I attached there. The efficiency of the design is useful in such a small space - very little extra cable to occupy space or catch on things.

Would recommend for the purpose described - a fairly permanent connection in a low-traffic area where space is limited. Otherwise, I'd recommend going with a more standard cable.

title: Great value for the money, works with Sony WF-1000XM3
text:
As I am sure is the case with many, I purchased this after seeing it listed by the New York Times in their portable BT transmitter review list. It was bought specifically to allow me to transmit BT audio from my computer to my Sony WF-1000XM3 earbuds. As the Sony earbuds only support SBC with these, I wasn't expecting stellar audio quality - I usually use them for lectures or podcast-like content, or for fairly low-bitrate music anyway. I wanted to see if the advantages of true-wireless earbuds were worth the sacrifice in quality before I invested in a more expensive BT transmitter and BT receiver+high-end IEMs. As such, I do not use the receive function, and I do not use the battery on the unit - it is always plugged in via USB. I did briefly test the battery though and can confirm it lasts at least 30m.

Note: I went with this type unit, instead of USB, because I wanted to have the ability to test it in multiple environments, including while running and in the car for single-ear usage. Normally, I'd go with a USB solution for computer use in order to avoid the conversion of the audio from to and back from analog.

Initial Setup

Dead simple - I connected the Line Out on my computer to the input on the transmitter, and alternately, the HP out on my stereo receiver to the input on the transmitter. I also tried it with a Sansa Clip+ MP3 player. It worked in all cases, though with the WF-1000XM3 I had to keep the input volume on the BT transmitter under 30% and allow the headphones to do the real amplification, as otherwise the audio would distort.

BT Setup

Fairly simple. I put my earbuds into pairing mode, the transmitter into pairing mode, and they connected within 10s. Afterward, they maintained their connection for the most part, I've had to re-pair a couple times over the last three weeks, but that is mostly a learning curve. Re-pairing is easy - just hold the pairing button down for two seconds and place the receiving device in pairing mode.

Range

Unpredictable, and sensitive. If the transmitter is located on a desk, at least twelve inches away from other electronics, then the range is remarkable. I can leave the room, pass through the adjacent room, and enter into the next room - a total of maybe thirty feet, through two or three walls - and start to lose audio at the end. This is despite being only five feet from a wireless router. However, if I move the transmitter six inches over so it is next to my monitor, or a couple feet so that it is within three feet of the router, the earbuds will begin to drop out even at ten feet. So it is very sensitive to environment.

Audio Quality

Decent. Better than I expected, but I haven't used bluetooth audio in ten years. It can be hard to really gauge it, because the Sony WF-1000XM3 are true wireless earbuds and I can't A/B test them to compare BT quality to a cable. I would say that the BT audio quality is equivalent to that produced when my Sony earbuds are connected to my smartphone. While it is decent, it can't compare to wired earbuds of even fairly middling quality. You lose highs and lows. For dialogue content, lectures and the like, no issue.

Summary

Seems to be a great entry-level transmitter for the average consumer. I'm glad I bought it, because it is reliable and easy to use, and has shown me that the freedom of using wireless earbuds is definitely worth the hit to quality - I can always use my full circumaural headphones if I want to watch a movie or listen critically. Would recommend.

title: Reliable 3.5mm audio cable
text:
I purchased this for connecting a bluetooth transmitter to the Line Out on my computer. It works as you would expect - audio quality is solid, no flaky connection when moving the transmitter around, the wire seems durable and well-made. The collector itself is a little odd, it has a sort of brass/metal collar at the end of the connector, right before it narrows into the plug - not sure why, but it does not interfere with use. It's a bit stiff, but that's only an issue because I have a very lightweight transmitter, less than 1oz, so I don't think anyone would normally notice much less comment on it. If you want something more flexible, go for a braided cable.

Would recommend as a basic, short 3.5mm audio cable.

title: Thin, strong adhesive tape
text:
I purchased this to attach LED strips to the back of a TV I repaired, and later, to the back of a battery in an MP3 player I repaired to secure it in place. It works very well as double-sided tape - very sticky, very thin, easy to apply once you free it from its backing. I cannot comment on its thermal conductivity, but since it is so thin I imagine that at least it will not impede the flow of heat.

Would recommend for general electronics use.

title: Would not connect with my Sony WF-1000XM3
text:
I purchased this specifically to connect to my Sony WF-1000XM3 headphones; it would not do so, regardless of my attempts to engage it. The same headphones connected to my Motorola Smartphone, and later, to a 1Mii Miilink Bluetooth transmitter/receiver. With this one, though, it would not.

May be a fine transmitter for other devices, and theoretically should work with the WF-1000XM3 as the protocols are supported, but it just would not pair. So would not recommend it for that purpose.

title: Great USB 3.0 hub, but don't expect much in the way of charging
text:
I purchased this to replace a Tripp-Lite 7-Port Mini Hub (U360-007-AL) (ASIN: ‎B06XDLXKW9). Don't get that one, it is terrible. I purchased two and returned one, and they all had issues with random disconnections, as did other units we had at my work. Some sort of hardware issue with splitting the hub into two groups of four and three ports respectively.

This one does not have issues - it's USB functionality is great. No disconnects, no issues with data transfer. Solid metal construction and doesn't move much around the table when plugging things in. This is almost everything I want in a desktop USB hub.

However, despite having a dedicated power supply, it delivers very little power to devices, it seems just enough to keep the things running. if you want to charge your phone/tablet while looking at data on it, you are going to waiting a while. Unfortunate, as I chose this unit over Startech's similar HB30C5A2CST, which does have the dedicated charging port.

The decent gauge, all-metal construction and solid performance are welcome. The price is not - this should be about half of what they are selling it for. At $45 it is an easy sell, at $90, you'd better really like the aesthetics and really need the durability to justify paying that much and not getting decent charging too.

So if you just want the ports, and don't mind the wimpy power delivery or price, strong recommendation. Otherwise, consider the equally expensive HB30C5A2CST or wait for a sale.

title: Easy install, does about what's expected
text:
I'm giving this a three star rating because it can only provide slow charging to my phone (a Motorola Moto X4), but I'm not entirely sure that's the transformer's fault. Phones are finicky things, after all, and it is possible that pretty much no charger will supply it with what it is looking for on the data lines. For what its worth, this prevents my phone from draining while I'm on a trip, and powers other USB devices without issue.

Install is easy if you know what you are doing, and if you are purchasing this you probably have an idea. Solders up very easily to the contacts on the back of a cigarette lighter in a car. Just make sure you choose one which isn't doesn't have power when the car is off, or you could run down the battery.

I installed this in combination with a recessed USB/Audio jack like ASIN: B07J4GVS65, worked without issue.

Would recommend.

title: Great little 3.5mm cable
text:
I installed a 3.5mm jack in my car so I could tie my phone/mp3 player into the audio system via an FM transmitter, and needed a short cable to just jump from the port to the device without leaving extra cable hanging around, looking unsightly or posing a snag risk. I needed a right angle to avoid putting pressure on the jack I installed, since it is inside the center console with other items and needs to make a right-angle bend anyway.

This was perfect for the task - makes the connection, snaps snugly into place, has as good of audio quality as you could expect. Also quite flexible and light, so not likely to torque your audio jacks.

Would recommend.

title: Not exactly flush, but quite functional nonetheless
text:
I purchased this for my '05 Subaru Outback, which was made before the days of USB ports and 3.5mm jacks being regular features of cars. I used this in conjunction with two other devices - an iSimple IS31 (ASIN: B002U5XPBE) and a YIPIN HEXHA Quick Charge QC3.0 USB Step Down Converter (ASIN: B0918CR35N), as well as a couple cable adapters. I installed it in the oddball center compartment above the Subaru's media console, so it is normally out of sight, and I can store any cables plugged into it in the compartment when no device is in use. The step-down adapter ties into a cigarette lighter which is inactive when the car is not turned on.

I checked my dimensions and runs first, deciding to install near the media console and run the wires behind the radio. I already had the iSimple and its own audio jack installed in the center console, so I was just going to tie this into the existing setup. Install was easy, if a bit fraught, due to the brittleness of 15+ year old vinyl and having one-shot at drilling the hole for it. I forewent the rubber gasket to I'd have a more flush mount, so you have to get the dimensions right within 1/16". I ended up using a stepper bit, and then an X-Acto to finish the hole.

The port sits quite nicely in place, the included nut makes it easy to tighten everything down. You might want a little bit of threadlocker on there so it doesn't vibrate loose, but it's not strictly necessary. You can shave down the back of this adapter a bit if you need the wires to make a tighter bend - I had to do so - but be careful, naturally. The port, even without the gasket, sits about 1/8" over the surface of the panel, so it isn't perfectly flush. However, it is tight enough that it is out of the way and will probably look more or less in place on a black panel.

For me, exercising care to get everything looking nice and clean and stock, it took about two hours total, not including the iSimple install - which was about two hours itself, with the same level of care - and the step-down converter, which was maybe 30m with the soldering.

So far the unit performs perfectly, power is transferred without issue - it seems to charge quickly, but I can't attest to full QC3 compatibility. The only odd-ball issue is that it looks like USB connectors don't seat all the way into the USB jack - some silver is exposed, more than you would expect. Not sure why this is, but it is the same with multiple USB plugs. Doesn't affect functionality, but might give you pause or encourage you to try pushing in hard to get it to seat fully.

Would recommend.

title: A bit stiff, but quite functional
text:
I have this connected from a USB I installed near the center console in my car to my phone, so it can charge while I'm driving. This prevents there from being a long wire dangling around the shifter/steering wheel. It works very well - fully capable to be sure. Only complaint is that it is a bit stiff, which can torque the connector on the phone if one isn't careful. In my case it isn't an issue since the wire is supported by features of the media console, but it might be for others, especially if you have other use cases where a lightweight device might be easily moved around by a cable of this kind.

Does what it is supposed to do, so no complaints. Would recommend for the purposes described.

title: Flexible, low-profile, great for MP3 players
text:
I use this to connect my MP3 player to a 3.5mm jack I installed in my car's center console. The low-profile 3.5mm connector was very important to me because I wanted to make the connection as slim as possible to avoid accidentally torquing it, catching things on it, or applying pressure to the jack when moving things in and out of the console.

It works quite well for this purpose. the connector is slim - about as slim as they come, such that it basically clamps right up against the side of the player and the wall of the console. The plug itself feels solid and has a small snap when connecting to things. The cable is soft and almost as flexible as a woven cord, even if it does prefer some orientations to others. Sound quality is typical - which is to say, as good as every other cable I've owned.

The only thing I didn't like about the cable was the colors - it really doesn't go with the car interior and stuck out as a result, a bit distracting. So I used a Sharpie Pro - the big chisel-tip type - to turn it black. It is cotton sheathing, so this is quite viable. I was careful - after inking the entire cable and letting it dry, I washed it in warm water, then dried it and ran a soft, clean rag over it about a hundred times, until it came away basically clean. After the fact, while you could tell the original black bits from the inked threads, it's just different shades of black, rather than looking blotchy. I imagine using something like RIT black dye would be about equally effective, if you heated it and let it soak for a good long while.

So I would recommend it. The braided cable looks premium and is much easier to work with than its equally-thick rubber counterparts. This makes it easy to handle the MP3 player while it is still plugged in.

title: Performs its function well
text:
This product is a pair of Y-RCA cables - that is to say, one male that splits into two female. The contacts of one Y-cable are colored red, the other, white. The length is approximately one foot, including the connectors.

I recently installed an FM-transmitter - the kind that attaches itself directly to the antenna cables of the radio - in my car, along with a 3.5mm audio jack in the center console. However, I discovered that It would also be useful to be able to connect my smartphone into the audio system in a similar way - this way, driving instructions can be heard over the music if necessary. or I could play music or media from my phone instead of my MP3 player. Ar the input on the FM-transmitter i RCA, I decided to use this splitter. One 3.5mm jack connects to one RCA cable, the other 3.5mm jack connects to the other.

This works about as well as it could. The cables are flexible, the contacts of good quality, the connectors tight. Audio quality is completely indistinguishable from a straight run, no loss in volume even. Connector size is reasonable, which is important to me, given the constraints imposed by placing the setup within the trim panels of the car.

Would recommend.

title: Good AUX cable for specific applications
text:
This is a fairly generic AUX cable, the right-angle connector works well to avoid unnecessary stress on the jack. I am using it in my car, where the AUX jack is located inside the compartment of the center console, so using the ribbon-like cable with the narrow cross-section makes sense - it means the lid of the compartment closes more easily. However, as expected, the wire flexes well in one direction (across the broad side of the cable) but not so well across the other (the narrow side). In most applications, I think you'd want the cable to flex equally well in all directions,

But this cable is fine if you prefer the flat type.

title: Great for connecting to a panel jack
text: The way this wire is set up, each channel has its own wire which is sheathed in the grounding mesh. Each wire also has some fiber reinforcement. I was able to cut the end off and solder the two wires (red for right channel, white for left channel) without issue, as well as the ground mesh to the chassis contact on a panel-mount jack. Seems well made, flexible, no real issue here.

title: Easy to install, consistent signal, fairly good sound quality
text:
Context: I have have an '05 Subaru Outback Limited, which has a 6-CD changer but no cassette deck or AUX-in. I have a decent amount of experience in audio, low-voltage electric, and soldering.

ASIN of other parts I purchased:

RCA-3.5mm cable: B00LM2Y2U4
3.5mm panel-mount jack: B00OGLCR3W
Antenna adapters for Subaru: B000K53QBA
3.5mm braided, right-angle cable: B01K3WYKW8

I installed this in my Outback after thinking about doing so for years. I've never used the sound system in my car and it felt like a bit of a waste, and I would like to listen to audiobooks and music on my commute or long trips. Previously I considered tying the audio into the wiring harness for the CD player in order to attain maximum quality, but it was sufficiently unapproachable that I put it off for years. I ended up going with the iSimple instead of a generic FM transmitter because I wanted to get the maximum possible quality at the maximum power, hopefully improving the battery life of my MP3 player (a Sandisk Sansa Clip+).

As for installation: I watched a video on Youtube by a guy named Dirtcheapdaily (How to add an auxiliary port to any car | Ep.81) which made the process very simple. It took me about three hours total from start to finish, and required that I remove the center console from the car and make some modifications on the workbench. However, I wanted my car to look stock, with everything hidden away - if you don't care about any of that, you could literally do this in 20m.

However, the steps I took were: remove some panels from center console and radio - pull antenna wires out from behind head unit- connect iSimple model to antenna wires via adapters to check length of wires - remove center console and bring to workbench - add velcro and attach iSimple to space inside center console where it won't interfere with anything - drill holes in wall of center console storage compartment - cut switch wires, feed through holes, resolder w/ heatshrink - feed audio wire through hole, solder to 3.5mm jack, seat in hole - trim, then solder power wires to back of cigarette lighter (only has power when ACC is on) - tie all wires down so they don't wander - return center console to car and temporarily reconnect to adjust gain and switch to best radio station, and make sure parking brake doesn't interfere with modules or wires - reassemble car and test one last time.

Regarding quality: after adjustment, I'd say the audio quality is pretty good. When the switch is on, there is no interference whatsoever from other stations. It is not as good as a true line in, but I don't see that as being very important as I frequently have the windows down, hear road noise, or have the car vents running, so for me fairly good is good enough. It is better than many external FM transmitters I've heard, and much more consistent.

I do wish the gain on the unit was a bit stronger, I have it maxed out an still have to crank my volume up to 50% if I have my MP3 player on ~50% volume, which isn't an issue it itself but at 20 the other radio stations are truly deafening. It is possible that the gain is limited by FCC regs, though. For now, I just set all my presets to the radio station I have selected on the unit to avoid accidentally shifting to a different one. This way I can run the MP3 on 50% and the battery will hold out longer than otherwise.

So, as for recommendations - I would say that if you want the best quality in the most unobtrusive form factor, this is a good investment so long as installing it into your car isn't -too- much of a hassle. I found the process educational myself but for some it might just be frustrating. If you just want audio and you aren't too attached to how you get it, I would order an external plug-in FM transmitter first and only upgrade if you feel it would be necessary.

title: Great for panel mounting in a car
text:
I wanted to add an AUX input to my '05 Subaru Outback via an iSimple transmitter, and this seemed to be what I was looking for. Since I like everything to look stock, I drilled out a hole for it in the wall of the storage compartment in the center console and mounted it right next to the switch that activates it. A 5/16" bit will do the trick, though if you have one, 11/32 makes it easier. For me, the panel was too thick to use the nut, so instead I just made barely made the hole big enough and press-fit the jack into it, then used some heat shrink tubing on the back.

Contacts could be larger, but soldering them up was a simple matter. I ended up using a bit of UV-activated glue to isolate the contacts and prevent a potential short, but hot glue, regular glue, or three individual sleeves of heatshrink will do the trick. If you are looking right at the back of the connector, the ground/chassis wire is on the bottom, the right channel (red, typically) is to the right, and the left channel (white, typically) is on the left.

Audio is fine, nice little snap when the connector goes in, retention isn't problematic in the least. Black bezel blends right into the mounting surface, like it belongs there. Durable enough that when I used the rubber-coated handle of my pliers to press-fit the jack into the panel, there was no damage at all to the surface of the jack.

Would recommend as a panel mount, it is compact, durable-feeling, and easy to use.

title: Great in a Sandisk Sansa Clip+ w/ rockbox
text:
I purchased this because I wanted to expand the internal storage of my Sansa Clip+ MP3 player. It's my old standby, I've been using it for nearly ten years now and the internal storage memory has become corrupted, but the external microSD works fine. In the past I have tried a 240GB card of a lower speed, but had constant issues getting it to operate reliably.

This card - the SanDisk Extreme Pro UHS-1 U3 A2 V30 works perfectly. I have loaded it two-thirds full of data and played it constantly on a 10h car trip and had no issue. No skipping, no access problems, nothing. The data also loaded onto the card using an microSD/SD adapter, with sustained xfer rates of about 90MB/s.

Quite happy with the outcome. I may even try the 512GB version when it comes down around $30.

Would recommend for purposes described.

title: Great general-purpose lithium cell charger
text:
This is a great charger for lithium batteries, including for 21700 cells. I am fairly happy with the design and function, and have been using it for a few months now with success. It charges cells reliably and quickly, and the interface is quite understandable after a quick perusal of the manual.

It has a couple weaknesses. First, it doesn't hold RC123A/16340 cells very well. Placement is finicky, and occasionally they shift out of alignment. It isn't a huge issue, but I have now had three lithium cell chargers and this is the first to have that problem. Second, i was surprised to discover it uses micro-USB instead of a USB-C jack, as the latter would support significantly higher wattage. I don't charge cells often, and when I do, I'm not generally pressed for time, but this seems like an obvious oversight, given when this was released USB-C was already well established. I'm guessing it is a cost-saving measure.

All in all, I would recommend it over other no-name chargers, but it's nothing to write home about. For a device like this, though, that's about all you need.

title: Decent for protecting a sketchpad/notebook
text:
If you have a nice sketching or art notebook, something with high-quality paper and good binding, this is great for protecting it. Even better, it has a little, separate side-pocket you can use to carry your pens/pencils/markers/etc. Soft on the inside, protects the notebook from moisture, dust, and contamination, and you can use it as a soft mat to set the notebook on while using it out in the real world.

A bit large, so better for larger notebooks than smaller ones, and not really thick enough to carry multiple notepads at a time. But great to throw into a backpack/messenger bag, ensuring that the edges of your notebook don't get chewed up over time.

Would recommend for that purpose.

title: Durable, simple case for a set of pens
text:
This is a decent, albeit somewhat bulky, case to organize your pens. I purchased it originally to keep my Pigmas, and works for this, but it doesn't fit into the tablet case I use to protect my notebook. Turns out I can just keep the pens in the charger pocket and it is small enough that they are all held in place.

This is good for a backpack or similar where you have the space to contain it, and it keeps everything reliably in order. If you want to carry the pens around in a laptop bag, for example, this is ideal - better than the plastic case the pens come in, if you carry them around and use them quite a bit.

Good quality material, feels durable, easy to use, no complaints here. Would recommend for those purposes.

title: Accurate, reliable, useful for experimentation
text:
I purchased this so I could easily run some experiments on LED strips, fans, and Peltier coolers. Very useful for that purpose, if you don't want to run a full-sized bench-top DC power supply, or are working with a circuit/setup that could damage your equipment. Display is bright, controls are easy to use, the unit is attractively designed and decently protected. Testing with a multimeter shows output is accurate.

Only critiques I have is that the voltage/amperage knobs are difficult to adjust, and the input/output terminals aren't very secure. I don't think they would come off, but they have small apertures and they twist in place when tightening things down. Aside from those two things, I would easily recommend this to hobbyists, tinkerers, and designers as a far preferable way to step up/down voltage without needing to use those tiny boards which require a meter to configure.

If they have a model that can handle greater amperage, I will be interested in procuring it.

Would recommend.

title: Decent value for money, but burn out quickly
text:
So I purchased these with the express purpose of testing out some ideas with Peltier devices; given the price, I didn't expect much. They arrived, and they both worked out of the box. One or both was cracked at the corner, but this did not seem to inhibit functionality; as many have mentioned, they aren't terribly well packed. I never ran them at even close to full voltage without a heat sink and paste. One failed mysteriously after maybe 30m of tinkering, the other failed when I put ~15V through it.

For me, if you have the Peltier unit on the table in front of you, with the wires emerging from the edge nearest to you, and the red wire is on your right, then the hot side is down and the cold side is up.

They work well if you want to get an idea about how these devices work and test out some designs, before investing in a higher quality model. I purchased my next set from TE Technologies, who make some nice units, but I avoided burning that one out by utilizing the lessons I learned with these, so I would recommend them for that purpose. On the other hand, one failed without any apparent reason, so only three stars from me.

title: Seems to work fairly well
text:
I like these little things - they are made of metal, and they stay closed on their own. In size and thickness they are discreet. I used it to cover the front camera on my phone and have been carrying it around with me for a week now; no accidental uncovers, no marks on the slide, and it is so thin I barely notice it is there at all. I'm using a Motorola Moto X4 with a Supershieldz protector and have had no issues with it attaching or detaching.

Only possible improvement I can think of is to make it smaller. The slide fits my phone well enough, but it may not fit others - make sure you check where all the sensors are before you attach the slide. On the Moto X4, for example, there is a light sensor located between the camera and the speaker, but it is totally invisible from the surface, even under inspection with a flashlight. I only knew to consult a teardown video because the Supershieldz protector had an aperture there.

So, would recommend. I will probably order a couple more for my tablets and the phones/tablets of friends and family.

title: Can't complain
text:
Ordered this memory to boost an old family laptop a bit, since it is really chugging on W10. Honestly, bumping it to 16GB didn't help as much as I would have liked, so we ended up replacing it with a newer model running a Ryzen 7 4700U. The old system I'll probably convert in to a Linux machine for testing purposes.

However, the memory itself is just fine, worked exactly as expected. Would recommend it for anything too resource intensive, since it is only 1600MHz, but what do you expect from DDR3?

title: Must-have for any PC tech or IT department
text:
I don't care if you have pounds of laptop screws you had the newbies extract from retired machines before the nice man took them off to the great electronics recycling bin in the sky, you should have at least one of these kits in the office at all times. No more trying to distinguish between the pitch on a 1.5mm machine screw, this tells you exactly what you are getting and where it is. Does it have everything? No. But just about - everything that you would need for typical laptop repair, for Dell systems anyway. I used to scrap and save screws in my desk so I'd have a few available, but this kit will save me all that time and annoyance for the foreseeable future.

The box is decent,but could be a little higher-quality, since you don't want the screws bouncing between parts of the tray, or the whole thing bursting open if it falls off the table. It's serviceable, but may consider getting your own pill-sorter type box with individually latching compartments instead.

PC techs - buy it, even if you have to use your own money. It's worth the 15m of your wage you'll use to pay for it.

title: Solid upgrade from the usual velcro ties
text:
I purchased these to use in a server room for cable management, specifically for managing UPS power cables. They work pretty well, haven't had one break yet.

These are a great improvement over the typical one-piece velcro cable ties. They are more durable and make it easier to tighten down straps, as well as loosen them if necessary - everything stays in place. They also look neater, in my opinion, due to being slightly wider and the rectangular plastic ring keeping the strap aligned with itself.

Quality of these is fine - you aren't likely to break them at these proportions, and they seem to be mostly well-aligned and made of a decent material. Nothing too incredible, but if its something you are strapping down and leaving in place, they'll do fine.

Maybe not for small bundles of cables, but great for power cords, Christmas lights, and that kind of thing.

title: Okay straps, build quality questionable
text:
I purchased these to use in a server room, specifically to strap cables to the racks for the purposes of cable management. I previously had 18" straps of a different, unknown brand and while they were good, they were just too long for some of the lower runs where there were fewer cables to tie up.

These are definitely the right length for just about everything the 18" can't handle. However, the quality isn't great - the hook part of the tab is fused onto the loop part of it, but on most they aren't perfectly aligned, and I broke three straps while cinching them down, all right at this juncture. Now it isn't a huge issue - to avoid straining the connection, you just pull on the main strap, not the end bit - but I really feel like that's something they should have gotten right. There just isn't that much to a cinch strap, after all.

Anyway, still three stars because only three broke and the rest were fine, and maybe I was pulling unreasonably hard on them in an attempt to corral the power cables, but maybe consider other brands and see if you have better luck there.

title: Does not fit the jabra Pro 920
text: The cushions feel like they are decent quality, for headset cushions anyway. Another review mentioned that these would work for the Jabra Pro 920 headset. This is not the case - it doesn't fit, and therefore would not fit the 930 either. The only reason I am making this review is to articulate that point.

title: Great cable to connect a DVI display to a DP output
text:
Not much to say about this sort of thing - it's a great cable, has been transferring video for a few weeks now without a hitch. Approximately 1/4" thick, plenty flexible, not too stiff. DVI plug is about as narrow as you can make it. DP plug lock in snugly. My setup has it so that the DP (the narrow side, with the one corner missing) is connected to my computer and the DVI (the wide side, with the pins) is connected to my monitor.

If you need a DP to DVI cable, this works.

title: Great for lightweight media/producitivy use
text: I installed this in my grandmother's laptop, since the 4GB she had in her older laptop wasn't cutting it with W10. Install easy, worked as expected - not much more required from a DIMM, to be honest. Not particularly fast, not for gaming or serous production work, but perfectly serviceable to refresh an old machine. Would recommend.

title: Strong, durable battery box
text:
I purchased this, initially, as part of a project to build out a small quick-access hiking kit which would contain batteries, electrolytes, and some other small necessities so I wouldn't have to dig through my pack to get them. It is a little large for that, I think, and a little heavy - though for some use cases it would be quite suitable. However, it does make for a great battery case - I now have it sitting right next to my battery charger, and keep all my 18650 cells stored in it while they are not in use. Both protected and unprotected cells fit without an issue. I am really quite happy with it in this regard - before, they were in open-air caddies, exposed to dust and moisture, but now they are well protected from everything.

The latch is very robust and snaps better than any other box I've seen on the market. This is not one of those cheap battery cases you see all over the internet, this is well made, it has heft and strength to it.

The two foam inserts are not secured in the frame, and will fall out on their own. Normally this would cost the product a star, but I find it useful, as I can use the box for some other purpose by removing the insert, if I wish. It is also a trivial matter to secure the insert into the bottom or lid using a mild spray adhesive, so it isn't really a problem.

If you are looking for a case to protect your 18650 cell, this one is is a great candidate.

title: Sturdy, well-sealed CR123A caddy
text:
This is probably a fairly niche product. I purchased it originally to convert it into a mixed battery/medicine holder to keep on the outer pocket of my hiking bag, but it is a bit too heavy for that. It isn't heavy in general - but in hiking you generally try to save as much weight as you can. This also isn't very space-efficient, as it has a large shock-absorbing interior designed to protect the cells.

That, it it was so well made, I felt a bit bad about modifying it. So, instead, It now sits on my shelf and holds my rechargeable RC123A/16350 cells instead, as well as 3x CR123A cells. The traction feet actually come into use now, and this is better than my prior setup where I had all the batteries secured in well-made, but open-air battery caddies.

This will offer significantly better protection against dust, moisture, and other general environmental degradation than the previous caddies.

So if you want something that will really protect your cells, either when hiking, in a toolbox, in your truck, or when you are going to be out in rough conditions, or you want something that will just keep them safe from moisture and dust on the shelf, then this is a good choice. If you wanted something that you can taking out in your daypack, it is probably more than you need, and I'd look for something a bit lighter and more compact.

title: Great for cleaning up your desk space
text:
I have my desktop, NAS array, router, and UPS all on the same desk, and so I did not need to have six-foot cables on everything. I purchased these, as well as some 18" CAT6 cables, to make cable management a little easier. It was successful in this regard; while before I had the excess cable tied in little spools, now I just have the cable going from one machine to another with minimal left over.

For pretty much every typical consumer, these cables will be more than sufficient for your power loads. If you have a 1500W+ power supply, you might want to consider going with 16GA instead of 18GA, but that's about it. I chose the 18GA so the cable would be a bit more flexible.

title: Great choice for a reliable, middle-of-the-road dashcam
text:
I purchased this for myself about six months ago ago, then again just recently for my sister to put in her car. The initial purchase was to replace an older Viofo, the original A119s (I think) when it failed after four years of use. This A119v3 is functionally quite similar to that one - it just has a higher picture quality due to improvements in technology. I wanted one that was 4k/60fps or 2k/120fps but the tech isn't quite there yet, at least not at a reasonable price.

I also purchased a pair of 128GB Samsung high-endurance microSD cards (primary and backup) and a hardware kit. I did not purchase a GPS unit, as I didn't see the need. Finally, I purchased a USB-C microSD reader so I could easily transfer a video to my phone for backup, in the case I ended up in an accident and needed to retain evidence.

Install was dead-simple - I mounted the camera in a location which as already blocked by my rear-view mirror, so I can't even see it while driving and it isn't conspicuous from the outside. I ran the wire up along under the lip where my car's internal ceiling meets the windshield, then down the a-pillar on the drivers-side, where it connects to the ACC and door-locks on the car. This is because I am using the hardware kit and wanted the camera to continue recording while parked, at least for a little while - if you are using the default wiring kit, you can run it own the passenger side and plug it into an car outlet or USB, as the unit comes with a cigarette-lighter-to-USB adapter and a very long USB cable. My sister used this latter option and was able to completely hide the cable without issue. After install, everything just stays put more or less permanently.

Functionally, the unit is straightforward. There are some settings should should configure, but not many. The menu is pretty tricky to navigate at first, it isn't clear what buttons do what, but you learn fairly quickly. Just read the manual to see what is available - all the basic features are there, file formats, date codes on the video, when to overwrite, what resolution and FPS you prefer, etc.

Daytime video quality is very good, close to exceptional. FOV (field of view) is wide enough to cover the entire windshield if you place the camera in the center. Resolution at 2K is good enough to resolve most license plates within two car lengths at rest, as well as with maybe 5mph difference, though it gets tricky quick. This will capture everything else pretty reliably.

Nighttime video quality is passable. Glare reduction is good, it comes with a polarizing filter to aid in that. You probably aren't resolving any license plates except under ideal conditions. It is more than enough for the average motorist, but if you do most of your driving at night, you might want to consider a dashcam specifically designed with the IR lamps for that purpose.

So far the camera has been very reliable. It chimes on startup to let me know it is on, and the record button has a soft red glow to confirm it is recording. The display is not normally lit while driving. I have already saved a couple videos of things I've seen on the road, quite successfully. I am much more comfortable having this dashcam in the car than not.

Overall, I think I'd recommend it to most people as their first camera, with the only alternative being the A129 Duo, which also has a rear-view camera to catch people behind you, in the case of a rear-end. That goes for about $170.

title: Great protective cover for a Galaxy Tab S4
text:
I purchased this for a basically new Galaxy Tab S4 tablet I purchased a couple months prior, in order to protect it from damage and incidental environmental exposure. I am quite content with it - the frame is quite rigid, protecting the tablet from flexing. The front cover isn't flimsy, and the material feels like it is high quality, with strong, distinct stitching. The case allows the tablet to be charged without issue. The internal pen holder - for me - is indispensable, as otherwise I would never have the S-pen and consequently never use it.

In terms of positioning, the cover is fine. Even sitting back on a recliner-like chair, I can find a position which is comfortable for viewing. It also works fairly well on a table. In terms of weight, it adds a bit to the tablet, I'm guessing 20% or so. Considerable, but the S4 isn't all that light to begin with and you'll have trouble beating this case's weight without sacrificing rigidity or durability. In terms of aesthetics, it is on point - hard, clean lines, subdued texturing and coloration, quite refined.

As for complaints, not many. It is hard to get the tablet out of the case once you put it in there, so make sure you have your SD and/or SIM card installed before you pop it in. It takes some time to get used to how the stand works, and it isn't the best at staying upright if you are moving things around on the table, though I have only had it slde flat a couple times. That's about it.

This isn't a case you want to use for a child or teenager - probably - or for a tablet you intend to bring out into the weather or while traveling in less-than-ideal environments. They have tablets cover for that purpose. This one is better for people bringing the tablet around the house, leaving it on the kitchen counter, maybe taking it by car to the office and back in a padded sleeve - I bought ASIN: B07Z4JZFWF, which works well for that purpose.

Would recommend.

title: Great replacement fans for a NAS
text:
The fan on my eight year-old QNAP TS-669 Pro's power supply finally began to fail recently, producing an unpleasant tone at odd intervals. After checking up the specs of the PS online, I found that the unit's fans were replaceable - and fairly easily too. As soon as I confirmed that the fans would fit, I ordered the 40mm PS fan as well as a pair of these 92mm to cut down on noise.

install was dead easy - while I had to solder the smaller PS fan to its connector, these plugged right in. Routing the wire was a bit tricky in the smaller box but the fans also contain an extension cord which is more than long enough for the task. They fired right up on start-up and are noticeably quieter than the original fans. Quite happy - I only wish I had thought of this half a decade ago instead of listening to those two fans running 24-7 on my desk. I'll know for sure i the summer, but right now this was definitely a good purchase.

I've replaced all my computer fans with Noctuas, with the interest in minimizing noise, and they have proven consistently reliable, so I would recommend them to others looking for fans for a similar application.

title: Excellent replacement fan for a power supply
text:
The fan on my eight year-old QNAP TS-669 Pro's power supply finally began to fail recently, producing an unpleasant tone at odd intervals. After checking up the specs of the PS online, I found that the fan was replaceable - and fairly easily too, so I picked up a Noctua not only for the PS but two more for the QNAP itself. Double-checked the specs, and since the voltage matched, and the amperage of the prior fan was higher than this one, I figured I was set.

Accurately, it seems. Install was dead simple. I did have to clip the wire off the old fan and solder it onto this one's - though the Noctua comes with several tie-ins you can use for this purpose, I wanted a cleaner install. After the install, it fired up perfectly, and it was so quiet I had to use a flashlight to make sure it was spinning at all. I'll know better in the summer, but so far I'm pretty happy with the outcome.

I've replaced all my computer fans with Noctua's, with the interest in minimizing noise, and they have proven consistently reliable, so I would recommend them to others looking for fans for a similar application.

title: Great replacement for a Zune 30GB
text:
I gave my father my old Zune a while back, since I moved onto the Sansa Zip Clip+ years and years ago. He has some trouble seeing, so the larger screen helps him out. However, it is an older device, the battery was dying in 45m, and I wanted to freshen it up a bit. So I figured, while I was replacing the battery, I'd replace the HDD with an SSD - mostly for the reduced weight, power usage and access times, rather than the increased storage size.

As others have said, it works great, first time in. What I did was carefully remove the little plastic bezel in the bottom of the Zune, remove two tiny Phillip's heads, gently pried the two halves apart, removed the battery by unclipping the cable, removed the HDD case via four tiny Phillip's heads screws, gently pried *that* up, starting from the end opposite where the battery was, gently pried the HDD from the cage, removed the ZIF cable from the HDD, inserted it into the SSD, put the SSD back in the cage (with shock absorbers attached, they fit the new drive), then reassembled the whole thing. It took about 30m total, moving at a very careful pace.

After reassembly, I reconnected the Zune to the computer, had to reinstall the firmware, then resync the Zune to the collection. This was a bit tricky, as the old Microsoft servers are no longer active, but there are guides online (search for ZuneUpdate for more info).

For reference, the original HDD is about 47g, the SSD is about 32g, so you are looking at a 30% savings in weight there. If you forgo the shock absorbing pads and the HDD case, you could probably save another 10g, Probably not worth it though.

It is a bit pricey, and there is a 64GB version for ~$30 less, but from what I understand, the KingSpec is one of the only drives that reliably works for the Zune upgrade. Converters, ZIF-SD for example, also don't seem to be reliable.

I'll leave an update if my father has any issues, but so far, I am happy.

title: Works well for a Samsung Galaxy Tab S4
text:
I purchased this for my Samsung Galaxy Tab S4 10.1, which I just picked up off eBay. The install was fairly easy - I used Supershieldz before and while their smartphone protectors are far easier to install than these on account of the smaller size, the experience was highly comparable. In the end did have a couple tiny air bubbles - so small that they were only iridescent patches - which I could not work to the edges of the screen no matter how I tried. However, I just left the Galaxy Tab in a warm room overnight, and the next day, they were totally gone and have not yet returned, more than month later.

Responsiveness is indistinguishable from the base touchscreen. Clarity is, so far as I can tell, perfect. Very low friction, though it still picks up fingerprints. I really like that it comes with two protectors, just in case one breaks in the future. The fact that the screen had a couple (very) minor scratches near the edges did not affect the install whatsoever.

Install notes are unremarkable. I followed the instructions closely. Basically, you need a clean area with good light and low airflow. You should wear tight-knit clothing, like nylon or linen, instead of something fuzzy. If you have long hair, tie it back. Wear latex gloves. Make sure you have 15m or so to devote to the install. Remove the tablet from its case, clean the screen up, inspect it from multiple angles, then do the hinge-type install as instructed. I also recommend cleaning the screen protector with the included cloth before you start, even though it still has its protective film on it, as this will prevent it from transferring dust to the screen during the fitting process.

Getting it centered is still kind of tricky, especially on the 10.1" tablet, you have to be more careful that you would be with the phone or a smaller tablet. Just decide in the beginning that you are going to devote 15-20m to this install and take your time with it.

I now have Supershieldz on three devices, and would recommend.

title: Fairly easy to install, no bubbles
text:
I purchased this for my Samsung Galaxy S2 8.0, which I recently bought used. The install was fairly easy - I used Supershieldz before and while their smartphone protectors are far easier to install than these on account of the smaller size, the experience was highly comparable. In the end did have a couple tiny air bubbles - so small that they were only iridescent patches - which I could not work to the edges of the screen no matter how I tried. However, I just left the S2 in a warm room overnight, and the next day, they were totally gone and have not yet returned, more than month later.

Responsiveness is indistinguishable from the base touchscreen. Clarity is, so far as I can tell, perfect. Very low friction, though it still picks up fingerprints, science hasn't brought us that far yet it seems. I really like that it comes with two protectors, just in case one breaks in the future. The fact that the screen had a couple (very) minor scratches on it already did not affect the install whatsoever.

Install notes are unremarkable. I followed the instructions closely. Basically, you need a clean area with good light and low airflow. You should wear tight-knit clothing, like nylon or linen, instead of something fuzzy. If you have long hair, tie it back. Wear latex gloves. Make sure you have 15m or so to devote to the install. Remove the tablet from its case, clean the screen up, inspect it from multiple angles, then do the hinge-type install as instructed.

Getting it centered is still kind of tricky, but it generally works. Much better than the old days with the flexible protectors.

I now have Supershieldz on three devices, and would recommend.

title: Would be a nice tablet case, if it actually fit the Galaxy Tab S2 8.0
text:
It would be nice - really, ideal - if it actually fit the tablet. Like many other users have said, the case fits on three edges but does not fit on the bottom - the lip does not lock over the bottom edge. This is so even after leaving the case on the tablet for several days, it never just "conforms" to shape. I've inspected it closely, and I can't quite tell *why* it has this problem - my guess is that, with all the apertures in the bottom edge of the case (to accommodate speakers and ports) the silicone just can't hold its structure.

More than this, though, the tablet cannot be charged when the case is on it. Well, it can be charged, but just barely - the material of the case prevents the charging cable from fully engaging, and it pops out at the slightest provocation.

Lastly, I've queried the seller in pursuit of a replacement so I can see if I just was unlucky - other reviews report having success when they ordered a replacement - but have not received a reply in weeks.

Too bad, it is precisely what I was looking for in terms of thinness.

I do not recommend.

title: Reliable sleeve for a Galaxy Tab S2 8.0
text:
I purchased this to hold my Samsung Galaxy Tab S2 8.0 while I am traveling, or while it is not in use. It works well for this purpose - even when the S2 is in its official Samsung Book Cover, it fits very nicely. This sleeve will keep dust, moisture, and sunlight off the tablet while protecting it from various impacts. The material is somewhat coarse but will likely soften in time.

Though this also can protect the bare tablet, I would recommend keeping it in a leather or protective case as well, as a sleeve like this will not protect a tablet from being bent or torqued. That said, I would recommend this sleeve for an inexpensive solution to protecting a somewhat fragile device. .

title: Great basic tablet sleeve for a Galaxy Tab S4
text:
I generally take care of my equipment and prefer for it to remain in good order for the entire time I own it, so I always pick up a tablet sleeve even if I rarely bring the device anywhere to begin with. This is a great, basic sleeve - plenty of space, plenty of padding, large zipper for easy zipping, and keeps the tablet out of the sun, dust, and moisture of an indoor environment. Material is a little coarse but doesn't feel cheap. Space for a charging cable and flattish USB charger in the front pocket. The sleeve easily fits my Galaxy Tab S4 while it is in its pseudo-leather case (ASIN: B07GF8K8ZW), which in turn is wide enough to have space for a stylus. .

it is a soft sleeve and not rigid. This means that while you could keep a bare tablet in it, or a tablet with just a thin gel case on it, and it would protect it from the environment and random impacts, I would still recommend getting a proper case for the tablet itself if you are going to be traveling with it.

title: Great cable for a receiver
text:
I use this cable to connect a pair of stereo headphones to my receiver, so I can wander around my study while still listening to music and other content. It works well for this purpose, there is minimal attenuation. The cable is sturdy and heavy enough not to get too tangled on things (including itself) and the connector seems to hold quite securely. No problems, despite it being kicked and pulled around corners for a few weeks.

Would recommend.

title: Seems robust enought to keep connected as a storage device
text: There are numerous most cost-effective solutions for internal storage, but I keep this connected to my USB hub so I can easily move files between my system and an isolated VM which has no access to the host system otherwise. I just move the files I want from the host system on the drive, then insert the USB into the VM via the hypervisor console. Easy to to, and largely maintains the isolation between the systems. It has been continuously connected for a couple months now and has no issues with capacity, speed, or detection.

title: Great replacement PS
text: I used this PS to replace a burnt-out one from a several decades old lamp which had failed (and used DC instead of AC for some reason). Since I wanted to re-use the original DC PS housing, I disassembled this one, completely insulated the inside of the old PS box, and connected this one into it. The compact size of the IBERLS power supply made it such that this was the only one that would really fit. After installing, and soldering it up, everything worked exactly as planned. I believe I was running the light at 1000mA without thermal or any other issues.

title: Low profile and work fairly well
text:
These are pretty easy to use and relatively small, to fit in confined spaces. The PCB solder points is of limited use if you aren't using a board, but if you are working with these you can certainly solder to wherever you need to. The battery locks in well and stays in place. I had no difficulty using this and testing it with a couple different components. .Plastic seems fairly durable, enough for a component anyway.

Would recommend.

title: It most works, with some limitations
text:
Specs
MSI B450M Mortar Max
Fractal Design Meshify C Mini

I purchased this just because my computer is not within arm's reach of my computer chair, which means when it locks up I have to walk over to reset it. I do some testing and experimental work so this is necessary slight more often for me than it would be for many people. I installed this device to facilitate this.

So here's the deal. Once I paired the remote, it stayed paired, regardless of how long I had the module off power. Some users have reported it losing its pairing, but mine didn't. I installed in as instructed. It works great when resetting the system during a soft or hard lock - the remote reboots the system without fail, even though the module in inside a metal computer case. This is still very useful to me, so I will keep the module installed.

It does not, however, turn the system on when it is already powered down. My guess is that the USB header isn't powered during shutdown and so the system cannot transmit a signal. This is true even if the system is on, so I am guessing that it may be a compatibility issue.

I tried a solution with a battery pack and a buck converter to get a 3V CR123A up to 5V, which delivered power to the module without issue, but still would not get it to send a signal to the motherboard to turn on. I metered it and tested extensively - the chip uses both sets of power pins, which is fine, and I had 5V on both sets, and the module's LED even illuminated showing me that it had a signal, but it the module wouldn't work on battery nonetheless. Neither reset not power on, when the system was off or on. Odd. Can't be a data pin issue since the adapter board supplied with the module doesn't even have traces for them. I assume there must be some other logic at work, since a CR123A can supply more current than the USB 2.0 standard demands.

Anyway, in the end, it seems that it draws about 20mA of power while idle, which, while minimal, generally means that a battery solution isn't viable, since that only gives you about three days on a 1.5aH cell. Not worth the effort.

However, if you want a module that lets you remotely reboot your system from across the room, this will probably work.

title: Works well as a battery holder, but oddly difficult to put battery into it
text:
I like that it holds the battery, and that it has a switch. It feels robust enough for what it is. However, it is oddly difficult to get the 9V to lock into place, The contacts are fixed in place, not on a little tail (which is how this issue is usually avoided). If the bottom opened, even a little, you could apply force to the bottom of the battery and press it onto the terminals, but the cell sits down in a little chamber instead. I had to use a wooden stirrer (like a paint stirring stick)) and slide it between the bottom of the battery and the edge of the case to pry it into place. As you can guess, removing the battery is also tricky.

Dealbreaker? Not really, for small projects it works just fine. But kind of an obvious oversight of design. My guess is a cost-saving measure. If a little trickiness like that described above doesn't bother you, then go ahead and order them.

title: Decent switch, but kept resetting on me
text:
Not sure how reliable it is. I was using this to briefly control two systems with a single mouse/keyboard, and it did work for this purpose. I could easily control both of them. However, I found that the hub would occasionally, without apparent cause, reset itself, causing the mouse and keyboard to be re-detected, flickering the keyboard backlight and triggering the beeps and chimes of the OS detected a connected device. Same occurred in two different power outlets, and multiple USB ports. It wasn't a major issue - everything was always redetected and working again within seconds, without my needing to do anything, but it was mildly annoying.

It is possible that it was one of my computers - the reason I was using it was that I was transitioning over to a new computer due to various issues, after all. Maybe the USB controller wasn't outputting a clean, consistent signal.

If you need this temporarily while transitioning over to a new system, or in a system which is isn't used that much, it should be fine. I wouldn't use it as a interface for my primary setup though.

title: Great memory, XMP to 3200 seems to work well
text:
I've been running two sets (total of 4x16GB) in my machine for a few months now. They work well - no memory issues whatsoever, I was able to clock it at ~2933 and 3200 without issue. Easy install.

Specs:

Ryzen 7 2700
MSI B450 Mortar Max on latest firmware

title: Perfect for meters
text:
These are perfect for keeping that spare 9V in your multimeter bag, or for whatever other tool you might use once once and find dead in a couple months because it got switched on in your bag. Previously I was keeping the battery in a small bag - because the contacts are close to each other and can be crossed pretty easily by a wayward bit of metal - but this is much better. Fits regular 9V, doesn't *quite* fit the lithiums, not a problem for most people.

Also great little boxes for spare parts, such as fuses if you are using a multimeter. Feels relatively robust - strong enough to keep in a case, maybe not to have bouncing around a metal toolbox with hammers and screwdrivers. Latches seems secure enough to stay closed under moderate jostling.

Would recommend.

title: Reliably steps up voltage to desired output
text:
I am specifically using these to step up 3v to either 5v (for USB devices) or 12v (for a strip of LEDs). I've set up two so far, and they work pretty well. The pot is very sensitive, so that you can bump it up by tenths of a volt or less. The pads are pretty easy to solder to. The power delivery is relatively clean, I have some flicker on the LED strip, but that seems to resolve itself fairly rapidly - for sensitive applications you might want to run through a capacitor to clean things up a bit.

The unit is moderately efficient, but becomes quite warm - when converting from 2xAAA Lithium batteries (3v) to 12v, with an approximate draw of 200mA the converter (both the top of the transformer and bottom of the board) temps at about 116F within three minutes or so of operation. Pretty warm, warmer than I would typically like. I might try hooking up a 9v instead to see if this knocks the temps down a bit, or if that fails, adding a thermistor to mitigate the risk of a thermal event.

Would recommend for general experimentation though.

title: Great for experimentation
text:
I purchased these strictly for experimentation when building circuits, specifically when attempting to integrate step up and buck converters with varying input voltages. There's plenty of test wires here, so I have no problem cutting them up, cutting them off, splicing them, and doing whatever else is needed. Wire is stout enough that I wouldn't mind using it in a finished circuit, at least for personal purposes. The pins are a bit wimpy, and they don't stick in the sockets all that well, but that is to be expected of this kind of connector, temporary only.

Only real complaint is that I'd like a set of only red/white/black, so it would be easier to track the charge throughout various connections. Other colors are okay, but with only two colors you can tell at a glance where everything is going. There are multiple red/white/black in this set, but getting to them requires peeling away other colors, which is suboptimal as it leaves them loose.

Would recommend.

title: Good for small projects, leads are a little flimsy
text:
These are great for small projects, the battery snaps in quite easily. Leads are a bit flimsy, though, it would be nice if they were a bit stouter. Also could use a small hole in the bottom to use to help ejecting the battery, but not strictly necessary.

Fit is otherwise good and current passes through as expected.

title: Passable, but unimpressive
text:
I purchased these for cleaning electronics contacts and circuit boards, using IPA and contact cleaner. They can perform this task better than q-tips, due to having a pointed foam tip - they leave no cotton threads behind when they are done - and they are quite useful for getting into small spaces (though not quite small enough to clean a micro-USB jack).

Better than q-tips, but otherwise deficient. The foam is very thin and doesn't hold up well to cleaning activities - every time I've used one, the foam has ended up torn and frayed within 30s. I always have to use two or three swabs to finish the job. It is possible that I'm not using them for their intended purpose - I often have to clean up small leads, solder pads, and chips which have sharp edges - but I'd like to see a little better durability from them.

I'll keep a few in my kit, and use them for cleaning smooth, delicate connectors, but I doubt I'd order them again.

title: Useful if you are connecting modules/expansion boards to internal USB headers.
text:
I purchased this because I was installing a small board which would allow me to reboot my system via a 2.4GHz remote control, something necessary because the system is some distance from my desk and am currently working on implementing an unconventional HW/SW virtualization setup which frequently hard locks on me. I would have attached the board directly to the MB, but as it turns out the graphics card is in the way; this is a relatively easy means of bypassing that issue by positioning the wireless receiver further from the motherboard.

It works quite well. The pins on the male side are delicate - you have to take care of them - and the wire is oddly beefy for what you are doing with it - but it does serve its purpose quite well. Would recommend for similar situations.

title: Great for a small apartment or upstairs WiFi router
text:
I purchased this specifically for my system in the upper-corner of the house, to compliment the main router in the basement and the first-floor router in the family room. The main draws of it were its reasonable range, decent price, and gigabit Ethernet jacks in the back, which allows me high-speed access to the NAS. I have been using it for almost two months now and am quite satisfied with its performance. I run mostly Ethernet up there; the WiFi is only for the smartphone and the tablets, which I rarely use while at home. So I can speak to the performance of the router's hardline connections more than its wireless ones.

I am an IT professional and work in system administration, among other domains, so setup for me was easy. The Archer offers more than sufficient customization options for a standard household, I found, but the basic guided setup option also seemed to me to be easy enough to follow. I don't think I'd recommend it as the primary router of a household of more than, say, three people or more than two floors, especially if data use is high, but it works as a secondary unit. I ended up setting it up with its own subnet, rather than making it a mere extender of the primary. I can send documents to the downstairs printer (all printers run via Ethernet to the primary router), but all traffic in that part of the house is kept local, which is fine for my purposes.

Would recommend.

title: Durable, practical caddy for storing cells near a charger
text:
I have a four-port charger I use to keep my 18650 cells topped off, and I like to keep the extras near at hand so I can swap them in as necessary. For that reason, I purchased a pair of these, one in black and one in orange, so I can easily tell one from the other. I have both protected and unprotected cells, and so I keep the four protected cells in one of these caddies and the unprotected ones in the other. Since the side of the caddy is open, I can tell which brand cell is inside for easy identification. If I need to take a sudden trip, I can bring a caddy with me and have an abundance of power at the ready. You can even insert the batteries into the caddy in either orientation, so I put used batteries in upside down and charged ones right-side up.

The caddy is strong and firmly holds the cells in place, and keeps everything in order. Not much more you can ask for in an item of this kind.

Would recommend.

title: Great for storing cells next to the charger
text:
I have a four-port charger I use to keep my batteries topped off, and I like to keep the extras near at hand so I can swap them in as necessary. For that reason, I purchased a pair of these, one in black and one in red. I have both protected and unprotected cells, and so I keep the four protected cells in one of these caddies and the unprotected ones in the other. Since the side of the caddy is open, I can tell which brand cell is inside for easy identification.

The caddy is strong and firmly holds the cells in place, and keeps everything in order. Not much more you can ask for in an item of this kind.

Would recommend.

title: Great, quite fans from a reputable company
text:
I just completed my new build, and decided to go with Noctua for the first time due to their stellar repuation. I'm running 2x 140mm and 1x 120mm in my Define Mini C, along with a Noctua nh-U12s chromax.Black CPU cooler. The whole thing operates with a quiet whoosh on startup, nice and gentle. The fans have some weight to them and a little springiness when starting and stopping. All have been operating for about three months now without any issue at all.

Installation was simple - no defects or even blemishes, the build quality on these is quite good. No power tools needed, of course.

I ran a couple cablemod fan power cables right to the fans themselves for a cleaner, more consistent look, but otherwise, I can't think of any complaints. A little overpriced, I suppose, but given the fact that the fans are going to stay with the system for its entire life, I'm not going to complain.

Would recommend.

title: Quiet, powerful
text:
Noctua makes great fans, and I'm pretty satisfied with these. I'm running 2x 140mm and 1x 120mm in my Define Mini C, along with a Noctua nh-U12s chromax.Black. The whole thing operates with a quiet whoosh on startup, nice and gentle. The fans have some weight to them and a little springiness when starting and stopping. All have been operating for about three months now without any issue at all.

Installation was simple - no defects or even blemishes, the build quality on these is quite good. No power tools needed, of course.

I ran a couple cablemod fan power cables right to the fans themselves for a cleaner, more consistent look, but otherwise, I can't think of any complaints. A little overpriced, I suppose, but given the fact that the fans are going to stay with the system for its entire life, I'm not going to complain.

Would recommend.

title: Durable, functional, a bit hefty
text:
