title: So far, so good
text:
I've been having occasional network issues. I have 75/75 Fios and have been using a ~5 year old verizon router as my main wired router (wifi is off). I have a separate mesh system for wifi. So, there's one cord that goes in for the WAN connection, and two that go out for the LAN: (1) Moca connection to a switch for wired machines, (2) main wifi AP.

We see sluggishness with 3 simultaneous video meetings. My corp laptop often has DNS issues after it comes out of sleep. The app controlling the mesh wifi is often surprisingly sluggish.

I got one of these ER-X boxes Friday. When I connected it to my computer, it didn't show the wizard, but holding the reset button for 10 seconds and powercycling fixed that. I found a Youtube video to guide me through basic setup for a home network. Those instructions were great and even pointed out some ways to make it faster via command line config. I love the fact that I can ssh into the box, though I laughed when I saw python running (I'm guessing for the web server).

I used iperf3 to test speeds. Upload didn't change (~78Mbps), but there was an increase in download (85Mbps vs. 77Mbps tested w/ old router). Also, everything involving the router seems faster and more responsive. And, the issues I noticed previously have disappeared (though we have yet to try with 3 video meetings simultaneously).

Before buying this, I had been trying to put openwrt on a cheap tp-link router. I got this after many tries with openwrt. So far, the ER-X is everything I wanted. One bonus was that it identified the fact that the incoming ethernet cable only supports 100Mbps. I have a Verizon upgrade in 1.5 weeks, so I know to make sure they upgrade the cable.

Update: Have had this for appx. 9 months now. It's rock solid. Current uptime is over 4 months. I've never seen slowness due to this router. Speed test records 500Mbps down 260Mbps up on a 400/400 Fios connection.

title: Lots to like, but somewhat flaky
text:
Been using for a few months now. Initially seemed like an excellent upgrade over an inexpensive single wifi router, but I've seen enough issues that I'm not sure I'd buy again. The worst failure was when I switched from Verizon Fios coax to ethernet and tried to use this as my main router. It worked... for about a week. At first, I just had trouble connecting to corp sites, so I thought it might be my corp network. Later that day, I saw issues with personal devices. Connecting to the router web page was super sluggish and the cpu was pegged. The next day, I went back to using the verizon router as the wired backbone and only using this set for wifi---much better. But, I still see occasional flakiness. Yesterday, one of the units wouldn't connect. I brought it closer to the other units---no dice. I rebooted. I connected it to the network via an ethernet cable. Finally, I rebooted the main/router unit and things went back to normal. Every 2-4 weeks one of the units has issues. Sometimes rebooting that unit is enough. Occasionally I have to reboot the main unit. One of the extender units connects via both wifi and powerline. The other extender unit only connects via powerline (it's too far to use wifi). The powerline-only unit is the one that tends to have issues. But, that was the point of buying this system.

So, the system seems good as long as you don't mind doing a ~weekly reboot. I see about 30Mbps over the powerline-only unit---not fast, but generally reliable.

I've started using MoCA (ethernet over coax) and will likely use that as my backbone in the near future---it's faster (I've seen ~300Mbps for a local transfer over MoCA/ethernet/wifi) and seems to be more reliable than this tp-link set over powerline.

Edit: I ditched this in favor of an EdgeRouter X and Ubiquity access points and am happier now. The Deco system was okay, but far from ideal.

title: Perfect for extending a network via coax
text:
It's important to understand what this is and is not. Considering the low price, I got it hoping that maybe I could use it to ditch my VZ Fios router. No dice---the coax light didn't come on when I disabled my VZ router. However, I found that the VZ router produces a MoCA signal over the coax line. So, with the VZ router connected, you can connect this to any coax in the house (assuming all your coax lines are connected) to yield a wifi or ethernet access point. This is similar to powerline adapters, but better because the speeds are higher.

Update: I'm now using two of these devices to extend my network via coax (to somewhere that would be difficult to wire via ethernet). My computer is connected to #1 via ethernet. #1 is connected to #2 via coax. #2 is connected to my router via ethernet. Now I understand that these are essentially repeaters which convert to/from MoCA. I'm about to have my Fios updated and converted from coax to ethernet. I'll be able to ditch the VZ router and connect my mesh wifi router to the main Fios cable. But, my computer isn't close to the Fios box, so I'll use these two devices and existing coax wiring to connect my computer (and other devices that need regular cables). Since the coax I'll be using is all internal (and my ethernet will be protected by my mesh router firewall), I won't need a coax filter.

Speed test screenshot is for a 75/75 Fios so the two devices don't seem to slow the speed at all---I get about the same with a direct ethernet connection.

Edit: This was the perfect solution for a room that only had coax wiring (where it wasn't worth running ethernet). Speeds max out around 150/200 (I now have a 400/400 Fios connect).

title: I'm impressed
text: I have a large house (> 2500 sf, 80 ft long) with modern-ish wiring (circuit breakers, 100 amp, 2nd panel was added in a 1990 addition). This worked exactly as the instructions described. For wiring that was on the same breaker box (but far enough away that wifi from the router was poor, around -70 dBm), I saw excellent speeds of 50+Mbps over wifi connected to the extender both up and down. I have Fios that goes up to 75-80 Mbps. For wiring that was on the 2nd box (so it had to go over a longer circuit to get to the adapter box wired to my router), speeds were a bit slower, around 30 Mpbs, but plenty fast as far as I'm concerned. I'm buying a 2nd extender so that I can have one extender at each end of my house. Oh, and copying my ssid/password/channel to the extender was a cinch. I found that I had to turn wifi off and back on again to get my device to connect to the nearest adapter, otherwise it was a piece of cake.

title: This is what you want for a normal desktop system
text:
At first I was confused about which Ryzen 3rd gen compatible board to get. After reading through specs, I learned that this was it. Here's what this board does NOT have:

- no RAID
- multiple PCIe x16 video card slots (i.e. no multi-card crossfire)

Here's what it has:

- BIOS updated for Ryzen 3rd gen (note that you will want to update to something more recent: mine came with a BIOS from August, I updated to October)
- 4 SATA ports
- 1 PCIe x16 slot
- 1 M.2 SLOT
- 4 DDR4 (3866Mhz max) slots for up to 64 gigs of memory
- built-in video w/ VGA, DVI and HDMI ports in rear
- lots of USB

My OS is Ubuntu 18.04 LTS. The on-board video didn't seem to work at first, so I tried the GeForce GT 1030 and that worked great. I didn't go back to trying the on-board video. I did need to make some updates to Ubuntu to eliminate some weird crashes (see howtogeek article on installing version 5 kernel and linuxconfig article on getting the latest nvidia drivers).

After updating my bios and setting the memory to 3200Mhz (it incorrectly detected 2400Mhz), the multi-core Geekbench came out ~10% higher than the normal score for my cpu (no OC), so MSI is doing something right. BIOS menu is graphical and easy to navigate.

Here are the rest of the parts I used to build my system:

- Ryzen 5 3600
- Timetec 2x16GB DDR4 3200MHz
- GIGABYTE GeForce GT 1030
- Thermaltake Smart 430W 80+

title: Impressive value; excellent cooler
text:
I upgraded a 6 yo machine, so I had HDs and an ATX case. Besides this, I installed:

- MSI ProSeries (B450M PRO-VDH Max)
- Timetec 2x16GB DDR4 3200MHz
- GIGABYTE GeForce GT 1030
- Thermaltake Smart 430W 80+

Geekbench lists 6920 as the typical Ryzen 5 3600 score. After updating to the latest stable bios (which was surprisingly easy) and manually setting the memory to 3200Mhz (auto setting was 2400Mhz), the system benchmarks at 7525 for muti-core (geekbench), slightly ahead of the Intel Core i7-9700K which is 8 core and almost twice as expensive. I don't game, but Chrome rendering is tons faster vs. my old machine.

Installing the hardware was easy. The fan had thermal paste pre-applied to the bottom, so after popping the cpu into the mobo and removing the fan brackets intended for other designs, it was easy to screw the fan into place.

Note that "Max" is MSI's indication that a board is Ryzen 3rd gen ready.

I initially had random crashes (Ubuntu 18.04 LTS). I learned that I needed to enable more recent versions of software. I followed a guide on howtogeek that described how to install version 5 of the kernel (plus some other goodies). I also found that I needed to install recent nvidia proprietary drivers (linuxconfig). After doing all that, the system seems completely stable.

title: Doesn't Fit
text:
I would love to give a higher rating, but I think "1 star" is the only way to summarize my experience with this product.

Amazon shipped quickly (as usual). I tried to put it together the night it arrived. It comes in 3 pieces: base, arm, and monitor. The only instructions were a simple diagram showing how they roughly fit together. The base and arm fit together nicely, but the arm would not snap into the monitor. I could see how it was designed to snap together, but the metal part was too large to fit into the space on the back of the monitor. I could technically place the monitor on top of the arm+base, but it was very loose and could easily fall over if bumped slightly.

I called Acer tech support, hoping there was some trick I couldn't figure out. There wasn't. After suggesting that I push harder (I had already pushed hard enough that I was worried about breaking the monitor), go back to the store for assistance (huh?), and return the entire monitor, they agreed to send a replacement part.

1.5 weeks later, I called back asking for a status update on the part. I was informed that the part hadn't been ordered (huh?) and that I could call back the next day to have it ordered (wtf?). The rep agreed that this was a less-than-wonderful customer experience, but explained that there was nothing she could do (she wasn't allowed to place the replacement part order).

At that point, I gave up and started the return process with Amazon (which, btw, is always awesome when I have to do it).

So, I guess this is mainly a review of Acer QA and customer service, both of which completely failed for me. Considering the other reviews, I'm hoping that my experience is rare, but I'll be trying a different brand for my next monitor.

title: Excellent value
text:
You can read other reviews to hear complaints about Windows 8.

This is an excellent piece of hardware for the price. Without any upgrades, desktop graphics in Ubuntu are very snappy; I expected to have to install a separate video card, but see no need to. The RAM is upgradeable to 16gb by adding two 4g simms (there are 4 slots; 2 are filled).

The build itself is reasonable. For example: There is no case fan, but the case is designed for one so it would be easy to add. But, I see no need---the machine runs very cool (<35C cpu temp at low cpu usage).

There is one spare 5.25" bay (e.g. 2nd DVD) and one spare 3.5" bay (e.g. 2nd internal HD). There is adequate spacing for air flow around the 3.5" bays. There is no mount for a front case fan, but I think the 3.5" bay spacing is sufficient for low-to-moderate usage.

This is an energy efficient machine. I plan to keep it running 24/7 and am happy to see that it consumes 45-50 watts when idle-ish in Ubuntu (measured using a kill-a-watt).

I was confused by the location of the DVD eject button: it's on the right side of the DVD bay.

To enter the BIOS, press the DEL key repeatedly during startup. If that doesn't work at first, try "restart" from Windows. Try using a PS2 keyboard (purple circular connector).

The machine uses UEFI. UEFI is is common on new machines, but was uncommon a few years ago and is likely a reason why installing a different operating system is not as straightforward as one would expect. Note that along with UEFI comes a different hard disk partition scheme: GPT (instead of the older MBR). I had trouble installing Ubuntu, but was eventually successful. Should be easier now since I helped isolate a bug in the boot-repair package.

Reinstall tips:

* From the BIOS, try disabling SecureBoot and/or FastBoot.
* If installing Ubuntu, start with the Ubuntu UEFI community documentation (not the older UEFIBooting page)
* If nothing else works, try enabling CSM (Compatibility Support Module), which should allow you to boot without UEFI. Note that you'll need to revert your disk to using MBR---I had mixed success with CSM.

The Motherboard is Acer AAHD3-VC. The BIOS is American Megatrends Aptio. I found that Tiger Direct's "Specifications" page had more useful details about this machine.

title: Great camera except for indoor no flash shots
text:
First, the bad: indoor, no flash pictures are poor. We took about 60 pictures this weekend for my brother's graduation, about half inside with no flash, and only 4 of them came out okay. Even the "good" ones weren't particularly sharp when I reduced them to 800x600. We mostly took pictures of people; any movement on the part of the subject or the camera made the picture very blurry. Guess it's using a slow shutter speed to compensate for the low light, though I'm surprised that it's as bad as it is! Though, this is the only digital camera that I've used, so it might just be that I had high expectations
Besides indoor no flash shots, this camera is great. It's pretty. It has some weight to it which makes it feel more solid. It's small---it easily slips into a jeans or shirt pocket. The lithium battery that comes with the battery is great---it lasts forever. The camera comes with a charger. I used the camera off and on over the weekend (~60 pictures) and didn't run out of battery. Outdoor shots are sharp and the colors are good. The memory is pretty speedy. I transferred over 100 meg worth of pictures in just a few minutes. Oh, and since the battery is so good, you don't need to worry about buying one of those special download hookups. Just plug the USB cable into the camera and start downloading!
One thing that I particularly love (being the computer geek that I am) is that I can mount the camera as a USB drive under linux, no special software needed. I just "mount -t vfat /dev/sda1 /mnt/usb" and copy the files over. No hassling with Windows!
In summary, if you don't mind using the flash for indoor pictures, this is a great little camera, well worth the money.

title: Only cancels about 5% of noise
text:
I thought "They're cheap, why not?" I expected that Sony would at least make a semi-descent product, but I was wrong. They only cut out about 5% of ambient noise. I tested them in a lot of different environments and it didn't perform well under any circumstance.

I compared them to a pair of low-end headphones ($20) to set a baseline, see below.

Test:
In flight - no noticeable difference between each pair
While driving - slightly better muffling of midrange noise, but slight (2% better)
Fan on high & low - slightly better canceling of low freq noise (2% better)
In crowed auditorium - slight better muffling (1% better)

They barely did any better than the cheap-o, non-noisecanceling, over the ear headphones I got for half the price.

The biggest thing I noticed is that the very little amount of noise that was actively cancelled was replaced fully by a hissing sound. This made the headset pretty much useless.

I would recommend not buying these headphones. I returned the set I bought, and got my money back. There are better headsets at this price.

title: Easy setup. Works perfect
text:
I have read some of the reviews with people complaining that they had problem getting them to work.
I don't know how the setup and operation could be any easier.
They are fantastic.
Just plug one into your existing ethernet network using the wide area network ethernet port.
Then run the Google Home app and add device.
It will even tell you if you have plugged into the wrong ethernet port.
Then plug in the second router on the other side of your house and run the Google Home app to add that device.
It becomes an extender to the first one you installed.

Works perfect in my house with no dropouts and a wireless speed of 450 Mbps.

title: Excellent 4k with HDMI but Displayport and USB-C has bad Colors
text:
When I first connected this LG 27UK850-W 27" monitor to my 2017 27" iMac, I was very disappointed in the colors.
I tried the USB-C and Displayport connections and they both looked really bad. I could not get the whitepoint color set correctly. It was never pure white.
When you have it connected that way, you are limited by the picture adjustments you can make with the monitor controls. So you need to use the display panel controls in MacOS to do the color adjustments.
But I could never get the colors to look good that way.

So I gave up and used the 4K HDMI connection and the colors look perfect.
When you use the 4K HDMI connection, you can customize all of the picture adjustments the way you want them.
I was able to adjust the colors and whitepoint to look the same as my iMac screen.
And it looks just as sharp with HDMI as it does with USB-C or Displayport.

So I am happy with this monitor. It looks just as good as my Retina iMac display.
I also like the adjustable stand which moves up and down and tilts.

Update 12/9/20
I returned my LG 27UK850-W 27" monitor and got the newer 2020 model LG 27UN850-W 27" Ultrafine monitor.
(Notice the "N" instead of "K" in the model number.)
The "N" model works perfect with my M1 Mac Mini using thunderbolt or HDMI

My network uses 10.0.1.xxx

You need to connect a computer directly with ethernet and log in to change the IP
A lot of reviews here say that the default IP address is 192.168.1.252

title: Weak Wireless but otherwise OK
text:
PROS:
Protects all internet connected devices in my home with no need to install software.
Works with my Apple Airport Extreme router. I am on Time Warner / Spectrum cable.
Just put the Airport Extreme in bridged mode and the Box 2 goes between my Cable modem and the Airport Extreme.
The Box 2 acts as the router and the Airport Extreme remains as my AC Wireless access point for my home.

Does not slow down internet traffic.

I also installed a Box 2 in my daughter's home. She has Verizon Fios with a uBee wireless router provided by Verizon.
The Box 2 is connected to the output of the uBee router. When you first do the setup, it clones the wireless settings of the uBee and then the Box2 becomes the wireless access point..

3/7/18 The latest firmware upgrade fixes port forwarding problems and lets you select the IP address range you want instead of forcing you to use 172.xxx.xxx.xxx

CONS:
If you need to use the wireless with this box, it has a poor range.
Also, it uses the same wireless name for both 2 Ghz and 5 Ghz which is very confusing.
When you go farther away from the box, the signal gets weaker and it switches from 5 Ghz to 2 Ghz and you have no idea that it did it.
Then when you move closer, it is stuck on the slower 2Ghz connection.
Also, if you try to use a Netgear range extender to get more wireless range, the range extender will try to connect to both 2 Ghz and 5 Ghz but will only be able to connect to 2 Ghz for a slow connection.

title: Good system, budget friendly, but lacks any personalization
text:
I’m 50/50 on the Blink XT2. It’s a decent system that has non contractual usage, which is very awesome... I just find a couple of issues with the system performance. There are no options for notification updates or changes to the system and the only tone that it will play doesn’t not work all me up at night. Also, you can arm the system on a schedule, which is cool, but again system options are limited. I have cameras that surround my house but, my dogs are always setting off the backyard cams... which happens all day and night. You can’t just arm the front yard cameras for all day use while turning off the rear cameras so the dogs don’t set them off in the day time. This means if you’re armed and home, your phone will go off alllllllllll day, and basically be ineffective for monitoring. We have a pool so all day long I’m also going in and out the house and it just adds to the notifications. I hoped this unit would allow more function in settings but it’s just very basic. There are a couple neat Alexa add one, but I refuse to buy Alexa for several reasons and feel there is a ploy to have to buy Alexa when those features like voice announcements or lights turning on upon motion. I like the system for its purpose, but the function and personalization falls flat on its face and that’s the reason it’s not 5 stars. I’ve read posts and there is AMPLE feedback to Blink/Amazon to correct the notifications (again notification ringer is ineffective unless awake and CANNOT BE CHANGED) but isn’t fixed. I have iphone, heard android users have a little more function??? Yet another uncorrected design flaw.

Also, the system crashes from WiFi for no identified reason and requires you to mess with the system. Doesn’t take long but had this a week and happened twice while I’m out and renders the system useless.

Another issue is that there is a 10-15 second delay to speak live through the cameras, even with early detection on. Still helpful, but trying to talk to someone through the cameras, like a delivery guy or unexpected guest, creates a lot of awkward conversations through the system.

Ideally... it works, and will help, but personalization and lack of settings to help your needs of the system can find a lot of improvement and hope these system flaws are improved as they are completely within the ability to improve function of their designs. Had these issues not been present the system would get 5 stars as the cameras are great, the system is very easy to install and get going, adds piece of mind that you otherwise wouldn’t have with out a high dollar monthly contract. All in all, it’s an improvement to safety, but many things can improve to make it effective and useful. Until then, it’s just bland

title: Great TV, Especially For The Money
text:
Had this for a few days now and it's been wonderful. In low light, the picture is perfect. In daylight, the edges can look a little dark, but it's still damn fine. The brightness is almost too much, but the dynamic picture settings seem to adjust the set with excellent results.

Could be easier to adjust between aspect ratios, but that's a small matter. The fact that the you can manually adjust the positioning of the image in different aspect ratios is nice, too, so you can, for instance, include or exclude the tickers or captions along the bottom of the screen. The generous amount of inputs is fantastic and so is the fact that they thought ahead and put them all within easy reach on the right side, not hidden away in the back like most others. When you have an 80 pound TV, it's nice not to have to move the thing to hook up a DVD player or cable box.

Looking forward to not having to replace bulbs thanks to the LED technology and not worrying about burn in. The picture is much more film-like than LCD or plasma - a great touch if you're a movie fan and like the look and feel of being in the cinema.

Speakers and sound are good, much better than most others. The surround sound mode really brings things to life. Of course, there is no substitute for adding a real surround sound system....

Last but not least, everything considered, for the money this is an unstoppable value. For less then $2000, you get a huge 61" screen with 1080p, good sound, lots of features, and intuitive design and usability. Helluva deal on a helluva TV!

Only docked it one star (would have docked it 1/2 star, but you can't do that here) because of its performance in high light condition, even though I almost never use it in those conditions. Buy it and enjoy!

title: GREAT DEVICE BUT PRIME SOFTWARE GETTING WORSE
text: I've been using Amazon FireStick and Amazon Prime video exclusively for TV viewing for almost 9 years. I don't even have cable, and I don't miss it a bit. In all that time, I only replaced my FireStick once, and that was because I stupidly lost the remote, and it arrived in about 4 hours thanks to Amazon Prime Now. It is high quality and very easy to use. But like most tech companies, Amazon keeps producing "upgrades" to the Prime Video channel software that sacrifice basic functions for bells and whistles. Movies are no longer included on the RECENTS list, and since I view documentaries I use to teach in my college classrooms, I do sometimes need to view a film more than once to ensure my notes are correct. Also, if I fell asleep watching a movie, it used to be easy to find it to watch again. Sometimes, even a TV series I'm watching disappears from the RECENTS list, even though it was there the day before. As with most "upgrades," each version gets a little bit worse in terms of basic functionality. I never upgrade software when I have a choice, but we're not given a choice in this case. Tech companies need to learn the expression "if it ain't broke, don't 'fix' it."

title: GREAT IMPROVEMENT OVER STANDARD MOUSE BUT NOT WORTH $78
text:
UPDATE FEB 2023 -- This is an excellent mouse. But it isn't worth $78. Similar devices are available for half that.

ORIGINAL FIVE-STAR REVIEW -- No matter what you do, a standard mouse and mouse pad become difficult to use after a time. I don't know whether the mouse surface gets worn down or the mouse pad does.

This is a vast improvement. I've been using one for a couple of years. It doesn't wear down. I'm not constantly picking the mouse up and moving it -- sometimes several times for one task. The mouse doesn't even have to be on the same surface as the computer, which adds flexibility, especially when you're using a laptop.

It's DEFINITELY better than the new generation of mouse that doesn't use batteries and has to be plugged in to charge. The plug has to go IN THE BOTTOM OF THE MOUSE, rendering it useless until it's charged. If I have work I need to get down, I don't have hours to wait for my mouse to work. Maybe someday tech people will learn the phrase "If it ain't broke, don't 'fix' it." Few things actually improve with "upgrades."

title: Are These Dangerous or Are the Designers Stupid?
text: I have a problem with the way ALL surge protectors are designed. Why can't they add plates with holes on each end so we can screw them into or onto cabinets, under counters, etc.? I am disabled and cannot get down onto or up off the floor. I have to keep these on table tops so I can plug in the endless chargers necessitated by modern technology. Since tech companies can't be consistent in how they shape and size transformers (I use all Apple products, and they can't be consistent within their own company), we have to be creative to get even three plugs to fit into a six-outlet adapter. Then the stupid surge protector falls on the floor, and we have to fish it out from under and behind furniture, along with transformers/plugs that have all been pulled out and then do the whole jigsaw puzzle again. The third time a day this happens, I let loose some serious profanity about the people who design the surge protectors. WE NEED TO BE ABLE TO ATTACH THEM TO/UNDER COUNTERS SO THEY STAY WHERE WE NEED THEM. How difficult is that for these brain trusts to figure out? It makes me wonder if surge protectors are such a fire hazard on the whole that it's dangerous to attach them to structures, which means they are actually too dangerous to use. What's the story? Are surge protectors dangerous, or are their designers just stupid?

title: Nice Solution to Portability Issue Created by Apple
text:
This just arrived, and it seems perfect. My 2017 13-inch MacBook Pro fits in perfectly. The front pockets provide ample space for even my trackball mouse and the cables we have to have to use ANYTHING external since Apple decided to create bus ports that nothing will fit into.

Of course, if I didn't need those darned little cables, I wouldn't need a case at all. Thank God someone's out there to protect us in at least small ways from the problems created by the engineered obsolescence that is putting us in debt almost as much as healthcare costs.

Here's a hint, Apple and other tech companies. Weight isn't the only factor in portability. Anything gained in that area by the thin profile of this MacBook is lost because it's necessary to carry two or three little cables with me. The more pieces I have to cart, the greater the chance something will get lost. I feel the same way about eliminating DVD drives. Not EVERYTHING is on the Web, and free Net access isn't available EVERYWHERE. I feel like I'm spending more money for less functionality.

I haven't bought an external DVD drive yet because I'm running out of ports, but I think one might fit in the larger outside pocket. I'm not entirely sure, but the pocket is a nice size, so I think it might.

title: The review that couldn't wait.
text:
Ordered at 7am PDT
Received at 5pm PDT
Plugged it in with the very very simple 6 step instruction. Don't let this fool you though. It's as easy as plugging in a cord into an outlet.
( note: do not use a power strip. It must be plugged directly into the wall.

No additional configuration was necessary. it just started working.

background: I needed this for my ps4, which is about 40 feet away from the router and hits 2-3 walls. I get about 300Mbps with Spectrum, but down at the 2.4 frequency. I can receive about 40-50Mbps depending on the strength of the the radio card on the device. The original PS4 wifi card is notorious for being extremely poor in quality. I was receiving about 2Mbps down and 599Kbps up. Yes, you read that right. a modern PS4 on a 2.4 frequency was getting shitty thruput. While at the same time, my other devices on a 2.4 frequency were receiving 10x that, even more on a 5g frequency.

I plugged in this unit and immediately got 10Mbps down and 5Mbps up. It's not a game changer, but will suffice.
Update after 12 hours: Reset the modem and did another speed test on the ps4. 25Mbps down and 10Mbps up.

text:
This case, overall, is very nice and sturdy. It looks a lot like a MacBook Pro or Air type design, But, it has its flaws. First off, the IPad Air II is NOT fully secured in place. So when you open and close, you have to continually push it back into place on the bottom, where there is a two centimeter-ish gap. This is a cause for concern as you are continually rubbing and most likely scratching your device. Huge downfall In My opinion, the case should hold the device securely and not move. SECOND and far biggest flaw is the so called ‘release’ button. Unless you have a 2-3 year old child’s help, your fingers will never fit even close to pushing the release button. This is utterly ridiculous that they advertise that it is so simple to release the iPad in the case that doesn’t fit the iPad correctly from the keyboard part. LAST but not least, the case DOES NOT line up once it’s closed. Instead of being straight and flat, there is a gap in the middle, which causes it to NOT shut the screen off unless you push on it, which then dislodges yours IPad the 2ish centimeter as explained before. See images for gaps!

These flaws are a huge disappointment because the overall looks and design of this keyboard case is really nice. The rubber feet are hard to find and a really good addition. Unlike Cooper Cases, you don’t have to click the keyboard for 5 seconds to get it out of sleep mode, and it saves the color.

title: One of the best things I've bought in a long time!
text:
I'm an organization freak and have been trying to figure out a way to organize the cords for my tech toys expecially during travel when I came upon this. The simple solution to my problem is to throw them in a bag, but that doesn't keep the cords from getting tangled. I could have bound the cords before throwing them in the bag, but the hassle of keeping track of the twisty ties, rubber bands, Velcro, or carrying tape around to re-tape them is too annoying. So when I came across the idea of a trapper keeper for cords and such I was excited! Will probably buy more in the future: one for general keeping while at home and one specifically for when I travel.

Pros:
-Love the bright color, will be so easy to spot wherever I am: bedroom/hotel, inside my backpack/luggage, in the car
-Double zipper pull tabs on both outside zippers with nicely sized pull tabs bearing the logo are very convenient and stylish
-Material and design reminds me of trapper keepers from back in the 90s: keeps everything organized! Plus, it feels somewhat water resistant but yet to be tested.
-Designed to have bulky stuff in it and still close!
-Well thought out design for organizing various things
-1ST COMPARTMENT:
--Can fit a lot of cords in varying lengths, the shorter cords I put in one of the zippered pockets.
--Elastic bands keep the cords from falling out, even when shaken while the compartment is open. It will be very handy while traveling or when not using a stable surface.
-2ND COMPARTMENT
-Bigger pockets for bigger things: plugs, power banks, small tablets, calculators, slim P&S cameras even
--2 pockets (1/3 & 2/3 of the length top to bottom) with elastic openings on one side. Pockets have pleats in them to store bulky items.
--1 large zippered pocket with pleats on the other side to store bulky items

Cons:
-Would be nice to have a plastic window pocket on the outside for an ID or business card just in case the item gets lost or left behind. (On the outside so that people won't need to open the compartments in order to contact the owner.)

title: $12 open box on Amazon?  Can't go wrong with this router for basic home needs...
text:
I have the 1300 Asus series at my work studio in the city and I love how many features it has, including the simple user interface. We purchased a vacation home in Wisconsin and needed a simple, cheap router with lots of options for bandwidth control and guest networks because we rent the home out. I found this 1200 series Asus for just $12 open box (and they have a LOT of returned units here!) and I'm super happy with it.

We don't have the fastest internet speed (like 25mb), so it's nice to have multiple wifi networks that I can throttle - one for my family (8mb), one for guests (5mb), and then the main 5G signal I use for work in case I need a fast connection for meetings and such. And then I use the QOS feature to super throttle our kids tablets down to like 4mb because...well they don't need their videos to load in HD quality and RIGHT NOW...they can wait haha!

Apparently the #1 complaint with Amazon user reviews is that the main LAN in/out master port is only 10/100 speed, not gigabit. For anyone that has less than 100mb connection, it doesn't matter. I dunno about everyone else, but the fastest line we have (even at my work place) is only 30mb. The connection at our cottage is only like 25mb.

But there are always going to be speed-junkies who look at pure numbers. This isn't the router for you if you want that pure speed.

But again - $12 - what do you expect? Even at its new $45 price tag, this Asus has SO many features. QOS, up to 6 guest networks (3x 2.4g and 3x 5g), and decent enough wifi strength. We have a 1500SF main level home and it reaches to all the corners of the house and basement without issue - in the FARTHEST part of the basement sometimes it gets down to 1 bar, but we don't need the nets there...so...

Anyway - it's a solid wifi router for basic home needs under 100mb connections. If you need something fast, you'll need to spend more than $50: don't get pissy about a basic router not fulfilling your not-basic needs!

title: Incredible range!  I recommend using high quality wifi router connected to their LAN port.
text:
**update - no more drop issues - in my review below I was having internet drop-outs, but I found out it was an issue with my source wifi connection. The CC Vector device is amazing and I'm super happy with it. The best way to sum it up, is that it's not a super "smart" device - so you'll need to connect to a strong source wifi signal - if you get ANY kind of drop out issues with the source wifi, you'll have issues. But if you have a WIFI source that is strong and consistent, this will allow you to connect to it from very far distances. I'm very happy with it!

**original review below**

We needed to get a wifi signal across a property to another building about 600 feet away, a property with scattered trees between the 2 locations. Nothing seemed to work, and I was hesitant to spend $300 for a solution, and I didn't want to pay for another internet line to the other building. I tried a few cheaper $100-$150 solutions, but they simply didn't work. The CCrane kit worked right away. It did take about an hour or so to assemble and setup, and it was by far the easiest long-range wifi solution in terms of the technical setup - it's no different than setting up a basic wifi range extender/repeater.

We connected the CCrane repeater to a 200Mb/s wifi connect connection, and with a 60% signal we were getting only about 10Mb/s download rate - it was slow, but usable. We generally range from 45-75% signal performance with where we setup the receiver antenna. I would HIGHLY recommend putting it as high as you can - we got about double performance when we put the antenna 15 feet high vs. 6 feet high (6 feet high gave us 10MB/s performance, 15 feet up we got about 18MB/s performance)

After a few months of on and off performance, I started to get tired of the slow and unreliable WIFI signal. It worked...good enough for browsing, but not good enough for taking business calls, Zoom meetings, etc. Wifi calling would constantly be unclear. We also ran into dead internet issues: a few times a week the wifi signal seemed fine, but would not allow for any internet activity and I'd have to turn off and turn on the wifi rebroadcaster to make it work again.

I almost gave up, but I decided to try to use the ethernet ports on the back of the unit. There is one wifi antenna and 2 ethernet ports on the CCrane unit. I simply stopped using the CCrane wifi, and I plugged an Asus AC1200 wifi router into the back of the CCrane unit. BOOM - we went from 10Mb/s performance up to 60Mb/s performance. NOW everything feels right. This number would be accurate - CCrane does say you get about 1/2 the performance of the base internet because it's a repeater and that's what they do.

Unfortunately I still get random internet drops - the CC Vector repeater will say it's connected to the internet, signals are strong, but the internet will not work. This happens about once a day and we have to reboot for it to work again. I'm currently working with their support to see if this can be resolved. (review update - this was because of an issue with the source wifi signal - I ended up connecting a Wavlink Ariel HD2 bridge to the source WIFI router, and now we're getting very strong and consistent speeds without any dropouts).

So all-in-all - I'm happy with it. The included CCrane wifi could use some technology improvements and updates, but I think they make these things for random couples who RV around the country and don't need blazing internet.

Once you bypass the CCrane wifi and use the ethernet in the back with your own high performance WIFI router, you'll notice much improved performance.

I hope they update the built in WIFI - it would have been nice to just use one router with a $300 setup!

title: Off camera is fine, but I'm unimpressed with on-camera recycle time
text:
I've been using the TT685N for years now, and I was excited to upgrade to the V1-N flash. I purchased 2 of them - one for on-camera, and one for off-camera. The on-camera, when shooting relatively slowly, is really fun and it works great. Thing is, for fast photographing, such as with wedding dance floors, intros, speeches, etc, the recycling time is painfully slow. I was shocked at how long the recycle time was, even when using ISO 800, 160 shutter, f/2.2 - this wouldn't require much light from a flash. My SB-700 can shoot 4-5 frames in a row without skipping a beat.

That said, it's a wonderful flash for off-camera, since I mostly shoot at around 1/64 and 1/32 settings in manual - and for that function it recycles fast enough. The reason I'm keeping it for the off-camera is because I don't have to charge AA batteries with this flash, and I really appreciate the magnetic modifiers. And on that note, the modifiers don't seem like quality construction - they were much lighter and cheaper feeling that I expected.

So yeah, give it a go, but be sure it fits your specific needs before committing to it!

title: Very happy with it!  Very similar to the BC-700
text:
I've been using the BC-700 for years now, but I can't stand how the buttons on them need to be pressed so hard.

I got the BlueTech because the price was incredible. I'm actually really happy with it. It goes up to 1000mah charging, which I was surprised about, and I like the additional 5V USB out charger port on it, too.

I use 2800mah rechargeable batteries, and I like to test/refresh them about once a month. Both of these functions work great, and the charger has all stats for display (voltage, mah rate, etc) - it really is a great charger for the price!

title: Love the charger, but batteries are not as good as Nikon brand.
text:
Disclosure: I was offered to purchase these EN-EL15 batteries/charger at a much reduced price for an honest review.

In my experience, aftermarket batteries take a few charge cycles to show their true colors. I've had aftermarket batteries gain almost 100% additional life after a few charges, and I've seen them go the other way. I will update this review after they go through 4-5 charge cycles, but the below review is after 1 initial charge and use.

When I first received, I charged the 2 batteries using the included USB charger - I do love this dual charger because it can charge 2x batteries at a time, and it's powered via USB port.

The quality of the charger and battery (construction) feel really good.

Unfortunately the batteries are not that great. I tested them on a Nikon Z6 and D850.

I used them at a wedding yesterday and below are the results:

- With the Z6 I got about 450 photos before it died. With Nikon brand battery I would have gotten about 800-900.

- With the D850 I got about 1400 photos before it died. With Nikon brand I would have gotten 2200-3000.

So for the price, I would just recommend getting Nikon brand batteries, because there's nothing worse than missing a shot because your battery dies.

For the casual photographer, these batteries might be fine.

I will update review when I go through a few charge cycles with these.

title: Works great!  Super happy that I can read XQD and SD at the same time
text: I was skeptical because I purchased this when there were no reviews, but I took a chance with it.  It actually works really well!  All at the same time I did the following and it still worked great:  plugged in an XQD card, an SD card, then an additional dual SD reader into the USB slot with 2 SD cards loaded into it - and the one USB port read all 4 cards - it was awesome!  I mainly got this just to read XQD and SD at the same time through the same USB port.  Speeds are spot on for USB 3 - so it's all good.  I guess time will tell on durability, so I can't speak on that yet.

title: Stunning lens - love it with my D850 and Z6 (after firmware update)
text: I've gone through a lot of 70-200's, and this is probably my favorite - it's just an all around really amazing lens - quick, accurate, and sharp.  The 3 VR/VC modes are really nice to choose from, too, and they actually work - I can handheld at 1/30th of a second and still get a sharp photograph, shockingly!  I was super bummed when it didn't work with the new Nikon Z6 at first, but then I saw there was a firmware update for the lens - you just need to purchase the additional Tamron Tap-in usb dock/console thing - it's a quick update and it now works with my Z6.  Overall one of my favorite lenses!  Tamron has really been stepping it up!  The lenses don't feel as professional as others, but they're good enough, and the optics are just stunning and accurate.

title: Absolutely amazing for basic full property coverage.  WAY better than wifi extenders.
text:
So I gotta first say that I'm not looking for any local gigabit connections with my home network - just reliable 2g/5g signal throughout the property. My main cable modem are in the corner basement of my home with my TV room, and I wanted coverage upstairs and in the detached garage, which is about 25 feet from my home, and about 70 feet from the cable modem and the primary Tenda Nova node in my basement (With the Tenda Nova installed, the garage node does switch between "good" and "fair" signal - but it does not effect the overall speed, and keep in mind it's going through the back of a TV, 3 home walls, my main electric box, and 2 garage walls to get to my garage utility room - that's pretty amazing!)

Previously I was having a heck of a time getting a good signal to the garage, event with a wifi extender (went through 2 of them with very broken and inconsistent results). With my prior Asus MIMO router (which is amazing!) my Amazon Tap was having trouble staying connected in the garage, and wifi was a inconsistent outside. I always wanted a whole home mesh router, but didn't want to spend $300 on it. The Nova system is absolutely fantastic for $100. They also have the model MW6, which does support gigabit, but as I said, I don't need that.

Also, their iPhone app is actually very convenient for both setup and monitoring the nodes and the overall usage - I was very skeptical about the app, but there are plenty of basic options like guest-network, QOS, firmware updating, maintenance rebooting, etc.

Setup is seriously a breeze. The only thing that I ran into was needing to turn off my modem, then turning it back on after initial plug in. It did not find the modem and internet connection type until I reset the modem - so be sure you do that! I setup the first note, set my own network information, and then connected the other 2 nodes. The other nodes connected and were up and running within about 2 minutes. Keep in mind the wifi signal goes in and out for about 2 minutes while it's connecting the other nodes, so just be patient and you'll see that they connect after about 2 minutes. So far, very satisfied - much much much better than wifi extenders! If you don't hear an update, then all is well!

**quick update - I read some reviews that said there is not a firewall in this router, but I contacted Tenda directly, and they said there IS a firewall: "Yes there is a firewall it is automatically enabled, if you need to get past it you can port forward." So good news there!

I also reconfigured where I placed the 3 nodes, and now I'm getting full/good signal on all of them, even in my garage. Still really happy with this kit!

title: Light, comfortable, good audio, good microphone, and the ANC is fine for $65 set of wireless headphones
text:
I wanted to find a cheaper alternative to my wife's wireless Bose headset, something with decent noise cancelling for flights and work. So far I've used Bose, the MPOW H5, Treblab, and Woltix with ANC.

Nothing will compare to Bose noise cancellation - but these Woltix are actually really nice for the money. The MPOW H5 don't have as good audio clarity as the Treblab, but at the end of the day I got noise cancelling headphones for the noise canceling. I ended up returning the Treblab and the MPOW H5 and I kept the Woltix because they are more comfortable than the MPOW and had the best low-price ANC. The MPOW also had some sound interference issues randomly when the ANC was on, and the Treblab had a slight hiss to them when ANC was on.

I ended up keeping the Woltix brand. They just work, they're very light, and they are not too tight on the ears. The Active Noise Cancellation isn't as good as Bose, but they actually work pretty well for a $65 set of wireless ANC headphones. For the price, I'm very happy.

The ONLY thing I don't like about these is that there is no battery meter display on my iPhone when these are connected via bluetooth. With the other brands there is a small battery meter. I have no idea when these are low, so I just charge them like once a week.

So, quick breakdown of my experience with these wireless ANC headsets:

Bose: Best noise cancellation, good audio, comfortable, but definitely expensive!
Treblab: Best audio, worst noise cancellation (you can hear a slight hiss when turned on), comfortable, but large and they don't fold down too small.
MPOW: Good audio, good noise cancellation, but was getting some weird sound interference with the ANC on sometimes. Tight on ears.
Woltix: Good audio, good noise cancellation, most comfortable (way lighter and less tight on the ears than the MPOW), and fold down the smallest. No battery meter displayed on phone.

title: The sound on these are first class - really great highs, mids, but ANC has slight hiss.
text:
I wanted to find a cheaper alternative to my wife's wireless Bose headset, something with decent noise cancelling for flights and work. So far I've used Bose, the MPOW H5, Treblab, and Woltix with ANC.

The sound on these are first class - really great highs, mids, and lows - tons of clarity (when active noise cancel is on...otherwise it sounds a bit muggy). Very comfortable and light. BUT - I got these because they are wireless with active noise cancellation, and although the ANC is effective, if you are in a quiet room you'll hear a slight hiss when the ANC is on - many people report the same thing in reviews, and it's true - you'll hear it. You won't notice this when music is on or during a flight. I often use these at coffee shops just to zone out and focus on work, and I could notice the slight hiss in quieter environments.

I've also used Bose, the MPOW H5, and Woltix with ANC. I didn't want to buy another Bose headset when my wife and I travel together. Nothing will compare to Bose noise cancellation, but the MPOW H5 and Woltix are actually really nice for the money. The MPOW H5 don't have as good audio clarity as the Treblab, but at the end of the day I got noise cancelling headphones for the noise canceling. I ended up returning the Treblab and the MPOW H5 and I kept the Woltix because they are more comfortable than the MPOW and had the best low-price ANC. The MPOW also had some sound interference issues randomly when the ANC was on.

So:

Bose: Best noise cancellation, good audio, comfortable, but definitely expensive!
Treblab: Best audio, worst noise cancellation (you can hear a slight hiss when turned on), comfortable, but large and they don't fold down too small.
MPOW: Good audio, good noise cancellation, but was getting some weird sound interference with the ANC on sometimes. Tight on ears.
Woltix: Good audio, good noise cancellation, most comfortable (way lighter and less tight on the ears than the MPOW), and fold down the smallest.

title: Works fine, but the life is way too short - 600-800 photographs on a D850.
text: Works fine in the new D850, but it doesn't last at all.  After 2 charges I'm still only getting about 600/700 photographs before it's totally dead.  I assume these 3rd party batteries take a few charges to see their full potential, but this is just junk.  Returning it.  I'm very happy with the RAVPower batteries I received with their dual charger.  Those last MUCH longer with about 2500 photos per battery.

title: Terrible!  Stay away from this stuff - does not evaporate and leaves dry residue on sensors.
text: This stuff is terrible - it does not evaporate completely - even 2 drops on a sensor swab and it still leaves too much wet residue on the sensors - when it does eventually dry it leaves dry marks on the sensor.  We've been doing this full-time for 5 years - we tried to clean a 6D, 5D-3, and Nikon D4, all of them left streaks and wet residue.  We followed directions.  Not recommended.  We are going back to the Eclipse cleaning solution.

title: Great for $35!  Averages about 4000 photos with my Nikon D4.
text:
So far so good! For $35 I can't complain. I have a Nikon D4 and photographed a wedding a 6 hour wedding this last weekend - it's down to 52% battery life and I took about 2100 photographs on it - so this battery is averaging about 4000 photos for a charge I'm guessing.

My official Nikon EN-EL18 batteries were getting old (age setting were at 1 on all 3 of mine) and I was only getting around 2000 photos per charge, which was no good because I don't like swapping batteries on wedding days.

I calibrated this battery when I first got it using my Nikon charger just to be sure it was charged completely.

I did notice that it slowly drains from 100% if I don't use the camera. After 4-5 days of sitting in the camera, it was down to about 96% charge, even with the camera off. But my Nikon batteries did the same thing, so I'm not worried.

Anyway - I'm happy with it! Really not bad for $35. I'll check in with everyone after this summer wedding season to let you know how it's holding up in its age.

title: Nicely built, but the sound is not clear.  Highs are muffled.
text:
For the price I couldn't expect much, but I did. I ended up returning these because the highs were muffled, and didn't sound natural. They are built very nicely, they look good, I like the cords included, but the sound just doesn't feel natural.

This was a good reminder to myself that I want something higher quality, and I shouldn't have been looking at this kind of price range to get that!

If you want good sound quality, I'd move on.

title: ALL of these reviews must be fake - this thing is a piece of junk!  USB ports do not work on 2015 12" MacBook Retina.
text: Piece of junk.  The reviews must be fake, they are way too vanilla.  The port doesn't fit snug into a 2015 12" MacBook retina.  The USB ports do not work.  Charging works fine, but that's about it.  Otherwise a total piece of crap.  I'm returning it.

title: Incredible picture and motion!  Upgraded from TCL and it's way better.  No HBO GO support is my only complaint.
text:
Really happy with this television! We upgraded from a TCL 48" and I couldn't be happier. We wanted a more crisp and clear picture that could handle blacks and dark shades better, and this Vizio delivers! The TCL we had was great for animated movies and shows, but the colors looked unrealistic and faded with most movies and shows.

This TV is intuitive, easy to use, clear, and has an amazing picture! Color reproduction is top, picture control is incredibly customizable, and apps are great.

The only thing I am not happy about is Vizio doesn't support HBO GO! We didn't know this until we had the TV for about a month. Not sure I would have purchased it had we known this, because now we have to connect our laptop or purchase a Roku to get that job done...

title: Not LTE compatible, but works great with 4G/2G signals on TMobile (as of Feb. 2016)
text:
First off: As of February 2016, this device only works with 4G/2G signals - so if you're expecting T-Mobiles new LTE coverage (which has been expanded, and is wonderful), don't! It's a fine device to use in big cities, but once you start heading out on the highways, small towns, etc, all you'll get is 2G signal.

I got this device for $18 and it costs me $10/month for 2GB of data on my Tmobile account - I use it for when I'm away from my studio and need to handle emails and what not. Definitely not as good as the LTE service, but works fine.

If you want LTE coverage, go for Tmobile's ZTE Z915 4G LTE Mobile Hotspot.

title: GREAT flash option for radio wireless setup - beautiful light quality.  iTTL + HSS work great.  Detailed comparison to Shanny:
text:
This past weekend I got to use both the SN600N and the Yongnuo YN568EX with the YN622 triggers. Basically both function completely with the YN622 triggers in both manual and iTTL modes. The only thing that I noticed with the SN600N was that manual power 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 all seem to be about the same output using the YN622 triggers - you have to lower it to 1/8 or less to start seeing lower outputs. Not a huge deal, but I'd like more output options. More on this below:

Here are a few details that a pretty important about these two alternatives to the Nikon SB series:

a) The 568 light is much higher quality - and I really mean the LIGHT quality. It is even, consistent, and clear. On the other hand, the SN600N is very scattered - what I mean by this is there are lines of brightness and darkness from the flash burst. This must be an internal flash "lens" issue - whatever the light is bouncing around and through within the flash is creating texture and light inconsistencies. This is not the case with the 568.

b) Yes, the SN600N is a more powerful flash, but in my opinion, it needs to have more levels of output on the lower end (1/256) because it's TOO bright for some situations. I use grids and modifiers during wedding receptions, and I like balancing the natural light with the flash output. 1/128 with the SN600N is equal to about 1/64 on the 568. I use the 568 at 1/128 quite a bit for details - so this was kinda a bummer to me.

c) The AF beam on the SN600N is better and more centered than the 568 - but they both need to improve designs. The ONLY reason I'm holding onto my Nikon SB900 at this point is the AF beam - which makes accurate AF possible in pitch black - no joke. The AF beam on the Yongnuo is a joke - they need to fix it on the 622 triggers too - it's basically worthless and too bright/annoying to the subject.

d) In my experience using the 568EX, the batteries get warm and stay warm, whether you're using the flash or not. If the flash is on, the batteries will get warm. It also EATS through batteries. I used to be able to photograph 2 weddings without recharging my Nikon SB setup (using SB600 previously) - now I have to recharge between weddings. I've upgraded to 2800mah EBL AA rechargeable (previously using Amazon 2000mah) and it has helped quite a bit.

So this is my current setup: SB900 on camera, 2x 568EX off camera group A+B for reception lighting, and then SN600N as group C for periodic fill. Rather than commit to a single brand, I'm using them all as tools for different situations, because they all work differently. I also am really enjoying the SN600N as on-camera if I don't need the AF beam - the quality of light is bright, crisp and rich - and the SN600N "brain" (basically how it works using iTTL mode) just works really well with Nikon - it's a very consistent flash, sometimes even better than my SB900. I like that it can zoom all the way to 200mm, too. If the SN600N had a better AF beam and better quality of light, I would ditch my SB900 and use it all the time. But I switch between the SB900 and the SN600N for different effects. I actually like the previously mentioned internal lens flash inconsistencies at times - it creates a grittiness that I like.

title: All screws fit perfectly into a Late 2010 MacBook Air.  Great screwdriver, too!
text: They fit a late 2010 MacBook Air perfectly.  The screwdriver is a lightly magnetic, hardened tip driver - which is to say it's actually really nice.  I purchased a separate set of screws (different listing) for the same computer from Amazon, but the long back screws were not long enough for the MBA.  This set is perfect!

title: Perfect fit, nice and snug.  Pain to take off, but worth the price.
text: Solid - holds the iPad Air 2 very nicely.  It's a pain in the rear to take it OFF the iPad, but it fits very nicely and snug when it is installed.

title: Definitely not as nice audio quality as the Wingz 4.0 - and the Wingz are 1/2 the price.
text:
I bought these from Fry's - didn't like them one bit. Muffled audio, not clear or crisp at all. For $85, I wanted something that at least offered crisp and clear audio.

I returned them and purchase the Wingz 4.0 bluetooth headphones. WAY happier, and they only cost $45. The Wingz 4.0 are almost identical design, sound much better, and offer Bluetooth 4.0 with battery level indicator on my iPhone 5.

title: The bodycap is fine, but the rear lens cap strips easily
text:
This was a great set of caps for about 2 weeks, then one day the rear lens cap stripped while I was tightening it on a lens. So now it's super loose and doesn't want to stay on.

The body cap works great though.

title: Great for wedding photography macro work, AF works with both AF-D and AF-S lenses
text:
I'm a professional wedding photographer who uses the D800, D600 and D3 Nikon bodies. I also use pretty basic lenses - 50mm 1.4 AFD and the 85mm 1.8 AFS most of the time.

I didn't want to carry around a dedicated macro lens as I like a light bag on wedding days, so I knew these macro tubes would do the trick.

To be honest with you, the 12mm extension on my 50mm AFD does the trick! And the 12mm is so slim! Super easy to throw into my bag. I can't imagine using the other 2 rings at this time, but I might play around with them eventually.

I like that these are compatible with both AF-D (the screw type, in-camera AF motor lenses) and the AF-S (lens motorized AF lenses) lenses.

They are made out of plastic and feel cheap, but they're also very light. If you're careful with them then you'll be fine.

Finally, there appears to be some lubrication or grease on the inside of the tubes. Not too much, but enough to give you some warning. I'm going to keep my eye on it for sure.

Anyway, for $65 can you really beat getting 3 different extension tubes for your kit?

I only wish I could have just bought the single 12mm alone!

title: Yup, works great on the D3100
text: I believe this is the only aftermarket EN-EL14 that will work on the D3100.  They've finally chipped these batteries so they work on Nikons "newer" bodies.  Just glad it works fine.

title: Really happy with this dual dock for $32
text:
I was a bit skeptical about purcahasing this drive, but it has been really nice to use. First off the obvious - it actually does hold 2x 3.5" SATA drives. I wasn't sure of this because the photo doesn't make it seem that way. The front slot does open enough to fit in a full 3.5" SATA drive along with the primary slot.

Besides that the dock works great on USB 3.0 with my 2012 Apple MacBook Pro (15"). The drives do spin down after about 10 minutes of inactivity, which is a nice feature.

Syba doesn't have a great reputation for their support. I asked them if the clone function would clone a Mac HSF+ formatted drive. Their reply email said that in their test situations no, it was not possible.

Well I tried it anyway. I copied about 700GB of data on a 3TB drive formatted on HSF+. It cloned perfectly.

One other minor complaint is that the power switch is on the back. It would be nice to have a push button power function on the front of the unit, or the top.

The USB cable included is only about 2.5 feet long as well. Way too short!

Anyway, you really can't complain for a $32 dual USB 3.0 SATA dock, right?!

title: Received defective unit, falls asleep too quickly - excellent Anker support, though
text:
Although the action of the keys feel great, the biggest issue with this drive (using with a late-2006 24" iMac) is that the first 2 keystrokes I typed with the keyboard would never respond - they only seemed to turn the keyboard back on. The keyboard falls asleep within 10 seconds, and it missed 1-2 keystrokes the next time I begin typing.

Otherwise it would be a good device.

**************************
***update 04/11/2013***

Anker emailed me and even called me directly (I have no idea how they got my phone number...) after they read my review to help resolve the issue. Aparently I simply received a defective unit. I believe them. I was really surprised at how proactive they were with trying to resolve my issue once I left the 2-star review.

They offered an updated product replacement without charge. However, I have since purchased an Apple brand keyboard. Otherwise I really appreciate their support. They offered me a complete refund.

So I'm currently waiting on a shipping label to return the keyboard for a full refund (apparently this is a part of their 18 month warranty - good stuff!)

Now THAT is customer service. I'll adjust my rating once I receive the refund.

**************************
***update 04/18/2013***

Received full refund via Amazon a few days ago. All good. I did change from 2-star rating to 4-star rating, trusting that Anker has fixed any bluetooth/sleeping issues with this, and trusting that I did receive a defective unit as they said I did. They get 4 stars for their stellar customer service.

title: Unfortunately the drivers strip and do not work after 2-3 turns!
text: I did accomplish one repair on my iphone 4 GSM with this kit, but I couldn't even finish screwing in the final 2 screws on the bottom of the iPhone.  So I gotta rate it at 1-star.  Might get 1 job done, but they should use better material.

title: Great bluetooth quality - great options
text:
This is a fantastic unit. I was getting sick of my basic Dual brand bluetooth car stereo and decided to upgrade. The bluetooth is crystal clear, no interference noise at all!

Also has plenty of options for Sub low-pass filter options and interior speaker high pass filter options. This really makes a difference with how a speaker setup sounds.

I was also surprised at how well it picks up FM radio information (broadcast information), and with bluetooth connected devices.

The bluetooth phone option with the included microphone works great too - crystal clear, and doesn't sound bad for the person on the other end.

Anyway, really liking this for $100 unit!

title: Bluetooth is fuzzy - only an okay car stereo.
text:
Although it's a great price on Amazon, I'd spend the extra $40 and get yourself a decent car stereo.

I installed this in my 2000 Toyota 4Runner with stock speakers and a 10" Kicker sub/200w amp. Althought it does the job, it doesn't do it with any real impact. It creates sound, and it functions, but don't expect amazing sound.

The biggest disappointment was the bluetooth performance. Although it's got all the phone gadgets, and includes a microphone, the connection with both my Android, iPhone 4 and iPhone 5 were all fuzzy. Yup - the louder you pumped the volume the louder the bluetooth fuzz was! It was really distracting, almost like using a tape deck aux converter. It's just poor quality.

I used it for about 8 months, but finally gave in and purchased a decent Pioneer unit that has crystal clear bluetooth connectivity, and much better control over stock speaker sound.

Just spend the extra money. Trust me.

title: Great for HD signals!  Self-powered!
text:
I was about to purchase a powered HD antena for my 1080p 40" Sony TV, KDL40BX450, but decided to keep it simple with this $15 unit. I'm really glad I did!

This thing works GREAT! I live in a very old 1940's cinder-block constructed house and the TV is next to some thick walls. But I get over 40HD channels about 26 miles west of Chicago. I couldn't believe it!

I really use my TV only for Blu-Ray, Netflix, Hulu, etc. Streaming content only. This is great for local TV, such as PBS and others.

Of course the signal, at times, does get fuzzy and distorts, but if you move it around a bit everything goes back to normal. This is most likely due to weather conditions.

title: Works great with the GoPro Hero3
text: I almost got myself a 16GB but decided on the 32GB last minute.  I'm so glad I did - I filled up my Hero3 White edition with over 20k time-lapse images and a few hours of HD footage.  These things are solid and reliable.  I filled it up over a 6 day period doing some work in Haiti.

title: Works great with my 30lbs 40'' Sony HDTV
text:
I use this with my Sony KDL-40BX450 - it's a 30lbs HDTV.

This is an incredible mount for the cost. At my local Fry's a mount like this would cost at least $75.

It feels very sturdy, and allows you to lock the tilt position of the television.

I mounted this on a wood stud on a house built in the 1940's. Feels great!

title: 2x the speed of USB 2.0 = good product
text:
I've previously used the Transcend USB 2.0 reader and sustained anywhere from 27-37MB/sec. 64GB cards were taking about 25-35 minutes to copy over, which was becoming a chore to wait for.

I only use this with CF cards, so I can't comment on the other slots.

Now that I have a USB 3.0 compatible MacBook Pro, this reader copies RAW images and compressed video at between 55-75MB/sec. Incredible!

I'm using Transcend 400x UDMA CF cards. Both 64GB and 32GB.

Well worth the money.

title: Works great in the new 2012 MacBook Pro
text:
I was using 12GB of 1333MHz sodimms on my new June 2012 MacBook Pro. It's supposedly backward compatible even though the system is designed to run at 1600MHz.

But the 12GB (8GB+4GB modules) I believe kept freezing my system after recovering from system sleep.

I decided to take the steps to fixing this issue. I heard that using 1333MHz memory might be the issue, so I opted to purchase some 1600MHz memory.

Honestly I chose Komputerbay brand because this 16GB set was so cheap.

But my system is working rock solid now - I'm pretty sure this indicates all the freezing was due to the slower memory installed in the updated system. All 16GB registers in OSX 10.8 and is running at 1600MHz.

Good stuff, and well worth the price.

Ben

title: Works well for MBP - Achieva Shimian QH270 27" monitor @ 2560x1440
text:
I've heard a lot of issues with getting the new Achieva Shimian QH270 monitors working with some laptop GPU video out.

Specifically the newer MacBook Pro models

I'm using an early 2011 i7, 15'' MBP with Thunderbolt @ AMD Radeon 6750M GPU.

I went through 2 previous DVI adapters which froze the laptop every time I plugged my new monitor in. Frustrating! Then I read somewhere that you need the USB powered adapter to support DVI Dual-Link and such a high resolution.

So glad to say it works GREAT. I know there are other non-Apple models for $60-$70, but I'm glad to have Apple quality. And it works, doesn't overheat, no flickering.

All good on this end.

Ben

title: Great for USB-powered external storage...
text:
I think the biggest issue with most self-powered portable USB drives is the casing they fit in: they are too small and do not have sufficient padding for shock damage within the external case.

I purchase these drives as backup products for my wedding image collections. I'm a professional photographer, so I need off-site backup for all of my photographs. These drives are great to dump all my images onto then throw into a fire-proof safe away from my office. They're not super fast - these drives are not something you purchase for speed - but they are great for usb-powered, external storage.

What I love about the Seagate is that they eliminate room for shock-damage. The external fitting is larger than most 2.5'' portable drives, but it's because they allow for some room on the inside and have greater shock damage resistance. I'd much rather something come crashing into this and break the case than the HDD within it.

Also great because they come in 1.5TB size. Most self-powered externals are only 1TB. The extra 500GB helps.

Ben

title: Great upgrade for MacBook Pro 8.2
text:
I wanted a faster OS experience on my Macbook Pro. Decided to setup a SSD boot disc and 1TB HDD storage to replace my optical drive.

It's been a great experience.

This is my first SSD and it has been super easy. I was so overwhelmed with people's opinions on SSD drives, but I kept hearing great things about the Crucial M4. After reading reviews, I figured it was a great drive to ease me into the SSD experience.

So far so good: I've never experienced any hangs, no issues with recovering from sleep, and I use hibernate quite often without issue. I use this computer as a workhorse for my photography business, so I'm regularly working with jpg and RAW images between 75MB and 150MB. You really need a zippy drive to make life easier when editing files this large.

Anyway, I purchased mine only 4 months ago at almost $322! Now that they are $100 cheaper! WOW! Lucky you guys. I would have just waited and gotten myself a 512GB.

Great product...highly recommended.

Ben

title: Faster than the WD equivalent...
text:
I own both this drive and the Western Digital WD10JPVT - nearly identical drives, but there are a few differences.

At the end of the day, I'd end up purchasing the Samsung M8 for a few reasons.

I'm usually a WD fan, but the Samsung M8 is faster in most practical user situations. Most reviews will state the WD drive as being faster, but that is only with very large file copy sequences - writing/reading files in this way is not what most people want a drive for.

The Samsung M8 is zippier with practical file operation - such as flowing through large batches of music or photography. If you edit photographs, the Samsung will be faster. If you are moving large batches of HUGE files (such as ISO's, disc images, etc), the WD will be faster, but only by 3-4 MB/s. For how much faster the Samsung is in most areas (nearly double the speed, 40mb/s vs. 20mb/s), getting the Samsung is more practical.

The Samsung is almost double the speed of the WD with most file operation, such as editing photography or flowing through music.

Ben

title: Nice and deep rail for the CF card
text:
Excellent product. I get about 35mb/sec transfer times with my Transcend 400x 64GB CF card using USB 2.0.

The biggest culprit with most CF card readers is that the rails that align the CF card to the pins (rails on the side of the CF card) are not deep enough. When you insert a CF card to a reader with shallow rails, it can be easy to bend the pins.

The Transcend P8 has very deep rails for the CF card reader, so a large majority of the CF card sinks into the reader before contacting the pins. This way you can be assured that the pins are aligned correctly without error for bending the pins.

Anyway, great product!

Ben

title: Works great - don't cover your breather holes!
text:
This product is very good for the price.

WARNING THOUGH: do not cover the breather holes for regular spinning (rotational) HDD's - after only about 3 months of use, I crashed a Hitachi HDD because I covered one of the breather holes. No good. I had all my data backed up so no worries!

Be sure to put a small amount of gaffers tape or duct tape or any kind of safe spacing device NEXT to the breather hole so the HDD doesn't lie flat on the metal of the caddy tray.

Ben

title: Good enough for $65
text:

Here's the thing: for $65 this product is fine.

BUT I give it 3-stars for quality check: one of the main screws that tighten the legs on one of the two stands did not thread deep enough, thus not tightening the legs which allowed the one-half of the backdrop to go limp: had I not checked this before going to the event, I would have looked like a fool with only one side working, the other not able to hold itself. It's a pretty minor issue that could cause a lot of inconvenience for a professional at a job if gone un-noticed.

I happened to have an extra screw sitting around that fit, but not sure if everyone would.

Could easily be a 5-star, if they got all their screws right. But the threads on a few of the screws/bolts are unfriendly.

Otherwise solid product. Great bag and good height for the cost.

title: Good product, but go for the bus-powered Nikon ME-1!
text:
I used this for a large video project this summer. It did the job well enough, but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone who is looking for decent DSLR HD video audio capture. Why? Because it is not bus-powered. You need to be sure this is powered on and the 9V battery is always good to go.

I used this in 2 different situations:

1) in camera audio capture, connected directly to D7000, 7D & 5DII bodies. It produced great audio, but many times I forgot to turn the mic on, which resulted in zero sound.
2) I used this in conjunction with an external audio device, such as the Zoom H1, to get more specifically located audio. Again, it did the job good enough.

But compared to the Nikon ME-1, you're missing a lot of handy features from the VideoMic. For example:

Nikon ME-1 is stereo. VideoMic is mono.
Nikon ME-1 is bus-powered. VideoMic requires on switch and 9V battery.
Nikon ME-1 is compact and small. VideoMic is large and bulky.
Nikon ME-1 is cheaper than the VideoMic.

After using both of them I sold my VideMic promptly. The Nikon ME-1 does the job much better.

Finally the included Fuzzy Windjammer on this kit doesn't do much more than the already included foam on the VideoMic. I compared the two in light wind situations and found the sound to be nearly the same.

Save some money and trouble, get the Nikon ME-1.

Ben

title: Excellent product for the price
text:

I knew I couldn't find many low-priced & compact units, so I decided to find what I could for around $30.

When I received the stand I was really surprised at how light it was. Yes, it is larger than my 7-foot Manfrotto, but I'm actually very happy with the build and the height for the price. $29?! I'm going to order another. They get above the average person just fine, and the feet stretch out enough to be very sturdy.

On that note, this 9 foot is much better built than my 6 foot Cowboystudio light stand (which I think is a piece of junk, but I'll continue to use it until it fails).

Good stuff!
