title: Great product, includes speed strap!
text:
I'd like to first say that I'm a professional, both journalism and wedding photography, and that I've been using the Honl Photo Professional Light System for almost 3 years now.

That being said, I needed a 1/4'' honeycomb grid, and I saw this Opteka for 1/3 of the price of the Honl product. I wasn't really hesitant, and I'm always game to try new products (at least try...)

Anyway, I received it and to my surprise it had an included speed strap with it! I had purchased an additional Honl strap for my 2nd flash, but now that I have 3 flashes, I'm just going to hold onto the extra strap. [...]

Anyway, kudos for a $13 product that includes the normally $10 strap.

The 1/4'' honey grid works as expected. I purchased the 1/4'' because my Honl 1/8'' was too tight in some situations (usually couples standing with one another, I needed a larger light circle). [...]

Some people complain about how loose these feel? Honestly, the Opteka (for some reason) stays on tighter than my Honl system.

The one issue I have is how the honeycomb grid is held together by the outer case - there was a gap on the side between the two cases holding together the grid. Some adhesive velcro was holding the two sides together. That's fine, but it didn't seem tight enough. Nothing a few strips of gaffers tape didn't solve!

LONG AND SHORT: if you need a 1/4'' honeycomb grid and a speed strap, you can't beat this price: I'm actually very happy with this product. I'll be looking into some other Opteka equipment in the future.

title: ***BUYER BEWARE, YOU NEED TO DOWNGRADE TO ENABLE UHD CAPABILITY***
text:
This product claims to be "UHD Friendly" however, they fail to mention that the software written into the drive completely disallows the drive from reading the disks out of the box.

The unit I received was manufactured with version 1.04 written to the hardware. This version, as well as version 1.03 will read a that it's a 4k disk, and stop reading any further. The user must flash the version they desire that allows 4k disks to be written. Version 1.00 through 1.02 work with 4k disks.

As a person who is computer literate, this was a relatively simple task, however, the way this product is advertised is very misleading to those who just want 4k Blu Ray capability in their PC out of the box.

title: Excellent keyboard case for your iPad!
text:
I don't need my personal laptop at the office, just my iPad, but typing on the iPad screen was a pain.

I did NOT get any compensation from anyone for this review.
This is a great product and my review reflects it: If I could give 10 stars, I would!

This keyboard case is genius!
It does a great job protecting your iPad, the keyboard feel is great and the Bluetooth connection is reliable and makes sense!
The special function keys - like screen dim and brighten, cut, copy and paste - actually work!

What is so clever about this is that it uses the iPad's built-in magnetic-sensing strip (the one that holds the original cover to the iPad)
to turn on the Bluetooth keyboard:

When you flip this case open and put your iPad in place on the clearly marked strip, you can FEEL the magnetic "click" and then the keyboard wakes up and turns on. Instant keyboard and very stable when sitting on your desk.

If you leave it alone for a while, it shuts down the Bluetooth connection, to save battery life.
But press any key for two seconds, and it's back up.

If you don't need the keyboard, it's very easy to open the case and flip the IPad over and use it without the keyboard:
The Bluetooth doesn't connect unless you "Click" the iPad into the magnetic strip.

I've had to recharge the keyboard once, in two months of use.
But the indicator lights warned me well in advance and it recharged in about two hours.

Great product!

The keyboard feel is great, though the keys are necessarily small

I bought another case that had a rotating pivot for portrait and landscape use, but it had bad keyboard reliability (what you typed didn't always appear) and the battery failed after one charge.

This case

text:

The construction is sturdier, the pop open feature is great (it fits better in my computer bag), the lip at the bottom holds the laptop more securely.

Best of all, now that it has two fans, it actually cools my laptop.

The location of the USB cord for the fans has been moved inside and seems much less prone to breakage (a broken and non-replaceable USB cord on the previous design is why I bought a new chill mat).

I have an older Apple PowerBook G4 that has its USB ports on the rear and the new design cable JUST makes it to the port.
If there was another inch of cable, it would be a better fit. That's why I'm giving four instead of five stars.
Most newer laptops have USB ports on either side so this should work well regardless of which side the USB port is on.

title: Made my "laptop" live up to its name
text:
UPDATE - December 2012
The non-replaceable USB cord sticking out of the back broke internally, causing intermittent fan operation - though mostly non-operation.
I've downgraded my review from 4 to 3 stars - it should have lasted more than a year!

Targus is now offering a significantly improved chill mat which I've purchased and that will hopefully hold up a little better.

------------
I was recently given an older PowerBook G4 800 laptop - not a cutting-edge computer, but up to what I need it for.
The computer's main problem was that it gets REALLY hot during extended, intense use, both on the bottom and at the keyboard.
Not just uncomfortably warm, but nearly hot enough to melt iron (just kidding!) even with its internal cooling fans running at max (very noisy -not kidding).

The near-perfect solution: The Targus Chill Mat Jr.

The width is the same as my PowerBook, and it's only one inch deeper.
When I'm using the Chill Mat, it seems like nothing is there.

It's incredibly light and fits very easily in my computer bag without bulking it up too much.
But it's a bit tall (about 2 inches) so that might be an issue for some computer bags.

The fan on the Targus is REALLY, REALLY quiet.
When I first plugged it into a USB port, I actually had to put my hand over the unit to make sure the fan was running - it was.
It doesn't solve the "screaming fans" problem when my computer is working hard. However, it takes a LOT longer before the fans kick in.

Most of the top area of the Targus (where the computer sits) is covered with holes that let passive cooling air flow under the computer without the USB fan running. I sometimes don't plug in the fan when on battery to conserve power - and still the computer runs a lot cooler.

Using it on my lap is very nice - it has a sort-of neoprene fabric-like wrapping that's both comfortable and doesn't slip around, whether you're wearing shorts or long pants. I'm a little concerned that the backing will not hold up well over time and how easy it will be to clean it up when it needs it.

The rubber feet that hold the computer in place work very well, too - the computer just doesn't move around.

The best of all for me, is that the Chill Mat raises the keyboard to the perfect angle for extended typing - whether used on a desk or on my lap.

The bottom line on the Targus Chill Mat, Jr., IMHO:

It's a great product at a great price:
Even if its fan fails over extended use (I don't think it will), it will still work to help keep my laptop cooler because of the cooling holes on its top.

And even if the fan fails and the fabric becomes uncleanably grungy, it costs less than $30.
I'll just buy another one.

But the best is that it has let me use my "laptop" on my lap!

title: Samsung used to be a great TV brand but not anymore.
text:
If all you watch is driven by an external device like a cable box or Roku or something, then this is probably an acceptable TV for you. However, you're paying a good chunk of money to have a "smart" TV that can connect to services like Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Hulu, and that "smart" technology is terrible.

- The video streaming apps crash regularly, or go unresponsive, or will have significant delays, or even lock up so badly that you have to reboot the TV. And since there's no volume-equalizing feature, sometimes a quiet TV show will crash and abruptly you'll be sent back to the default "TV Plus" music channels, blaring a country song at ear-splitting volumes.

- Those same apps sometimes receive forced updates without any notice. One day you'll turn on the TV and discover that the controls are different or even missing. For example, my son loves the "Classical Baby" series via Amazon, and would frequently used the "restart season from the beginning" button to watch it again. Then one day, poof, no more button. To watch it again, we have to navigate back to the first episode, resume it (which picks up about 4 seconds from the end), and quickly start rewinding all the way back to the beginning of the episode. This itself is not a huge deal but the same type of unexpected, forced-on-you changes have happened many times in the last 2 years of owning the TV.

- The "dynamic" picture mode looks good on a few shows but on others will seriously distort colors. Skin will be bluish, or someone's red coat will be super-saturated into a weird blob of red on the screen. It also increases the refresh rate so things suddenly lose the normal movie feel and instead get that soap opera feel to them.

- It doesn't support the normal phone "cast" features that pretty much every other TV and phone supports. It supposedly supports a screen mirroring feature via their own SmartThings mobile app but the configuration is so awful and inconsistent that I have yet to get any casting to work (I'm a techie so these things are not often difficult). Why wouldn't they just go with the normal way that everyone else does it, which works flawlessly? Who knows.

Maybe in the future, Samsung will get their act together but right now it's a very bad buy for most people.

title: Okay Cooling, Flimsy Quality, But Hey, It's Cheap!
text:
This worked fairly well - not QUITE as much of a reduction in heat as I'd hoped, but still decent. I had previously owned a Microsoft brand cooling pad with one fan - the practical difference was about 2-3 degrees when running a graphics-intensive app. I had bought this one specifically because the graphics card in my laptop is in the top-left corner underneath the keyboard, and this cooler has a fan in that exact spot.

The quality of the cooling pad isn't that great, but I guess you get what you pay for. The body feels flimsy, with the pop-up tabs flying off every time they get the slightest jarring. The fans themselves are a little TOO exposed on the bottom - EVERY time I pick it up, my fingers touch the fan blades. They're flimsy plastic blades, so it's not like it hurts, but it's pretty annoying after the 5th time and you realize it's going to keep happening EVERY time you pick it up.

In retrospect, if I'm going to be annoyed by a cooling device, I think I would have preferred one of those devices that have a little vacuum thing that attach to the exhaust near the graphics card.

UPDATE: Less than a year later, the two back fans have started to die. My guess is that some wires have gotten loose, based on what I'm seeing (it's not a gradual dying effect but rather flipping on/off rapidly as if there's a bad wire connection). Overall, not too durable. I may need to chuck this and buy a different one. I'm not sure $20 for intermittent use throughout a year is worth it.

title: Perfect replacements for my G930, some people must not know how to install them
text:
My old G930 ear pads were flaking like crazy after several years of daily, all-day use, and I was hesitant to buy these at first because several people said they were too small. But I figured it's only $5, so it's worth a shot.

They arrived this morning and all I can think of is that whoever thought these were too tight or too small wasn't putting them on correctly. Maybe they thought they were just push-on instead of realizing that they have a flap (just like the ones that come with the headset) that needs to be lifted to go over the plastic part of the earpiece. That's what actually holds these things in place, people - otherwise they'd just fall off! Or maybe people aren't actually matching up the shape correctly. Either way - if you install them CORRECTLY, they fit perfectly.

These things are the correct size and I took some photos to compare the old Logitech-made pads with these. I also measured separately and they are the exact same size. If you take the time to look at how the original ear pads come off, you'll know exactly how to put these replacements on, and it'll take you all of about 10-15 seconds per ear pad.

These are virtually indistinguishable from the originals. I put these on and at first they seemed a little firmer than the original ear pads. However, I actually have a total of three G930 headsets (different purposes), so I was able to compare the feel of these ear pads to the original ear pads on one of the lesser-used, newer headsets. Again, pretty much identical - I guess they just get softer with use. Still, they are very comfortable even in their brand-new state, and I'm happy not to finish the day with black flakes on the sides of my face again.

PHOTOS:
I have three photos, two that are just comparing the back and front of the old pad to the replacement pad (and showing where the flap is that some people are apparently missing). The third photo is just showing the headset with one pad replaced so you can actually see that it looks pretty much the same as the original when installed correctly on the headset.

title: Nice Drive but Old Software = Hidden Costs to Upgrade
text:
I bought this so I could play Blu-Ray movies on my computer or my laptop.

Interestingly enough, the drive itself seems to be recognized by Windows, and Windows can actually see the files on the discs, so the drive seems to work in that respect. However, the drive comes bundled with an older version of CyberLink's media playing software (PowerDVD 12), which is supposed to be able to play Blu-Ray discs.

However, the software just doesn't want to play Blu-Ray movies. I popped in "The Equalizer" and it showed me the thumbnail icon for it, but when I tried to play, it just took me back to the home screen of the PowerDVD 12 player. I tried updating the software with no luck, and I tried it on a different computer that is almost brand-new, and got the same results. I even installed CyberLink's "Advisor" tool that analyzes your system to see if there are any items that could cause issues with playing such content, and it told me everything passed.

From what I've read, it sounds like you need to constantly upgrade to newer versions of PowerDVD (up to version 15 now, which is an extra $99 upgrade fee) in order to play newer movies.

So while this might be a good drive for data-driven usage of Blu-Ray discs, just be aware that the packaged software is just too old to be useful nowadays. You'll need to account for another $99 upgrade charge to watch more recently-released movies unless you already have a newer version of that software.

As of today, if you can find a version of PowerDVD that is version 13 or 14, the upgrade fee to version 15 is $49, I think, so the included version is just one version too old.

It's unfortunate, since the drive itself seems like a really nice piece of hardware. It's very convenient in terms of being able to be plugged in, it's very small, and seemed very quiet, too.

title: Beware the high star reviews! Over four years, 6 out of 9 of these have failed!
text:
I've had a RAID-5 array running with four of these Spinpoint F3 (HD103SJ) drives running since 2010. Over the past four years, I've had to replace SIX of these drives. That's right, I've owned a total of NINE of these, and I've replaced ALL of the original four.

Last year, I decided to stop wasting money on these and decided to just pay a little more for a different drive (WD Black), and today I'm running with three of the Samsung drives and one WD Black. Guess what? Two days ago, one of the remaining Samsung F3s started reporting a SMART failure. I ordered a replacement, and just today - TWO days after that Samsung F3 drive reported the SMART failure, a second Samsung F3 started reporting SMART failures, too.

So today, I've got three Spinpoint F3 drives left, two of which are about to die. That means in four years, I will have had 8 out of 9 of these drives die. None of them have lasted more than 1 1/2 years.

Just as a side note, I have another WD Black operating as my boot drive, a Caviar Green drive as a secondary data drive, and yet another WD Black as a final data drive (yes, my computer is a monstrosity). So of all of the drives in the system, ALL of them have held up for 2-4 years so far and the ONLY drives that have failed are these Spinpoint F3s.

Also, I've bought the drives from a variety of sources - NewEgg, Amazon, and MicroCenter, at different times, so it's not just like I happened to buy a bunch from a bad batch.

BOTTOM LINE: Don't waste your money. The high-star reviews are likely from new owners. Take it from someone who has tried these drives again and again for four years - they're junk.

title: Good laptop, keyboard needs an adjustment period
text:

PROS:

CONS:
- Came with Windows 8
- The mSATA SSD drive was too small for my tastes.
- Had an issue with battery not charging that apparently was a Windows bug and was easily fixed
- Keyboard takes some adjustment

I mistakenly purchased a 2.5" 256Gb SSD for this, and when it arrived, I realized that the included 16Gb SSD was an mSATA drive. So I ended up buying a 256Gb mSATA drive and swapped out both drives for a total of 512Gb of SSD. I get great performance out of it without it running hot.

When it arrived, I tried out Windows 8 for a while but gave up on it and switched back to Windows 7 during the aforementioned drive swap.

The keys on the keyboard feel a little spread out, so it took some time to get used to the layout, but it's working fine for me now. I think I'd still prefer the typical keyboard layout provided by most Dell and ASUS laptops.

Lenovo offers a feature that will keep the battery charged at 60% to prevent the battery life from being sucked away too early when you keep it plugged in all the time. Didn't even expect this, but I love this feature. My laptop batteries always die too quickly, so hopefully this will work well in the long-term. So far so good!

title: Wireless needs a lot of work - go with the G35
text:
MY HISTORY WITH THIS PRODUCT:
I've owned this headset for almost a full year. Technically, I've had two of them, since the boom mic snapped off the first one and had it replaced. I use these every day, for multiple hours and a variety of uses (VoIP calls, gaming, music, and movies).

PROS:
The audio quality, when it is working, is good. The bass in 7.1 mode is great, and the overall surround sound is pretty convincing. They are comfortable and rechargeable via USB.

CONS:
The biggest problem here is the wireless connection. Both headsets I owned suffered from this same problem - they would frequently just restart or lose the signal and reconnect. The process takes about 3-5 seconds each time, and sometimes you get multiple restarts in a row. It doesn't sound too bad until it happens when you're watching a movie and you have to quickly pause or rewind a bit because you suddenly couldn't hear anything they were saying (which also completely pulls you out of the movie), or when it drops out in the middle of a phone conversation, or drops out at the worst possible moment in a game... It happens probably two dozen times a day, if not more. At first, I didn't care too much about it, but the first time you have it drop out 3 times in a matter of a single minute, it's simply maddening. Imagine going randomly deaf for several seconds throughout every day of your life, and you'll get a sense of what it's like.

If I could simply plug the cable in and it would use the USB cable to transmit the audio instead of wireless, that would be perfect, but when it's plugged in, it simply charges the internal battery - you still get audio interruptions all the time. The interruptions will also reset the "mute" status on the mic, which can be troublesome if you're intentionally muted on a conference call and suddenly your mic is on and people hear you eating lunch.

Second problem is that the power button is a bit flaky. If the headset is plugged in via USB and powered off, sometimes it will not power on unless you unplug the headset and THEN power it on (and then you can plug it back in to continue charging). I thought it was a defect in my first headset until the same thing happened with the second one.

A minor third problem is that the boom mic is a little flimsy on the construction. I am careful with my toys, but it still cracked and finally snapped off one day when I was lowering the mic to use it, and that was only a few months into owning it.

OVERALL:
If they would fix the wireless, I would rate this 4 stars in a heartbeat. If they fixed the power button, it would go up to 5. That said, the G35 seems to be the G930 but wired, and cheaper. The number of times that I've wanted to really make good use of the wireless (go to another room and keep the audio going) is far less frequent than the dozens upon dozens of times that the audio cuts out, so it's just an unacceptable point for me, since that is what this headset is about.

title: If you buy Iomega products: 50/50 chance you'll get a lemon.
text:
There's just no in-between, and this drive is no exception.
My drive will connect and be recognized by the computer, but it won't recognize any CDs that are put in, no matter what brand of CD. It doesn't matter what software you install, either - it's simply a hardware defect, and if you buy one of Iomega's cheap products, there's just about a 50/50 chance you'll get a broken one. If you're lucky, you'll get a unit that actually works fine.
Take it from a network admin who has had to use many, many Iomega products over the years (with about half being unusable) - don't buy this product unless you're a compulsive gambler and you just have to take every chance.

title: Stop looking and buy this. It is exactly what you are looking for
text:
If you are thinking about getting a wireless keyboard and mouse then stop here and buy this set. I have been using this set for about 6 months and I am extremely happy with it. They connect to a usb plugged into the computer that is about the size of a nickel. The keyboard and mouse have just about 0 lag from motion or keystroke to output. I've played GTA V, Fallout, Diablo 3 + 2, and now Grim dawn on my computer, all from my couch because of this set. I have had no issues at all. They also barely use batteries. The mouse takes 1 AA battery and I still have not changed it. and the Keyboard I believe take 1 or 2 AA batteries and I also have no changed them. I spent a while looking for a keyboard and mouse set and I kept coming back to this one wondering if it was worth the money or was this set too cheap. I wish I had just bought this the second I found it rather than wait and waste time.

Also the mouse is one of the best I have used. I have used razors, cyborgs, and a few others and I still would prefer this mouse over them for how comfortable it is and also how well it works on almost any surface. Because I use my computer that is connected to my TV, I sometimes walk around and use the mouse, or sit on the couch and forget a mousepad. It does not matter what I put it on this mouse still moves perfectly. Sometimes I just use the cushion next to me for a mouse pad and I play games and have no issues.

The battery life is pretty good, I typically use them for between 60 and 90 minutes at a go and I only charge the case every week to 2 weeks depending. The absolute best thing about these is they don't lose connection when you walk more than 7 ft away or when they're sync to your wrist and you only have the right earbud in. That was a common problem when using my garment on my left hand and running with only the right earbud in and other brands. But this one keeps connection the whole time when I'm running no issues. title: Great for off-roading trails
text:
First time using a GMRS system and this was exactly what I needed for how I'm using it. My off-road group has switched from CB to GMRS and this was the model I went with to make sure we could all keep comms up. With no modifications or aftermarket purchases, I was able to keep up 2-way comms with vehicles out to at least 2 miles away from inside my Jeep (never got further than that). It was all very clear transmissions and having the 2 button PTT option was nice for a private conversation to one other driver.

I can't speak to the battery too much but having it on and using it 2 days in a row, while keeping it off during the night, I never showed less than the 3/3 bars on the battery. That was even after resting it at night in below freezing temps. Very impressed with the life so I don't have to carry a separate charger or extra battery.

Setup for basic usage was very easy although getting into more advanced functions is fairly complex. Being able to switch between channel and ferq mode is simple, just turn it on/off while holding a single button. Also, I like that you can turn on high power with a single button push. Anything more than those adjustments and setting a frequency is complex however. Its possible to access the menu on the unit but its really to small to display a lot of text so you need the manual in front of you to really be able to make any useful changes. Not a huge issue for me as I don't need to do much more than set a channel and go, but for those that want to really dive into how the unit operates, its going to be somewhat of a chore.

Overall highly recommend the unit for anyone wheeling in a group that needs a simple comms setup and doesn't want to deal with mounting a more permeant unit. Don't forget to get your callsign to stay legal!

title: Fantastic smart & fitness watch
text:
With all the options out for watches that double as smartwatches and fitness watches, I settled on this one for really 2 reasons. First, its from Garmin so you can expect that the GPS functions are going to be spot on. In that regard this watch is solid. The GPS is automatic as soon as you tell it that you are going to work out and it acquires quickly and its accurate. All you have to do is hit the single button on the side once, and select your activity. It usually locks in after about 10-15 seconds and off you go. This is critical for someone like me that pushes a stroller, steps never count right if you don't have GPS.

Second huge thing with this watch is the music function. I hate carrying my phone when i run and now, I don't! I set up spotify in a few minutes, downloaded 3 playlists (about 200 songs) and I'm good to go for my whole run. It makes it easy to hook to bluetooth and lets me either leave my phone behind when running or pull up a weight training app. The only drawback at all is that for the first about 2 minutes, it can have tiny skips if you are also running GPS, probably something to do with the watch not quite keeping up initially.

All in all this has been a great purchase and at a cost less than other options. We liked it so much, my wife got one too!

title: Great headphones for average use, wires seem very sturdy & never get tangled
text:
These are great headphones for music and movies for the price. I have never owned a big-money pair of headphones & after buying cheap ones that I had to replace multiple times due to breakage, I decided to get these after a recommendation from a friend. After buying them for myself, I also bought them for each of my kids. They're great for average use... i've never been bothered by outside noise, they are comfortable, and the sound is of good quality. They also are much sturdier than the cheapie $10-$20 ones I've gotten before. (My kids haven't broken them, which is a minor miracle)

I do recommend getting a bag or carrying case for them (I use a Crown Royal bag:) it certainly helps protect them and they do seem vulnerable at the hinges where they collapse for storage.

The only thing my kid complains about is the wire is kind of short. title: Fabulous Lens - Tack Sharp
text:
I received this lens on 4/22/17 and have had one day out shooting with it. I'm not a professional photographer, but I've been making photographs for decades, and I like to use only excellent cameras and lenses. I do general photography - urban and rural landscapes, and street photography as well.
The lens, like the Sigma 35 Art and the Sigma 50 Art lens, is incredibly sharp even wide open at 1.8. IMO the Sigma 135 seems like it is even sharper than the other Sigma Art lenses. And it renders colors better than any lens I've ever used.
I'm not into bokeh that is "bubblely", but more interested in a soft transition to the out of focus background, and this lens proved beautiful for that effect. I'm confident that if I wanted to produce bokeh balls that I could.
The lens barrel has 3 different focus distances from which to use. There is one focus distance that I did not try yet, and that I've seen on the internet, and appears to take excellent flower photos.
The barrel is not as long as my Nikon 70-200 2.8 VR II, but it is fat and not a light-weight at 44 ounces. After a couple of solid hours shooting with it, I was wishing that it had optical stabilization. It's a fantastic addition to my relatively small stable of lenses that I will use frequently, and will definitely find a consistent spot in my camera bag. I currently shoot with a Nikon D810 and D750.

title: Two Years and Still Incredible Sound and Comfort
text:
I bought the Bose QC25 headphones in February 2015 and they're still awesome. The noise canceling couldn't be better, the sound quality is impeccable, and they are the MOST comfortable headphones that I have ever had.
I use them in the house to listen to my iPod, which sets in a Yamaha dock that is connected to my Yamaha receiver. I also have my TV hooked up to my Yamaha receiver so that I can listen to the TV with the Bose headphones. They get a lot of use, but no abuse.
I have not had any problems with the headphones, just the expected maintenance of replacing the pads after two years, but that was easy to do with the Bose replacement pads.
From my experience I highly recommend the QC25 phones. Worth every penny!

title: Promaster HGX - The Best
text:
I've used many lens filters in my life, but the Promaster HGX are far and away the best. They aren't cheap, but they rarely need cleaning. I simply use a lens brush to very quickly get rid of any rust, because they rarely smudge, and when they do, a quick wipe with a microfiber cloth easily removes the smudge.
Just as a comparison, I previously purchased expensive B+W filters, which cost as much or more than the Promaster filters, but trying to clean was a major headache whether I was at home or out shooting. Microfiber cloths would simply move the dirt and smudges around on the B+W filters, and for some reason seemed to attract dirt. They were way too frustrating.
What a relief it is to use the Promaster HGX. I suspect they have a coating that makes these filters unique.
Oh, I wasn't asked to write this review and I paid full price, but worth every penny.

title: Nikon D810 body only
text:
I have had this camera since July 2015 and I find that this camera to be the most incredible camera I have ever owned. I have owned the D700, D800, D600, D610 and still own the D750.The clarity and dynamic range surpasses all of my previous cameras, including my D750.
However, the D810 is very demanding on lenses. Inferior lenses will provide either inconsistent performance, or just plain horrendous results.
Edit: 11/29/2017: After over two years of regular use I have had no problems with this camera. I have never had to clean my sensor, and I change lenses frequently, as I most often use prime lenses. So, I don’t understand why so many people have the need to frequently to “dust off” or clean their sensor. Nor do I understand why some people complain about the fact that most of the outer shell is made of carbon fiber. For years I worked with advanced composites, and carbon fiber is not just cheap plastic, but is used in many high-tech products for its superior strength and light weight.
I can only speak from my own experience and knowledge.

title: Fantastic lens
text: The Nikon 85 1.4G is the best lens I own. Fast focus on my D750 even handheld @ 1.4 in the city at night. And the bokeh is incredible. title: No documentation, constant beeping when computer asleep, audio only through one channel
text:
While I can get it so work as a basic KVM with MacBooks, there are some serious problems. For one, the switch makes the most ear-piercing beep nit only when the two computers are toggled, but also when Athena computer’s display signal turns off for power saving and does so repeated and random intervals (30-90 seconds) as the displays flick on and off. Therefore, when your machine is in sleep mode and notifications wake it up briefly to be displayed (like when you get new mail) it beeps when it goes back to sleep. This means it beeps incessantly when not in use which will drive you insane. You either have to disable sleep notifications or configure the display to be powered on 24/7 - neither are good options.

I looked for a solution to this problem as well as info for other functions but the “documentation” is a single sheet of paper that has literally no instructions. It’s just a list of specifications, diagrams for connections, and a list of hot-key combinations fans they actions the invoke - half of which have no explanation. For instance, I have no idea what “auto scan mode every 10 seconds” means. I couldn’t find anything on line either. Of course there is no hot-key listed to toggle the horrific beeping on and off.

Another problem is the audio only worked through the left channel and then after "fiddling" with the connections it now doesn't work at all.

Junk.

title: So good, I bought two!
text:
This is unquestionably the best docking station for any MacBook that supports Thunderbolt 3. I have tried several other similar devices and they all had serious problems, while this provides 87W of power, dual display support (DisplayPort 1.2), both an analogue and digital audio (TOSLINK) device, SD card reader, and extra 5 Gbps Thunderbolt 3/USB-C and USB 3.0 ports.

Regarding the 1 star reviews, with the exception of the person with the defective unit, I am almost positive the problems people have been having are because of their cables. Most people don't realize that the white USB-B cable that comes with their MacBook (which they probably just use for power) is Thunderbolt 2 and will NOT support Thunderbolt 3 devices! To connect your computer to the dock, use the cable they provide. If you need a longer cable, be sure to buy an actual Thunderbolt 3 cable that is less than 2 meters long. As for your display cables, it is critical the cable is DisplayPort 1.2. I also connected the second monitor to the Thunderbolt 3 port that converted to DisplayPort 1.2 (I just got the Amazon Basics brand and it works as it should. I have used this on both my 2017 and 2019 MacBooks and they both work flawlessly. Its so nice to just have one cable to plug and unplug for all devices!

title: Whatever you think this dock is, it isn’t that
text:
Everything about this dock is either confusing, misleading, or falsely. First of all, I’m not quite sure I see the point of having two hosts connect to it as I it does not seem to be a like a KVM switch in any way. For one, video output is dedicated to one or the other host depending on the port. There is no switch to toggle between hosts so USB devices seem to be shared? Honestly it’s not at all clear. The power supply also can only charge one host, I believe whichever is plugged in first. Since there is a single ethernet jack that both hosts share it also shares a single MAC ID. The only explanation for any of this seems to be to give a buyer some impression that it behaves like a KVM switch that allows you to share peripherals. In fact it’s not even clear what it does as the instructions are incomplete. Since I was unable to get a keyboard to work connected to it I presume can you either use the built-in keyboard or plug it directly into the laptop.

I honestly didn’t even fully unboxed this thing after reading the instructions and trying to make sense of them. Once I saw that video was not shared and that the resolution was appallingly low, all of the other issues were already moot. It is advertised as a thunderbolt 3 dock but it’s apparent that thunderbolt 3 support is quite limited and it’s really a USB-C dock. Seeing how the function of this device is very unclear a pure its existence only serves to fool customers like me into not having to use a KVM. Since the description and the instructions appear to be deliberately vague, it would seem this is the point. This also explains why it’s so much less expensive than a single host dock or a dual host KVM.

Back to Amazon with you!

title: A DisplayPort KVM that works reliably with late model MacBook Pros, but there are issues..
text:
2nd Update: Virtiv support confirmed that the display wake-up issue described below with the MacBook Pros is a known issue with this switch's firmware. I am told they will swap out your switch with one that is updated. Unfortunately, it would seem that Amazon's stock of this item as well the 2 display version have this issue. Since this is literally the only DisplayPort KVM that even remotely works with a MacBook Pro I would suggest this is worth the trouble if you fall in that category. (I haven't gotten mine back yet but I will update this when I do to confirm it's working properly.)

I also purchased the two display version and there is a problem where it creates a "stutter" in mouse movement that makes it painful to use. Even the MacBook Pro's built-in trackpad is affected by this problem! Vertiv again said that this is a firmware issue that is known about and has been fixed in later versions so a replacement is necessary.

UPDATE: I finally ran into a case where the display wouldn't show a signal even though my MacBook behaved like the monitor was attached. The case is when the MacBook wakes up from sleep. Otherwise, it works flawlessly. Also, I discovered that a "premium UHD" DisplayPort I bought on Amazon actually created problems where there wasn't one before. (If it aint broke...). When I swapped out my no-name DP cable for the fancy new one all I accomplished was creating the same problem I just described (the problem that afflicts all display switching with cheaper KVMs) where my original no-name 4K cable worked fine (except for the sleep issue.) Therefore, if you see this problem with your MacBook and your dock or KVM, try swapping out the DP cable! It would appear that Apple's DP support over USB-C is really bad.
Original Review:
For whatever reason, the new MacBook Pro support of DisplayPort from the USB-C port is very flakey. With other high-end KVMs I found that when switching back to my MBP, nearly all KVMs - even the renowned, industry-standard Black Box KVM had problems Getting sync emulation to work reliably switched to another computer and I had to replug my display cable to get the monitor to work even though the graphics card still thought the display was connected. Even with this switch, using some DisplayPort cables had the same problem with this switch but using standard 4K cables (not the flashy woven kind) worked great. Just be careful what cables you use with your MBP and you’ll be fine. The audio and USB lock feature is also super useful.

Also, you should get a good dock if for your MBP that provides full power to the USB-C port as this makes everything work better. I have found the USB-C to DisplayCables are not very good and require resets a lot. Again, I think it’s because Apple’s doing a bad job with DisplayPort. The dock has its own conversion so DisplayPort is native at that point. The CalDigit dock is worth every penny,

title: Unreliable with Inconsistent Support
text: As a USB docking station and power supply, it doesn't work very well. Found that when connected to a new MacBook with a single USB connection many functions didn't reliably work. I had some issues getting Ethernet to work consistently most frequently and USB A support for Keyboards and Mice would occasionally stop working required one of many cables to be replugged. It also seems to have problems charging at times for reasons that don't form any sort of pattern. Finally, the usability is poor. For one, only one of the HDMI ports seems to function when connected via USB C. There is no DisplayPort/Thunderbolt port. A friend had the same unit that overheated so badly that it started to smoke! It also feels cheap as it is made from ABS plastic so it's hard to deal with all of that and stomach the price that you can get a mid-grade dock for that works much better with a higher-powered power supply. I would keep looking.

title: Nice way to turn two smaller drives into a single volume in nice, quiet USB enclosure.
text: This is a great way to make two smaller drives into a single volume that’s a sum of its size in a USB 3 enclosure. (There are not many that do this.) The aluminum case dissipates heat well. It has multiple modes of operation so you can have two separate drive volumes as well as run in hardware mirroring mode for a cheap RAID 1 solution.

title: Very unsexy, very reliable
text: Anker makes good cables. They don’t charge as quickly with consistent times as Belkin cables do which probably explains the huge price difference, but they do charge better than any of the dozens of no-name brand cables available on Amazon. Also, they don’t spontaneously stop working after three months like the expensive woven cables end up doing 9/10 of the time. They also don’t overheat and they last longer than any other cable I have found. The only problem Is after a year they tend to to split a little on the plastic around the grommet that encircles the lightening plug end but it doesn’t affect function. No, the6 aren’t as cool looking as the braided cables, but they work better.

title: Good Sound, Bad UI
text:
I used to be a big Ultimate Ears guy from the aughts before they were bought by Logitech who killed their best product lines and replaced it with stuff like... THIS. The tiresome photos of impossibly gleeful adult-babies listening to music underwater and having the times of their lives thanks to this f——g speaker really gets cloying when it’s printed on literally everything except the device itself. But that’s Logitech for you. Of all things I have to complain about with this speaker, the sound isn’t one of them. Unlike its predecessors and smaller cousins, the Megaboom 3 doesn’t peak out the bass quite so much when it would otherwise be distorted. (This is the most common bit of digital audio gimmickry to fool you into think it sounds “crystal clear”.) The people complaining about this speaker in these reviews who say other brands are better are just brands more notorious for “loudness fakery” to make the sound seem more bass-heavy but is really just slick audio post-processing. It’s makes hip hop sound a little better but everything else is a murky mess. But I digress. This speaker does all of the digital trickery, sure, but at least the actual amplifier and speaker drivers aren’t rubbish so that’s I plus. I was playing System of a Down cranked in my bedroom and it sounded amazing, especially compared to my former Boom speaker which someone nicked from my garage. Where the Boo crumpled trying to product screeching highs and thumping lows the Megaboom 3 dominated. Of course I don’t use any of the EQ tomfoolery and let it play as close to how the music was engineered to play and its just dandy. Okay then, good sound: check.
The problem with this speaker, like all of the other UE speakers, is the brain-dead user interface and obnoxious audio feedback that you can’t properly adjust without hacking the device configs (allegedly). There is literally a single on/off switch for all audio feedback. Wut? No relative volume of system sounds compared to music, or selection of which sounds you want to hear and which ones you don’t, like that HORRIBLY OBNOXIOUS LOUD BEEP it makes that’s louder than the music if you accidentally lean in on your volume up button? Of course every sound is as loud as or louder than the music your playing. That’s just great. Furthermore, if you are listening to music through your iPad or iPhone, it decides to insert little beeps for certain feedback notifications that never happen when you are just using your device without the speaker. It’s horribly distracting and unnecessary, but worse is that you NEED audio feedback on if you want to be able to Bluetooth connect to it as audio feedback is the only feedback you get.

Ugh. Sorry, had a bit of a rant there.

It’s tough because I think the speak sounds decent and almost worth the price, but the UI team at Logite... excuse me... Ultimate Ears are clearly huffing paint fumes as each product they subsequently release is even more unpleasant to use than the last. Don’t let the coked-out looking teens with bright, expensive clothing printed on the box fool you.

title: Best quality 10' lightening cable I can find
text: After so many "premium" 10' cables that die promptly and stop charing my iPad, this basic cords hold up and keep working. They are also built well. Great value too. I have tried at least 5 different cloth sheathed 10' cords and this is the only one that didn't die or have the poly/silicone bushing around the aluminum lightening plug casing crack. Even the spendy Belkin cords craak hereafter a few months! This is the one to get and take a beating. Plus they're the right price. My search for a good 10' lightening cord has finally ended!

title: Outstanding compatibility and fidelity
text:
This is the first aftermarket dongle for lightening to 1/8" jack where the inline mic works as well as controls. I was amazed by this. What's much more impressive is that the fidelity of these DAC is outstanding and I experience much less distortion across the the full dynamic range on 15Ω dual-driver headphones from as low as 7 Hz. In fact, they performed flawlessly where other expensive amplifiers which no mic headphone controls (only the amps own buttons) worked at all. The Apple dongle doesn't really do a good job with larger headphone drivers which is why so many people get in line amps for their expensive earbuds. So
far, I’ve yet to try an in-line amp that’s worth what I paid for it. This guy is $20 and it does the job much better. I will never buy an Apple dongle or in-line "amplifier" again for an iPhone X series where there is no jack. This is clearly the way to go. Granted, there is no way to charge and have this control at the same time, but I guess this is a problem with the MFI spec from Apple. It's crappy, but no fault of this vendor. (It’d be great if Apple could be less thick about thinks like this and realize that people don’t always want to use a charge pad. It’s so silly.)

The design of this dongle is super rugged and I have not had any issues with distortion or phone problems. It seems just as reliable as the Apple dongle on an iPhone XS Max at minimum. I'm buying a couple more just to have them around since I hate not having my dongle nearby. (Tee-hee.) I’d just rather not have to pay the dongle tax to Apple anymore. They do wear out.

Also, I highly recommend the ERJIGO KZ ZS6 earbuds: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0756WVBZ9 as they pair incredibly with this dongle even at high volumes. I couldn’t believe that they sounded better on this than a fancy in-line amp! They sound as good or better than my UE Triple Fi 10's on the standard Apple dongle! For a total spend of $70 you are getting your money's worth and then some! Note, the fit of the Triple Fi is definitely superior to pretty much any earbud made, not to mention their noise-blocking capabilities. I doubt anyone will beat them there, but they are discontinued. (Thanks, Logitech.)

title: Excellent sound, but but in-line mic does NOT work
text:
I was reasonably impressed with this amp's fidelity, especially using dual driver headphones which the dinky DA converters Apple's builds into their hardware simply don't come close to cutting the mustard and end up distorting any low end sound, even at nominal volumes. With this amp I had the volume at levels which sustained listening would have caused hearing loss, but just to test it I could detect zero low end distortion that would indicate an underpowered amp. On the other hand, midrange performance is only mediocre. There is some faint crackle. It’s not terrible but it’s occasionally noticeable and shouldn’t be for a $69 accessory. This sort of amp is absolutely necessary for the ERJIGO KZ ZS6 (best value ever at less than $50 for dual-driver 15Ω earbuds). Unless you're an audiophile who wouldn't bother listening to music through an iPhone anyway, this is an okay solution but there are better DAC amps out there for less money.
Also, the lack of the in-line microphone function is a drag, but this is nothing new for in-line amplifiers. You can hear calls just fine, but you need to use the iPhone's built-in microphone as the headphones' in-line mic will be inactive. I only mention this because some miscreant's Q&A responses for this product indicates just the opposite, but I assure you this is NOT the case. The controls are nice, but the in-line microphone signal on your headphones will NOT be recognized for calls or making voice memos so I am not sure what the heck that person was smoking when he said that. Anyway, aside from that, this is a decent amp though a bit overpriced for what it does.

title: Not the original formula
text:
At first these seemed like excellent replacements for my tripleFi leads which the dog destroyed but it became clear there are some serious design problems. Aside from the mic being mediocre, the headphone lead from the junction is the weak link and within 45 days the lead was bent at this point and felt like it was break at any moment as there seemed to be no longer structural integrity at the most vulnerable location. It was less than a mo th from this that the wire severed enough to cut the connections and only the insulation was barely holding it together. If I bought another I feel like just a little gaffers tape at this point would avoid inevitable damage even with light use, but hindsight is always 20/20.
Otherwise, aside from the slightly weak mic, audio fidelity seemed on par with the stock leads. I wish it was just designed to be more durable.

title: Decent cable but comes with some quality issues
text:
Initially, this appears to be a fairly well built cable and the cordage seems fairly resilient to filth. Being electrum-colored I assumed it would look like trash in a few weeks but it holds up rather well even after being left out on the floor every day. It does seem to be fully supported by iOS. My problem with it is the aluminum cowling on the Lightening end of the cord has already become unglued and it easily slides off, and if I don’t find some glue soon I’m going to lose it. I’ve had it for less than a month!

It otherwise seems adequate, but being priced to be in the “premium” cord market I call “nah-uh”. Note to vendor: Drop the price on this as there are better woven-sheathed cords out there for about the same price that don’t fall apart, but I have had a hard time finding them in the gigantic 10’ and 12’ lengths which are great for being able to charge your phone while doing whatever without being leashed to the electrical outlet.

title: Excellent all-purpose wireless router explodes with flavor!
text:
ASUS makes excellent routers overall with the added bonus of being compatible with a variety of free-ware router software like DD-WRT, Tomato, and Merlin-WRT (recommended). It includes all of the features you need for a proper home LAN, far better than the junky wireless routers offered by your internet provider, especially Comcast XFinity. (Don't believe the hype- their equipment is terrible.)

Some great features include
- Great 802.11ac support (5 GHz wireless support)
- Legacy 802.11b support (2.4 Ghz wireless support used in most cheap IOT devices)
- DHCP support which includes local DNS and MAC ID binding to make NAT and Firewall rules effective with having to manually configure your devices with easy to use client management
- Easy to use QOS with instrumentation features
- VPN support
- Many storage solution variants to allow for of personal cloud and LAN network storage (NAS-like functionality)
- Gaming networking enhancements galore
- Excellent security features
- Excellent compatibility with other devices
- Excellent and easy to use web-base administration software
- Excellent community support on countless on-line forums
- Best router for the money; Similarly featured Netgear routers are significantly more expensive without a real edge

Some downsides:
- Terrible vendor support (not really necessary unless you need a warranty replacement, but they are okay here)
- Some software limitations make many features will only work when you use local subnets within the 192.168.0.0/16 class B network
- Network storage throughput somewhat slow

It is devices like this that have had me a loyal ASUS customer for routers for nearly a decade. The fact that you can use Merlin-WRT as your software which IMHO more stable than the factory firmware makes it a slam-dunk.

title: NOT a cheaper replacement for the other Arris DOCSIS 3.1 modems
text: This doesn't work properly with Comcast Xfinity as it is described here. Speeds are reduced to 3-6 Mbps. Just buy the proper Arris DOCSIS 3.1 cable modem.

title: Not a good solution to give standard headphones "mobile" features due to basic design
text: There are not a lot of M-F line extenders out there that have controls and a mic built in. Find an in-line extender with a separate line with controls and a mic on the end is impossible to find. If you use a pair of reference headphones that have no controls or mic, you might thing this is a good solution, however the positioning of the control/mic module will be all wrong which is evident the first time you attempt to use it. I ended up fastening it to my desk so the controls are handy, but because the mic is about 18" from my head it is not attenuated to capture my voice at that distance so people can barely hear me. Therefore, this cord is a bit of an anathema. Putting the controls and mic in-line makes it unsuitable for a set of headphones that have a long cord, particularly if you are walking, and mic is designed to reproduce sounds at very close range, so it's not useful as any sort of "proximity" microphone. Again, if the controls were on the end a separate cord that's about 2' to 3' in length and offered the extender line to be as short as 6", this would be perfect for people who wish to make their standard headphones become "phone" headphones. Since this is not the design, it fails in this regard.

title: Solid design, great size, and a bonus net-pouch inside
text: This is a great case that protects well and has an handy net-pouch for accessories. There is ample room so your cans won't be crushed inside, deforming the ear-pads, but it is not to cavernous for them to flop around inside very much or be to bulky overall. The zipper is a heady gauge and built to last. The style is very plain so it's not exactly aesthetically interesting in any way, but it does their job perfectly. If you travel with a pair of nice over-the-ear headphones, this case is a must have.

title: Great bass response at the expense of fidelity
text:
The first thing I noted when I listened to these much-celebrated headphones (at least the Prestige line at any rate) is how incredibly exaggerated the low-end is. While getting that kind of bass response from a headphone driver is impressive, showing it off at the expense of fidelity is not something I particularly care for. When using these on a device where a DAC is involved, such as an iPad, I have to use the 'bass reducer' EQ profile on the device or the sound will otherwise will be muddy with distortion. I am sure this has a lot to do with the dinky amplifier inside the iPad being unable to fully drive the the whopping 32 ohms of resistance the SR80e pushes back with. As a rule, underpowered amplifiers are what ruin the drivers inside speakers or headphones so when you hear distortion it means your amplifier is underpowered when matched with the driver and you need to change one of those two things. When you hear distortion from a crappy amplifier that's the sound of your speakers being slowly ruined so you really want to avoid this. (I always have a sad chuckle when some punk is walking the streets with ghetto blaster at maximum volume and the sound is atrocious- little does he know that what people are annoyed by is not the volume, but the distortion! Plus he's ruining his equipment.)

Using the SR80e with a mobile device is a case where an external headphone amplifier would be highly desirable, if not required, so this is a bit of an ask. I have not had a lot of success with the in-line amplifiers designed to run off of the device's power (specifically the Lightning-DAC-and-amplifier combos that you can buy to replace the dongle that Apple ships with their new iPhones) where I played recordings which have very high amplitude levels. For these recordings, the distortion is intolerable even though records at a nominal recording level sound great. The lack of gain control is a real problem with these gadgets- something that is de-facto on any headphone amp that you don't put in your pocket. Therefore, you'll be reduced to using headphones like these at home or work, which is where I use mine.

The fact that you have to significantly alter the EQ profile of your audio player to even have these cans reproduce a sound that is remotely like the original recording violates "high fidelity" by definition. Compare this to a sound engineer style headphone set like Sony MDR Pros which are designed to reproduce the source signal as accurately as possible. This is what "high fidelity" actually means. Some people may not like this and will end up using some artificial bass boost on their device to compensate, which the MDRs will gladly deliver. Most people who listen to popular music are generally accustomed to excessive bass. If that is the sort of listener that you are, then these headphones are for you because once you get the SR80s tuned properly, the sound these cans deliver is very impressive. Very. Impressive.

Unfortunately, when using an IOS device, playing this profile with even high end earbuds like the UE Triple Fis, the sound will be tinny, so toggling between the two modes by way of a shortcut would be a nice bonus, but as it stands I have to go deep into the preferences to change this setting. Therefore, I would only recommend these headphones if you intend to use them in a stationary location. Since these are very high resistance earphones (even higher than most loudspeakers for that matter) you really ought to get an headphone amplifier if you want these to shine.

One other issue is with the minimalist foam cup pads. While they are comfy, they do not block sound in or out whatsoever, so if you use them in a noisy office you will be annoyed at how loud you have to play these to drown out ambient noise. Also, your workmates will probably be annoyed by the bleed through. I ended up getting a different cup pad kit which is marginally better, but it changes the fit somewhat so it takes a little fiddling to get them to sit on your skull around your ears evenly. Otherwise, the headphones are incredibly comfortable as they are very lightweight, which is surprising considering the size of the driver. Grado has found the sweet spot between having a massive (and heavy) drive coil magnet and being featherweight, even if I might take issue with their choices about fidelity reproduction.

Tl;DR: If you really like your sound overcharged with bass, these are the headphones for you. Otherwise, if you are looking for a quality but moderately priced pair of headphones, you might be better off with a more reference-style set like the Sony MDRs.

title: One of the nicest pieces of worthless junk ever conceived
text:
I really wanted to love this keyboard. In fact, I have purchased three of them over the past 18 months. If it weren't for the fact that two of them simply stopped working altogether with the steady red LED problem along with complete lack of function, I would probably have given this deice a 5 star review, and that is all of the variants that exist of this keyboard. When it works, it is a wonderful device. The problem is, there are clearly some major quality issues.

First off, what is it about this keyboard that is so fantastic that makes it so popular if it has so many problems? Answer, it feels wonderful, and when it works, it's a dream. It is the right shape and size even for practically all typically sized hands. Maybe even for some of the more tiny-handed men out there. Microsoft has perfected the bezel curve of the ergonomic keyboard in the Sculpt, and the amount of travel it gives each key is perfect. The feedback of the keys (as in the feel) is perfect as well. The apparently physical quality of the device seems well made (if though it clearly has some design flaws). Even the amount of "clack" that the keyboard makes is satisfying without being obnoxious.

So what's the problem? Aside form the things people have talked about ad nauseam (broken keys, losing that tiny transceiver means the keyboard is useless, etc.. being the seemingly biggest issues) so along with practically all of Microsoft's consumer-grade products, support is nowhere to be found. While MS offers comprehensive support plans for their corporate products, you are on your own with accessories, even if they are expensive bluetooth accessories. They don't even host proper forums for their accessories (there is no category for this on their official forum) and any information elsewhere on the internet about the Sculpt is strangely scant, so trying to find out what the steady red LED means is definitely a no-go. Anything I find is either for another model or simply doesn't map to this condition. Therefore, I can't even find out what the red LED light even means, let alone attempt to resolve the problem. Their phone and chat support offers no meaningful help as they are unfamiliar with the device. Since I have a Mac they balk and say the device isn't supported on a Mac, even though I have been using it for 9 months beforehand without incident. Also, the red LED turns on immediately after the new batteries go in so it's probably nothing to do with signal and a failure of the device itself. This seems further evident since the bottom of the keyboard that is underneath the light actually gets warm to the touch, so I should assume the keyboard is fried. This would be the second Sculpt keyboard that this has happened to in less than a year so this is not an outlier. I don't do anything to my keyboards that would kill them like this. My old Logitech Wave that I keep having to go back to keeps on ticking.

Also, note that apparently USB 3 interferes with the wireless signal between the USB dongle and the keyboard, a problem I have personally experienced when my keyboard strangely stopped receiving input temporarily for a few seconds and then resume. I thought I solved the problem by using an old USB 2 hub to get the dongle physically closer to the keyboard as I thought it was a reception issue that is so common with Bluetooth devices. (I am not even sure if this even uses Bluetooth and it might just be some proprietary RF signal.) But in fact, I later learned that it was the use of a USB 2 port that was far away from my USB 3 ports!

Sadly, as tantalizing as this device may be, I would steer clear of it. It's nothing but trouble.

title: Great high output cable and well built
text: This is a great cable and charges my iPad faster than any other cable, assuming you have a high output wall charger for it.

title: Audio recorded with high gain become profoundly distorted
text:
When I received this DAC adaptor I was really ready to love it. Like many other late-model iPhone owners I was disappointed in the signal reproduction of Apple's stock Lightening-to-Headphone-Plug adaptor with its cheap DAC and was trying to find a replacement that had a better frequency response and sampling rate. This device, while oddly bulky, seemed to fit the bill. The device has controls for volume and track selection like pretty much all headphones that are designed to be used with smartphones so unless you are using old-school or audiophile headphones all these controls manage to do is render the controls on your headphones inoperable. Considering this means you a reaching for controls that are going to be right next to your phone anyway, it definitely reduces the convenience factor in your controls are located up the wire near so you don't have to fishing for it in your pocket. The devices is well built out of machines aluminum, it's unnecessarily bulky and the short lightening cord makes it awkward and likely to put torsional strain on the lightening port of your iPhone- something you really don't want to do.

But how does it sound?

Initially, I was really impressed with the sound reproduction playing an album that was mixed at a lower gain amplitude, like what you'd find from a streaming service or Apple Music. In combination with my Ultimate Ears TripleFi 10s I was pleased to finally hear the full sound reproduction so that trouble of encoding my music at a 320k bitrate finally wasn't a complete waste of storage space as it was before since the stock adaptor steps bitrate down to something like 192k. (Don't quote me on that.) Anyway, all seemed well, even if the device was kind of bulky and the black finish on the aluminum started to rub off after the first day, until I played some music that was encoded with an unusually high gain. The sounds was UNLISTENABLE. It was so distorted that I was worried I was damaging my headphones. I checked the SoundWise App that you can download to update firmware and boost the signal if need be, but none of that was in use. The DAC simply couldn't handle the signal! Even the cheap Apple adaptor could play that signal without butchering the sound, albeit it in its flat, lossy way that it usually does.

Therefore, I do not recommend this product. I was really hoping to love it and that it would solve the crappy DAC problem Apple created, but it simply was not designed well. Keep looking...

title: These cheap Al heatsinks will make you wish you bought Cu if you have a real heat dissipation concern
text: Meh, these heatsinks are so-so. Since they are aluminum and don't conduct as well as copper, you may have issues if you are dissipating a lot of therms. I am also skeptical about the peel-and-eat thermal adhesive (which is not the old-fashioned gooey variety that conducts heat wonderfully.) I have them on the processors of a pair of 1 TB m2.SSD modules on my NAS' tiered storage and one of the modules is frequently crossing the 70°C mark under moderate load. The sinks are directly in the forced airflow and should get plenty of cooling, so the only thing to do is double down on the sinks by sticking a second one on the memory core to see if that helps with the overheating. If that doesn't help, I guess I will be very carefully yoinking the sinks off the modules and replacing them with copper.

title: Extend your RCA cabling without looking like a dummy!
text:
These are pretty much as basic an RCA cable you can find that will extend the length of your existing RCA cables without the need for another male-to-male adapter. While for components that have RCA hookups that allow you to use any RCA cable that your can find, I would recommend buying a single longer cable as every connection point is a place for potential signal loss. However, for components that have their RCA cables integrated with the device, you have little choice but to buy an extender such as this. Turntables, especially the older variety, are the most notable components that have this configuration, and since most people like to be able to play records from a location that is easy to reach and has plenty of headroom, this is often far away from your receiver and the built-in cables on the turntable are usually far too short for this. This is why these cables are a perfect way to add an extra 3' while only introducing one additional connection in your linkage, where using a standard RCA cable with a male-to-male adapter introduces two.

Also, since the cables which are connected to turntables are almost always of bare-bones quality with the minimum gauge of copper necessary to carry a signal (that's assuming the wire is made from copper at all, and not from some other cheaper alloy), these are probably going to be the same gauge. Your connection is only as good as the weakest link, so buying some thick gauge cable that is made out of magnetically polarized copper probably would only serve to drive the price up with no actual benefit to you except for being able to brag about them. Therefore, this RCA cable extenders is all that you really need and will spare you the embarrassment of spending money on something that you actually do not need at all. Some "high end" users might complain about them being of a small gauge because they have convinced themselves that they have to use overpriced Monster cables to connect their gear to be able to fully enjoy it., but I don't necessarily buy into this. True, good cable makes a difference, especially when you are sending a signal over a longer distance (10' or more) chances are the mid-grade cable of 16 gauge copper wire with gold plated contacts is all you're going to need. This cable solves your short cable problem while telling the world "I am care about how my music sounds, but I am neither a sucker nor a fool!"

title: Still the best value for high-end earbuds
text:
This was one of the last Ultimate Ears earbud lines before Logitech bought the company which resulted in an immediate drop in product quality and increase in product price. Yes, these are still wired headphones, but the sound fidelity is unmatched, and instead of complicated noise cancelling algorithms this simply employs noise isolation to block out ambient sound. These headphones have been out of production for some time, but for whatever reason you can still find them NIB from many vendors. They charge about a little more than what cut-rate vendors charged when they were new about 6 years ago, but they were way ahead of their time and frankly nothing on the market in this price range sounds even close to this good. Plus, these original UE headphones (I don't evangelize anything UE after Logitech bought them) have a lot of great design features. The earbud units are modular, so if you ever destroy the leads, you can always replace them for $10. Also, the standard leads these ship with do NOT have the mic and volume/start-stop control on the leads, but you can buy them in various levels of quality for about $20-60 aftermarket and swap them out. It's money well spent if you want to make calls on them. Also, the lead up to 6" from each bud is cased in memory metal so they can be bent to shape and hold in place to are a comfy fit on he outside of your ears- great idea.

All around the best earbud headphones for the money, if you can find them!

title: The Best Plex Client Appliance for your TV
text: Without repeating what everyone has said here, I will speak for Roku's support of the Plex media streaming software which is a free Roku channel. If you have never heard of it, it is a fantastic solution that allows you to use Roku (as well as all your portable devices and remote computers, including ones on the internet-at-large) to stream all of the movies on your computer, regardless of the format. On Roku, you can browse the movie collection on your computer using a slick interface and watch it in full resolution. (This is only if you have a fast connection like a home wireless network, and you need to configure it to do this- an easy settings change.) If your computer can play it, so can your Roku. The key to this is because all the transcoding of the video file happens on your computer so all Roku has to do is play the video stream. The result is that you can easily fast-forward and rewind, as well and have the jump-back feature like the TiVo has. This was the primary reason that I bought the Roku as it is a lot easier to use than trying to connect your computer directly to your TV and muddling about with computer controls to watch movies. The Plex interface on Roku is easy to use and very slick. It does nice things like look up movie data so you have the cover art, theme music, and movie info for you to peruse as you are browsing your library. Finally, there is the "Plex it!" feature which you can use with your computer's browser, so that when you find a video on the internet on your computer, you want to queue it up for later to watch on your TV, and it will appear in your movie queue in Plex on Roku, regardless of the video format! This also gets around the one annoying thing about Roku and that it doesn't have a native YouTube channel for some reason.

title: Great Alternative To Yubbi Key
text:
Thus far this is the only hardware USB key that I have tried that compare to Yubbi. These are about half the price and as you should know if shopping these, you need a minimum of 2. I recommend having at least 3 to 5. If you lose, break, damage or anything causing your device to be innaccessable then in some cases, especially in Crypto exchanges you will not be able to regain access to your assets.

I keep one on me, one in a safe at my house, one in a safety deposit box and another with a trusted friend that has no idea what it goes to. These things are the best protection you can own for logging in to accounts using MFA.

This has the same compatibility as other brands. Worked everywhere it said and more. If you do anything in finance or even online banking or shopping, I would highly recommend looking into these. Not sure why Amazon hasn't added support on here for this type of MFA. Wish they would hurry up and do so. You would think that since they sell them, they would at least add in support for hardware keys to help protect our accounts.

As I said the best security available for a great price. Just make sure to have at least two or you will end up regretting it later.

title: Worked In My Alienware M17R4
text:
I was told it wouldn't work in here but mine already had a Killer Wireless installed in the m.2 slot that says for Wireless/Bluetooth only. It has a PCI-E one in there also Intel I believe that's built onto the motherboard. I disabled all the network devices and removed the Killer wireless. I installed this, installed new drivers and just like that it was working. Adjusted a few setting and was using WiFi 6 or 802.11AX that quick. I don't use wireless or bluetooth that often on this as I prefer an ethernet connection when possible but the speeds on .AX rivals my ethernet speed on a 2GB Google Fiber network. Very impressive. I have photos of the install but they have disappeared so I will upload them all later when I find them.

This was simple to install as long as you have worked inside computers before. Instructions were a little limited considering it could be complicated to some. I did notice on this card the antenna plugs were opposite so I had to plug them in the way it showed on their board. It was opposite my own but guess that's manufacturers preference. This is a great upgrade and I highly recommend if you have a WiFi 6 home network that you upgrade to the AX. This Wise Tiger AX210NGW is truly astonishing in the speed difference.

Photos will follow because I have to get a new SSD and they install in the same area so I can take new photos for everyone.

Updated by adding the promised photos of in in the Alienware M17xR4 Still no problems and running on an all AX WiFi.

I am still trying to figure out exactly which of the three video cards this device is using but it has to using the one in the AGA considering the internal GeForce 1070 is disabled, it could be using the Intel that runs the laptops built in monitor but that's not being used and I have 3 monitors and a VR headset already attached to the GeForce 1080 Ti on the AGA.

I didn't purchase this for the graphics though but I do want to see exactly how it's going to work on this system and if it's going to cause a slow down at all. It will take a lot more time for me to figure all that out. I will update it as I do if there is any interest.

The data transfer rate is incredible and it has plenty of ports and added value everywhere. I honestly didn't expect it to work with the Alienware and AGA since the AGA acts like a dock of it's own but it's working perfectly. My only problem and I am going to contact them about it is the front two USB ports appear upside down and that's hard to use my security keys in them. It doesn't matter with regular cables but those have a button that must be pressed and it's hard to reach. It also comes with a good usb C to usb C cable to connect it.

I am extremely happy with this Tiergrade Docking station and look forward to using it for even more in the future. I will update this as I have an answer to the upside down ports and which video card is being used when I connect to it.
